Polar coordinates

Cartesian coordinates answer two questions:

\text{How far left or right?} \qquad \text{How far up or down?}

Polar coordinates answer different questions:

\text{How far from the origin?} \qquad \text{At what angle?}

This is often the natural language of rotation, spirals, circular motion, and orbits.

 Distance and angle as coordinates

Fix an origin O and a positive x-axis. A point P can be described by:

r=\text{directed distance from the origin},

and

\theta=\text{angle measured from the positive \(x\)-axis}.

The pair

(r,\theta)

is called a pair of polar coordinates.

If r>0, the point lies r units from the origin in the direction of angle \theta.

The angle \theta is measured in radians unless stated otherwise. Positive angles are measured counterclockwise. Negative angles are measured clockwise.

For example,

\left(2,\frac{\pi}{3}\right)

means: go distance 2 from the origin in the direction 60^\circ above the positive x-axis.

Polar coordinates are not unique

The point

\left(2,\frac{\pi}{3}\right)

is the same as

\left(2,\frac{\pi}{3}+2\pi\right),

because adding 2\pi makes one full turn.

More generally,

(r,\theta)

and

(r,\theta+2k\pi)

represent the same point for any integer k.

There is another source of nonuniqueness. A negative r means that the point is plotted in the opposite direction from the angle \theta. Thus

(-r,\theta)

represents the same point as

(r,\theta+\pi).

For example,

\left(-2,\frac{\pi}{3}\right)

is the same point as

\left(2,\frac{4\pi}{3}\right).

The origin is even more nonunique. It can be written as

(0,\theta)

for every angle \theta.

Polar warning

A Cartesian point usually has one coordinate pair.

A polar point has many coordinate pairs:

(r,\theta)=(r,\theta+2\pi)=(-r,\theta+\pi)=\cdots.

This nonuniqueness is useful, but it also makes polar graphs easy to misread.

 Why are polar coordinates not unique?

The pairs (r,\theta), (r,\theta+2\pi), and (-r,\theta+\pi) can name the same point. In your own words, why is that nonuniqueness both useful and dangerous, especially when two polar curves appear to miss each other?

Adding a full turn does not move the point, and negative r plots in the opposite direction. Intersections can occur under different polar names.

Converting between polar and Cartesian coordinates

The right triangle in Figure gives the conversion formulas.

If a point has polar coordinates (r,\theta), then

x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.

Conversely, if a point has Cartesian coordinates (x,y), then

r^2=x^2+y^2.

When r>0, the angle satisfies

\tan\theta=\frac{y}{x}

when x\neq0. The quadrant must be chosen from the signs of x and y.

What questions do polar coordinates answer?

Cartesian coordinates ask how far left or right and how far up or down. In your own words, what two questions do polar coordinates ask instead, and why is that language natural for rotation, spirals, and orbits?

Polar coordinates use an angle from the positive x-axis and a signed radial coordinate. The distance from the origin is |r|; for r\ge0, it is r itself.

 polar to Cartesian

Convert

\left(2,\frac{\pi}{6}\right)

to Cartesian coordinates.

Use

x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.

Then

x=2\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\sqrt3,

and

y=2\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=2\cdot\frac12=1.

So

\left(2,\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=(\sqrt3,1).

Cartesian to polar

Convert

(-1,\sqrt3)

to polar coordinates with r>0 and 0\le\theta<2\pi.

First,

r^2=(-1)^2+(\sqrt3)^2=1+3=4,

so

r=2.

Next,

\tan\theta=\frac{\sqrt3}{-1}=-\sqrt3.

The point lies in Quadrant II, so

\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}.

Thus one polar representation is

(-1,\sqrt3)=\left(2,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right).

Other representations include

\left(2,\frac{2\pi}{3}+2\pi\right)

and

\left(-2,-\frac{\pi}{3}\right).

 a circle in polar form

Convert

r=2\cos\theta

to a Cartesian equation.

Multiply both sides by r:

r^2=2r\cos\theta.

Now use

r^2=x^2+y^2

and

r\cos\theta=x.

So

x^2+y^2=2x.

Complete the square:

x^2-2x+y^2=0,

(x-1)^2+y^2=1.

Thus

r=2\cos\theta

is the circle centered at (1,0) with radius 1.

This example is important. A circle that is slightly awkward in Cartesian coordinates may be very simple in polar coordinates.

 a line through the origin

The equation

\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}

means all points whose direction from the origin is 45^\circ. This is the line

y=x.

If we allow r to be negative as well as positive, then one equation

\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}

traces the whole line. Positive r gives the ray in Quadrant I. Negative r gives the opposite ray in Quadrant III.

 Polar graphs

A polar equation usually gives r as a function of \theta:

r=f(\theta).

For each angle \theta, we compute the distance r, then plot the point

(r,\theta).

But there is a second way to see the same graph. Every polar equation

r=f(\theta)

is automatically a parametric curve:

x=f(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y=f(\theta)\sin\theta.

The angle \theta is the parameter.

This is why polar coordinates belong in the same chapter as parametric curves. A polar graph is a curve traced by a rotating ray.

the circle <m>r=2</m>

The equation

r=2

means that every point on the graph has distance 2 from the origin. Therefore the graph is the circle

x^2+y^2=4.

In parametric form,

x=2\cos\theta, \qquad y=2\sin\theta.

So the polar circle is the same circle parametrization we already know.

 the spiral <m>r=\theta</m>

The equation

r=\theta, \qquad \theta\ge0,

says that the distance from the origin grows at the same rate as the angle.

At

\theta=0,

we have

r=0.

At

\theta=2\pi,

we have

r=2\pi.

After one full turn, the point is farther from the origin. After another full turn, it is farther still. The curve is a spiral.

This curve is called an Archimedean spiral. More generally,

r=a\theta

has radius increasing linearly with angle.

 How to sketch a polar graph

A polar graph is easier to sketch if we ask four questions.

How to sketch a polar graph Question Why it helps What values of \theta are needed? The curve may be traced once on a smaller interval than 0\le\theta\le2\pi. When is r=0? These angles send the curve through the origin. When is r largest or smallest? These angles locate the outermost and innermost points. Can r be negative? Negative r plots the point in the opposite direction.

The last question is the one most students forget.

Negative <m>r</m> is not an error

If a polar equation gives r<0, plot the point by turning the ray through angle \theta, then moving |r| units in the opposite direction.

Equivalently,

(r,\theta)=(-r,\theta+\pi).

 Why is negative <m>r</m> not an error?

A polar equation may give r<0 at some angles. In your own words, how should that value be plotted, and why is forgetting negative r one of the most common sketching mistakes?

Turn the ray through angle \theta, then move |r| units the other way. Equivalently, (r,\theta)=(-r,\theta+\pi).

Circles, spirals, roses, and limacons

Polar coordinates make several families of curves appear with simple equations.

Circles

The equation

r=a

is the circle centered at the origin with radius a, assuming a>0.

The equation

r=2a\cos\theta

is a circle centered at (a,0) with radius a. To see this, multiply by r:

r^2=2ar\cos\theta.

Convert:

x^2+y^2=2ax.

Complete the square:

(x-a)^2+y^2=a^2.

Similarly,

r=2a\sin\theta

is the circle centered at (0,a) with radius a.

Spirals

The equation

r=a\theta, \qquad a>0,

is an Archimedean spiral. Each full turn increases the radius by

2\pi a.

Indeed, increasing \theta by 2\pi changes r by

a(\theta+2\pi)-a\theta=2\pi a.

So the turns of the spiral are evenly spaced.

This is different from exponential spirals, where the radius multiplies after each turn. Polar coordinates make both kinds natural because the angle is already part of the coordinate system.

Roses

Equations such as

r=a\cos(n\theta) \qquad\text{or}\qquad r=a\sin(n\theta)

produce flower-shaped curves called roses when a>0 and n is a positive integer. The petal count below uses these assumptions.

For example,

r=2\cos(3\theta)

has three petals. The factor 3\theta makes the radius oscillate three times as the angle runs from 0 to 2\pi.

A useful rule of thumb is:

Circles, spirals, roses, and limacons rose equation number of petals r=a\cos(n\theta) or r=a\sin(n\theta), n odd n petals r=a\cos(n\theta) or r=a\sin(n\theta), n even 2n petals

This rule describes the usual full polar graph. The reason comes from periodicity and negative r. When r becomes negative, the graph is not discarded; it is plotted in the opposite direction, which may create another petal or retrace one already drawn.

Limacons and cardioids

Equations of the form

r=a+b\cos\theta \qquad\text{or}\qquad r=a+b\sin\theta

produce curves called limacons. The name comes from a word for snail, and the curves often have a rounded shell-like shape.

The special case

a=b

is called a cardioid. For example,

r=1+\cos\theta

is a cardioid. It has a cusp at the origin because

r=1+\cos\pi=0.

The largest radius occurs at

\theta=0,

where

r=2.

So the curve points to the right and pinches at the origin on the left.

If b>a>0, then r=a+b\cos\theta becomes negative for some angles. The graph develops an inner loop.

Why polar coordinates matter

Curves involving circles, rotations, angles, or distance from a fixed point often have simple polar equations and complicated Cartesian equations.

Polar coordinates do not replace Cartesian coordinates. They give us another language, better suited to radial and angular geometry.

A polar equation

r=f(\theta)

is already a parametric curve:

x=f(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y=f(\theta)\sin\theta.

So the calculus we built for parametric curves should also give slopes, areas, and lengths for polar curves. The next section does exactly that.

Why do polar coordinates not replace Cartesian coordinates?

Circles, roses, and limaçons often have simple polar equations and complicated Cartesian ones. In your own words, what does it mean to choose coordinates that match the geometry rather than to abandon x and y?

Polar coordinates are another language, better suited to radial and angular geometry. Conversion still connects the two descriptions.

When r>0, the angle satisfies

\tan\theta=\frac{y}{x}

when x\neq0. The quadrant must be chosen from the signs of x and y.

What questions do polar coordinates answer?

Cartesian coordinates ask how far left or right and how far up or down. In your own words, what two questions do polar coordinates ask instead, and why is that language natural for rotation, spirals, and orbits?

Polar coordinates use an angle from the positive x-axis and a signed radial coordinate. The distance from the origin is |r|; for r\ge0, it is r itself.

 polar to Cartesian

Convert

\left(2,\frac{\pi}{6}\right)

to Cartesian coordinates.

Use

x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.

Then

x=2\cos\frac{\pi}{6}=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\sqrt3,

and

y=2\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=2\cdot\frac12=1.

So

\left(2,\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=(\sqrt3,1).

Cartesian to polar

Convert

(-1,\sqrt3)

to polar coordinates with r>0 and 0\le\theta<2\pi.

First,

r^2=(-1)^2+(\sqrt3)^2=1+3=4,

so

r=2.

Next,

\tan\theta=\frac{\sqrt3}{-1}=-\sqrt3.

The point lies in Quadrant II, so

\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}.

Thus one polar representation is

(-1,\sqrt3)=\left(2,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right).

Other representations include

\left(2,\frac{2\pi}{3}+2\pi\right)

and

\left(-2,-\frac{\pi}{3}\right).

 a circle in polar form

Convert

r=2\cos\theta

to a Cartesian equation.

Multiply both sides by r:

r^2=2r\cos\theta.

Now use

r^2=x^2+y^2

and

r\cos\theta=x.

So

x^2+y^2=2x.

Complete the square:

x^2-2x+y^2=0,

(x-1)^2+y^2=1.

Thus

r=2\cos\theta

is the circle centered at (1,0) with radius 1.

This example is important. A circle that is slightly awkward in Cartesian coordinates may be very simple in polar coordinates.

 a line through the origin

The equation

\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}

means all points whose direction from the origin is 45^\circ. This is the line

y=x.

If we allow r to be negative as well as positive, then one equation

\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}

traces the whole line. Positive r gives the ray in Quadrant I. Negative r gives the opposite ray in Quadrant III.

 Polar graphs

A polar equation usually gives r as a function of \theta:

r=f(\theta).

For each angle \theta, we compute the distance r, then plot the point

(r,\theta).

But there is a second way to see the same graph. Every polar equation

r=f(\theta)

is automatically a parametric curve:

x=f(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y=f(\theta)\sin\theta.

The angle \theta is the parameter.

This is why polar coordinates belong in the same chapter as parametric curves. A polar graph is a curve traced by a rotating ray.

the circle <m>r=2</m>

The equation

r=2

means that every point on the graph has distance 2 from the origin. Therefore the graph is the circle

x^2+y^2=4.

In parametric form,

x=2\cos\theta, \qquad y=2\sin\theta.

So the polar circle is the same circle parametrization we already know.

 the spiral <m>r=\theta</m>

The equation

r=\theta, \qquad \theta\ge0,

says that the distance from the origin grows at the same rate as the angle.

At

\theta=0,

we have

r=0.

At

\theta=2\pi,

we have

r=2\pi.

After one full turn, the point is farther from the origin. After another full turn, it is farther still. The curve is a spiral.

This curve is called an Archimedean spiral. More generally,

r=a\theta

has radius increasing linearly with angle.

 How to sketch a polar graph

A polar graph is easier to sketch if we ask four questions.

How to sketch a polar graph Question Why it helps What values of \theta are needed? The curve may be traced once on a smaller interval than 0\le\theta\le2\pi. When is r=0? These angles send the curve through the origin. When is r largest or smallest? These angles locate the outermost and innermost points. Can r be negative? Negative r plots the point in the opposite direction.

The last question is the one most students forget.

Negative <m>r</m> is not an error

If a polar equation gives r<0, plot the point by turning the ray through angle \theta, then moving |r| units in the opposite direction.

Equivalently,

(r,\theta)=(-r,\theta+\pi).

 Why is negative <m>r</m> not an error?

A polar equation may give r<0 at some angles. In your own words, how should that value be plotted, and why is forgetting negative r one of the most common sketching mistakes?

Turn the ray through angle \theta, then move |r| units the other way. Equivalently, (r,\theta)=(-r,\theta+\pi).

Circles, spirals, roses, and limacons

Polar coordinates make several families of curves appear with simple equations.

Circles

The equation

r=a

is the circle centered at the origin with radius a, assuming a>0.

The equation

r=2a\cos\theta

is a circle centered at (a,0) with radius a. To see this, multiply by r:

r^2=2ar\cos\theta.

Convert:

x^2+y^2=2ax.

Complete the square:

(x-a)^2+y^2=a^2.

Similarly,

r=2a\sin\theta

is the circle centered at (0,a) with radius a.

Spirals

The equation

r=a\theta, \qquad a>0,

is an Archimedean spiral. Each full turn increases the radius by

2\pi a.

Indeed, increasing \theta by 2\pi changes r by

a(\theta+2\pi)-a\theta=2\pi a.

So the turns of the spiral are evenly spaced.

This is different from exponential spirals, where the radius multiplies after each turn. Polar coordinates make both kinds natural because the angle is already part of the coordinate system.

Roses

Equations such as

r=a\cos(n\theta) \qquad\text{or}\qquad r=a\sin(n\theta)

produce flower-shaped curves called roses when a>0 and n is a positive integer. The petal count below uses these assumptions.

For example,

r=2\cos(3\theta)

has three petals. The factor 3\theta makes the radius oscillate three times as the angle runs from 0 to 2\pi.

A useful rule of thumb is:

Circles, spirals, roses, and limacons rose equation number of petals r=a\cos(n\theta) or r=a\sin(n\theta), n odd n petals r=a\cos(n\theta) or r=a\sin(n\theta), n even 2n petals

This rule describes the usual full polar graph. The reason comes from periodicity and negative r. When r becomes negative, the graph is not discarded; it is plotted in the opposite direction, which may create another petal or retrace one already drawn.

Limacons and cardioids

Equations of the form

r=a+b\cos\theta \qquad\text{or}\qquad r=a+b\sin\theta

produce curves called limacons. The name comes from a word for snail, and the curves often have a rounded shell-like shape.

The special case

a=b

is called a cardioid. For example,

r=1+\cos\theta

is a cardioid. It has a cusp at the origin because

r=1+\cos\pi=0.

The largest radius occurs at

\theta=0,

where

r=2.

So the curve points to the right and pinches at the origin on the left.

If b>a>0, then r=a+b\cos\theta becomes negative for some angles. The graph develops an inner loop.

Why polar coordinates matter

Curves involving circles, rotations, angles, or distance from a fixed point often have simple polar equations and complicated Cartesian equations.

Polar coordinates do not replace Cartesian coordinates. They give us another language, better suited to radial and angular geometry.

A polar equation

r=f(\theta)

is already a parametric curve:

x=f(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y=f(\theta)\sin\theta.

So the calculus we built for parametric curves should also give slopes, areas, and lengths for polar curves. The next section does exactly that.

Why do polar coordinates not replace Cartesian coordinates?

Circles, roses, and limaçons often have simple polar equations and complicated Cartesian ones. In your own words, what does it mean to choose coordinates that match the geometry rather than to abandon x and y?

Polar coordinates are another language, better suited to radial and angular geometry. Conversion still connects the two descriptions.

Calculus in polar coordinates

The last section ended with one important observation:

r=f(\theta)

is already a parametric curve, because

x=f(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y=f(\theta)\sin\theta.

So polar calculus is not a new kind of calculus. It is parametric calculus with the angle \theta as the parameter.

The polar picture, however, gives new geometry. A small change in \theta sweeps out a small sector. A small change in r moves the point in or out along a ray. That is why the formulas for slope, area, and length look different from the ones for ordinary graphs.

 Slope of a polar curve

Start with a simple polar curve:

r=\theta, \qquad \theta\ge0.

This is a spiral. It is not naturally a graph y=f(x). But it is naturally a moving point:

x=\theta\cos\theta, \qquad y=\theta\sin\theta.

The slope is still

\frac{dy}{dx}.

Because both x and y depend on \theta, we use the parametric slope formula:

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta}.

For the spiral,

\frac{dx}{d\theta} = \cos\theta-\theta\sin\theta,

and

\frac{dy}{d\theta} = \sin\theta+\theta\cos\theta.

Therefore

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sin\theta+\theta\cos\theta} {\cos\theta-\theta\sin\theta}.

At

\theta=\pi,

the point is

r=\pi,

so

x=\pi\cos\pi=-\pi, \qquad y=\pi\sin\pi=0.

The slope is

\frac{\sin\pi+\pi\cos\pi} {\cos\pi-\pi\sin\pi} = \frac{0-\pi}{-1-0} = \pi.

So the tangent line to the spiral at the point (-\pi,0) has slope \pi.

Now do the same calculation for a general polar curve

r=f(\theta).

To keep the notation light, write

r=r(\theta).

Then

x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.

Differentiate with respect to \theta. By the product rule,

\frac{dx}{d\theta} = \frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta-r\sin\theta,

and

\frac{dy}{d\theta} = \frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta+r\cos\theta.

Therefore

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta+r\cos\theta} {\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta-r\sin\theta}

whenever the denominator is not zero.

Slope of a polar curve

For a polar curve

r=r(\theta),

the slope is

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{r'(\theta)\sin\theta+r(\theta)\cos\theta} {r'(\theta)\cos\theta-r(\theta)\sin\theta}.

This is just the parametric formula

\frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta}

applied to

x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.

 a circle in polar form

The polar equation

r=2\cos\theta

is the circle

(x-1)^2+y^2=1.

Find the slope when

\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}.

First,

r=2\cos\theta, \qquad r'=-2\sin\theta.

The numerator of the slope formula is

r'\sin\theta+r\cos\theta = (-2\sin\theta)\sin\theta+(2\cos\theta)\cos\theta.

So

r'\sin\theta+r\cos\theta = 2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta) = 2\cos(2\theta).

The denominator is

r'\cos\theta-r\sin\theta = (-2\sin\theta)\cos\theta-(2\cos\theta)\sin\theta.

Thus

r'\cos\theta-r\sin\theta = -4\sin\theta\cos\theta = -2\sin(2\theta).

Therefore

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2\cos(2\theta)}{-2\sin(2\theta)} = -\cot(2\theta).

At

\theta=\frac{\pi}{4},

we get

\frac{dy}{dx} = -\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0.

The point is

r=2\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=\sqrt2,

so

x=r\cos\theta=1, \qquad y=r\sin\theta=1.

This is the top of the circle (x-1)^2+y^2=1, where the tangent is horizontal.

 Horizontal and vertical tangents

The polar slope formula also tells us when tangents are horizontal or vertical.

A horizontal tangent occurs when

\frac{dy}{d\theta}=0

and

\frac{dx}{d\theta}\neq0.

So for a polar curve,

r'(\theta)\sin\theta+r(\theta)\cos\theta=0

with

r'(\theta)\cos\theta-r(\theta)\sin\theta\neq0.

A vertical tangent occurs when

\frac{dx}{d\theta}=0

and

\frac{dy}{d\theta}\neq0.

So

r'(\theta)\cos\theta-r(\theta)\sin\theta=0

with

r'(\theta)\sin\theta+r(\theta)\cos\theta\neq0.

Warning

If both

\frac{dx}{d\theta}=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{dy}{d\theta}=0,

then the quotient gives 0/0. The tangent is not decided by direct substitution. Study the nearby motion.

This warning is especially important at cusps.

For the cardioid

r=1+\cos\theta,

the point \theta=\pi gives

r=0, \qquad r'=-\sin\pi=0.

Thus

x'(\pi)=0, \qquad y'(\pi)=0.

The moving point has stopped at the origin. The curve still has a tangent there, but the simple slope formula cannot find it by direct substitution.

 Why is polar calculus not a new kind of calculus?

The equation r=f(\theta) is already parametric through x=r\cos\theta and y=r\sin\theta. In your own words, why do slope, area, and length formulas then look different from the graph formulas, even though they come from the same ideas?

Polar calculus is parametric calculus with angle as the parameter. The new look comes from sector geometry and from expressing the coordinate rates in terms of r and r'.

Area in polar coordinates

The ordinary area formula for a graph uses vertical strips:

dA=y\,dx.

A polar graph suggests a different small piece. When \theta changes by a small amount \Delta\theta, the radius sweeps out a thin sector.

For a circle of radius r, a sector with angle \Delta\theta has area

\frac12 r^2\Delta\theta.

For a polar curve r=f(\theta), if \Delta\theta is small, the radius is nearly constant on that small angular interval. So the small sector area is approximately

\Delta A\approx \frac12 r^2\Delta\theta.

Adding these small sectors gives the polar area formula.

Area in polar coordinates

If the polar curve

r=f(\theta), \qquad \alpha\le\theta\le\beta,

traces a region once, then the area swept out by the radius vector is

A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta \bigl(f(\theta)\bigr)^2\,d\theta.

This formula is easy to remember:

dA=\frac12r^2\,d\theta.

It is the small area of a thin sector.

There is also a parametric reason for the same formula. For a closed curve traced counterclockwise,

A=\frac12\int (x y'-y x')\,d\theta.

With

x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta,

we have

x y'-y x'=r^2.

So

A=\frac12\int r^2\,d\theta.

The sector picture and the parametric area formula agree.

Why is polar area built from sectors rather than from vertical strips?

A small change in \theta sweeps a thin sector of area about \frac12 r^2\,d\theta. In your own words, why is that the natural small piece in polar coordinates, and why must you check that the interval of \theta traces the region exactly once?

Polar coordinates organize the plane by rays from the origin. Retracing, negative r, or the wrong interval can count the same region more than once.

area of a circle

The polar equation

r=R

traces a circle of radius R centered at the origin when

0\le\theta\le2\pi.

The polar area formula gives

A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}R^2\,d\theta.

Thus

A=\frac12R^2(2\pi)=\pi R^2.

The familiar circle area formula is a sector accumulation.

 area inside a cardioid

Find the area enclosed by

r=1+\cos\theta.

The cardioid is traced once for

0\le\theta\le2\pi.

So

A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(1+\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta.

Expand:

(1+\cos\theta)^2=1+2\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta.

Therefore

A = \frac12\int_0^{2\pi} \left(1+2\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta\right)\,d\theta.

Now

\int_0^{2\pi}1\,d\theta=2\pi,

\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\,d\theta=0,

and

\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\pi.

Thus

A=\frac12(2\pi+\pi)=\frac{3\pi}{2}.

 Area between two polar curves

If two polar curves share the same angular interval and one lies outside the other, then we subtract sector areas.

Suppose

r=R(\theta)

is the outer curve and

r=\rho(\theta)

is the inner curve, with 0\le\rho(\theta)\le R(\theta), on

\alpha\le\theta\le\beta.

Then

A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta \left(R(\theta)^2-\rho(\theta)^2\right)\,d\theta.

In words,

\text{polar area between curves} = \frac12\int \left((\text{outer radius})^2-(\text{inner radius})^2\right)\,d\theta.

The square is not optional. Sector area depends on r^2, not on r.

 one petal of a rose

Find the area of one petal of

r=2\cos(3\theta).

One petal is traced while r\ge0 around \theta=0. The zeros occur when

2\cos(3\theta)=0,

so

3\theta=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}.

Thus one petal is traced for

-\frac{\pi}{6}\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{6}.

The area is

A=\frac12\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}4\cos^2(3\theta)\,d\theta.

So

A=2\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}\cos^2(3\theta)\,d\theta.

Let

u=3\theta, \qquad du=3\,d\theta.

Then

A=\frac23\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2 u\,du.

Since

\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2u\,du=\frac{\pi}{2},

we get

A=\frac{\pi}{3}.

The whole rose has three petals, so its total area is

\pi.

 Warning

Before using

A=\frac12\int r^2\,d\theta,

check what interval traces the region exactly once. Polar curves can retrace themselves, and negative r can send points to the opposite side of the origin.

 Arc length in polar coordinates

A polar curve is parametric:

x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.

So its length is

L=\int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{d\theta}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{dy}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta.

We already computed

\frac{dx}{d\theta} = r'\cos\theta-r\sin\theta,

and

\frac{dy}{d\theta} = r'\sin\theta+r\cos\theta.

Now square and add:

\left(r'\cos\theta-r\sin\theta\right)^2 + \left(r'\sin\theta+r\cos\theta\right)^2.

Expand:

(r')^2\cos^2\theta-2rr'\sin\theta\cos\theta+r^2\sin^2\theta

+ (r')^2\sin^2\theta+2rr'\sin\theta\cos\theta+r^2\cos^2\theta.

The cross terms cancel. The remaining terms give

(r')^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta) + r^2(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta).

So the square of the speed is

(r')^2+r^2.

Therefore

L=\int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{\left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2+r^2}\,d\theta.

Arc length in polar coordinates

For

r=r(\theta), \qquad \alpha\le\theta\le\beta,

assuming r has a continuous derivative, the distance traveled along the polar curve is

L=\int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{r(\theta)^2+\bigl(r'(\theta)\bigr)^2}\,d\theta.

The formula has a nice geometric meaning. As \theta changes, the point may move radially because r changes, and it may move around the origin because the angle changes. The two effects combine by the Pythagorean theorem.

Why can two polar curves meet without sharing the same <m>r</m> at the same <m>\theta</m>?

Polar names are not unique, so the same-angle equation r_1(\theta)=r_2(\theta) can miss intersections. In your own words, what other meetings should you look for, and why does the origin need a separate check?

Curves can meet under different angles, or both pass through the pole at different times. Nonuniqueness is useful for graphing and dangerous for solving.

circumference of a circle

For

r=R,

we have

r'=0.

Thus

L=\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{R^2+0^2}\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}R\,d\theta = 2\pi R.

 length of a cardioid

Find the length of

r=1+\cos\theta, \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi.

We have

r'=-\sin\theta.

So

r^2+(r')^2 = (1+\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta.

Expand and simplify:

(1+\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta = 1+2\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta = 2+2\cos\theta.

Using

1+\cos\theta=2\cos^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right),

we get

2+2\cos\theta = 4\cos^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right).

Therefore

\sqrt{r^2+(r')^2} = 2\left|\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right|.

So

L=\int_0^{2\pi} 2\left|\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right|\,d\theta.

On 0\le\theta\le\pi, \cos(\theta/2)\ge0. On \pi\le\theta\le2\pi, it is nonpositive. Therefore

L= \int_0^\pi 2\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\,d\theta + \int_\pi^{2\pi} -2\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\,d\theta.

Compute:

\int 2\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\,d\theta = 4\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right).

Thus the first integral is

4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)-4\sin0=4.

The second integral is

-4\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\Big|_\pi^{2\pi} = -4\sin\pi+4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 4.

So

L=8.

A small absolute value warning

The expression

\sqrt{4\cos^2(\theta/2)}

equals

2|\cos(\theta/2)|,

not always 2\cos(\theta/2). Dropping the absolute value would incorrectly make the length cancel to zero.

 Intersections and repeated tracing

Polar coordinates are not unique. That nonuniqueness is useful, but it makes intersections more delicate than in Cartesian coordinates.

Two polar curves can meet even when their equations do not give the same r at the same \theta.

There are three common issues.

Intersections and repeated tracing Issue What to check Same ray intersections Solve r_1(\theta)=r_2(\theta). The origin Check whether each curve reaches r=0, possibly at different angles. Negative r and alternate angles Remember (r,\theta)=(-r,\theta+\pi).
an intersection missed by the same-angle equation

Consider

r=2\cos\theta

and

r=2\sin\theta.

These are two circles:

(x-1)^2+y^2=1

and

x^2+(y-1)^2=1.

Solving with the same angle gives

2\cos\theta=2\sin\theta.

So

\cos\theta=\sin\theta,

and hence

\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.

At this angle,

r=\sqrt2,

so the point is

(1,1).

But the circles also meet at the origin.

Why did the same-angle equation miss it?

For

r=2\cos\theta,

the origin occurs when

\cos\theta=0,

for example at

\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}.

For

r=2\sin\theta,

the origin occurs when

\sin\theta=0,

for example at

\theta=0.

The two curves reach the same Cartesian point with different polar angles. Therefore the same-angle equation did not see that intersection.

 Repeated tracing

Polar curves can also trace the same geometric curve more than once.

For example,

r=2\cos\theta

is one circle. The interval

-\frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2}

traces it once.

But the interval

0\le\theta\le2\pi

traces the same circle twice.

If we blindly use the polar area formula on 0\le\theta\le2\pi, we get

A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta.

This becomes

A=2\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta = 2\pi.

But the circle has radius 1, so its area is only

\pi.

The integral doubled the answer because the parametrization traced the circle twice.

Using the once-around interval gives

A=\frac12\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta.

So

A=2\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta = 2\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \pi.

That is correct.

Polar checklist before computing area or length

Before using a polar formula, ask:

  1. What interval of \theta traces the desired curve?

  2. Is the curve traced once or more than once?

  3. Does r become negative, creating points on the opposite ray?

  4. Does the curve pass through the origin?

  5. If two curves intersect, are there intersections reached at different angles?

Polar coordinates are powerful because they match circular and radial geometry. But the price is that the same point may have many names.

The next family of curves makes especially good use of polar coordinates. It includes parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas. These curves can be described by distance from a fixed point and a fixed line, and in polar form they appear in one equation.

 What should you ask before computing polar area or length?

The section ends with a checklist: interval, repeated tracing, negative r, the origin, and hidden intersections. In your own words, why does skipping those questions turn a correct formula into a wrong geometric count?

The formula integrates the parametrization you feed it. If the tracing is wrong, the integral is faithfully wrong.

Therefore

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sin\theta+\theta\cos\theta} {\cos\theta-\theta\sin\theta}.

At

\theta=\pi,

the point is

r=\pi,

so

x=\pi\cos\pi=-\pi, \qquad y=\pi\sin\pi=0.

The slope is

\frac{\sin\pi+\pi\cos\pi} {\cos\pi-\pi\sin\pi} = \frac{0-\pi}{-1-0} = \pi.

So the tangent line to the spiral at the point (-\pi,0) has slope \pi.

Now do the same calculation for a general polar curve

r=f(\theta).

To keep the notation light, write

r=r(\theta).

Then

x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.

Differentiate with respect to \theta. By the product rule,

\frac{dx}{d\theta} = \frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta-r\sin\theta,

and

\frac{dy}{d\theta} = \frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta+r\cos\theta.

Therefore

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta+r\cos\theta} {\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta-r\sin\theta}

whenever the denominator is not zero.

Slope of a polar curve

For a polar curve

r=r(\theta),

the slope is

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{r'(\theta)\sin\theta+r(\theta)\cos\theta} {r'(\theta)\cos\theta-r(\theta)\sin\theta}.

This is just the parametric formula

\frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta}

applied to

x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.

 a circle in polar form

The polar equation

r=2\cos\theta

is the circle

(x-1)^2+y^2=1.

Find the slope when

\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}.

First,

r=2\cos\theta, \qquad r'=-2\sin\theta.

The numerator of the slope formula is

r'\sin\theta+r\cos\theta = (-2\sin\theta)\sin\theta+(2\cos\theta)\cos\theta.

So

r'\sin\theta+r\cos\theta = 2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta) = 2\cos(2\theta).

The denominator is

r'\cos\theta-r\sin\theta = (-2\sin\theta)\cos\theta-(2\cos\theta)\sin\theta.

Thus

r'\cos\theta-r\sin\theta = -4\sin\theta\cos\theta = -2\sin(2\theta).

Therefore

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2\cos(2\theta)}{-2\sin(2\theta)} = -\cot(2\theta).

At

\theta=\frac{\pi}{4},

we get

\frac{dy}{dx} = -\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0.

The point is

r=2\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=\sqrt2,

so

x=r\cos\theta=1, \qquad y=r\sin\theta=1.

This is the top of the circle (x-1)^2+y^2=1, where the tangent is horizontal.

 Horizontal and vertical tangents

The polar slope formula also tells us when tangents are horizontal or vertical.

A horizontal tangent occurs when

\frac{dy}{d\theta}=0

and

\frac{dx}{d\theta}\neq0.

So for a polar curve,

r'(\theta)\sin\theta+r(\theta)\cos\theta=0

with

r'(\theta)\cos\theta-r(\theta)\sin\theta\neq0.

A vertical tangent occurs when

\frac{dx}{d\theta}=0

and

\frac{dy}{d\theta}\neq0.

So

r'(\theta)\cos\theta-r(\theta)\sin\theta=0

with

r'(\theta)\sin\theta+r(\theta)\cos\theta\neq0.

Warning

If both

\frac{dx}{d\theta}=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{dy}{d\theta}=0,

then the quotient gives 0/0. The tangent is not decided by direct substitution. Study the nearby motion.

This warning is especially important at cusps.

For the cardioid

r=1+\cos\theta,

the point \theta=\pi gives

r=0, \qquad r'=-\sin\pi=0.

Thus

x'(\pi)=0, \qquad y'(\pi)=0.

The moving point has stopped at the origin. The curve still has a tangent there, but the simple slope formula cannot find it by direct substitution.

 Why is polar calculus not a new kind of calculus?

The equation r=f(\theta) is already parametric through x=r\cos\theta and y=r\sin\theta. In your own words, why do slope, area, and length formulas then look different from the graph formulas, even though they come from the same ideas?

Polar calculus is parametric calculus with angle as the parameter. The new look comes from sector geometry and from expressing the coordinate rates in terms of r and r'.

Area in polar coordinates

The ordinary area formula for a graph uses vertical strips:

dA=y\,dx.

A polar graph suggests a different small piece. When \theta changes by a small amount \Delta\theta, the radius sweeps out a thin sector.

For a circle of radius r, a sector with angle \Delta\theta has area

\frac12 r^2\Delta\theta.

For a polar curve r=f(\theta), if \Delta\theta is small, the radius is nearly constant on that small angular interval. So the small sector area is approximately

\Delta A\approx \frac12 r^2\Delta\theta.

Adding these small sectors gives the polar area formula.

Area in polar coordinates

If the polar curve

r=f(\theta), \qquad \alpha\le\theta\le\beta,

traces a region once, then the area swept out by the radius vector is

A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta \bigl(f(\theta)\bigr)^2\,d\theta.

This formula is easy to remember:

dA=\frac12r^2\,d\theta.

It is the small area of a thin sector.

There is also a parametric reason for the same formula. For a closed curve traced counterclockwise,

A=\frac12\int (x y'-y x')\,d\theta.

With

x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta,

we have

x y'-y x'=r^2.

So

A=\frac12\int r^2\,d\theta.

The sector picture and the parametric area formula agree.

Why is polar area built from sectors rather than from vertical strips?

A small change in \theta sweeps a thin sector of area about \frac12 r^2\,d\theta. In your own words, why is that the natural small piece in polar coordinates, and why must you check that the interval of \theta traces the region exactly once?

Polar coordinates organize the plane by rays from the origin. Retracing, negative r, or the wrong interval can count the same region more than once.

area of a circle

The polar equation

r=R

traces a circle of radius R centered at the origin when

0\le\theta\le2\pi.

The polar area formula gives

A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}R^2\,d\theta.

Thus

A=\frac12R^2(2\pi)=\pi R^2.

The familiar circle area formula is a sector accumulation.

 area inside a cardioid

Find the area enclosed by

r=1+\cos\theta.

The cardioid is traced once for

0\le\theta\le2\pi.

So

A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(1+\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta.

Expand:

(1+\cos\theta)^2=1+2\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta.

Therefore

A = \frac12\int_0^{2\pi} \left(1+2\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta\right)\,d\theta.

Now

\int_0^{2\pi}1\,d\theta=2\pi,

\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\,d\theta=0,

and

\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\pi.

Thus

A=\frac12(2\pi+\pi)=\frac{3\pi}{2}.

 Area between two polar curves

If two polar curves share the same angular interval and one lies outside the other, then we subtract sector areas.

Suppose

r=R(\theta)

is the outer curve and

r=\rho(\theta)

is the inner curve, with 0\le\rho(\theta)\le R(\theta), on

\alpha\le\theta\le\beta.

Then

A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta \left(R(\theta)^2-\rho(\theta)^2\right)\,d\theta.

In words,

\text{polar area between curves} = \frac12\int \left((\text{outer radius})^2-(\text{inner radius})^2\right)\,d\theta.

The square is not optional. Sector area depends on r^2, not on r.

 one petal of a rose

Find the area of one petal of

r=2\cos(3\theta).

One petal is traced while r\ge0 around \theta=0. The zeros occur when

2\cos(3\theta)=0,

so

3\theta=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}.

Thus one petal is traced for

-\frac{\pi}{6}\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{6}.

The area is

A=\frac12\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}4\cos^2(3\theta)\,d\theta.

So

A=2\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}\cos^2(3\theta)\,d\theta.

Let

u=3\theta, \qquad du=3\,d\theta.

Then

A=\frac23\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2 u\,du.

Since

\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2u\,du=\frac{\pi}{2},

we get

A=\frac{\pi}{3}.

The whole rose has three petals, so its total area is

\pi.

 Warning

Before using

A=\frac12\int r^2\,d\theta,

check what interval traces the region exactly once. Polar curves can retrace themselves, and negative r can send points to the opposite side of the origin.

 Arc length in polar coordinates

A polar curve is parametric:

x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.

So its length is

L=\int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{d\theta}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{dy}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta.

We already computed

\frac{dx}{d\theta} = r'\cos\theta-r\sin\theta,

and

\frac{dy}{d\theta} = r'\sin\theta+r\cos\theta.

Now square and add:

\left(r'\cos\theta-r\sin\theta\right)^2 + \left(r'\sin\theta+r\cos\theta\right)^2.

Expand:

(r')^2\cos^2\theta-2rr'\sin\theta\cos\theta+r^2\sin^2\theta

+ (r')^2\sin^2\theta+2rr'\sin\theta\cos\theta+r^2\cos^2\theta.

The cross terms cancel. The remaining terms give

(r')^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta) + r^2(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta).

So the square of the speed is

(r')^2+r^2.

Therefore

L=\int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{\left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2+r^2}\,d\theta.

Arc length in polar coordinates

For

r=r(\theta), \qquad \alpha\le\theta\le\beta,

assuming r has a continuous derivative, the distance traveled along the polar curve is

L=\int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{r(\theta)^2+\bigl(r'(\theta)\bigr)^2}\,d\theta.

The formula has a nice geometric meaning. As \theta changes, the point may move radially because r changes, and it may move around the origin because the angle changes. The two effects combine by the Pythagorean theorem.

Why can two polar curves meet without sharing the same <m>r</m> at the same <m>\theta</m>?

Polar names are not unique, so the same-angle equation r_1(\theta)=r_2(\theta) can miss intersections. In your own words, what other meetings should you look for, and why does the origin need a separate check?

Curves can meet under different angles, or both pass through the pole at different times. Nonuniqueness is useful for graphing and dangerous for solving.

circumference of a circle

For

r=R,

we have

r'=0.

Thus

L=\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{R^2+0^2}\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}R\,d\theta = 2\pi R.

 length of a cardioid

Find the length of

r=1+\cos\theta, \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi.

We have

r'=-\sin\theta.

So

r^2+(r')^2 = (1+\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta.

Expand and simplify:

(1+\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta = 1+2\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta = 2+2\cos\theta.

Using

1+\cos\theta=2\cos^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right),

we get

2+2\cos\theta = 4\cos^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right).

Therefore

\sqrt{r^2+(r')^2} = 2\left|\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right|.

So

L=\int_0^{2\pi} 2\left|\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right|\,d\theta.

On 0\le\theta\le\pi, \cos(\theta/2)\ge0. On \pi\le\theta\le2\pi, it is nonpositive. Therefore

L= \int_0^\pi 2\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\,d\theta + \int_\pi^{2\pi} -2\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\,d\theta.

Compute:

\int 2\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\,d\theta = 4\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right).

Thus the first integral is

4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)-4\sin0=4.

The second integral is

-4\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\Big|_\pi^{2\pi} = -4\sin\pi+4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 4.

So

L=8.

A small absolute value warning

The expression

\sqrt{4\cos^2(\theta/2)}

equals

2|\cos(\theta/2)|,

not always 2\cos(\theta/2). Dropping the absolute value would incorrectly make the length cancel to zero.

 Intersections and repeated tracing

Polar coordinates are not unique. That nonuniqueness is useful, but it makes intersections more delicate than in Cartesian coordinates.

Two polar curves can meet even when their equations do not give the same r at the same \theta.

There are three common issues.

Intersections and repeated tracing Issue What to check Same ray intersections Solve r_1(\theta)=r_2(\theta). The origin Check whether each curve reaches r=0, possibly at different angles. Negative r and alternate angles Remember (r,\theta)=(-r,\theta+\pi).
an intersection missed by the same-angle equation

Consider

r=2\cos\theta

and

r=2\sin\theta.

These are two circles:

(x-1)^2+y^2=1

and

x^2+(y-1)^2=1.

Solving with the same angle gives

2\cos\theta=2\sin\theta.

So

\cos\theta=\sin\theta,

and hence

\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}+k\pi,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.

At this angle,

r=\sqrt2,

so the point is

(1,1).

But the circles also meet at the origin.

Why did the same-angle equation miss it?

For

r=2\cos\theta,

the origin occurs when

\cos\theta=0,

for example at

\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}.

For

r=2\sin\theta,

the origin occurs when

\sin\theta=0,

for example at

\theta=0.

The two curves reach the same Cartesian point with different polar angles. Therefore the same-angle equation did not see that intersection.

 Repeated tracing

Polar curves can also trace the same geometric curve more than once.

For example,

r=2\cos\theta

is one circle. The interval

-\frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2}

traces it once.

But the interval

0\le\theta\le2\pi

traces the same circle twice.

If we blindly use the polar area formula on 0\le\theta\le2\pi, we get

A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta.

This becomes

A=2\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta = 2\pi.

But the circle has radius 1, so its area is only

\pi.

The integral doubled the answer because the parametrization traced the circle twice.

Using the once-around interval gives

A=\frac12\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta.

So

A=2\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta = 2\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \pi.

That is correct.

Polar checklist before computing area or length

Before using a polar formula, ask:

  1. What interval of \theta traces the desired curve?

  2. Is the curve traced once or more than once?

  3. Does r become negative, creating points on the opposite ray?

  4. Does the curve pass through the origin?

  5. If two curves intersect, are there intersections reached at different angles?

Polar coordinates are powerful because they match circular and radial geometry. But the price is that the same point may have many names.

The next family of curves makes especially good use of polar coordinates. It includes parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas. These curves can be described by distance from a fixed point and a fixed line, and in polar form they appear in one equation.

 What should you ask before computing polar area or length?

The section ends with a checklist: interval, repeated tracing, negative r, the origin, and hidden intersections. In your own words, why does skipping those questions turn a correct formula into a wrong geometric count?

The formula integrates the parametrization you feed it. If the tracing is wrong, the integral is faithfully wrong.

Conic sections

Circles, parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas look like different curves. But they belong to one family.

One way to discover them is to slice a cone. A horizontal slice gives a circle. A slanted slice may give an ellipse, a parabola, or a hyperbola.

There is another way, better suited to calculus and polar coordinates: compare distances.

A conic is controlled by a fixed point and a fixed line.

\text{fixed point: focus} \qquad \text{fixed line: directrix}

The curve consists of all points whose distance to the focus has a constant ratio to their distance to the directrix.

That ratio is called the eccentricity.

 Parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas from focus and directrix

Start with the most familiar focus-directrix example.

Let the focus be

F=(0,p), \qquad p>0,

and let the directrix be the horizontal line

y=-p.

A point P=(x,y) is on the parabola if its distance to the focus equals its distance to the directrix.

The distance from P=(x,y) to the focus F=(0,p) is

\sqrt{x^2+(y-p)^2}.

The distance from P=(x,y) to the directrix y=-p is

y+p

for points above the directrix.

Set the distances equal:

\sqrt{x^2+(y-p)^2}=y+p.

Square both sides:

x^2+(y-p)^2=(y+p)^2.

Expand:

x^2+y^2-2py+p^2=y^2+2py+p^2.

Cancel y^2 and p^2:

x^2-2py=2py.

So

x^2=4py.

This is the standard upward-opening parabola with vertex at the origin.

The parabola is only one member of the family. To get the whole family, allow a constant ratio.

Focus-directrix definition of a conic

Fix a point F, called the focus, and a line \ell not containing F, called the directrix. For a positive number e, the conic with eccentricity e is the set of points P such that

\operatorname{dist}(P,F)=e\,\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell).

The number e is called the eccentricity.

The value of e determines the kind of conic.

Parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas from focus and directrix eccentricity type of conic 0<e<1 ellipse e=1 parabola e>1 hyperbola

A circle is the perfectly symmetric special case of an ellipse. In the usual two-focus description of ellipses, a circle has eccentricity e=0. The focus-directrix description above is most useful for e>0.

Why the ratio matters

If

e=1,

then the point is equally far from the focus and the directrix. This gives a parabola.

If

0<e<1,

then

\operatorname{dist}(P,F)<\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell).

The focus distance is smaller than the directrix distance. The resulting curve closes up into an ellipse.

If

e>1,

then

\operatorname{dist}(P,F)>\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell).

The focus distance is larger than the directrix distance. The resulting curve opens into a hyperbola.

 What single comparison produces the whole conic family?

A conic is the set of points whose distance to a focus has a constant ratio to their distance to a directrix. In your own words, why does that one comparison unify parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas, and what role does the eccentricity e play?

For a nondegenerate focus-directrix conic, the positive ratio is e. The cases 0<e<1, e=1, and e>1 give ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola. A circle is the limiting case of an ellipse as eccentricity tends to zero.

 Standard equations

The focus-directrix definition gives the geometry. The standard equations give the algebra.

Parabolas

We already derived

x^2=4py.

This parabola has

\text{vertex }(0,0), \qquad \text{focus }(0,p), \qquad \text{directrix }y=-p.

It opens upward when p>0 and downward when p<0.

The sideways form is

y^2=4px.

This parabola has

\text{focus }(p,0), \qquad \text{directrix }x=-p.

It opens right when p>0 and left when p<0.

Example

Find the focus and directrix of

y^2=12x.

Compare with

y^2=4px.

So

4p=12, \qquad p=3.

Therefore the focus is

(3,0),

and the directrix is

x=-3.

Ellipses

An ellipse can be described as the set of points whose distances to two fixed foci have constant sum.

For the horizontal ellipse centered at the origin,

\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1, \qquad a\ge b>0.

The longer axis is along the x-axis. The vertices are

(\pm a,0),

and the endpoints of the shorter axis are

(0,\pm b).

The foci are

(\pm c,0),

where

c^2=a^2-b^2.

The eccentricity is

e=\frac{c}{a}.

Because c<a, an ellipse has

0\le e<1.

If a=b, then c=0, the two foci coincide at the center, and the ellipse is a circle.

 Example

Find the foci and eccentricity of

\frac{x^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{9}=1.

Here

a^2=25, \qquad b^2=9.

So

a=5, \qquad b=3.

Then

c^2=a^2-b^2=25-9=16,

so

c=4.

The foci are

(\pm4,0).

The eccentricity is

e=\frac{c}{a}=\frac45.

Hyperbolas

A hyperbola can be described as the set of points whose distances to two fixed foci have a constant positive absolute difference.

For the horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin, with a,b>0,

\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1.

The vertices are

(\pm a,0).

The foci are

(\pm c,0),

where

c^2=a^2+b^2.

The eccentricity is

e=\frac{c}{a}.

Because c>a, a hyperbola has

e>1.

The asymptotes are

y=\pm\frac{b}{a}x.

What does eccentricity measure geometrically?

For ellipses, e=c/a. In your own words, why does e=0 recover a circle, why does e approaching 1 stretch the ellipse, and what changes when e crosses 1?

Eccentricity measures how far the conic is from circular. Crossing e=1 opens the curve: a parabola is no longer closed, and a hyperbola splits into branches.

Example

Find the foci and asymptotes of

\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{16}=1.

Here

a^2=9, \qquad b^2=16,

so

a=3, \qquad b=4.

For a hyperbola,

c^2=a^2+b^2=9+16=25,

so

c=5.

The foci are

(\pm5,0).

The asymptotes are

y=\pm\frac{4}{3}x.

The eccentricity is

e=\frac{c}{a}=\frac53.

Polar equations of conics

The focus-directrix definition becomes especially simple in polar coordinates if we place the focus at the origin.

Let the focus be the pole. Let the directrix be the vertical line

x=d, \qquad d>0.

First use r\ge0 for a point P to the left of the directrix. Its distance to the focus is

r.

The Cartesian x-coordinate of P is

x=r\cos\theta.

So the distance from P to the directrix x=d, for points to the left of the directrix, is

d-r\cos\theta.

The focus-directrix condition is

r=e(d-r\cos\theta).

Solve for r:

r=ed-er\cos\theta.

Move the r-terms together:

r+er\cos\theta=ed.

Factor:

r(1+e\cos\theta)=ed.

Therefore

r=\frac{ed}{1+e\cos\theta}.

If we write

p=ed,

then

r=\frac{p}{1+e\cos\theta}.

For an ellipse or parabola, these nonnegative radii describe the whole conic. For a hyperbola they describe the branch to the left of the directrix. Allowing negative radii in the same algebraic polar formula also traces the other branch; there the focus distance is |r| and the directrix distance is |d-r\cos\theta|. The number p is called the semi-latus rectum. It is the radius when

\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}

or

\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2},

provided those points are on the curve.

Changing the position of the directrix changes the sign or replaces cosine by sine. The common polar forms are

r=\frac{p}{1\pm e\cos\theta}

and

r=\frac{p}{1\pm e\sin\theta}.

The same eccentricity test applies:

Polar equations of conics eccentricity in polar equation conic 0<e<1 ellipse e=1 parabola e>1 hyperbola
Why do polar coordinates put every conic in one equation?

With the focus at the pole, conics take the form r=p/(1+e\cos\theta). In your own words, why is that a natural language for the focus-directrix definition, and how does the single number e become visible in the formula?

Polar coordinates measure distance from the focus directly when r\ge0. In the standard focus form, after normalizing the constant denominator term to one, the absolute value of the cosine or sine coefficient is the eccentricity.

 identify a polar conic

Classify

r=\frac{6}{2+\cos\theta}.

First rewrite the denominator so that it has the form 1+e\cos\theta:

r = \frac{6}{2+\cos\theta} = \frac{3}{1+\frac12\cos\theta}.

Thus

p=3, \qquad e=\frac12.

Since

0<e<1,

the conic is an ellipse.

 a parabola in polar form

Consider

r=\frac{4}{1+\cos\theta}.

Here

e=1,

so the curve is a parabola.

We can also convert it to Cartesian form. Multiply both sides by the denominator:

r(1+\cos\theta)=4.

Since

r\cos\theta=x,

this becomes

r+x=4.

Thus

r=4-x.

Now use

r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.

So

\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=4-x.

Square both sides:

x^2+y^2=(4-x)^2.

Expand:

x^2+y^2=16-8x+x^2.

Cancel x^2:

y^2=16-8x.

So

y^2=-8(x-2).

This is a parabola opening left. Its focus is at the origin, exactly as the polar setup promised.

 classify several polar conics

Classify each curve.

r=\frac{10}{3+2\cos\theta}.

Rewrite:

r=\frac{10/3}{1+\frac23\cos\theta}.

So

e=\frac23.

This is an ellipse.

Next,

r=\frac{5}{1-\sin\theta}.

Here

e=1.

Conic sections

Circles, parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas look like different curves. But they belong to one family.

One way to discover them is to slice a cone. A horizontal slice gives a circle. A slanted slice may give an ellipse, a parabola, or a hyperbola.

There is another way, better suited to calculus and polar coordinates: compare distances.

A conic is controlled by a fixed point and a fixed line.

\text{fixed point: focus} \qquad \text{fixed line: directrix}

The curve consists of all points whose distance to the focus has a constant ratio to their distance to the directrix.

That ratio is called the eccentricity.

 Parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas from focus and directrix

Start with the most familiar focus-directrix example.

Let the focus be

F=(0,p), \qquad p>0,

and let the directrix be the horizontal line

y=-p.

A point P=(x,y) is on the parabola if its distance to the focus equals its distance to the directrix.

The distance from P=(x,y) to the focus F=(0,p) is

\sqrt{x^2+(y-p)^2}.

The distance from P=(x,y) to the directrix y=-p is

y+p

for points above the directrix.

Set the distances equal:

\sqrt{x^2+(y-p)^2}=y+p.

Square both sides:

x^2+(y-p)^2=(y+p)^2.

Expand:

x^2+y^2-2py+p^2=y^2+2py+p^2.

Cancel y^2 and p^2:

x^2-2py=2py.

So

x^2=4py.

This is the standard upward-opening parabola with vertex at the origin.

The parabola is only one member of the family. To get the whole family, allow a constant ratio.

Focus-directrix definition of a conic

Fix a point F, called the focus, and a line \ell not containing F, called the directrix. For a positive number e, the conic with eccentricity e is the set of points P such that

\operatorname{dist}(P,F)=e\,\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell).

The number e is called the eccentricity.

The value of e determines the kind of conic.

Parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas from focus and directrix eccentricity type of conic 0<e<1 ellipse e=1 parabola e>1 hyperbola

A circle is the perfectly symmetric special case of an ellipse. In the usual two-focus description of ellipses, a circle has eccentricity e=0. The focus-directrix description above is most useful for e>0.

Why the ratio matters

If

e=1,

then the point is equally far from the focus and the directrix. This gives a parabola.

If

0<e<1,

then

\operatorname{dist}(P,F)<\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell).

The focus distance is smaller than the directrix distance. The resulting curve closes up into an ellipse.

If

e>1,

then

\operatorname{dist}(P,F)>\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell).

The focus distance is larger than the directrix distance. The resulting curve opens into a hyperbola.

 What single comparison produces the whole conic family?

A conic is the set of points whose distance to a focus has a constant ratio to their distance to a directrix. In your own words, why does that one comparison unify parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas, and what role does the eccentricity e play?

For a nondegenerate focus-directrix conic, the positive ratio is e. The cases 0<e<1, e=1, and e>1 give ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola. A circle is the limiting case of an ellipse as eccentricity tends to zero.

 Standard equations

The focus-directrix definition gives the geometry. The standard equations give the algebra.

Parabolas

We already derived

x^2=4py.

This parabola has

\text{vertex }(0,0), \qquad \text{focus }(0,p), \qquad \text{directrix }y=-p.

It opens upward when p>0 and downward when p<0.

The sideways form is

y^2=4px.

This parabola has

\text{focus }(p,0), \qquad \text{directrix }x=-p.

It opens right when p>0 and left when p<0.

Example

Find the focus and directrix of

y^2=12x.

Compare with

y^2=4px.

So

4p=12, \qquad p=3.

Therefore the focus is

(3,0),

and the directrix is

x=-3.

An ellipse can be described as the set of points whose distances to two fixed foci have constant sum.

For the horizontal ellipse centered at the origin,

\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1, \qquad a\ge b>0.

The longer axis is along the x-axis. The vertices are

(\pm a,0),

and the endpoints of the shorter axis are

(0,\pm b).

The foci are

(\pm c,0),

where

c^2=a^2-b^2.

The eccentricity is

e=\frac{c}{a}.

Because c<a, an ellipse has

0\le e<1.

If a=b, then c=0, the two foci coincide at the center, and the ellipse is a circle.

Find the foci and eccentricity of

\frac{x^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{9}=1.

Here

a^2=25, \qquad b^2=9.

So

a=5, \qquad b=3.

Then

c^2=a^2-b^2=25-9=16,

so

c=4.

The foci are

(\pm4,0).

The eccentricity is

e=\frac{c}{a}=\frac45.

A hyperbola can be described as the set of points whose distances to two fixed foci have a constant positive absolute difference.

For the horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin, with a,b>0,

\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1.

The vertices are

(\pm a,0).

The foci are

(\pm c,0),

where

c^2=a^2+b^2.

e=\frac{c}{a}.

Because c>a, a hyperbola has

e>1.

The asymptotes are

y=\pm\frac{b}{a}x.

What does eccentricity measure geometrically?

For ellipses, e=c/a. In your own words, why does e=0 recover a circle, why does e approaching 1 stretch the ellipse, and what changes when e crosses 1?

Eccentricity measures how far the conic is from circular. Crossing e=1 opens the curve: a parabola is no longer closed, and a hyperbola splits into branches.

Example

Find the foci and asymptotes of

\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{16}=1.

Here

a^2=9, \qquad b^2=16,

a=3, \qquad b=4.

c^2=a^2+b^2=9+16=25,

c=5.

The foci are

(\pm5,0).

The asymptotes are

e=\frac{c}{a}=\frac53.

Warning examples

This chapter gave us three new languages for plane curves:

x=x(t),\quad y=y(t),

r=f(\theta),

and

z=re^{i\theta}.

Each language is powerful because it carries more information than a plain Cartesian equation. It can tell direction, speed, repeated tracing, and rotation.

That extra information is useful. It is also dangerous if we forget what the parameters are doing.

The safest habit is simple:

\text{Before using a formula, ask how the curve is being traced.}

A parametrization stops even when the curve continues

A moving point can pause without the geometric curve having a corner or endpoint.

Consider

x=t^3, \qquad y=t^6.

Eliminate the parameter. Since

x=t^3,

we have

y=t^6=(t^3)^2=x^2.

So the geometric curve is the parabola

y=x^2.

As t increases through 0, the point moves along the parabola through the origin.

But the velocity is

\frac{dx}{dt}=3t^2, \qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=6t^5.

At t=0,

\frac{dx}{dt}=0, \qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=0.

The point has zero speed at the origin.

The curve, however, is perfectly smooth there. The parabola y=x^2 has horizontal tangent at (0,0).

For t\neq0, the parametric slope is

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{6t^5}{3t^2} = 2t^3.

As t\to0,

2t^3\to0.

Thus the tangent slope at the origin is 0, even though direct substitution into

\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}

would give the meaningless quotient

\frac00.

This is the first warning.

A zero velocity may be a feature of the parametrization, not a feature of the curve

When

x'(t_0)=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad y'(t_0)=0,

the moving point stops at t=t_0. The curve may still be smooth. The tangent must be found by looking nearby, not by substituting into the slope quotient.

A parametrization is a schedule. A bad or unusual schedule can pause on an otherwise ordinary road.

Why can a parametrization stop even when the curve continues?

If both coordinate derivatives vanish, the moving point has zero velocity. In your own words, why might that pause be a feature of the schedule rather than a corner of the geometric curve, and how should the tangent then be found?

Look nearby instead of substituting into the slope quotient. A traveler can rest on an otherwise smooth road.

A polar curve traced twice

Polar coordinates have another kind of trap. The same point can have many polar names.

(r,\theta)=(r,\theta+2\pi)=(-r,\theta+\pi).

Because of this, a polar equation may trace a geometric curve more than once.

Consider

r=2\cos\theta.

We converted this earlier:

r^2=2r\cos\theta,

so

x^2+y^2=2x.

Completing the square,

(x-1)^2+y^2=1.

Thus the curve is the circle centered at (1,0) with radius 1.

A once-around interval is

-\frac{\pi}{2}\le \theta\le \frac{\pi}{2},

because on that interval

\cos\theta\ge0.

But if we use

0\le\theta\le2\pi,

the circle is traced twice. The second half is not a new region. It is the same circle again, because r becomes negative and the points are plotted in the opposite direction.

The area formula reveals the mistake.

If we blindly use 0\le\theta\le2\pi, then

A= \frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta.

So

A = 2\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta = 2\pi.

But the circle has radius 1, so its area is

\pi.

The integral doubled the area because the curve was traced twice.

Use a once-around interval instead:

A= \frac12\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta.

Then

A= 2\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta = 2\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \pi.

Polar warning

The formula

A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta r^2\,d\theta

counts how the polar curve is traced on the interval [\alpha,\beta].

If the same region is swept twice, the integral counts it twice.

The square r^2 makes negative r look harmless algebraically. But negative r can still change the tracing.

Why can a polar area integral count a region twice?

The circle r=2\cos\theta is traced twice on [0,2\pi]. In your own words, why does \frac12\int r^2\,d\theta then double the geometric area, and what question should you ask about the interval of \theta before integrating?

The formula counts how the polar curve is traced. Choose an interval that sweeps the region exactly once.

A tangent formula fails when both derivatives vanish

The parametric slope formula is

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}.

It works when

\frac{dx}{dt}\neq0.

For horizontal and vertical tangent tests, we used

\frac{dy}{dt}=0,\quad \frac{dx}{dt}\neq0

and

\frac{dx}{dt}=0,\quad \frac{dy}{dt}\neq0.

Both tests deliberately avoid the case

x'(t)=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad y'(t)=0.

Here is why.

At t=0, all three parametrizations below have

x'(0)=0, \qquad y'(0)=0.

But their tangent behavior is different.

P_1(t)=(t^2,t^3),

P_2(t)=(t^3,t^2),

P_3(t)=(t^2,t^2).

For P_1,

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^2}{2t} = \frac32t \qquad (t\neq0).

As t\to0,

\frac32t\to0.

So P_1 has a horizontal tangent at the cusp.

For P_2,

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2t}{3t^2} = \frac{2}{3t} \qquad (t\neq0).

As t\to0, this becomes unbounded. The tangent is vertical.

For P_3,

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2t}{2t} = 1 \qquad (t\neq0).

The curve is the line

y=x

with x\ge0, traced in and out. Its tangent slope is 1.

The same direct substitution,

\frac00,

has hidden three different outcomes.

The <m>0/0</m> tangent warning

When both coordinate derivatives vanish, the slope formula does not decide the tangent.

Look at the nearby slopes, eliminate the parameter if possible, or study the local geometry.

The same warning applies to polar curves. For

x=r(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y=r(\theta)\sin\theta,

if

\frac{dx}{d\theta}=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{dy}{d\theta}=0,

then the polar slope formula gives 0/0. A cusp, a smooth pause, a retracing, or a more complicated behavior may be hiding there.

Why does a <m>0/0</m> slope formula fail to decide the tangent?

The parametric slope formula is illegal when both derivatives vanish, and the same warning applies to polar curves. In your own words, what different geometric behaviors can hide behind that 0/0, and what extra tools can distinguish them?

A cusp, a smooth pause, or a retracing may all produce vanishing derivatives. Nearby slopes, elimination of the parameter, or a local picture can tell them apart.

The chapter’s main cautions

The formulas in this chapter are reliable when their hypotheses match the tracing.

The chapter’s main cautions situation what to check Parametric slope Is dx/dt\neq0? If both dx/dt and dy/dt vanish, study nearby motion. Parametric length Does the parametrization retrace the curve? The length integral counts distance traveled. Parametric area Is the curve traced once? What is the orientation? Polar area What interval of \theta sweeps the region exactly once? Does r become negative? Polar intersections Did the curves meet at the origin or with different polar names? Conic classification First rewrite the denominator so the constant term is 1, then read eccentricity. Complex polar form Remember that arguments are not unique: \theta and \theta+2\pi k describe the same direction.

A formula is a tool, not a substitute for the picture.

What habit protects every formula in this chapter?

Parametric, polar, and complex languages all carry more information than a plain Cartesian equation. In your own words, why is ask how the curve is being traced the safest habit before using a length, area, or tangent formula?

Extra information about direction, speed, and repeated tracing is useful only if you remember that the formula follows the tracing, not just the set of points.

\text{model the rate, then understand the function.}

The first task in a differential equation is not to solve. It is to recognize what kind of equation is in front of us and what kind of answer is reasonable.

The following examples review the central skills.

What pattern unites the models of this chapter?

Cooling, logistic growth, mixing, springs, and interacting populations look different. In your own words, what common pattern do they share, and why is recognizing the kind of equation as important as producing a formula?

Model the rate, then understand the function. A direction field, a phase line, a separation, or an integrating factor answers a different first question.

separable growth

Solve

y'=3ty, \qquad y(0)=2.

Separate:

\frac{dy}{y}=3t\,dt.

Integrate:

\ln|y|=\frac32t^2+C.

Since y(0)=2,

C=\ln2.

Therefore

y(t)=2e^{(3/2)t^2}.

The exponent is the accumulated relative growth rate:

\int_0^t 3s\,ds=\frac32t^2.

 cooling toward equilibrium

Solve

T'=-0.1(T-22), \qquad T(0)=82.

This has the equilibrium-difference form

Q'=-k(Q-Q_{\text{eq}}).

So

T(t)=22+(82-22)e^{-0.1t}.

Thus

T(t)=22+60e^{-0.1t}.

The temperature approaches 22^\circ\text{C}, not 0^\circ\text{C}, because 22 is the surrounding temperature.

Solve

y'+2y=4e^{-t}, \qquad y(0)=3.

Here

p(t)=2, \qquad q(t)=4e^{-t}.

\mu(t)=e^{\int 2\,dt}=e^{2t}.

Therefore

e^{2t}y=4e^t+C.

P=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad P=800.

P>800,

    y'=1-y

Solve or analyze each problem.

    y(t)=2e^{-3t}

    solves

Let A(t) be the grams of salt in the tank. Set up and solve the initial value problem if the tank initially contains pure water.

  1. The equation

    M'=-0.02M

    models the mass of a radioactive substance. Explain in words what the equation says. What are the units of 0.02 if time is measured in years?

    T'=-k(T-T_s)

  3. A population satisfies

    P'=0.1P\left(1-\frac{P}{1000}\right).

  4. A population satisfies the threshold model

    P(0)=15

    and if

    P(0)=25.

  5. A fish population satisfies

    P'=0.4P\left(1-\frac{P}{1000}\right)-h.

    Find the largest sustainable constant harvest rate in this model.

  6. The solution of a cooling model is

    T(t)=20+70e^{-0.05t}.

    What are the surrounding temperature, the initial temperature, and the cooling constant?

 Project: model a cooling cup of coffee

Newton’s law of cooling says

T'=-k(T-T_s),

where T_s is the surrounding temperature and k>0.

The solution is

T(t)=T_s+(T_0-T_s)e^{-kt}.

This project asks you to test that model with data.

Data collection

Use a hot drink, soup, or warm water in a cup.

  1. Measure the room temperature T_s.

  2. Measure the initial temperature T_0.

  3. Record the temperature every 2 or 3 minutes for at least 20 minutes.

  4. Make a table of t, T(t), and T(t)-T_s.

 Linearizing the model

If the cooling model is correct, then

T(t)-T_s=(T_0-T_s)e^{-kt}.

Assuming T(t)>T_s, take logarithms:

\ln(T(t)-T_s)=\ln(T_0-T_s)-kt.

So a plot of

\ln(T(t)-T_s)

against t should be approximately a straight line with slope

-k.

 Project tasks

  1. Plot T(t) against t. Does the curve look like exponential approach to room temperature?

  2. Plot \ln(T(t)-T_s) against t. Does the graph look approximately linear?

  3. Estimate k from the slope of the logarithmic plot.

  4. Use your estimated k to predict when the drink will reach a chosen temperature, such as 45^\circ\text{C}.

  5. Compare your prediction with the observed data.

  6. Describe at least two possible reasons why real data might not perfectly follow the model.

Model reflection

A differential equation is a simplified law. Real cups lose heat through the cup, the surface, evaporation, stirring, and changing room conditions. The model is useful because it captures the main pattern, not because it records every physical detail.

 Project: compare Euler approximations with exact solutions

Euler’s method turns a differential equation into a sequence:

y_{k+1}=y_k+hF(x_k,y_k).

This project compares Euler approximations with exact solutions.

Part A: a stable approach

Use

y'=1-y, \qquad y(0)=0.

The exact solution is

y=1-e^{-x}.

For each step size

h=0.5,\qquad h=0.25,\qquad h=0.1,

use Euler’s method to approximate y(2).

Make a table:

Part A: a stable approach step size Euler approximation exact value absolute error 0.5 0.25 0.1

Then answer:

  1. Does the error decrease as h decreases?

  2. Does Euler’s method overestimate or underestimate the exact solution?

  3. How does the concavity of y=1-e^{-x} help explain the sign of the error?

 Part B: a step-size warning

Use

y'=-4y, \qquad y(0)=1.

The exact solution is

y=e^{-4x}.

Use Euler’s method up to x=2.4 with

h=0.2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad h=0.6.

Then answer:

  1. Which step size gives values that behave like the exact solution?

  2. Which step size gives values that alternate sign?

  3. For this equation, Euler’s multiplier is

    1-4h.

    Explain why the condition

    |1-4h|<1

    is related to numerical decay.

 Part C: optional improved Euler

Repeat Part A with improved Euler’s method:

k_1=F(x_k,y_k),

\widetilde y_{k+1}=y_k+hk_1,

k_2=F(x_k+h,\widetilde y_{k+1}),

y_{k+1}=y_k+\frac h2(k_1+k_2).

Compare its error with ordinary Euler’s method for the same step sizes.

Project conclusion

A numerical method should be judged by both computation and behavior. A table of numbers is not enough. The numbers should agree with the direction field, the phase line, and any exact solution available.

 What extra information turns a law of change into one history?

A first-order equation usually needs one starting value; a second-order equation usually needs two. In your own words, why is that count part of the meaning of the model, not a bookkeeping afterthought?

The law describes a family of possible motions. The starting state chooses which motion actually happens.

A final map of the chapter

The main ideas of the chapter can be summarized in one picture of dependencies.

\text{law of change} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{differential equation}

and then we choose a route:

\text{qualitative route} \amp:\quad \text{direction field, phase line, equilibria}, \text{numerical route} \amp:\quad \text{Euler's method and step-size checks}, \text{exact route} \amp:\quad \text{separation or integrating factors}, \text{modeling route} \amp:\quad \text{interpret constants, units, and long-term behavior}.

No one route is the whole subject. Often the best solution uses several at once.

For example, in a logistic model, the phase line tells us that a positive solution should approach K. The exact formula tells us when it reaches K/2. Euler’s method can approximate values when parameters are changing or when the equation becomes too complicated to solve exactly. The model interpretation tells us which values of P make physical sense.

What differential equations add to calculus

Earlier, calculus measured change and accumulated change. Differential equations use those ideas to describe laws.

They turn

\text{the derivative}

from something we compute into something we are given.

This chapter ends one story and opens another.

Differential equations often describe motion by using time as the input:

t\longmapsto y(t).

But many curves are not naturally graphs of the form

y=f(x).

A point on a wheel, a planet moving in an orbit, or a particle tracing a loop may pass above the same x-value more than once. The curve may still be easy to describe if we let time trace both coordinates:

x=x(t), \qquad y=y(t).

That is the next idea. Instead of forcing every curve to be a graph, we let a moving point draw it.

What do differential equations add to calculus?

Earlier, calculus measured change and accumulated change. In your own words, how do differential equations change the role of the derivative, and why does that turn an unknown function into the object we seek?

The derivative becomes something we are given by a law, not only something we compute from a known formula.

k_1=F(x_k,y_k),

 What extra information turns a law of change into one history?

A first-order equation usually needs one starting value; a second-order equation usually needs two. In your own words, why is that count part of the meaning of the model, not a bookkeeping afterthought?

The law describes a family of possible motions. The starting state chooses which motion actually happens.

The main ideas of the chapter can be summarized in one picture of dependencies.

\text{law of change} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{differential equation}

and then we choose a route:

\text{qualitative route} \amp:\quad \text{direction field, phase line, equilibria}, \text{numerical route} \amp:\quad \text{Euler's method and step-size checks}, \text{exact route} \amp:\quad \text{separation or integrating factors}, \text{modeling route} \amp:\quad \text{interpret constants, units, and long-term behavior}.

No one route is the whole subject. Often the best solution uses several at once.

Earlier, calculus measured change and accumulated change. Differential equations use those ideas to describe laws.

They turn

\text{the derivative}

from something we compute into something we are given.

This chapter ends one story and opens another.

Differential equations often describe motion by using time as the input:

t\longmapsto y(t).

But many curves are not naturally graphs of the form

y=f(x).

A point on a wheel, a planet moving in an orbit, or a particle tracing a loop may pass above the same x-value more than once. The curve may still be easy to describe if we let time trace both coordinates:

x=x(t), \qquad y=y(t).

That is the next idea. Instead of forcing every curve to be a graph, we let a moving point draw it.

What do differential equations add to calculus?

Earlier, calculus measured change and accumulated change. In your own words, how do differential equations change the role of the derivative, and why does that turn an unknown function into the object we seek?

The derivative becomes something we are given by a law, not only something we compute from a known formula.

A first-order differential equation of the form

y'=F(t,y)

assigns a slope to each point in the (t,y)-plane. At the point (t,y), a solution curve passing through that point must have slope

Return to the equation

y'=1-y.

At a point where y=0,

y'=1-0=1.

So the solution curve has slope 1.

At a point where y=1,

y'=1-1=0.

So the solution curve is horizontal.

At a point where y=2,

y'=1-2=-1.

So the solution curve has slope -1.

Notice that the right side does not depend on t. Every point along the same horizontal line has the same slope.

The little segments are not solution curves. They are instructions for solution curves. A true solution curve must pass through the field by matching the local direction at each point.

y'=F(t,y),

a direction field or slope field is a plot of small line segments, where the segment at (t,y) has slope F(t,y).

The equation y'=F(t,y) assigns a slope to each point (t,y). In your own words, why are the little segments not themselves solution curves, and what instruction do they give to any true solution that passes through a point?

Each segment is a local direction, not a whole history. A solution curve must match the prescribed slope at every point it visits.
