Simpson’s Rule

The midpoint and trapezoidal rules replaced the graph by something simple: a horizontal line or a straight line. Those approximations are easy to compute, and their errors are controlled by curvature.

But a curve is not usually straight. On a short interval, a better first picture may be a parabola.

That is the idea behind Simpson’s Rule.

\text{Use a quadratic curve instead of a line.}

The reward is surprisingly large. Midpoint and trapezoidal errors usually shrink like 1/n^2. Simpson’s Rule, for smooth functions, usually shrinks like 1/n^4.

 Quadratic approximation on pairs of intervals

A polynomial of degree at most one is determined by two points with distinct inputs. A polynomial of degree at most two is determined by three points with distinct inputs.

So Simpson’s Rule uses three equally spaced sample points:

x_0,\qquad x_1,\qquad x_2,

where

x_1=x_0+\Delta x, \qquad x_2=x_0+2\Delta x.

The middle point x_1 is the midpoint of [x_0,x_2].

The function values are

f(x_0),\qquad f(x_1),\qquad f(x_2).

Through the three points

(x_0,f(x_0)),\qquad (x_1,f(x_1)),\qquad (x_2,f(x_2)),

there is exactly one quadratic polynomial. Simpson’s Rule integrates that quadratic instead of the original function.

The formula is simple:

\int_{x_0}^{x_2} f(x)\,dx \approx \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0)+4f(x_1)+f(x_2) \right].

The middle value receives weight 4. The endpoint values receive weight 1.

Where the weights come from

To see the weights, shift and scale the interval so that the three sample points become

-1,\qquad 0,\qquad 1.

Let

p(u)=Au^2+Bu+C

be the quadratic through

(-1,y_0),\qquad (0,y_1),\qquad (1,y_2).

Then

p(0)=C=y_1.

Also

p(-1)=A-B+C=y_0,

and

p(1)=A+B+C=y_2.

Adding these last two equations gives

2A+2C=y_0+y_2.

Since C=y_1,

A=\frac{y_0+y_2-2y_1}{2}.

Now integrate p from -1 to 1:

\int_{-1}^{1}p(u)\,du = \int_{-1}^{1}(Au^2+Bu+C)\,du.

The odd term integrates to zero:

\int_{-1}^{1}Bu\,du=0.

So

\int_{-1}^{1}p(u)\,du = A\int_{-1}^{1}u^2\,du+C\int_{-1}^{1}1\,du.

Since

\int_{-1}^{1}u^2\,du=\frac23

and

\int_{-1}^{1}1\,du=2,

we get

\int_{-1}^{1}p(u)\,du = \frac23A+2C.

Substitute the values of A and C:

\frac23\cdot\frac{y_0+y_2-2y_1}{2}+2y_1 = \frac13(y_0+y_2-2y_1)+2y_1.

Therefore

\int_{-1}^{1}p(u)\,du = \frac13(y_0+4y_1+y_2).

Finally, returning to x-coordinates multiplies the integral by the spacing \Delta x. Thus

\int_{x_0}^{x_2}p(x)\,dx = \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ y_0+4y_1+y_2 \right].

That is Simpson’s Rule.

One-panel Simpson’s Rule

If

m=\frac{a+b}{2},

then

\int_a^b f(x)\,dx \approx \frac{b-a}{6}\left[ f(a)+4f(m)+f(b) \right].

This is the same formula as above, written for one interval [a,b] with midpoint m.

 Why does Simpson’s Rule use three sample points at a time?

Linear interpolation uses two distinct inputs, while interpolation by a polynomial of degree at most two uses three. In your own words, why does Simpson’s Rule therefore work on pairs of subintervals, and why must composite Simpson’s Rule use an even number of subintervals?

Three equally spaced values determine one quadratic interpolant. Pairing subintervals means n is even.

exact for a quadratic

Use Simpson’s Rule to compute

\int_0^2 x^2\,dx.

Here

a=0,\qquad m=1,\qquad b=2.

The Simpson approximation is

\frac{2-0}{6}\left[f(0)+4f(1)+f(2)\right].

Since f(x)=x^2,

f(0)=0,\qquad f(1)=1,\qquad f(2)=4.

So

S=\frac{2}{6}(0+4+4)=\frac{8}{3}.

The exact value is

\int_0^2 x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \frac83.

So Simpson’s Rule is exact in this example.

That should not be surprising. Simpson’s Rule integrates the quadratic interpolating polynomial. If the original function is already quadratic, the approximation is the function itself.

 Composite Simpson’s Rule

One parabola over a wide interval may not be enough. As before, we divide the interval into smaller pieces.

Let [a,b] be divided into n equal subintervals, where n is even. Define

\Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n},

and

x_i=a+i\Delta x, \qquad i=0,1,2,\ldots,n.

Because Simpson’s Rule uses pairs of subintervals, n must be even. We apply Simpson’s Rule on

[x_0,x_2],\quad [x_2,x_4],\quad [x_4,x_6],\quad \ldots,\quad [x_{n-2},x_n].

On the first pair,

\int_{x_0}^{x_2} f(x)\,dx \approx \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0)+4f(x_1)+f(x_2) \right].

On the second pair,

\int_{x_2}^{x_4} f(x)\,dx \approx \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_2)+4f(x_3)+f(x_4) \right].

Adding the pieces, the shared endpoint values such as f(x_2) are counted twice. That is why the even interior indices receive weight 2.

Composite Simpson’s Rule

Suppose n is even. Then

S_n= \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0) +4f(x_1) +2f(x_2) +4f(x_3) +2f(x_4) +\cdots +4f(x_{n-1}) +f(x_n) \right].

The weights follow the pattern

1,\ 4,\ 2,\ 4,\ 2,\ \ldots,\ 4,\ 1.

A compact way to remember the formula is:

S_n = \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0)+f(x_n) + 4\sum_{\substack{i=1\\i\text{ odd}}}^{n-1} f(x_i) + 2\sum_{\substack{i=2\\i\text{ even}}}^{n-2} f(x_i) \right].

The odd interior points get weight 4. The even interior points get weight 2.

Warning: <m>n</m> must be even

Composite Simpson’s Rule pairs neighboring subintervals. If n is odd, one subinterval is left unpaired.

For example, n=5 gives five subintervals. Simpson’s Rule can cover four of them in two pairs, but one remains. In that situation, either change n to an even number or combine Simpson’s Rule with another rule on the leftover interval.

For this course, when using Simpson’s Rule, choose n even.

 Example: Simpson’s Rule for <m>\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx</m>

Approximate

I=\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx

using Simpson’s Rule with n=4.

Here

\Delta x=\frac{1-0}{4}=\frac14.

The grid points are

x_0=0,\quad x_1=0.25,\quad x_2=0.50,\quad x_3=0.75,\quad x_4=1.

The function values are:

\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x_i \amp 0 \amp 0.25 \amp 0.50 \amp 0.75 \amp 1.00\\ \hline e^{-x_i^2} \amp 1.000000 \amp 0.939413 \amp 0.778801 \amp 0.569783 \amp 0.367879 \end{array}

Since n=4, the weights are

1,\ 4,\ 2,\ 4,\ 1.

Therefore

S_4 = \frac{0.25}{3} \left[ 1.000000 +4(0.939413) +2(0.778801) +4(0.569783) +0.367879 \right].

Compute the weighted sum:

1.000000 +3.757652 +1.557602 +2.279132 +0.367879 = 8.962265.

Thus

S_4=\frac{0.25}{3}(8.962265)\approx 0.746855.

So

\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx\approx 0.746855

using Simpson’s Rule with only four subintervals.

A more accurate value is

0.746824\ldots,

so this approximation is already quite good.

Example: Simpson’s Rule for <m>\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx</m> rule with n=4 approximation to \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx midpoint 0.748747 trapezoidal 0.742984 Simpson 0.746855

The Simpson value is much closer in this example. The next subsection explains why this often happens.

 Why Simpson’s Rule is often much better

The midpoint and trapezoidal rules approximate a graph using degree 0 and degree 1 shapes:

\text{horizontal line}, \qquad \text{straight line}.

Simpson’s Rule uses degree 2:

\text{parabola}.

So it should be exact for quadratic functions. The surprise is that it is also exact for cubic functions.

To see why, work on the symmetric interval [-1,1]. Simpson’s Rule says

\int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,dx \approx \frac13\left[f(-1)+4f(0)+f(1)\right].

Check the four basic powers 1,x,x^2,x^3.

For f(x)=1,

\int_{-1}^{1}1\,dx=2,

and Simpson gives

\frac13(1+4+1)=2.

For f(x)=x,

\int_{-1}^{1}x\,dx=0,

and Simpson gives

\frac13(-1+0+1)=0.

For f(x)=x^2,

\int_{-1}^{1}x^2\,dx=\frac23,

and Simpson gives

\frac13(1+0+1)=\frac23.

For f(x)=x^3,

\int_{-1}^{1}x^3\,dx=0,

and Simpson gives

\frac13(-1+0+1)=0.

So Simpson’s Rule is exact for all polynomials of degree at most 3. Any cubic is a linear combination of

1,\quad x,\quad x^2,\quad x^3.

Since both integration and Simpson’s formula are linear, exactness for these four powers gives exactness for every cubic.

Key fact

Simpson’s Rule is built from a quadratic approximation, but it integrates every cubic polynomial exactly.

This is why Simpson’s Rule can outperform what its construction suggests.

There is also a useful geometric way to remember the improvement. On a concave-up graph, the trapezoidal rule tends to overestimate and the midpoint rule tends to underestimate. Simpson’s Rule is the weighted average

S=\frac13T+\frac23M

on a single interval, where T is the one-trapezoid approximation and M is the midpoint approximation.

Indeed,

T=\frac{b-a}{2}\bigl(f(a)+f(b)\bigr),

and

M=(b-a)f(m).

Then

\frac13T+\frac23M = \frac{b-a}{6}\bigl(f(a)+f(b)\bigr) + \frac{2(b-a)}{3}f(m).

So

\frac13T+\frac23M = \frac{b-a}{6} \left[ f(a)+4f(m)+f(b) \right],

which is Simpson’s Rule.

The leading curvature errors of T and M have opposite signs. Simpson’s Rule combines them in just the right proportion to cancel much of that error.

Why is Simpson’s Rule exact for cubics, not only quadratics?

Simpson’s Rule is built by integrating a quadratic interpolant, yet it also integrates every cubic exactly. In your own words, why is that possible, and how does writing Simpson as the weighted average \frac13 T+\frac23 M help explain the improvement?

On a symmetric interval, the odd cubic term integrates to zero in both the true integral and Simpson’s formula. The leading curvature errors of the trapezoid and midpoint have opposite signs.

Simpson error bound

The midpoint and trapezoidal error bounds were controlled by f'', because lines fail when curvature is present.

Simpson’s Rule is exact for cubics. So its first possible error comes from behavior beyond cubic. That is why the fourth derivative appears.

Error bound for composite Simpson’s Rule

Suppose f^{(4)} is continuous on [a,b], and suppose

|f^{(4)}(x)|\le K

for all x\in[a,b].

Let S_n be the composite Simpson approximation using n equal subintervals, where n is even. Then

\left| \int_a^b f(x)\,dx-S_n \right| \le \frac{K(b-a)^5}{180n^4}.

The important feature is

\frac{1}{n^4}.

Doubling n divides the error bound by

2^4=16.

That is a much faster improvement than the 1/n^2 behavior of the midpoint and trapezoidal rules.

a guaranteed Simpson approximation

Use Simpson’s Rule to approximate

\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx

with guaranteed error less than 0.0005.

For

f(x)=e^{-x^2},

a calculation gives

f^{(4)}(x)=\left(16x^4-48x^2+12\right)e^{-x^2}.

On [0,1], a derivative check shows

|f^{(4)}(x)|\le 12.

So we may take

K=12.

The Simpson error bound gives

|I-S_n| \le \frac{12(1)^5}{180n^4} = \frac{1}{15n^4}.

We want

\frac{1}{15n^4}<0.0005.

This is equivalent to

15n^4>2000,

or

n^4>\frac{2000}{15}\approx 133.33.

Taking fourth roots,

n>3.40.

Since Simpson’s Rule requires n even, we take

n=4.

So 4 subintervals are enough to guarantee error less than 0.0005.

With n=4, we found

S_4\approx0.746855.

The actual error is even smaller than the guaranteed bound.

 A bound is a guarantee, not a prediction

An error bound tells us the approximation cannot be worse than a certain amount. It does not usually tell us the actual error exactly.

 Why the hypotheses matter

The Simpson error bound assumes that f^{(4)} exists, is continuous, and is bounded on the interval.

For example,

f(x)=\sqrt{x}

is continuous on [0,1], and the integral

\int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,dx

exists. But the derivatives of f become singular near x=0. In particular, the fourth derivative is unbounded near 0.

Simpson’s Rule may still produce useful approximations, but the standard Simpson error bound does not apply on [0,1].

\text{The numerical rule can still be used. The guarantee is what fails.}

That warning is important in computation. A formula can return a number even when the theorem that estimates its error does not apply.

Numerical integration approximates accumulation. But the other half of calculus can also be approximated. If we know values of a function from data, can we estimate its derivative?

That question leads to numerical differentiation.

 Why does Simpson’s error bound involve the fourth derivative?

Midpoint and trapezoidal errors are controlled by f''. Simpson’s bound is controlled by f^{(4)} and shrinks like 1/n^4. In your own words, why does exactness through cubics push the first possible error to the next derivative, and why is a bound still only a guarantee?

A rule that is exact for polynomials up through degree 3 first feels the failure of a degree-4 term. Doubling n divides the bound by 16, but the actual error may be smaller.

What fails when the fourth derivative is unbounded?

Simpson’s Rule can still be applied to \int_0^1\sqrt{x}\,dx, even though f^{(4)} blows up at x=0. In your own words, what exactly fails in that situation, and what does that teach about trusting a formula that still returns a number?

The numerical rule can still be used. The theorem that estimates its error is what no longer applies.

 Why does Simpson’s Rule use three sample points at a time?

Linear interpolation uses two distinct inputs, while interpolation by a polynomial of degree at most two uses three. In your own words, why does Simpson’s Rule therefore work on pairs of subintervals, and why must composite Simpson’s Rule use an even number of subintervals?

Three equally spaced values determine one quadratic interpolant. Pairing subintervals means n is even.

exact for a quadratic

Use Simpson’s Rule to compute

\int_0^2 x^2\,dx.

Here

a=0,\qquad m=1,\qquad b=2.

The Simpson approximation is

\frac{2-0}{6}\left[f(0)+4f(1)+f(2)\right].

Since f(x)=x^2,

f(0)=0,\qquad f(1)=1,\qquad f(2)=4.

So

S=\frac{2}{6}(0+4+4)=\frac{8}{3}.

The exact value is

\int_0^2 x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \frac83.

So Simpson’s Rule is exact in this example.

That should not be surprising. Simpson’s Rule integrates the quadratic interpolating polynomial. If the original function is already quadratic, the approximation is the function itself.

 Composite Simpson’s Rule

One parabola over a wide interval may not be enough. As before, we divide the interval into smaller pieces.

Let [a,b] be divided into n equal subintervals, where n is even. Define

\Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n},

and

x_i=a+i\Delta x, \qquad i=0,1,2,\ldots,n.

Because Simpson’s Rule uses pairs of subintervals, n must be even. We apply Simpson’s Rule on

[x_0,x_2],\quad [x_2,x_4],\quad [x_4,x_6],\quad \ldots,\quad [x_{n-2},x_n].

On the first pair,

\int_{x_0}^{x_2} f(x)\,dx \approx \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0)+4f(x_1)+f(x_2) \right].

On the second pair,

\int_{x_2}^{x_4} f(x)\,dx \approx \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_2)+4f(x_3)+f(x_4) \right].

Adding the pieces, the shared endpoint values such as f(x_2) are counted twice. That is why the even interior indices receive weight 2.

Composite Simpson’s Rule

Suppose n is even. Then

S_n= \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0) +4f(x_1) +2f(x_2) +4f(x_3) +2f(x_4) +\cdots +4f(x_{n-1}) +f(x_n) \right].

The weights follow the pattern

1,\ 4,\ 2,\ 4,\ 2,\ \ldots,\ 4,\ 1.

A compact way to remember the formula is:

S_n = \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0)+f(x_n) + 4\sum_{\substack{i=1\\i\text{ odd}}}^{n-1} f(x_i) + 2\sum_{\substack{i=2\\i\text{ even}}}^{n-2} f(x_i) \right].

The odd interior points get weight 4. The even interior points get weight 2.

Warning: <m>n</m> must be even

Composite Simpson’s Rule pairs neighboring subintervals. If n is odd, one subinterval is left unpaired.

For example, n=5 gives five subintervals. Simpson’s Rule can cover four of them in two pairs, but one remains. In that situation, either change n to an even number or combine Simpson’s Rule with another rule on the leftover interval.

For this course, when using Simpson’s Rule, choose n even.

 Example: Simpson’s Rule for <m>\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx</m>

Approximate

I=\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx

using Simpson’s Rule with n=4.

Here

\Delta x=\frac{1-0}{4}=\frac14.

The grid points are

x_0=0,\quad x_1=0.25,\quad x_2=0.50,\quad x_3=0.75,\quad x_4=1.

The function values are:

\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x_i \amp 0 \amp 0.25 \amp 0.50 \amp 0.75 \amp 1.00\\ \hline e^{-x_i^2} \amp 1.000000 \amp 0.939413 \amp 0.778801 \amp 0.569783 \amp 0.367879 \end{array}

Since n=4, the weights are

1,\ 4,\ 2,\ 4,\ 1.

Therefore

S_4 = \frac{0.25}{3} \left[ 1.000000 +4(0.939413) +2(0.778801) +4(0.569783) +0.367879 \right].

Compute the weighted sum:

1.000000 +3.757652 +1.557602 +2.279132 +0.367879 = 8.962265.

Thus

S_4=\frac{0.25}{3}(8.962265)\approx 0.746855.

So

\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx\approx 0.746855

using Simpson’s Rule with only four subintervals.

A more accurate value is

0.746824\ldots,

so this approximation is already quite good.

Example: Simpson’s Rule for <m>\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx</m> rule with n=4 approximation to \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx midpoint 0.748747 trapezoidal 0.742984 Simpson 0.746855

The Simpson value is much closer in this example. The next subsection explains why this often happens.

 Why Simpson’s Rule is often much better

The midpoint and trapezoidal rules approximate a graph using degree 0 and degree 1 shapes:

\text{horizontal line}, \qquad \text{straight line}.

Simpson’s Rule uses degree 2:

\text{parabola}.

So it should be exact for quadratic functions. The surprise is that it is also exact for cubic functions.

To see why, work on the symmetric interval [-1,1]. Simpson’s Rule says

\int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,dx \approx \frac13\left[f(-1)+4f(0)+f(1)\right].

Check the four basic powers 1,x,x^2,x^3.

For f(x)=1,

\int_{-1}^{1}1\,dx=2,

and Simpson gives

\frac13(1+4+1)=2.

For f(x)=x,

\int_{-1}^{1}x\,dx=0,

and Simpson gives

\frac13(-1+0+1)=0.

For f(x)=x^2,

\int_{-1}^{1}x^2\,dx=\frac23,

and Simpson gives

\frac13(1+0+1)=\frac23.

For f(x)=x^3,

\int_{-1}^{1}x^3\,dx=0,

and Simpson gives

\frac13(-1+0+1)=0.

So Simpson’s Rule is exact for all polynomials of degree at most 3. Any cubic is a linear combination of

1,\quad x,\quad x^2,\quad x^3.

Since both integration and Simpson’s formula are linear, exactness for these four powers gives exactness for every cubic.

Key fact

Simpson’s Rule is built from a quadratic approximation, but it integrates every cubic polynomial exactly.

This is why Simpson’s Rule can outperform what its construction suggests.

There is also a useful geometric way to remember the improvement. On a concave-up graph, the trapezoidal rule tends to overestimate and the midpoint rule tends to underestimate. Simpson’s Rule is the weighted average

S=\frac13T+\frac23M

on a single interval, where T is the one-trapezoid approximation and M is the midpoint approximation.

Indeed,

T=\frac{b-a}{2}\bigl(f(a)+f(b)\bigr),

and

M=(b-a)f(m).

Then

\frac13T+\frac23M = \frac{b-a}{6}\bigl(f(a)+f(b)\bigr) + \frac{2(b-a)}{3}f(m).

So

\frac13T+\frac23M = \frac{b-a}{6} \left[ f(a)+4f(m)+f(b) \right],

which is Simpson’s Rule.

The leading curvature errors of T and M have opposite signs. Simpson’s Rule combines them in just the right proportion to cancel much of that error.

Why is Simpson’s Rule exact for cubics, not only quadratics?

Simpson’s Rule is built by integrating a quadratic interpolant, yet it also integrates every cubic exactly. In your own words, why is that possible, and how does writing Simpson as the weighted average \frac13 T+\frac23 M help explain the improvement?

On a symmetric interval, the odd cubic term integrates to zero in both the true integral and Simpson’s formula. The leading curvature errors of the trapezoid and midpoint have opposite signs.

Simpson error bound

The midpoint and trapezoidal error bounds were controlled by f'', because lines fail when curvature is present.

Simpson’s Rule is exact for cubics. So its first possible error comes from behavior beyond cubic. That is why the fourth derivative appears.

Error bound for composite Simpson’s Rule

Suppose f^{(4)} is continuous on [a,b], and suppose

|f^{(4)}(x)|\le K

for all x\in[a,b].

Let S_n be the composite Simpson approximation using n equal subintervals, where n is even. Then

\left| \int_a^b f(x)\,dx-S_n \right| \le \frac{K(b-a)^5}{180n^4}.

The important feature is

\frac{1}{n^4}.

Doubling n divides the error bound by

2^4=16.

That is a much faster improvement than the 1/n^2 behavior of the midpoint and trapezoidal rules.

a guaranteed Simpson approximation

Use Simpson’s Rule to approximate

\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx

with guaranteed error less than 0.0005.

For

f(x)=e^{-x^2},

a calculation gives

f^{(4)}(x)=\left(16x^4-48x^2+12\right)e^{-x^2}.

On [0,1], a derivative check shows

|f^{(4)}(x)|\le 12.

So we may take

K=12.

The Simpson error bound gives

|I-S_n| \le \frac{12(1)^5}{180n^4} = \frac{1}{15n^4}.

We want

\frac{1}{15n^4}<0.0005.

This is equivalent to

15n^4>2000,

or

n^4>\frac{2000}{15}\approx 133.33.

Taking fourth roots,

n>3.40.

Since Simpson’s Rule requires n even, we take

n=4.

So 4 subintervals are enough to guarantee error less than 0.0005.

With n=4, we found

S_4\approx0.746855.

The actual error is even smaller than the guaranteed bound.

 A bound is a guarantee, not a prediction

An error bound tells us the approximation cannot be worse than a certain amount. It does not usually tell us the actual error exactly.

 Why the hypotheses matter

The Simpson error bound assumes that f^{(4)} exists, is continuous, and is bounded on the interval.

For example,

f(x)=\sqrt{x}

is continuous on [0,1], and the integral

\int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,dx

exists. But the derivatives of f become singular near x=0. In particular, the fourth derivative is unbounded near 0.

Simpson’s Rule may still produce useful approximations, but the standard Simpson error bound does not apply on [0,1].

\text{The numerical rule can still be used. The guarantee is what fails.}

That warning is important in computation. A formula can return a number even when the theorem that estimates its error does not apply.

Numerical integration approximates accumulation. But the other half of calculus can also be approximated. If we know values of a function from data, can we estimate its derivative?

That question leads to numerical differentiation.

 Why does Simpson’s error bound involve the fourth derivative?

Midpoint and trapezoidal errors are controlled by f''. Simpson’s bound is controlled by f^{(4)} and shrinks like 1/n^4. In your own words, why does exactness through cubics push the first possible error to the next derivative, and why is a bound still only a guarantee?

A rule that is exact for polynomials up through degree 3 first feels the failure of a degree-4 term. Doubling n divides the bound by 16, but the actual error may be smaller.

What fails when the fourth derivative is unbounded?

Simpson’s Rule can still be applied to \int_0^1\sqrt{x}\,dx, even though f^{(4)} blows up at x=0. In your own words, what exactly fails in that situation, and what does that teach about trusting a formula that still returns a number?

The numerical rule can still be used. The theorem that estimates its error is what no longer applies.

Numerical differentiation

Integration is forgiving. It averages values over an interval.

Differentiation is less forgiving. It subtracts nearby values and divides by a small number.

That difference matters.

If we know a formula for f, exact differentiation may be best. But in experiments, we may only know values from a table. A motion sensor records position. A weather station records temperature. A lab instrument records concentration. We then ask:

\text{Can we estimate the instantaneous rate of change from sampled values?}

The answer is yes, but with a warning: smaller steps are not always better.

 Forward, backward, and centered differences

The derivative at a is

f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

If h is small but not zero, the quotient

\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}

is a natural approximation to f'(a). It uses the point a and a point to the right. This is called a forward difference.

There are three basic finite-difference formulas.

Finite-difference approximations to <m>f'(a)</m>

For h>0,

D_h^+f(a)=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}

is the forward difference,

D_h^-f(a)=\frac{f(a)-f(a-h)}{h}

is the backward difference, and

D_h^0f(a)=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a-h)}{2h}

is the centered difference.

Geometrically, all three are slopes of secant lines.

The forward difference looks right. The backward difference looks left. The centered difference balances both sides.

What are forward, backward, and centered differences measuring?

Each finite-difference formula is the slope of a secant. In your own words, what geometric distinction is there among looking right, looking left, and balancing both sides, and why does that distinction matter at the endpoint of a data table?

A centered difference needs a point on each side. At a left endpoint there is no data to the left, so a forward difference may be the only available estimate.

differentiating from values

Estimate

\frac{d}{dx}e^x\Big|_{x=0}

using h=0.1.

The true derivative is

\left(e^x\right)'=e^x,

so

f'(0)=1.

Now compare the numerical approximations.

The forward difference is

D_{0.1}^+f(0) = \frac{e^{0.1}-e^0}{0.1} \approx 1.051709.

The backward difference is

D_{0.1}^-f(0) = \frac{e^0-e^{-0.1}}{0.1} \approx 0.951626.

The centered difference is

D_{0.1}^0f(0) = \frac{e^{0.1}-e^{-0.1}}{0.2} \approx 1.001668.

differentiating from values method approximation absolute error forward difference 1.051709 0.051709 backward difference 0.951626 0.048374 centered difference 1.001668 0.001668

The centered difference is much better here because the errors from the left and right partly cancel.

 Truncation error

A finite-difference formula replaces a limit by a finite step. The error from doing that is called truncation error.

The word means: we stopped a limiting process early.

Assume f''' is continuous near a, with |f'''|\le K. Repeated use of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives the finite identity

f(a+s)=f(a)+f'(a)s+\frac12f''(a)s^2+R_3(s),\qquad R_3(s)=\frac12\int_0^s(s-t)^2f'''(a+t)\,dt.

The orientation of the integral makes the identity valid for negative s too. In either direction, |R_3(s)|\le K|s|^3/6. Therefore

D_h^+f(a)=f'(a)+\frac12f''(a)h+\frac{R_3(h)}h,\qquad D_h^-f(a)=f'(a)-\frac12f''(a)h-\frac{R_3(-h)}h.

Each remainder quotient has absolute value at most Kh^2/6. The one-sided errors generally have opposite leading terms proportional to h. Averaging the quotients cancels those terms:

D_h^0f(a)=f'(a)+\frac{R_3(h)-R_3(-h)}{2h},\qquad |D_h^0f(a)-f'(a)|\le\frac{Kh^2}{6}.

Continuity of f''' also gives R_3(s)/s^3\to f'''(a)/6: subtract f'''(a) in the integral and bound the difference by its maximum near a. Consequently

\lim_{h\to0}\frac{D_h^0f(a)-f'(a)}{h^2}=\frac16f'''(a).

The leading centered error is usually proportional to h^2. These are finite remainder estimates; Taylor polynomials will be developed in Chapter 16.

Truncation error pattern

For smooth functions,

D_h^+f(a)-f'(a) \quad\text{and}\quad D_h^-f(a)-f'(a)

are usually of size roughly proportional to h, while

D_h^0f(a)-f'(a)

is usually of size roughly proportional to h^2.

This explains why centered differences are often much better than one-sided differences when the same step size is used.

Why is a centered difference usually more accurate than a one-sided one?

Truncation error is the error from replacing a limit by a finite step. In your own words, why are forward and backward errors typically of size about h, while the centered error is typically of size about h^2?

The finite quadratic remainder identities show that the terms proportional to the step have opposite signs and cancel in the centered quotient.

why the centered error is small

For f(x)=e^x, all derivatives equal e^x. At a=0,

f'(0)=f''(0)=f'''(0)=1.

The forward difference has leading error approximately

\frac12h.

With h=0.1, this predicts error near

0.05,

which matches the observed forward error

0.051709.

The centered difference has leading error approximately

\frac16h^2.

With h=0.1, this predicts error near

\frac{0.01}{6}=0.001667,

which matches the observed centered error

0.001668.

The finite remainder estimate tells us how the error behaves.

 Roundoff error

Truncation error suggests a simple strategy:

\text{make \(h\) smaller.}

But computation has another error source.

A computer does not usually store real numbers exactly. It stores rounded approximations. When two nearly equal rounded numbers are subtracted, the small difference may lose important digits.

That is exactly what finite differences do.

f(a+h)-f(a)

subtracts two nearby values. When h is very small, these values are very close.

Suppose the computed values of f(a+h) and f(a) each have possible absolute error at most \eta. Then the numerator

f(a+h)-f(a)

may have absolute error as large as

2\eta.

After dividing by h, the derivative approximation may have roundoff error as large as

\frac{2\eta}{h}.

So roundoff error grows as h shrinks.

\text{Small \(h\) reduces truncation error but can increase roundoff error.}

This is the central tension in numerical differentiation.

A typical floating-point experiment

Compute

\frac{e^h-1}{h}

as an approximation to f'(0) for f(x)=e^x. The true value is 1.

A typical double-precision computation may look like this:

\begin{array}{c|c|c} h \amp \dfrac{e^h-1}{h} \amp \text{absolute error}\\ \hline 10^{-1} \amp 1.0517091808 \amp 5.17\cdot10^{-2}\\ 10^{-4} \amp 1.0000500017 \amp 5.00\cdot10^{-5}\\ 10^{-8} \amp 0.9999999939 \amp 6.08\cdot10^{-9}\\ 10^{-10} \amp 1.0000000827 \amp 8.27\cdot10^{-8}\\ 10^{-12} \amp 1.0000889006 \amp 8.89\cdot10^{-5} \end{array}

At first the error decreases. Then it increases.

The mathematical limit is still true:

\lim_{h\to0}\frac{e^h-1}{h}=1.

But the computer is not taking a mathematical limit. It is doing arithmetic with rounded numbers.

 Why smaller <m>h</m> is not always better

There are two competing errors.

For a forward difference,

\text{truncation error}\approx C_1h,

while

\text{roundoff error}\approx \frac{C_2\eta}{h}.

So a rough total error model is

\text{total error}\approx C_1h+\frac{C_2\eta}{h}.

The first term decreases when h decreases. The second term increases when h decreases.

There is usually a best middle range.

For a centered difference,

\text{truncation error}\approx C_1h^2,

while roundoff still behaves like

\frac{C_2\eta}{h}.

So centered differences often allow a smaller error before roundoff takes over, but they do not escape the problem entirely.

Practical lesson

For numerical derivatives, do not blindly make h extremely small.

Use a moderately small h, compare several step sizes, and prefer centered differences when the data allow them.

 Why is smaller <m>h</m> not always better?

Making h smaller reduces truncation error, yet a computer experiment can show the error decreasing and then increasing. In your own words, what competing error is growing, and why is numerical differentiation more delicate than numerical integration?

Finite differences subtract nearby values and divide by a small number. Roundoff (or measurement noise) is magnified by division by h. Integration averages; differentiation magnifies.

Data, endpoints, and one-sided differences

Experimental data often come in a table.

\begin{array}{c|ccccc} t \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \amp 3 \amp 4\\ \hline s(t) \amp 0.0 \amp 1.8 \amp 7.9 \amp 18.2 \amp 32.1 \end{array}

If s(t) is position, then finite differences estimate velocity.

At t=2, the centered difference with h=1 is

\frac{s(3)-s(1)}{2} = \frac{18.2-1.8}{2} = 8.2.

So the estimated velocity at t=2 is

8.2

position units per time unit.

At the left endpoint t=0, a centered difference using t=-1 is not available. We may use a forward difference:

\frac{s(1)-s(0)}{1} = 1.8.

At the right endpoint t=4, we may use a backward difference:

\frac{s(4)-s(3)}{1} = 13.9.

Data, endpoints, and one-sided differences point available estimate reason left endpoint forward difference no data to the left interior point centered difference data on both sides right endpoint backward difference no data to the right

This is common in applications. The best formula is not only a matter of accuracy. It also depends on which measurements are available.

 Warning example: a difference quotient may hide a corner

Numerical differentiation can produce a number even when the derivative does not exist.

Let

f(x)=|x|.

At x=0, the graph has a corner. The derivative does not exist.

The forward difference is

D_h^+f(0)=\frac{|h|-|0|}{h}=1

for h>0.

The backward difference is

D_h^-f(0)=\frac{|0|-|-h|}{h}=-1.

The centered difference is

D_h^0f(0)=\frac{|h|-|-h|}{2h}=0.

So the three numerical formulas give

1,\qquad -1,\qquad 0.

None of these means that f'(0) exists.

Warning

A finite-difference formula can return a number even when the derivative does not exist.

Numerical evidence must be interpreted with the graph, the data, and the hypotheses in mind.

This warning is especially important with noisy data. If the measurements contain small errors, dividing by a small h can turn small measurement errors into large derivative errors.

Differentiation magnifies noise. Integration averages noise.

That is one reason numerical differentiation is usually more delicate than numerical integration.

Why can a difference quotient return a number even when the derivative does not exist?

For f(x)=|x| at x=0, the three finite-difference formulas give 1, -1, and 0. In your own words, why none of those numbers means that f'(0) exists, and what extra evidence should accompany a numerical derivative?

A formula can compute a quotient even when left and right slopes disagree. Interpret the number with the graph, the data, and the hypotheses.

Where this points

Numerical integration and numerical differentiation both replace a limit by a finite calculation. Each method has an error story.

For integration, smaller subintervals usually improve the approximation, and the error bounds can be very strong for smooth functions.

For differentiation, smaller steps reduce truncation error but may increase roundoff error. The best computation is a compromise.

The next natural place where approximation, derivatives, and error meet is Newton’s method. We already used Newton’s method to find roots. Now we can ask sharper computational questions:

\text{When should the iteration stop?}

\text{How close is the current guess to the root?}

\text{What happens when the derivative is small or the root is repeated?}

Those questions bring Newton’s method back, this time as a numerical algorithm rather than only a tangent-line idea.

The finite quadratic remainder identities show that the terms proportional to the step have opposite signs and cancel in the centered quotient.

why the centered error is small

f'(0)=f''(0)=f'''(0)=1.

\frac12h.

With h=0.1, this predicts error near

0.05,

which matches the observed forward error

0.051709.

The centered difference has leading error approximately

\frac16h^2.

With h=0.1, this predicts error near

\frac{0.01}{6}=0.001667,

which matches the observed centered error

0.001668.

Truncation error suggests a simple strategy:

\text{make \(h\) smaller.}

But computation has another error source.

A computer does not usually store real numbers exactly. It stores rounded approximations. When two nearly equal rounded numbers are subtracted, the small difference may lose important digits.

f(a+h)-f(a)

subtracts two nearby values. When h is very small, these values are very close.

f(a+h)-f(a)

may have absolute error as large as

2\eta.

\frac{2\eta}{h}.

So roundoff error grows as h shrinks.

This is the central tension in numerical differentiation.

Compute

\frac{e^h-1}{h}

as an approximation to f'(0) for f(x)=e^x. The true value is 1.

\begin{array}{c|c|c} h \amp \dfrac{e^h-1}{h} \amp \text{absolute error}\\ \hline 10^{-1} \amp 1.0517091808 \amp 5.17\cdot10^{-2}\\ 10^{-4} \amp 1.0000500017 \amp 5.00\cdot10^{-5}\\ 10^{-8} \amp 0.9999999939 \amp 6.08\cdot10^{-9}\\ 10^{-10} \amp 1.0000000827 \amp 8.27\cdot10^{-8}\\ 10^{-12} \amp 1.0000889006 \amp 8.89\cdot10^{-5} \end{array}

At first the error decreases. Then it increases.

The mathematical limit is still true:

\lim_{h\to0}\frac{e^h-1}{h}=1.

But the computer is not taking a mathematical limit. It is doing arithmetic with rounded numbers.

There are two competing errors.

\text{truncation error}\approx C_1h,

while

\text{roundoff error}\approx \frac{C_2\eta}{h}.

So a rough total error model is

\text{total error}\approx C_1h+\frac{C_2\eta}{h}.

The first term decreases when h decreases. The second term increases when h decreases.

There is usually a best middle range.

For a centered difference,

\text{truncation error}\approx C_1h^2,

while roundoff still behaves like

\frac{C_2\eta}{h}.

So centered differences often allow a smaller error before roundoff takes over, but they do not escape the problem entirely.

Practical lesson

For numerical derivatives, do not blindly make h extremely small.

Use a moderately small h, compare several step sizes, and prefer centered differences when the data allow them.

Making h smaller reduces truncation error, yet a computer experiment can show the error decreasing and then increasing. In your own words, what competing error is growing, and why is numerical differentiation more delicate than numerical integration?

Finite differences subtract nearby values and divide by a small number. Roundoff (or measurement noise) is magnified by division by h. Integration averages; differentiation magnifies.

Data, endpoints, and one-sided differences

Experimental data often come in a table.

\begin{array}{c|ccccc} t \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \amp 3 \amp 4\\ \hline s(t) \amp 0.0 \amp 1.8 \amp 7.9 \amp 18.2 \amp 32.1 \end{array}

At t=2, the centered difference with h=1 is

\frac{s(3)-s(1)}{2} = \frac{18.2-1.8}{2} = 8.2.

So the estimated velocity at t=2 is

8.2

position units per time unit.

At the left endpoint t=0, a centered difference using t=-1 is not available. We may use a forward difference:

\frac{s(1)-s(0)}{1} = 1.8.

At the right endpoint t=4, we may use a backward difference:

\frac{s(4)-s(3)}{1} = 13.9.

This is common in applications. The best formula is not only a matter of accuracy. It also depends on which measurements are available.

 Warning example: a difference quotient may hide a corner

Numerical differentiation can produce a number even when the derivative does not exist.

Let

f(x)=|x|.

At x=0, the graph has a corner. The derivative does not exist.

The forward difference is

D_h^+f(0)=\frac{|h|-|0|}{h}=1

for h>0.

The backward difference is

D_h^-f(0)=\frac{|0|-|-h|}{h}=-1.

The centered difference is

D_h^0f(0)=\frac{|h|-|-h|}{2h}=0.

So the three numerical formulas give

1,\qquad -1,\qquad 0.

None of these means that f'(0) exists.

Warning

A finite-difference formula can return a number even when the derivative does not exist.

Numerical evidence must be interpreted with the graph, the data, and the hypotheses in mind.

This warning is especially important with noisy data. If the measurements contain small errors, dividing by a small h can turn small measurement errors into large derivative errors.

Differentiation magnifies noise. Integration averages noise.

That is one reason numerical differentiation is usually more delicate than numerical integration.

Why can a difference quotient return a number even when the derivative does not exist?

For f(x)=|x| at x=0, the three finite-difference formulas give 1, -1, and 0. In your own words, why none of those numbers means that f'(0) exists, and what extra evidence should accompany a numerical derivative?

A formula can compute a quotient even when left and right slopes disagree. Interpret the number with the graph, the data, and the hypotheses.

Where this points

Numerical integration and numerical differentiation both replace a limit by a finite calculation. Each method has an error story.

For integration, smaller subintervals usually improve the approximation, and the error bounds can be very strong for smooth functions.

For differentiation, smaller steps reduce truncation error but may increase roundoff error. The best computation is a compromise.

The next natural place where approximation, derivatives, and error meet is Newton’s method. We already used Newton’s method to find roots. Now we can ask sharper computational questions:

\text{When should the iteration stop?}

\text{How close is the current guess to the root?}

\text{What happens when the derivative is small or the root is repeated?}

Newton’s method revisited

Numerical differentiation taught us a useful warning: a formula can be mathematically correct and still be delicate in computation. Newton’s method has the same personality.

Earlier, Newton’s method came from tangent lines. To solve

f(x)=0,

we replaced the curve by its tangent line at a current guess x_n, then used the x-intercept of that tangent line as the next guess:

x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.

That formula is simple. The computational questions are not.

\text{When should we stop?}

\text{How close is the current guess to the root?}

\text{What changes when the root is multiple?}

\text{What can go wrong if we iterate from a bad starting point?}

These are not side questions. They are the questions that turn Newton’s method from a geometric idea into a numerical algorithm.

 Stopping criteria

A computer almost never lands on the exact root. It produces a sequence

x_0,\ x_1,\ x_2,\ \ldots

and we must decide when the sequence is good enough.

There are two numbers we can easily monitor.

First, we can monitor the residual:

|f(x_n)|.

This tells us how close the function value is to 0.

Second, we can monitor the step size:

|x_n-x_{n-1}|.

This tells us how much the iterates are still moving.

Both are useful. Neither is perfect by itself.

square root of <m>2</m>

To compute \sqrt2, solve

f(x)=x^2-2=0.

Newton’s method gives

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{x_n^2-2}{2x_n} = \frac12\left(x_n+\frac2{x_n}\right).

Start with

x_0=1.5.

The iterates are:

square root of 2 n x_n |f(x_n)| |x_n-x_{n-1}| 0 1.500000000 2.500000\cdot10^{-1} -- 1 1.416666667 6.944444\cdot10^{-3} 8.333333\cdot10^{-2} 2 1.414215686 6.007305\cdot10^{-6} 2.450980\cdot10^{-3} 3 1.414213562 4.510614\cdot10^{-12} 2.123900\cdot10^{-6} 4 1.414213562 4.440892\cdot10^{-16} 1.594946\cdot10^{-12}

By n=3, the residual is tiny and the step is small enough for a moderate decimal tolerance. The required precision determines whether another step is needed.

 A practical stopping rule

Choose tolerances \varepsilon_{\text{res}}>0 and \varepsilon_{\text{step}}>0. Stop when

|f(x_n)|<\varepsilon_{\text{res}}

and

|x_n-x_{n-1}|<\varepsilon_{\text{step}}.

Also choose a maximum number of iterations, so the method cannot run forever.

A typical algorithm therefore asks for three pieces of numerical judgment:

\text{residual tolerance},\qquad \text{step tolerance},\qquad \text{maximum number of iterations}.

The maximum iteration count is not mathematical decoration. It protects us from cycles, divergence, and programming mistakes.

Why residual alone can mislead

A small residual does not always mean a small error in x. The reason is slope.

If the graph is very flat near the axis, then the function value can be small even when the input is not very close to the root.

For example, consider

f(x)=10^{-8}(x-10^6).

The root is

r=10^6.

At x=0,

f(0)=-10^{-2}.

If a careless stopping rule accepts every residual less than 0.02, then x=0 would be accepted even though it is one million units away from the root.

The residual must be interpreted together with the scale of the function and the slope near the root.

\text{Small \(f(x_n)\) is strongest evidence when \(f'\) is not small near the root.}

Why step size alone can mislead

A small step size can also be misleading. An iteration may stop moving because of roundoff error, because the derivative is badly scaled, or because the method is trapped near a point that is not a root.

So a step-size test should usually be paired with a residual test. We want the iterates to stop moving and the function value to be close to zero.

 Why is neither residual nor step size enough by itself?

A Newton iteration can monitor |f(x_n)| and |x_n-x_{n-1}|. In your own words, why can a small residual occur far from a root, and why can a small step occur even when the current point is not a trustworthy root?

A flat graph can have a small function value far from the axis. An iteration can also stall from roundoff, a tiny derivative, or a trap that is not a root. Pair the two tests.

Error estimates

A residual is easy to compute. The actual error

|x_n-r|

is usually not easy to compute, because the root r is the thing we are trying to find.

Still, we can sometimes bound the error.

Suppose r is a root, so

f(r)=0.

If x_n and r lie in an interval where

|f'(x)|\ge m>0,

then the Mean Value Theorem gives

|f(x_n)-f(r)|=|f'(c)|\,|x_n-r|

for some c between x_n and r. Since f(r)=0,

|f(x_n)|=|f'(c)|\,|x_n-r|.

Because |f'(c)|\ge m, we get

|x_n-r|\le \frac{|f(x_n)|}{m}.

This is an a posteriori error estimate: it uses information from the approximation we have already computed.

How can a residual bound the unknown error <m>|x_n-r|</m>?

The root r is what we are trying to find, so the true error is not directly available. In your own words, why does a lower bound on |f'| near the root convert a small residual into a bound on |x_n-r|?

The Mean Value Theorem says |f(x_n)|=|f'(c)|\,|x_n-r|. If the slope cannot be too small, a small function value forces a small input error.

residual gives an error bound

Suppose we use Newton’s method on

f(x)=x^2-2

and obtain

x_3=1.4142135623746899.

We know the positive root lies between 1 and 2. On this interval,

f'(x)=2x,

so

|f'(x)|\ge 2.

For the displayed decimal input, the residual satisfies

|f(x_3)|<4.52\cdot10^{-12}.

Therefore

|x_3-\sqrt2| \le \frac{4.52\cdot10^{-12}}{2} = 2.26\cdot10^{-12}.

So the approximation is guaranteed to be within about

2.26\cdot10^{-12}

of the true root.

This bound is not the same thing as the actual error. It is a guarantee based on a lower bound for the derivative.

 The Newton step as an error estimate

The Newton step is

s_n=x_{n+1}-x_n=-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.

Near a simple root, the tangent line predicts that the root is approximately

x_n+s_n.

So

|s_n|

is often a rough estimate of the current error |x_n-r|.

This is why the step size is useful as a stopping test. If the next tangent correction is tiny, then the current approximation is probably close to a root, provided the residual is also tiny and the derivative is not causing trouble.

But there is something even better near a simple root.

Earlier, the quadratic remainder argument using Rolle’s Theorem gave the Newton error relation

x_{n+1}-r = \frac{f''(c_n)}{2f'(x_n)}(r-x_n)^2

for some point c_n between x_n and r. So near a simple root,

|x_{n+1}-r|\approx C|x_n-r|^2.

This is quadratic convergence.

If the current error is about 10^{-3}, the next error may be about 10^{-6}. If the current error is about 10^{-6}, the next error may be about 10^{-12}.

That is why Newton’s method can suddenly gain many digits.

Practical lesson

When Newton’s method is converging well to a simple root, the number of correct digits often roughly doubles from one step to the next.

When it is not converging well, no stopping rule should pretend that it is.

 Multiple roots

Newton’s method is fastest near a simple root. A simple root is a root r for which

f(r)=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad f'(r)\neq0.

If

f'(r)=0,

then the graph meets the axis with zero slope; it may touch the axis or cross it flatly. Newton’s method may still converge, but the convergence often becomes much slower.

Why does a multiple root slow Newton’s method?

Near a simple root, Newton’s method often doubles the number of correct digits. Near a double root, the error may merely be cut in half each step. In your own words, what geometric difference between a simple crossing and a flat touch explains the change?

Quadratic convergence near a simple root uses a nonzero derivative there. At a root of finite multiplicity m>1, ordinary Newton iteration usually has only linear convergence, with leading error factor (m-1)/m. Such a root can touch or cross the axis.

 a double root

Let

f(x)=(x-1)^2.

The root is

r=1,

and it is a double root. More generally, a root has multiplicity m if, near the root, f(x)=(x-r)^m g(x), where m is a positive integer and g is continuous with g(r)\ne0. For the differentiations below we also assume g is sufficiently differentiable. Here m=2 and g=1. Since

f'(x)=2(x-1),

we have

f'(1)=0.

Newton’s method gives, for x_n\neq1,

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{(x_n-1)^2}{2(x_n-1)}.

Cancel one factor:

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{x_n-1}{2}.

So

x_{n+1}=\frac{x_n+1}{2}.

Starting from x_0=2, the iterates are:

a double root n x_n |x_n-1| 0 2.000000 1.000000 1 1.500000 0.500000 2 1.250000 0.250000 3 1.125000 0.125000 4 1.062500 0.062500

The error is cut in half each time. That is convergence, but it is not quadratic convergence. It is only linear convergence.

The same pattern appears for higher multiplicity. If

f(x)=(x-r)^m,

then

f'(x)=m(x-r)^{m-1}.

Newton’s method gives

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{(x_n-r)^m}{m(x_n-r)^{m-1}} = x_n-\frac{x_n-r}{m}.

Therefore

x_{n+1}-r = \left(1-\frac1m\right)(x_n-r).

So the error is multiplied by

1-\frac1m

each step.

For a double root, this factor is 1/2. For a triple root, it is 2/3. The larger the multiplicity, the slower the basic Newton iteration becomes.

 Multiple-root warning

If Newton’s method converges only linearly, one possible reason is that the root is multiple.

Repeatedly small residuals with slow-moving iterates may indicate a flat crossing or a flat touch near the axis.

If the multiplicity m is known, a modified Newton step can help:

x_{n+1}=x_n-m\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.

For

f(x)=(x-r)^m,

this modified method reaches the root in one step. For more general functions with a root of multiplicity m, it can restore much faster convergence near the root.

But the multiplicity is not always known. That is why observing the behavior of the iteration matters.

 A first glimpse of chaotic iteration

Newton’s method is an iteration:

x_{n+1}=N(x_n),

where

N(x)=x-\frac{f(x)}{f'(x)}.

So Newton’s method is not only a root-finding formula. It is also a dynamical system: a rule that sends each point to a next point.

When the starting point is close to a simple root, the dynamics are friendly. The root attracts nearby iterates.

Far from a root, the dynamics can be complicated.

What can Newton’s method do far from a good root?

Near a simple root the iteration is friendly, but the same formula is a dynamical system. In your own words, what kinds of failure can occur from a bad starting point, and why should a safe workflow monitor iterates rather than trust the formula blindly?

The method can jump to another root, cycle, divide by zero, or behave unpredictably. Record residual and step size, and restart or switch methods if the residual does not drop.

asking for a real root that does not exist

Let

f(x)=x^2+1.

This function has no real root. Still, Newton’s formula produces an iteration.

Since

f'(x)=2x,

we get

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{x_n^2+1}{2x_n}.

Simplify:

x_{n+1} = \frac12\left(x_n-\frac1{x_n}\right).

This formula is defined whenever x_n\neq0.

Start with

x_0=1.

Then

x_1=\frac12(1-1)=0.

The next step is impossible because the formula would require division by 0.

Start instead with

x_0=1.01.

Then

x_1 = \frac12\left(1.01-\frac1{1.01}\right) \approx 0.0099505.

Now the next step contains 1/x_1, which is huge:

x_2 \approx \frac12(0.0099505-100.4975) \approx -50.2438.

A tiny change from 1 to 1.01 has produced a very different next story.

This example is not here because we need to solve x^2+1=0 over the real numbers. We already know there is no real solution.

It is here because it shows something deeper: an iteration can have a simple rule and complicated behavior.

 Computational warning

Newton’s method can be extremely fast near a good root. Far from a good root, it can move to a different root, enter a cycle, become undefined, or behave unpredictably.

Always monitor the iterates.

This warning does not make Newton’s method less valuable. It makes it more honest. In serious computation, a fast method and a safety check belong together.

 A safe Newton workflow

When using Newton’s method as a numerical algorithm, follow a disciplined workflow.

  1. Choose a function f whose root solves the original problem.

  2. Choose a starting value x_0 from a graph, table, physical estimate, or bracket.

  3. Compute

    x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}

    only when f'(x_n)\neq0.

  4. At each step, record x_n, f(x_n), and x_n-x_{n-1}.

  5. Stop only when the residual and step size are both small enough.

  6. If the method leaves the physical domain, cycles, or fails to reduce the residual, restart with a better initial guess or use a safer method such as bisection.

Newton’s method is a perfect example of this chapter’s theme. Calculus gives the idea: follow the tangent line. Computation adds the discipline: check whether the idea is working.

The same discipline belongs to numerical integration. We have formulas, but formulas become understanding only when we test them.

for some point c_n between x_n and r. So near a simple root,

|x_{n+1}-r|\approx C|x_n-r|^2.

This is quadratic convergence.

If the current error is about 10^{-3}, the next error may be about 10^{-6}. If the current error is about 10^{-6}, the next error may be about 10^{-12}.

That is why Newton’s method can suddenly gain many digits.

Practical lesson

When Newton’s method is converging well to a simple root, the number of correct digits often roughly doubles from one step to the next.

When it is not converging well, no stopping rule should pretend that it is.

 Multiple roots

Newton’s method is fastest near a simple root. A simple root is a root r for which

f(r)=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad f'(r)\neq0.

If

f'(r)=0,

then the graph meets the axis with zero slope; it may touch the axis or cross it flatly. Newton’s method may still converge, but the convergence often becomes much slower.

Why does a multiple root slow Newton’s method?

Near a simple root, Newton’s method often doubles the number of correct digits. Near a double root, the error may merely be cut in half each step. In your own words, what geometric difference between a simple crossing and a flat touch explains the change?

Quadratic convergence near a simple root uses a nonzero derivative there. At a root of finite multiplicity m>1, ordinary Newton iteration usually has only linear convergence, with leading error factor (m-1)/m. Such a root can touch or cross the axis.

 a double root

Let

f(x)=(x-1)^2.

The root is

r=1,

and it is a double root. More generally, a root has multiplicity m if, near the root, f(x)=(x-r)^m g(x), where m is a positive integer and g is continuous with g(r)\ne0. For the differentiations below we also assume g is sufficiently differentiable. Here m=2 and g=1. Since

f'(x)=2(x-1),

we have

f'(1)=0.

Newton’s method gives, for x_n\neq1,

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{(x_n-1)^2}{2(x_n-1)}.

Cancel one factor:

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{x_n-1}{2}.

So

x_{n+1}=\frac{x_n+1}{2}.

Starting from x_0=2, the iterates are:

a double root n x_n |x_n-1| 0 2.000000 1.000000 1 1.500000 0.500000 2 1.250000 0.250000 3 1.125000 0.125000 4 1.062500 0.062500

The error is cut in half each time. That is convergence, but it is not quadratic convergence. It is only linear convergence.

The same pattern appears for higher multiplicity. If

f(x)=(x-r)^m,

then

f'(x)=m(x-r)^{m-1}.

Newton’s method gives

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{(x_n-r)^m}{m(x_n-r)^{m-1}} = x_n-\frac{x_n-r}{m}.

Therefore

x_{n+1}-r = \left(1-\frac1m\right)(x_n-r).

So the error is multiplied by

1-\frac1m

each step.

For a double root, this factor is 1/2. For a triple root, it is 2/3. The larger the multiplicity, the slower the basic Newton iteration becomes.

 Multiple-root warning

If Newton’s method converges only linearly, one possible reason is that the root is multiple.

Repeatedly small residuals with slow-moving iterates may indicate a flat crossing or a flat touch near the axis.

If the multiplicity m is known, a modified Newton step can help:

x_{n+1}=x_n-m\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.

For

f(x)=(x-r)^m,

this modified method reaches the root in one step. For more general functions with a root of multiplicity m, it can restore much faster convergence near the root.

But the multiplicity is not always known. That is why observing the behavior of the iteration matters.

 A first glimpse of chaotic iteration

Newton’s method is an iteration:

x_{n+1}=N(x_n),

where

N(x)=x-\frac{f(x)}{f'(x)}.

So Newton’s method is not only a root-finding formula. It is also a dynamical system: a rule that sends each point to a next point.

When the starting point is close to a simple root, the dynamics are friendly. The root attracts nearby iterates.

Far from a root, the dynamics can be complicated.

What can Newton’s method do far from a good root?

Near a simple root the iteration is friendly, but the same formula is a dynamical system. In your own words, what kinds of failure can occur from a bad starting point, and why should a safe workflow monitor iterates rather than trust the formula blindly?

The method can jump to another root, cycle, divide by zero, or behave unpredictably. Record residual and step size, and restart or switch methods if the residual does not drop.

asking for a real root that does not exist

Let

f(x)=x^2+1.

This function has no real root. Still, Newton’s formula produces an iteration.

Since

f'(x)=2x,

we get

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{x_n^2+1}{2x_n}.

Simplify:

x_{n+1} = \frac12\left(x_n-\frac1{x_n}\right).

This formula is defined whenever x_n\neq0.

Start with

x_0=1.

Then

x_1=\frac12(1-1)=0.

The next step is impossible because the formula would require division by 0.

Start instead with

x_0=1.01.

Then

x_1 = \frac12\left(1.01-\frac1{1.01}\right) \approx 0.0099505.

Now the next step contains 1/x_1, which is huge:

x_2 \approx \frac12(0.0099505-100.4975) \approx -50.2438.

A tiny change from 1 to 1.01 has produced a very different next story.

This example is not here because we need to solve x^2+1=0 over the real numbers. We already know there is no real solution.

It is here because it shows something deeper: an iteration can have a simple rule and complicated behavior.

 Computational warning

Newton’s method can be extremely fast near a good root. Far from a good root, it can move to a different root, enter a cycle, become undefined, or behave unpredictably.

Always monitor the iterates.

This warning does not make Newton’s method less valuable. It makes it more honest. In serious computation, a fast method and a safety check belong together.

 A safe Newton workflow

When using Newton’s method as a numerical algorithm, follow a disciplined workflow.

  1. Choose a function f whose root solves the original problem.

  2. Choose a starting value x_0 from a graph, table, physical estimate, or bracket.

  3. Compute

    x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}

    only when f'(x_n)\neq0.

  4. At each step, record x_n, f(x_n), and x_n-x_{n-1}.

  5. Stop only when the residual and step size are both small enough.

  6. If the method leaves the physical domain, cycles, or fails to reduce the residual, restart with a better initial guess or use a safer method such as bisection.

Newton’s method is a perfect example of this chapter’s theme. Calculus gives the idea: follow the tangent line. Computation adds the discipline: check whether the idea is working.

The same discipline belongs to numerical integration. We have formulas, but formulas become understanding only when we test them.

Computing experiments

Numerical methods become real when we use them.

The purpose of these experiments is not only to produce decimals. A calculator can produce decimals. The purpose is to learn how numerical answers behave when the step size changes, when the function becomes less smooth, and when an algorithm is implemented by an actual person or machine.

Each experiment follows the same pattern:

\text{compute},\qquad \text{compare},\qquad \text{explain}.

 Experiment 1: approximate <m>\pi</m> by integration

The number \pi can be computed from an integral.

Since

\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x=\frac{1}{1+x^2},

we have

\int_0^1 \frac{1}{1+x^2}\,dx = \arctan(1)-\arctan(0) = \frac{\pi}{4}.

Therefore

\pi=4\int_0^1 \frac{1}{1+x^2}\,dx.

So we can approximate \pi by approximating the integral

\int_0^1 \frac{4}{1+x^2}\,dx.

Let

f(x)=\frac{4}{1+x^2}.

Use the midpoint rule, trapezoidal rule, and Simpson’s Rule on [0,1].

Experiment 1: approximate <m>\pi</m> by integration n M_n T_n S_n 4 3.146801 3.131176 3.141569 8 3.142895 3.138988 3.141593 16 3.141918 3.140942 3.141593 32 3.141674 3.141430 3.141593

The true value begins

\pi=3.1415926535\ldots.

Simpson’s Rule performs very well here because the integrand is smooth on the whole interval.

Project tasks

Complete the following.

  1. Reproduce the table above using a calculator, spreadsheet, or program.

  2. Add a column for the absolute error

    |\pi-\text{approximation}|.

  3. When n doubles, how does the error change for each rule?

  4. Which rule gives the best answer for the same n?

  5. Which rule gives the best answer for the same number of function evaluations?

  6. Use the Simpson error bound to explain why the Simpson values stabilize so quickly.

  7. Repeat the experiment using the quarter-circle formula

    \pi=4\int_0^1 \sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx.

    Which formula is numerically friendlier? Why might the endpoint x=1 cause trouble for error bounds?

The last question is important. Two different integrals can equal the same number, but they may not be equally good for computation.

 What is a computing experiment supposed to teach?

A calculator can already produce decimals. In your own words, why is the pattern compute–compare–explain the real purpose of these experiments, and what should change in your explanation when the integrand becomes less smooth?

Watch how answers behave when the step size changes and when the function is no longer smooth. Observed error should match the smoothness the theory assumes.

Experiment 2: estimate a probability from a density

A probability density is a function whose accumulated area gives probability.

The standard normal density is

\phi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}.

It is centered at 0, symmetric, and bell-shaped.

The probability that a standard normal quantity lies between -1 and 1 is

P(-1\le Z\le1) = \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}\,dx.

This integral has no elementary antiderivative. Numerical integration is the natural tool.

Using Simpson’s Rule gives:

Experiment 2: estimate a probability from a density n Simpson approximation to P(-1\le Z\le1) 4 0.683058 8 0.682711 16 0.682691 32 0.682690

A more refined computation gives approximately

P(-1\le Z\le1)\approx0.682689.

So about 68.27\% of the probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean.

Project tasks

Complete the following.

  1. Use the midpoint, trapezoidal, and Simpson rules to approximate

    \int_{-1}^{1}\phi(x)\,dx.

    Use n=4,8,16,32.

  2. Compare your answers with

    0.682689.

  3. Use symmetry to explain why

    \int_{-1}^{1}\phi(x)\,dx = 2\int_0^1\phi(x)\,dx.

  4. Estimate

    \int_{-2}^{2}\phi(x)\,dx.

    How much larger is this probability?

  5. Estimate

    \int_{-4}^{4}\phi(x)\,dx.

    Why is this close to 1, even though the true total probability is the improper integral

    \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(x)\,dx?

This experiment connects three ideas: numerical integration, improper integrals, and probability.

 Experiment 3: compare rules on smooth and rough functions

Error bounds have hypotheses. Simpson’s Rule needs a bounded fourth derivative for its standard error bound. The midpoint and trapezoidal bounds need a bounded second derivative.

Smooth functions reward high-order methods. Less smooth functions may not.

Compare these two integrals:

I_1=\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx

and

I_2=\int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,dx.

The first integrand is smooth. The second is continuous, but its derivatives become large near x=0. In fact,

\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\sqrt{x} = -\frac{1}{4x^{3/2}}

for x>0, which is unbounded near 0.

The exact value of I_2 is

I_2=\frac23.

A refined value of I_1 is

I_1\approx0.7468241328.

Using Simpson’s Rule gives the following comparison.

Experiment 3: compare rules on smooth and rough functions n Simpson for \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx Simpson for \int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,dx 4 0.746855 0.656526 8 0.746826 0.663079 16 0.746824 0.665398 32 0.746824 0.666218

Project tasks

Complete the following.

  1. For each integral, compute midpoint, trapezoidal, and Simpson approximations with n=4,8,16,32.

  2. Compute the absolute errors using

    \int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,dx=\frac23

    and the refined value

    \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx\approx0.7468241328.

  3. For each rule, estimate how the error changes when n doubles.

  4. Which rule benefits most from smoothness?

  5. Explain why the standard midpoint, trapezoidal, and Simpson error bounds are not directly available for \sqrt{x} on [0,1].

  6. Try splitting the square-root integral:

    \int_0^1\sqrt{x}\,dx = \int_0^{0.01}\sqrt{x}\,dx+\int_{0.01}^{1}\sqrt{x}\,dx.

    Compute the first part exactly, and approximate the second part numerically. Does this improve the result?

This experiment is a counterexample to a lazy belief:

\text{``A more powerful rule always gives its promised error behavior.''}

The rule’s error theorem has hypotheses. The function must meet them.

 Why is a small change between successive approximations not a proof?

One experiment keeps doubling n until two successive approximations differ by less than a tolerance. In your own words, why is that difference useful evidence, and why is it still not the same thing as an error bound?

Two close wrong answers can agree with each other. Stabilization supports confidence; a theorem or independent estimate supplies a guarantee.

Experiment 4: build a small numerical-integration program

A numerical method becomes clearer when you implement it yourself.

The goal is not to build a professional scientific library. The goal is to translate the formulas into an algorithm and test the algorithm on examples where you know what should happen.

Midpoint rule

M_n=\Delta x\sum_{i=1}^{n} f\left(a+\left(i-\frac12\right)\Delta x\right), \qquad \Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n}.

 Trapezoidal rule

T_n=\Delta x\left[ \frac12f(a)+f(a+\Delta x)+\cdots+f(a+(n-1)\Delta x)+\frac12f(b) \right].

 Simpson’s Rule

For even n,

S_n= \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0)+f(x_n) + 4\sum_{\substack{1\le i\le n-1\\i\text{ odd}}}f(x_i) + 2\sum_{\substack{2\le i\le n-2\\i\text{ even}}}f(x_i) \right].

 Pseudocode

The following language-neutral pseudocode gives the structure. Supply a function defined throughout [a,b], with a<b and a positive integer subdivision count n. Simpson’s Rule also requires even n.

function midpoint(f, a, b, n):
    if n is not a positive integer or a >= b:
        stop with message "Require positive integer n and a less than b"
    dx = (b-a)/n
    total = 0
    for i = 1 to n:
        xmid = a + (i - 0.5)*dx
        total = total + f(xmid)
    return dx*total

function trapezoid(f, a, b, n):
    if n is not a positive integer or a >= b:
        stop with message "Require positive integer n and a less than b"
    dx = (b-a)/n
    total = 0.5*f(a) + 0.5*f(b)
    for i = 1 to n-1:
        x = a + i*dx
        total = total + f(x)
    return dx*total

function simpson(f, a, b, n):
    if n is not a positive integer or a >= b:
        stop with message "Require positive integer n and a less than b"
    if n is odd:
        stop with message "Simpson's Rule requires even n"
    dx = (b-a)/n
    total = f(a) + f(b)
    for i = 1 to n-1:
        x = a + i*dx
        if i is odd:
            total = total + 4*f(x)
        else:
            total = total + 2*f(x)
    return dx*total/3
Testing your program

A numerical program should be tested on simple cases before it is trusted on hard ones.

Use these tests.

Testing your program test integral exact value what should happen \displaystyle \int_0^1 5\,dx 5 all three rules exact \displaystyle \int_0^1 x\,dx 1/2 all three rules exact \displaystyle \int_0^1 x^2\,dx 1/3 Simpson exact; midpoint and trapezoid converge \displaystyle \int_0^1 x^3\,dx 1/4 Simpson exact when n is even \displaystyle \int_0^1 \frac{4}{1+x^2}\,dx \pi approximates \pi

If your program fails one of these tests, do not move on. A mistake in the loop limits or weights can produce convincing-looking wrong numbers.

 Project tasks

Build the three functions above in a spreadsheet, calculator, or programming language. Then complete the following.

  1. Verify the five tests in the table.

  2. Use your program to approximate

    \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx

    with n=4,8,16,32,64.

  3. Use your program to approximate

    \int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,dx

    with the same values of n.

  4. Use your program to approximate

    \pi=4\int_0^1 \frac{1}{1+x^2}\,dx.

  5. Make a table of errors for each rule.

  6. For each rule, estimate the factor by which the error shrinks when n doubles.

  7. Write one paragraph explaining when Simpson’s Rule looks dramatically better, and one paragraph explaining when its advantage is less dramatic.

  8. Add a safety check to your Simpson function so that it refuses odd n.

  9. Add an optional feature that keeps doubling n until two successive approximations differ by less than a chosen tolerance.

What the project tests

A numerical answer should not arrive alone. It should come with checks:

\text{Does the algorithm reproduce simple exact cases?}

\text{Do the approximations stabilize as \(n\) increases?}

\text{Do the observed errors match the smoothness of the function?}

\text{Does the code enforce the hypotheses of the rule?}

 Why should a numerical program reproduce simple exact cases?

Before trusting a homemade integrator on a hard integral, we test it on cases whose exact values we know. In your own words, why is that a mathematical check and not just a programming convenience?

If the code cannot recover a line, a quadratic, or another exact case the rule should get right, later decimals have no authority.

A final computational habit

Numerical computation is not button pressing. It is mathematical experimentation with responsibility.

For every numerical answer, ask:

  1. What exact quantity is being approximated?

  2. Which rule or algorithm produced the approximation?

  3. What hypotheses does the rule need?

  4. What error estimate or stability evidence supports the answer?

  5. What simple test case confirms that the implementation is working?

This chapter began with numerical integration: approximating accumulated quantities. It then returned to numerical root-finding: approximating solutions of equations.

Both stories have the same lesson.

\text{An approximation is useful only when we understand its error.}

The next chapter carries this lesson into a new setting. A differential equation gives a law for a derivative, but the unknown function may not have a formula we can write down. Then we must do for functions what we have done for numbers and integrals: build approximations step by step, and ask how much to trust them.

What five questions should travel with every numerical answer?

The section ends with a computational habit: name the exact quantity, the rule, the hypotheses, the error evidence, and a test case. In your own words, why would omitting any one of those five leave the answer incomplete?

A decimal without a method, a method without hypotheses, or a result without a check is still only a number with arithmetic attached.

        total = total + f(x)
    return dx*total

    if n is not a positive integer or a >= b:
        stop with message "Require positive integer n and a less than b"
    if n is odd:
        stop with message "Simpson's Rule requires even n"
    dx = (b-a)/n
    total = f(a) + f(b)
    for i = 1 to n-1:
        x = a + i*dx
        if i is odd:
            total = total + 4*f(x)
        else:

Testing your program

A numerical program should be tested on simple cases before it is trusted on hard ones.

If your program fails one of these tests, do not move on. A mistake in the loop limits or weights can produce convincing-looking wrong numbers.

 Project tasks

Build the three functions above in a spreadsheet, calculator, or programming language. Then complete the following.

  1. Verify the five tests in the table.

  2. Use your program to approximate

    \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx

    with n=4,8,16,32,64.

  3. Use your program to approximate

    \int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,dx

    with the same values of n.

  4. Use your program to approximate

    \pi=4\int_0^1 \frac{1}{1+x^2}\,dx.

  5. Make a table of errors for each rule.

  6. For each rule, estimate the factor by which the error shrinks when n doubles.

  7. Write one paragraph explaining when Simpson’s Rule looks dramatically better, and one paragraph explaining when its advantage is less dramatic.

What the project tests

A numerical answer should not arrive alone. It should come with checks:

\text{Does the algorithm reproduce simple exact cases?}

\text{Do the approximations stabilize as \(n\) increases?}

\text{Do the observed errors match the smoothness of the function?}

\text{Does the code enforce the hypotheses of the rule?}

 Why should a numerical program reproduce simple exact cases?

Before trusting a homemade integrator on a hard integral, we test it on cases whose exact values we know. In your own words, why is that a mathematical check and not just a programming convenience?

If the code cannot recover a line, a quadratic, or another exact case the rule should get right, later decimals have no authority.

A final computational habit

Numerical computation is not button pressing. It is mathematical experimentation with responsibility.

For every numerical answer, ask:

  1. What exact quantity is being approximated?

  2. Which rule or algorithm produced the approximation?

  3. What hypotheses does the rule need?

  4. What error estimate or stability evidence supports the answer?

  5. What simple test case confirms that the implementation is working?

This chapter began with numerical integration: approximating accumulated quantities. It then returned to numerical root-finding: approximating solutions of equations.

Both stories have the same lesson.

\text{An approximation is useful only when we understand its error.}

The next chapter carries this lesson into a new setting. A differential equation gives a law for a derivative, but the unknown function may not have a formula we can write down. Then we must do for functions what we have done for numbers and integrals: build approximations step by step, and ask how much to trust them.

What five questions should travel with every numerical answer?

The section ends with a computational habit: name the exact quantity, the rule, the hypotheses, the error evidence, and a test case. In your own words, why would omitting any one of those five leave the answer incomplete?

A decimal without a method, a method without hypotheses, or a result without a check is still only a number with arithmetic attached.

Essential formulas

Divide [a,b] into n equal subintervals:

\Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n}, \qquad x_i=a+i\Delta x.

The midpoint of the ith subinterval [x_{i-1},x_i] is

\overline{x}_i=\frac{x_{i-1}+x_i}{2}.

Composite midpoint rule

M_n=\Delta x\sum_{i=1}^n f(\overline{x}_i).

Composite trapezoidal rule

T_n= \Delta x\left[ \frac12 f(x_0)+f(x_1)+f(x_2)+\cdots+f(x_{n-1})+\frac12 f(x_n) \right].

Composite Simpson’s Rule

For even n,

S_n= \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0)+f(x_n) + 4\sum_{\substack{1\le i\le n-1\\i\text{ odd}}} f(x_i) + 2\sum_{\substack{2\le i\le n-2\\i\text{ even}}} f(x_i) \right].

The weights are

1,\ 4,\ 2,\ 4,\ 2,\ \ldots,\ 4,\ 1.

 Error bounds

If f'' is continuous on [a,b] and

|f''(x)|\le K

on [a,b], then

\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-M_n\right| \le \frac{K(b-a)^3}{24n^2}

and

\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-T_n\right| \le \frac{K(b-a)^3}{12n^2}.

If f^{(4)} is continuous on [a,b], n is even, and

|f^{(4)}(x)|\le K

on [a,b], then

\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-S_n\right| \le \frac{K(b-a)^5}{180n^4}.

The powers of n are the main message:

\text{midpoint and trapezoidal errors shrink like } \frac1{n^2},

while

\text{Simpson errors shrink like } \frac1{n^4},

when the hypotheses are satisfied.

 Finite differences

For h>0,

D_h^+f(a)=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}

is the forward difference,

D_h^-f(a)=\frac{f(a)-f(a-h)}{h}

is the backward difference, and

D_h^0f(a)=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a-h)}{2h}

is the centered difference.

For smooth functions, we use the notation R(h)=O(h^p) to mean that there are constants C,\delta>0 such that |R(h)|\le C|h|^p whenever 0<|h|<\delta. With this notation,

D_h^+f(a)=f'(a)+O(h),

D_h^-f(a)=f'(a)+O(h),

and

D_h^0f(a)=f'(a)+O(h^2).

The centered difference is usually more accurate for the same step size, but no finite difference formula escapes roundoff error when h becomes too small.

To solve

f(x)=0,

Newton’s method uses

x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.

The residual is

|f(x_n)|.

The step size is

|x_n-x_{n-1}|.

A practical stopping rule should monitor both.

If r is a root and

|f'(x)|\ge m>0

between x_n and r, then

|x_n-r|\le \frac{|f(x_n)|}{m}.

Near a simple root, Newton’s method often has quadratic convergence:

|x_{n+1}-r|\approx C|x_n-r|^2.

Near a multiple root, the convergence may slow to linear.

Integration averages values over an interval. Differentiation subtracts nearby values and divides by a small step. In your own words, why do those two personalities lead to different computational warnings?

End-of-chapter habit

For every numerical answer, ask four questions:

\text{What exact quantity is being approximated?}

\text{Which method produced the approximation?}

\text{What assumptions does the method need?}

\text{What evidence or theorem supports the claimed accuracy?}

The next section turns this habit toward a new kind of problem. So far, numerical methods have mostly produced numbers: values of integrals, derivatives, and roots. But many laws of science ask for more than one number. They ask for a whole unknown function.

End-of-chapter habit

For every numerical answer, ask four questions:

\text{What exact quantity is being approximated?}
