Chapter review and discovery problems

This chapter began with a moving endpoint:

A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt.

That small change turned an integral from a number into a function. Then the Fundamental Theorem revealed the main hinge of calculus:

\text{accumulation and instantaneous change undo each other.}

Part I says that differentiating an accumulation gives back the integrand:

\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt=f(x).

Part II says that integrating a derivative gives net change:

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).

These are not two unrelated formulas. They are the same story read in opposite directions.

The most common mistakes come from forgetting one of these meanings. A definite integral is signed accumulation. An indefinite integral is a family of functions. Why are the two parts of the Fundamental Theorem the same story?

Part I differentiates an accumulation and recovers the integrand. Part II integrates a derivative and recovers net change. In your own words, why are these not two unrelated formulas, but the same hinge of calculus read in opposite directions?

One direction starts with a rate and builds a running total. The other starts with a running total and reads its rate. Each undoes the other.

A rate tells how a quantity changes. The Fundamental Theorem tells how to rebuild the quantity from the rate, once one starting value is known.

Q(x)=Q(a)+\int_a^x Q'(t)\,dt.

This project reconstructs a quantity from both an exact rate formula and sampled rate data.

Part 1: exact reconstruction

A tank starts with

Q(0)=12

liters of water. Water flows into the tank at the rate

R(t)=2+\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{4}\right)

liters per minute, for

0\le t\le 8.

Since R(t)=Q'(t), the amount of water in the tank at time x is

Q(x)=12+\int_0^x R(t)\,dt.

  1. Write

    Q(x)=12+\int_0^x \left( 2+\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{4}\right) \right)\,dt.

  2. Evaluate the integral to find an explicit formula for Q(x).

  3. Find Q(4) and Q(8).

  4. Differentiate your formula for Q(x). Check that

    Q'(x)=R(x).

  5. The rate R(t) increases on some subintervals and decreases on others. Does Q(t) ever decrease on [0,8]? Explain using the sign of R(t).

Part 2: reconstruction from data

Now suppose the rate is measured once per minute instead of given by a formula.

\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc} t\text{ (minutes)} \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \amp 3 \amp 4 \amp 5 \amp 6 \amp 7 \amp 8\\ \hline R(t)\text{ (liters/minute)} \amp 2.0 \amp 2.8 \amp 3.4 \amp 3.0 \amp 2.2 \amp 1.6 \amp 1.2 \amp 0.8 \amp 0.5 \end{array}

Again assume

Q(0)=12.

Use trapezoids to estimate the accumulated water. For example, from t=0 to t=1,

\Delta Q \approx \frac12\bigl(R(0)+R(1)\bigr)(1) = \frac12(2.0+2.8) = 2.4.

So

Q(1)\approx 12+2.4=14.4.

Project tasks

  1. Complete the cumulative trapezoid table.

    \begin{array}{c|c|c} t \amp \text{estimated accumulated water from }0\text{ to }t \amp \text{estimated }Q(t)\\ \hline 0 \amp 0 \amp 12\\ 1 \amp 2.4 \amp 14.4\\ 2 \amp \amp\\ 3 \amp \amp\\ 4 \amp \amp\\ 5 \amp \amp\\ 6 \amp \amp\\ 7 \amp \amp\\ 8 \amp \amp \end{array}

  2. Estimate the total amount of water added during the 8 minutes.

  3. Estimate Q(8).

  4. Sketch the reconstructed graph of Q(t). It should be increasing, but its slope should change.

  5. At what time does the rate R(t) appear largest? What does that say about the graph of Q(t)?

  6. Does the maximum of R(t) correspond to a maximum of Q(t)? Explain.

  7. Suppose the tank can hold 30 liters. Based on your reconstruction, does it overflow by t=8?

  8. What additional measurements would make the reconstruction more reliable?

What the project tests

A rate graph is not the same thing as the quantity graph. The rate tells the slope of the quantity. The quantity is reconstructed by accumulation.

 Where this points

The Fundamental Theorem has made integration computable.

Before this chapter, a definite integral was a limit of sums:

\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.

Now, when we can find an antiderivative,

\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).

That changes what we can do.

The next chapter asks what integrals can measure. Area under a curve was only the first picture. The same accumulation idea will measure many quantities:

\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{quantity} \amp \textbf{small piece} \amp \textbf{integral}\\ \hline \text{area between curves} \amp \text{height difference}\cdot dx \amp \displaystyle\int (\text{top}-\text{bottom})\,dx\\ \text{volume by slices} \amp \text{cross-sectional area}\cdot dx \amp \displaystyle\int A(x)\,dx\\ \text{mass of a rod} \amp \text{density}\cdot dx \amp \displaystyle\int \rho(x)\,dx\\ \text{work by a variable force} \amp \text{force}\cdot dx \amp \displaystyle\int F(x)\,dx\\ \text{average value} \amp \text{accumulated height divided by length} \amp \displaystyle \frac1{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx \end{array}

The pattern will not change:

\text{identify a small piece, add all the pieces, and take the limit.}

What changes is the shape of the small piece. That is where applications of the integral begin.

What must you carry along when you change variables or reverse direction?

A substitution changes the integrand, and reversing an interval changes the sign. In your own words, why are orientation and the new limits part of the meaning of the integral rather than extra bookkeeping?

The small piece being added is height times oriented step. Changing the coordinate or the direction changes that step, so the description of the accumulation must change with it.

Related rates

Some quantities change alone. Many do not.

If a balloon is being inflated, its radius changes, its surface area changes, and its volume changes. These quantities are linked. Knowing how fast one changes can tell us how fast another changes.

That is the idea of a related rates problem.

\text{an equation relating quantities} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{an equation relating their rates}.

The bridge is the chain rule.

 Quantities changing together

A spherical balloon has radius r, surface area S, and volume V. They satisfy

S=4\pi r^2

and

V=\frac43\pi r^3.

If the balloon is growing, then r, S, and V all depend on time. We should write

r=r(t),\qquad S=S(t),\qquad V=V(t).

The formulas become

S(t)=4\pi \bigl(r(t)\bigr)^2

and

V(t)=\frac43\pi \bigl(r(t)\bigr)^3.

Usually we do not write every t. But we must remember it is there.

Why does an equation relating quantities become an equation relating rates?

If two quantities are linked by a formula that remains true as time passes, the chain rule turns that formula into a relation among derivatives. In your own words, why is that the idea of a related rates problem, and why must we remember that each quantity is secretly a function of time?

An equation relating quantities implies an equation relating their rates. The bridge is the chain rule, not a new kind of derivative.

Example

Air is pumped into a spherical balloon at the rate

\frac{dV}{dt}=24\pi

cubic centimeters per second. How fast is the radius increasing when

r=3

centimeters?

The volume and radius are related by

V=\frac43\pi r^3.

Differentiate both sides with respect to t. Since r depends on t, the chain rule gives

\frac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^2\frac{dr}{dt}.

Now substitute the known values:

24\pi=4\pi(3)^2\frac{dr}{dt}.

Thus

24\pi=36\pi\frac{dr}{dt},

so

\frac{dr}{dt}=\frac23

centimeters per second.

The radius is increasing at 2/3 centimeter per second at that instant.

 What changed?

The volume was given as a rate. The radius was asked for as a rate. The formula

V=\frac43\pi r^3

connected the quantities, and differentiating connected the rates.

Notice that the radius is not always increasing at 2/3 centimeter per second. The equation

\frac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2\frac{dr}{dt}

shows that, if \frac{dV}{dt} stays constant, then \frac{dr}{dt} gets smaller as r gets larger. The same amount of new air is spread over a larger sphere.

 Differentiating a relation with respect to time

The balloon example used a direct formula. Other related rates problems use an implicit relation.

Suppose two quantities x and y are connected by

x^2+y^2=100.

If both quantities depend on time, then we really have

\bigl(x(t)\bigr)^2+\bigl(y(t)\bigr)^2=100.

Differentiate with respect to t:

2x\frac{dx}{dt}+2y\frac{dy}{dt}=0.

That equation relates the rates \frac{dx}{dt} and \frac{dy}{dt}.

Related rates workflow

\begin{array}{ll} \text{1.} \amp \text{Draw a picture, if the problem is geometric.}\\ \text{2.} \amp \text{Name the changing quantities.}\\ \text{3.} \amp \text{Write an equation relating the quantities.}\\ \text{4.} \amp \text{Differentiate the relation with respect to time.}\\ \text{5.} \amp \text{Substitute the values known at the instant in question.}\\ \text{6.} \amp \text{Solve for the desired rate and check units and sign.} \end{array}

The order matters. First differentiate. Then substitute the values for the particular instant.

If we substitute too early, the changing quantities disappear.

For example, if x=6 and y=8, the equation

x^2+y^2=100

becomes

6^2+8^2=100.

Differentiating that gives only

0=0,

which says nothing about the rates. The numbers 6 and 8 describe one instant. The variables x and y describe the changing situation.

Why must we differentiate before substituting the values of one instant?

The numbers x=6 and y=8 describe one snapshot of x^2+y^2=100. Differentiating after substituting them yields only 0=0. In your own words, why does that destroy the rate information, and what is the difference between the changing variables and the numbers that describe one moment?

First differentiate the relation that remains true over time. Then plug in the values known at the instant in question.

Geometry problems: ladders, shadows, cones

Geometry supplies many clean related rates problems because lengths, areas, and volumes are linked by familiar formulas.

a sliding ladder

A 10-foot ladder leans against a wall. The bottom of the ladder slides away from the wall at

2\text{ ft/s}.

How fast is the top of the ladder sliding down the wall when the bottom is 6 feet from the wall?

Let

x(t)=\text{distance from the wall to the bottom of the ladder},

and

y(t)=\text{height of the top of the ladder}.

The ladder has fixed length 10, so

x^2+y^2=10^2=100.

We are given

\frac{dx}{dt}=2.

We want \frac{dy}{dt} when x=6. At that instant,

6^2+y^2=100,

so

y^2=64, \qquad y=8.

Differentiate the relation

x^2+y^2=100

with respect to time:

2x\frac{dx}{dt}+2y\frac{dy}{dt}=0.

Now substitute

x=6,\qquad y=8,\qquad \frac{dx}{dt}=2.

We get

2(6)(2)+2(8)\frac{dy}{dt}=0.

Thus

24+16\frac{dy}{dt}=0,

so

\frac{dy}{dt}=-\frac32

feet per second.

The negative sign matters. It says the height is decreasing. The top of the ladder is sliding downward at 3/2 feet per second.

 a growing shadow

A 6-foot person walks away from a 15-foot lamp post at

4\text{ ft/s}.

How fast is the tip of the person’s shadow moving?

Let

x(t)=\text{distance from the lamp post to the person},

s(t)=\text{length of the shadow},

and

p(t)=x(t)+s(t)=\text{distance from the lamp post to the tip of the shadow}.

We are given

\frac{dx}{dt}=4.

The similar triangles give

\frac{15}{x+s}=\frac{6}{s}.

Cross-multiply:

15s=6(x+s).

So

15s=6x+6s,

hence

9s=6x,

and therefore

s=\frac23x.

Differentiate:

\frac{ds}{dt}=\frac23\frac{dx}{dt}.

Since \frac{dx}{dt}=4,

\frac{ds}{dt}=\frac23(4)=\frac83.

The tip of the shadow is at

p=x+s.

Therefore

\frac{dp}{dt} = \frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{ds}{dt} = 4+\frac83 = \frac{20}{3}

feet per second.

The tip of the shadow moves faster than the person because the shadow is stretching while the person moves.

 water in a cone

An inverted cone has height 12 feet and radius 4 feet at the top. Water flows into the cone at

2\text{ ft}^3/\text{min}.

How fast is the water level rising when the water height is 6 feet?

Let

h(t)=\text{height of the water},

r(t)=\text{radius of the water surface},

and

V(t)=\text{volume of water}.

The volume of a cone is

V=\frac13\pi r^2h.

But this formula contains two changing variables, r and h. We need one relation between them.

The water cone is similar to the full tank cone, so

\frac{r}{h}=\frac{4}{12}=\frac13.

Thus

r=\frac{h}{3}.

Substitute into the volume formula:

V = \frac13\pi\left(\frac{h}{3}\right)^2h = \frac{\pi}{27}h^3.

Differentiate with respect to time:

\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{\pi}{9}h^2\frac{dh}{dt}.

Now use

\frac{dV}{dt}=2, \qquad h=6.

Then

2= \frac{\pi}{9}(6)^2\frac{dh}{dt} = 4\pi\frac{dh}{dt}.

Therefore

\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{1}{2\pi}

feet per minute.

 Units as a guardrail

Related rates problems are easy to damage by a small algebra mistake. Units help catch many of those mistakes.

In the balloon problem,

\frac{dV}{dt}

had units

\text{cm}^3/\text{s},

while

4\pi r^2\frac{dr}{dt}

had units

\text{cm}^2\cdot \frac{\text{cm}}{\text{s}} = \text{cm}^3/\text{s}.

The units match.

In the ladder problem,

2x\frac{dx}{dt}+2y\frac{dy}{dt}=0.

Both terms have units

\text{ft}\cdot\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}} = \text{ft}^2/\text{s}.

The units match because we differentiated an equation whose terms had units of square feet.

Signs are also part of the meaning.

\frac{dx}{dt}>0

means x is increasing. In the ladder problem,

\frac{dy}{dt}<0

means y is decreasing. If a result says the ladder top is moving “down” but gives a positive \frac{dy}{dt}, something has been mislabeled or misread.

A rate is not just a number

A rate carries units and direction. Before trusting an answer, ask:

\text{Does the sign make sense?}

\text{Do the units make sense?}

\text{Was the equation differentiated before instant-specific values were substituted?}

Related rates tell how quantities change together. The next problem is different. Instead of asking how fast something changes, we ask which choice is best.

Why is a rate not just a number?

A related-rates answer carries units and a sign. In your own words, why do matching units catch many algebra mistakes, and why does a positive \frac{dy}{dt} for a ladder sliding down the wall mean the labels, not the calculus, have gone wrong?

Before trusting an answer, ask whether the sign makes sense and whether the units make sense. A rate remembers direction as well as size.

Optimization problems

The previous chapter taught us how to find high and low points of a function. Optimization turns that skill into a method for solving word problems.

A real question rarely arrives as

\text{maximize } f(x).

It arrives as a sentence:

\text{Build the largest box from this sheet of cardboard.}

\text{Use the least metal for this can.}

\text{Enclose the most area with this much fence.}

The first task is not calculus. The first task is translation.

\text{situation} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{function} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{derivative} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{decision}.

 Translating a word problem into a function

A farmer has 200 meters of fencing and wants to enclose a rectangular field along a straight river. The river forms one side of the rectangle, so fencing is needed only for the other three sides.

What dimensions give the largest area?

Let

x=\text{the width perpendicular to the river}

and

y=\text{the length parallel to the river}.

The fencing is used for two widths and one length:

2x+y=200.

The area is

A=xy.

We want to maximize A, but right now A uses two variables. Use the constraint

2x+y=200

to solve for y:

y=200-2x.

Then

A(x)=x(200-2x)=200x-2x^2.

Now the problem is a one-variable calculus problem.

The physical domain is

0\le x\le 100.

If x=0, the rectangle has no width. If x=100, then y=0. Both give area 0. For 0<x<100, the rectangle has positive area.

Differentiate:

A'(x)=200-4x.

Set the derivative equal to 0:

200-4x=0.

Thus

x=50.

Then

y=200-2(50)=100.

Since A''(x)=-4<0, the area is concave down; also A(0)=A(100)=0 and A(50)=5000. Thus the absolute maximum area occurs when

x=50,\qquad y=100.

The farmer should build a field 50 meters wide and 100 meters long.

The optimization translation

\begin{array}{ll} \text{objective} \amp \text{the quantity to maximize or minimize}\\ \text{constraint} \amp \text{the condition that limits the choices}\\ \text{domain} \amp \text{the physically meaningful values of the variable} \end{array}

In the fencing problem, the objective was area, the constraint was the amount of fencing, and the domain came from requiring nonnegative side lengths.

Why is the first task of optimization translation, not calculus?

A real question arrives as a sentence about a box, a fence, or a can, not as maximize f(x). In your own words, why must we first name the objective, the constraint, and the domain, and why is that translation already most of the mathematics?

The derivative can only act on a function. Until the situation has been written as a function of one variable, there is nothing to differentiate.

Constraints in one variable

Many optimization problems begin with several quantities. The constraint is what lets us reduce to one variable.

The general pattern is:

\text{objective } Q=Q(x,y)

together with

\text{constraint relating }x\text{ and }y.

Use the constraint to write

y=\text{a formula in }x.

Then

Q=Q(x)

becomes a one-variable function.

Optimization workflow

\begin{array}{ll} \text{1.} \amp \text{Identify the quantity to optimize.}\\ \text{2.} \amp \text{Name the variables.}\\ \text{3.} \amp \text{Write the objective function.}\\ \text{4.} \amp \text{Write the constraint.}\\ \text{5.} \amp \text{Use the constraint to get one variable.}\\ \text{6.} \amp \text{Find the physical domain.}\\ \text{7.} \amp \text{Use derivatives and endpoint checks.}\\ \text{8.} \amp \text{Translate the answer back into the problem.} \end{array}

The domain is not optional. It is part of the model.

A critical number outside the physical domain is not a possible solution. An endpoint inside the domain may be the best solution.

Why does a constraint reduce an optimization problem to one variable?

Many problems begin with two quantities linked by a restriction, such as a fixed amount of fencing. In your own words, why do we use that restriction to eliminate a variable, and what would go wrong if we differentiated an objective that still contained two independent inputs?

The constraint is what makes the choices depend on one another. After substituting, the objective becomes an ordinary one-variable function.

Geometry: boxes, fences, cans, and light paths

Geometry problems are good training because the constraints are visible.

the largest open box from a square sheet

A square sheet of cardboard is 12 inches by 12 inches. Equal squares of side length x are cut from the four corners. The sides are folded up to make an open box.

After cutting, the base has side length

12-2x.

The height is

x.

So the volume is

V(x)=x(12-2x)^2.

The physical domain is

0\le x\le 6.

At x=0, no box is formed. At x=6, the base has side length 0. Both endpoints give volume 0.

V(x)=x(12-2x)^2.

Using the product and chain rules,

Factor:

V'(x) = (12-2x)\bigl((12-2x)-4x\bigr).

Thus

V'(x) = (12-2x)(12-6x).

x=6 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=2.

The number x=6 is an endpoint. The interior critical number is x=2.

Check the volumes:

V(0)=0,

V(2)=2(12-4)^2=2(8)^2=128,

V(6)=0.

Therefore the largest volume occurs at

x=2

inches. The box dimensions are

8\text{ in}\times 8\text{ in}\times 2\text{ in}.

A closed cylindrical can must hold volume V_0. What shape uses the least surface area?

r=\text{radius}

and

h=\text{height}.

The volume constraint is

\pi r^2h=V_0.

The surface area of a closed cylinder is

S=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh.

Use the constraint to solve for h:

Thus

0\le x\le L.

Optimization problems are not finished when we find a critical number.

A critical number is a candidate. It may give a maximum, a minimum, neither, or it may not be physically allowed.

q=20.

A formula alone does not know what choices are possible. The domain tells the formula which choices are allowed.

Newton’s method

Linear approximation estimates a function by a line.

Newton’s method uses that line to solve an equation.

Suppose we want to solve

f(x)=0.

A solution is an input where the graph of f meets the x-axis; it may cross the axis or merely touch it. If we already have a nearby guess x_0, the tangent line at x_0 is often easier to use than the curve itself. The tangent line crosses the x-axis at a new guess.

Then we do it again.

 Tangent lines as root finders

We begin with a familiar problem:

\sqrt2.

Instead of asking directly for \sqrt2, solve

x^2=2.

Equivalently, find a zero of

f(x)=x^2-2.

A reasonable first guess is

x_0=1.5.

At this point,

f(1.5)=1.5^2-2=2.25-2=0.25,

and

f'(x)=2x,

so

f'(1.5)=3.

The tangent line at x_0=1.5 is

y=f(x_0)+f'(x_0)(x-x_0).

Thus

y=0.25+3(x-1.5).

Newton’s idea is to follow this tangent line down to the x-axis. Set y=0:

0=0.25+3(x-1.5).

Then

3(x-1.5)=-0.25,

so

x-1.5=-\frac{0.25}{3}=-\frac{1}{12}.

Therefore

x=1.5-\frac{1}{12} = \frac32-\frac{1}{12} = \frac{17}{12} \approx1.4166667.

This is already closer to \sqrt2 than 1.5.

Now repeat the same process using

x_1=\frac{17}{12}.

Newton’s next approximation is

x_2 = \frac{577}{408} \approx 1.414215686.

Already the first five decimal places are correct.

Why can a tangent line be used to hunt for a root?

Newton’s method replaces the curve y=f(x) by its tangent line and solves the linear equation instead. In your own words, why should the x-intercept of that tangent be a better guess for a nearby root, and why do we then repeat the process?

Near a simple root, the graph looks like a line. Solving the linear problem is easy, and each new intercept becomes the next expansion point.

The iteration formula

The same tangent-line calculation works for any differentiable function.

Suppose x_n is the current guess for a zero of f. The tangent line at x_n is

y=f(x_n)+f'(x_n)(x-x_n).

Set y=0 to find where this tangent line crosses the x-axis:

0=f(x_n)+f'(x_n)(x-x_n).

Solve for x:

f'(x_n)(x-x_n)=-f(x_n),

so

x-x_n=-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.

Therefore

x=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.

This is the next guess.

Newton’s method

To solve

f(x)=0,

start with an initial guess x_0. Then define

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}

as long as f'(x_n)\neq0.

Newton’s method is a repeated linear approximation. At each step, we throw away the curve for a moment and use its tangent line.

square roots

For

f(x)=x^2-2,

Newton’s method gives

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{x_n^2-2}{2x_n}.

Simplify:

x_{n+1} = \frac{2x_n^2-(x_n^2-2)}{2x_n} = \frac{x_n^2+2}{2x_n}.

So

x_{n+1} = \frac12\left(x_n+\frac{2}{x_n}\right).

Starting with

x_0=1.5,

we get

\begin{array}{c|c} n \amp x_n\\ \hline 0 \amp 1.500000000\\ 1 \amp 1.416666667\\ 2 \amp 1.414215686\\ 3 \amp 1.414213562\\ 4 \amp 1.414213562 \end{array}

The numbers settle quickly.

 solving <m>\cos x=x</m>

The equation

\cos x=x

cannot be solved by ordinary algebra. Write it as

f(x)=\cos x-x=0.

Then

f'(x)=-\sin x-1.

Newton’s method gives

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{\cos x_n-x_n}{-\sin x_n-1}.

Equivalently,

x_{n+1} = x_n+\frac{\cos x_n-x_n}{\sin x_n+1}.

Starting with

x_0=1,

and using radians, we get

\begin{array}{c|c} n \amp x_n\\ \hline 0 \amp 1.000000000\\ 1 \amp 0.750363868\\ 2 \amp 0.739112891\\ 3 \amp 0.739085133\\ 4 \amp 0.739085133 \end{array}

So the solution is approximately

x\approx0.739085133.

The method works well here because the starting guess is reasonable and the tangent lines point toward the root.

 Convergence when the starting point is good

Newton’s method can be fast. But it is not magic. It is a local method, just like linear approximation.

The method works best when:

\begin{array}{ll} \text{1.} \amp \text{the starting guess is close to the root,}\\ \text{2.} \amp \text{the function is smooth near the root,}\\ \text{3.} \amp \text{the derivative at the root is not zero.} \end{array}

The third condition means the graph crosses the axis with a real slope, not with a flat touch.

Newton convergence principle

Suppose f has a zero r, so

f(r)=0.

If f has two continuous derivatives near r, and

f'(r)\neq0,

then Newton’s method converges to r whenever the starting guess is close enough to r.

The phrase “close enough” is important. The theorem does not say every starting point works. It says that near a good root, Newton’s method behaves well.

Idea of the proof

Let x_n be close to the root r. We can obtain a quadratic error formula using Rolle’s Theorem twice, without assuming a later Taylor formula. Choose C so that F(t)=f(t)-f(x_n)-f'(x_n)(t-x_n)-C(t-x_n)^2 satisfies F(r)=0. We also have F(x_n)=F'(x_n)=0. Rolle’s Theorem first gives a zero of F' between x_n and r, and then a zero of F'' between that point and x_n. Thus C=f''(c_n)/2 for a point c_n between x_n and r. (If x_n=r, the root has already been found.) Therefore

f(r) = f(x_n)+f'(x_n)(r-x_n) + \frac12 f''(c_n)(r-x_n)^2

for some point c_n between x_n and r.

Since

f(r)=0,

we have

0 = f(x_n)+f'(x_n)(r-x_n) + \frac12 f''(c_n)(r-x_n)^2.

Solve this for the Newton correction. Because

x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)},

one obtains

x_{n+1}-r = \frac{f''(c_n)}{2f'(x_n)}(r-x_n)^2.

So the next error is roughly a constant times the square of the previous error:

|x_{n+1}-r|\approx C|x_n-r|^2.

This is why Newton’s method can suddenly become very accurate. If an error is about 10^{-3}, its square is 10^{-6}. If an error is about 10^{-6}, its square is 10^{-12}.

This behavior is called quadratic convergence. To make the convergence claim precise, continuity bounds |f''| above and |f'| away from zero in a small interval about r. Hence |x_{n+1}-r|\le C|x_n-r|^2 there for a fixed C. Choose the starting error small enough that C|x_0-r|\le1/2 and the starting point lies in that interval. Each next error is at most half the previous one, so all iterates remain in the interval and converge to r.

The reason Newton can be fast

Near a simple root, Newton’s method does not merely reduce the error. It roughly squares the error.

 Why is Newton’s method a local method?

The method is fast when the starting guess is close, the function is smooth, and f' is nonzero at the root. In your own words, why does close enough matter, and why does a flat touch at the root (a multiple root) slow or spoil the process?

Linear approximation is local, so Newton’s method is local. Near a simple root the error is roughly squared at each step; a horizontal tangent at the root is a different story.

Failure modes: cycles and bad tangents

Newton’s method depends on tangent lines. A bad tangent can send the method to the wrong place, make it cycle, or stop it entirely.

The hypotheses are not decoration.

Failure mode 1: a horizontal tangent

Newton’s formula

x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}

requires

f'(x_n)\neq0.

If

f'(x_n)=0,

then the tangent line is horizontal. It does not cross the x-axis in the way the method needs.

For example, let

f(x)=x^3-x.

This function has roots

-1,\quad 0,\quad 1.

But

f'(x)=3x^2-1.

At

x_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt3},

we have

f'(x_0)=0.

The Newton formula cannot even produce x_1. The function has roots, but this starting point gives a horizontal tangent.

 Failure mode 2: a cycle

Let

f(x)=x^3-2x+2.

Then

f'(x)=3x^2-2.

Start Newton’s method at

x_0=0.

We get

x_1 = 0-\frac{f(0)}{f'(0)} = 0-\frac{2}{-2} = 1.

Now compute the next step:

x_2 = 1-\frac{f(1)}{f'(1)} = 1-\frac{1}{1} = 0.

So the method repeats:

0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ldots

It never reaches a root.

But the function does have a real root. Since

f(-2)=-8+4+2=-2

and

f(-1)=-1+2+2=3,

the Intermediate Value Theorem tells us that there is a root between -2 and -1.

Newton’s method failed because the tangent lines from 0 and 1 point back to each other.

 Failure mode 3: a multiple root

If a root r satisfies

f'(r)=0,

then Newton’s method may still converge, but often more slowly.

For example,

f(x)=(x-1)^2

has a double root at

x=1.

Newton’s method gives

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{(x_n-1)^2}{2(x_n-1)} = x_n-\frac{x_n-1}{2} = \frac{x_n+1}{2},

as long as x_n\neq1.

This moves halfway toward 1 each time. It converges, but the error is cut in half rather than squared. The fast convergence is lost.

 Why can a bad tangent send Newton’s method astray?

Newton’s method

Linear approximation estimates a function by a line.

Newton’s method uses that line to solve an equation.

Suppose we want to solve

f(x)=0.

A solution is an input where the graph of f meets the x-axis; it may cross the axis or merely touch it. If we already have a nearby guess x_0, the tangent line at x_0 is often easier to use than the curve itself. The tangent line crosses the x-axis at a new guess.

Then we do it again.

 Tangent lines as root finders

We begin with a familiar problem:

\sqrt2.

Instead of asking directly for \sqrt2, solve

x^2=2.

Equivalently, find a zero of

f(x)=x^2-2.

A reasonable first guess is

x_0=1.5.

At this point,

f(1.5)=1.5^2-2=2.25-2=0.25,

and

f'(x)=2x,

so

f'(1.5)=3.

The tangent line at x_0=1.5 is

y=f(x_0)+f'(x_0)(x-x_0).

Thus

y=0.25+3(x-1.5).

Newton’s idea is to follow this tangent line down to the x-axis. Set y=0:

0=0.25+3(x-1.5).

Then

3(x-1.5)=-0.25,

so

x-1.5=-\frac{0.25}{3}=-\frac{1}{12}.

Therefore

x=1.5-\frac{1}{12} = \frac32-\frac{1}{12} = \frac{17}{12} \approx1.4166667.

This is already closer to \sqrt2 than 1.5.

Now repeat the same process using

x_1=\frac{17}{12}.

Newton’s next approximation is

x_2 = \frac{577}{408} \approx 1.414215686.

Already the first five decimal places are correct.

Why can a tangent line be used to hunt for a root?

Newton’s method replaces the curve y=f(x) by its tangent line and solves the linear equation instead. In your own words, why should the x-intercept of that tangent be a better guess for a nearby root, and why do we then repeat the process?

Near a simple root, the graph looks like a line. Solving the linear problem is easy, and each new intercept becomes the next expansion point.

The iteration formula

The same tangent-line calculation works for any differentiable function.

Suppose x_n is the current guess for a zero of f. The tangent line at x_n is

y=f(x_n)+f'(x_n)(x-x_n).

Set y=0 to find where this tangent line crosses the x-axis:

0=f(x_n)+f'(x_n)(x-x_n).

Solve for x:

f'(x_n)(x-x_n)=-f(x_n),

so

x-x_n=-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.

Therefore

x=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.

This is the next guess.

Newton’s method

To solve

f(x)=0,

start with an initial guess x_0. Then define

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}

as long as f'(x_n)\neq0.

Newton’s method is a repeated linear approximation. At each step, we throw away the curve for a moment and use its tangent line.

square roots

For

f(x)=x^2-2,

Newton’s method gives

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{x_n^2-2}{2x_n}.

Simplify:

x_{n+1} = \frac{2x_n^2-(x_n^2-2)}{2x_n} = \frac{x_n^2+2}{2x_n}.

So

x_{n+1} = \frac12\left(x_n+\frac{2}{x_n}\right).

Starting with

x_0=1.5,

we get

\begin{array}{c|c} n \amp x_n\\ \hline 0 \amp 1.500000000\\ 1 \amp 1.416666667\\ 2 \amp 1.414215686\\ 3 \amp 1.414213562\\ 4 \amp 1.414213562 \end{array}

The numbers settle quickly.

 solving <m>\cos x=x</m>

The equation

\cos x=x

cannot be solved by ordinary algebra. Write it as

f(x)=\cos x-x=0.

Then

f'(x)=-\sin x-1.

Newton’s method gives

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{\cos x_n-x_n}{-\sin x_n-1}.

Equivalently,

x_{n+1} = x_n+\frac{\cos x_n-x_n}{\sin x_n+1}.

Starting with

x_0=1,

and using radians, we get

\begin{array}{c|c} n \amp x_n\\ \hline 0 \amp 1.000000000\\ 1 \amp 0.750363868\\ 2 \amp 0.739112891\\ 3 \amp 0.739085133\\ 4 \amp 0.739085133 \end{array}

So the solution is approximately

x\approx0.739085133.

The method works well here because the starting guess is reasonable and the tangent lines point toward the root.

 Convergence when the starting point is good

Newton’s method can be fast. But it is not magic. It is a local method, just like linear approximation.

The method works best when:

1.the starting guess is close to the root,2.the function is smooth near the root,3.the derivative at the root is not zero.

The third condition means the graph crosses the axis with a real slope, not with a flat touch.

Newton convergence principle

Suppose f has a zero r, so

f(r)=0.

If f has two continuous derivatives near r, and

f'(r)\neq0,

then Newton’s method converges to r whenever the starting guess is close enough to r.

The phrase “close enough” is important. The theorem does not say every starting point works. It says that near a good root, Newton’s method behaves well.

Idea of the proof

Let x_n be close to the root r. We can obtain a quadratic error formula using Rolle’s Theorem twice, without assuming a later Taylor formula. Choose C so that F(t)=f(t)-f(x_n)-f'(x_n)(t-x_n)-C(t-x_n)^2 satisfies F(r)=0. We also have F(x_n)=F'(x_n)=0. Rolle’s Theorem first gives a zero of F' between x_n and r, and then a zero of F'' between that point and x_n. Thus C=f''(c_n)/2 for a point c_n between x_n and r. (If x_n=r, the root has already been found.) Therefore

f(r) = f(x_n)+f'(x_n)(r-x_n) + \frac12 f''(c_n)(r-x_n)^2

for some point c_n between x_n and r.

Since

f(r)=0,

we have

0 = f(x_n)+f'(x_n)(r-x_n) + \frac12 f''(c_n)(r-x_n)^2.

Solve this for the Newton correction. Because

x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)},

one obtains

x_{n+1}-r = \frac{f''(c_n)}{2f'(x_n)}(r-x_n)^2.

So the next error is roughly a constant times the square of the previous error:

|x_{n+1}-r|\approx C|x_n-r|^2.

This is why Newton’s method can suddenly become very accurate. If an error is about 10^{-3}, its square is 10^{-6}. If an error is about 10^{-6}, its square is 10^{-12}.

This behavior is called quadratic convergence. To make the convergence claim precise, continuity bounds |f''| above and |f'| away from zero in a small interval about r. Hence |x_{n+1}-r|\le C|x_n-r|^2 there for a fixed C. Choose the starting error small enough that C|x_0-r|\le1/2 and the starting point lies in that interval. Each next error is at most half the previous one, so all iterates remain in the interval and converge to r.

The reason Newton can be fast

Near a simple root, Newton’s method does not merely reduce the error. It roughly squares the error.

 Why is Newton’s method a local method?

The method is fast when the starting guess is close, the function is smooth, and f' is nonzero at the root. In your own words, why does close enough matter, and why does a flat touch at the root (a multiple root) slow or spoil the process?

Linear approximation is local, so Newton’s method is local. Near a simple root the error is roughly squared at each step; a horizontal tangent at the root is a different story.

Failure modes: cycles and bad tangents

Newton’s method depends on tangent lines. A bad tangent can send the method to the wrong place, make it cycle, or stop it entirely.

The hypotheses are not decoration.

Failure mode 1: a horizontal tangent

Newton’s formula

x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}

requires

f'(x_n)\neq0.

If

f'(x_n)=0,

then the tangent line is horizontal. It does not cross the x-axis in the way the method needs.

For example, let

f(x)=x^3-x.

This function has roots

-1,\quad 0,\quad 1.

But

f'(x)=3x^2-1.

At

x_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt3},

we have

f'(x_0)=0.

The Newton formula cannot even produce x_1. The function has roots, but this starting point gives a horizontal tangent.

 Failure mode 2: a cycle

Let

f(x)=x^3-2x+2.

Then

f'(x)=3x^2-2.

Start Newton’s method at

x_0=0.

We get

x_1 = 0-\frac{f(0)}{f'(0)} = 0-\frac{2}{-2} = 1.

Now compute the next step:

x_2 = 1-\frac{f(1)}{f'(1)} = 1-\frac{1}{1} = 0.

So the method repeats:

0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ldots

It never reaches a root.

But the function does have a real root. Since

f(-2)=-8+4+2=-2

and

f(-1)=-1+2+2=3,

the Intermediate Value Theorem tells us that there is a root between -2 and -1.

Newton’s method failed because the tangent lines from 0 and 1 point back to each other.

 Failure mode 3: a multiple root

If a root r satisfies

f'(r)=0,

then Newton’s method may still converge, but often more slowly.

For example,

f(x)=(x-1)^2

has a double root at

x=1.

Newton’s method gives

x_{n+1} = x_n-\frac{(x_n-1)^2}{2(x_n-1)} = x_n-\frac{x_n-1}{2} = \frac{x_n+1}{2},

as long as x_n\neq1.

This moves halfway toward 1 each time. It converges, but the error is cut in half rather than squared. The fast convergence is lost.

The hypotheses are not decoration. A tangent can fail to cross the axis, or it can point somewhere the original curve never intended.

Chapter review and applications

This chapter began with a simple change in perspective. Instead of being handed a function and asked to differentiate it, we were asked to build the function first.

A ladder slides. A box is folded. A cup cools. A population grows. A light ray chooses a path. In each case, the derivative did not appear at the beginning. It appeared after we translated the situation into mathematics.

That is the main skill of the chapter:

\text{real situation} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{mathematical model} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{derivative information} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{interpretation}.

The last step is as important as the first. A derivative answer without units, sign, domain, and meaning is not yet an answer to the problem.

 The chapter in one map

The chapter used derivatives in several different ways. The same derivative idea kept returning with different names.

\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{topic} \amp \textbf{main question} \amp \textbf{derivative role}\\ \hline \text{related rates} \amp \text{How fast is one quantity changing?} \amp \text{differentiate a relation}\\ \text{optimization} \amp \text{Which choice is best?} \amp \text{find and test candidates}\\ \text{linear approximation} \amp \text{How much does the output change?} \amp \Delta y\approx f'(x)\Delta x\\ \text{Newton's method} \amp \text{Where is a zero?} \amp \text{use tangent-line correction}\\ \text{exponential models} \amp \text{What grows at a rate proportional to itself?} \amp y'=ky\\ \text{logistic models} \amp \text{How does growth slow near a limit?} \amp P'=rP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{K}\right)\\ \text{least-time paths} \amp \text{Which path makes time stationary?} \amp \text{differentiate time or distance} \end{array}

A derivative answer must still pass three checks

\text{Does the sign make sense?}

\text{Do the units make sense?}

\text{Is the answer allowed by the domain of the model?}

These checks are not afterthoughts. They are part of the mathematics.

Why is the main skill of the chapter building the function first?

A ladder slides, a box is folded, a cup cools, a population grows. In your own words, why did the derivative appear after we translated the situation into mathematics, and why is that change of perspective the chapter’s central idea?

Real situation, then model, then derivative information, then interpretation. We were not handed a function and asked to differentiate it.

Formulas to remember

The formulas below are not separate tricks. Each is a compact version of an idea from the chapter.

\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{idea} \amp \textbf{formula}\\ \hline \text{linear approximation} \amp f(a+\Delta x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)\Delta x\\ \text{differential estimate} \amp dy=f'(x)\,dx\\ \text{Newton's method} \amp x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\\ \text{exponential growth or decay} \amp y'=ky,\qquad y(t)=y_0e^{kt}\\ \text{doubling time} \amp D=\dfrac{\ln2}{k}\quad(k>0)\\ \text{half-life} \amp H=-\dfrac{\ln2}{k}\quad(k<0)\\ \text{Newton's law of cooling} \amp T(t)=T_s+\bigl(T(0)-T_s\bigr)e^{-kt}\\ \text{logistic growth} \amp P'=rP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{K}\right)\\ \text{logistic solution} \amp P(t)=\dfrac{K}{1+\left(\dfrac{K-P_0}{P_0}\right)e^{-rt}} \end{array}

For related rates and optimization, the most important formulas are often not fixed in advance. The formula comes from the geometry or the constraint.

A ladder problem uses

x^2+y^2=L^2.

A cone problem uses

V=\frac13\pi r^2h

together with similar triangles. A box problem uses a volume formula and a physical domain. A can problem uses surface area and a fixed-volume constraint.

The hard part is not memorizing formulas. The hard part is choosing the right quantities and keeping the model honest.

 Skills: related rates and optimization

Related rates and optimization are the two main problem-solving skills of this chapter. They look similar because both begin with translation, but they ask different questions.

\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{problem type} \amp \textbf{what changes?} \amp \textbf{what is the goal?}\\ \hline \text{related rates} \amp \text{quantities change with time} \amp \text{find an unknown rate}\\ \text{optimization} \amp \text{a choice variable changes} \amp \text{maximize or minimize a quantity} \end{array}

Related rates checklist

\begin{array}{ll} \text{1.} \amp \text{Draw a picture, if geometry is involved.}\\ \text{2.} \amp \text{Name the changing quantities as functions of time.}\\ \text{3.} \amp \text{Write an equation relating the quantities.}\\ \text{4.} \amp \text{Differentiate with respect to time.}\\ \text{5.} \amp \text{Substitute values for the instant in question.}\\ \text{6.} \amp \text{Solve for the desired rate.}\\ \text{7.} \amp \text{Check sign and units.} \end{array}

The most common mistake is substituting the instant-specific numbers too early. The variables must remain variables until after the relation has been differentiated.

 Optimization checklist

\begin{array}{ll} \text{1.} \amp \text{Name the quantity to optimize.}\\ \text{2.} \amp \text{Name the variables.}\\ \text{3.} \amp \text{Write the objective function.}\\ \text{4.} \amp \text{Write the constraint.}\\ \text{5.} \amp \text{Use the constraint to get one variable.}\\ \text{6.} \amp \text{Find the physical domain.}\\ \text{7.} \amp \text{Find critical numbers and check endpoints.}\\ \text{8.} \amp \text{Translate the result back into the situation.} \end{array}

The most common mistake is finding a critical point and stopping. A critical point is a candidate, not a conclusion.

 Why do related rates, optimization, and models use the same derivative differently?

Related rates differentiate a relation. Optimization finds and tests candidates. Exponential and logistic models begin with a law for y'. In your own words, why is the derivative doing one job with several names, and how do you tell which question a problem is asking?

Ask whether the problem wants a rate, a best choice, a small-error estimate, a root, or a function obeying a rate law.

Review problems

The problems below are meant to mix the chapter’s ideas. For each one, write a complete solution with units and a sentence interpreting the answer.

  1. Inflating sphere. Air is pumped into a spherical balloon at a constant rate of

    30\pi\text{ cm}^3/\text{s}.

    How fast is the radius increasing when the radius is 5 cm?

  2. Sliding ladder. A 13-foot ladder leans against a wall. The bottom slides away from the wall at

    3\text{ ft/s}.

    How fast is the top sliding down when the bottom is 5 feet from the wall?

  3. Water in a cone. An inverted cone has height 10 feet and radius 5 feet at the top. Water is flowing in at

    3\text{ ft}^3/\text{min}.

    How fast is the water level rising when the water height is 4 feet?

  4. Two cars. One car travels east from an intersection at 40 mph. Another travels north from the same intersection at 30 mph. How fast is the distance between the cars increasing 2 hours later?

  5. Largest rectangle under a parabola. A rectangle has its base on the x-axis and its upper two vertices on the graph

    y=12-x^2.

    Assume the rectangle is symmetric about the y-axis. What dimensions give the largest area?

  6. Open box. A 20-inch by 30-inch sheet of cardboard has equal squares of side length x cut from its corners. The sides are folded up to make an open box. What value of x gives the largest volume?

  7. Fence along a river. A farmer has 300 meters of fencing and wants to make a rectangular field along a river, using the river as one side. What dimensions maximize the area?

  8. Least material can. A closed cylindrical can must hold

    1000\text{ cm}^3.

    Ignoring seams and thickness, find the radius and height that minimize surface area.

  9. Newton’s method. Use Newton’s method to approximate the positive solution of

    x^3=10.

    Start with x_0=2. Compute x_1, x_2, and x_3.

  10. Cooling model. A metal object is heated to 100^\circ\text{C} and placed in a room at 20^\circ\text{C}. After 5 minutes, its temperature is 70^\circ\text{C}. Assuming Newton’s law of cooling, estimate its temperature after 15 minutes.

  11. Logistic growth. A population satisfies

    P'=0.6P\left(1-\frac{P}{800}\right), \qquad P(0)=100.

    Find P(t). When does the population reach 400?

  12. A warning problem. A model for profit is

    P(q)=-q^2+60q-500.

    A factory is allowed to produce only

    40\le q\le 80

    units. Find the production level that maximizes profit on the allowed domain. Explain why the unconstrained critical point is not the answer.

 Project: design a least-material container

A basic can problem assumes that all material costs the same. Real containers are not always like that. The top and bottom may need thicker material. The side wall may be cheaper. The seams may matter.

This project keeps the model simple but makes the design question more realistic.

Design brief

A closed cylindrical container must hold a fixed volume

V_0

cubic centimeters. The side wall costs 1 unit per square centimeter. The top and bottom cost c units per square centimeter, where

c>0.

Find the radius and height that minimize material cost.

 Step 1: Build the cost function

The side area is

2\pi rh.

The top and bottom together have area

2\pi r^2.

Since the top and bottom cost c units per square centimeter, the material cost is

M=2\pi rh+2c\pi r^2.

The volume constraint is

\pi r^2h=V_0.

Solve the constraint for h:

h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}.

Substitute into the cost:

M(r) = 2\pi r\left(\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}\right)+2c\pi r^2.

Thus

M(r)=\frac{2V_0}{r}+2c\pi r^2, \qquad r>0.

 Step 2: Minimize

Differentiate:

M'(r)=-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}+4c\pi r.

Set M'(r)=0:

-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}+4c\pi r=0.

Multiply by r^2:

-2V_0+4c\pi r^3=0.

So

4c\pi r^3=2V_0,

and therefore

r^3=\frac{V_0}{2c\pi}.

Thus

r=\left(\frac{V_0}{2c\pi}\right)^{1/3}.

Now find the height:

h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}.

Since

V_0=2c\pi r^3,

we get

h=\frac{2c\pi r^3}{\pi r^2}=2cr.

Therefore the optimal shape satisfies

h=2cr.

When c=1, this gives

h=2r.

So the height equals the diameter, which matches the equal-cost can from Section .

 Step 3: Interpret the parameter <m>c</m>

The ratio

\frac{h}{r}=2c

shows how the design changes with material cost.

\begin{array}{c|c|c} c \amp h/r \amp \text{interpretation}\\ \hline 1 \amp 2 \amp \text{height equals diameter}\\ 2 \amp 4 \amp \text{top and bottom are expensive, so use smaller ends}\\ 4 \amp 8 \amp \text{ends are very expensive, so make the can tall and narrow} \end{array}

The formula tells a physical story. If the circular ends are expensive, the design tries to reduce their area by using a smaller radius. To keep the same volume, the height must increase.

 Report questions

Write a short report answering these questions.

  1. Derive the cost function M(r) from the geometry and the volume constraint.

  2. Prove that the critical point gives an absolute minimum. One way is to use

    M''(r)=\frac{4V_0}{r^3}+4c\pi>0.

    Another way is to examine what happens to M(r) as r\to0^+ and as r\to\infty.

  3. For

    V_0=1000\text{ cm}^3

    compute the optimal r and h for

    c=1,\qquad c=2,\qquad c=4.

  4. Make a graph of M(r) for each value of c. Mark the minimizing radius.

  5. Explain, in words, why increasing c makes the optimal container taller and narrower.

  6. Extension. Suppose the container has no top. If the bottom costs c units per square centimeter and the side costs 1, build and minimize the new cost function.

 Project: model cooling data

Chapter 2 used cooling coffee as an example of data that should not be modeled by a line forever. This chapter gives the derivative law behind the better model.

Newton’s law of cooling says

T'=-k(T-T_s), \qquad k>0,

where T_s is the surrounding temperature. The solution is

T(t)=T_s+\bigl(T(0)-T_s\bigr)e^{-kt}.

The quantity that decays exponentially is not T itself. It is the excess temperature

T-T_s.

Data

A cup of coffee sits in a room whose temperature is

22^\circ\text{C}.

The measured temperatures are:

\begin{array}{c|cccccc} t\text{ (minutes)} \amp 0 \amp 5 \amp 10 \amp 15 \amp 20 \amp 25\\ \hline T(t)\text{ }(^\circ\text{C}) \amp 90 \amp 73 \amp 60 \amp 51 \amp 44 \amp 39 \end{array}

 A first model from two points

Since

T_s=22

and

T(0)=90,

the model has the form

T(t)=22+68e^{-kt}.

Use T(5)=73:

73=22+68e^{-5k}.

Thus

51=68e^{-5k},

so

e^{-5k}=\frac{51}{68}=\frac34.

Therefore

k=-\frac15\ln\left(\frac34\right).

Numerically,

k\approx0.0575.

So a two-point model is

T(t)=22+68e^{-0.0575t}.

Equivalently,

T(t)=22+68\left(\frac34\right)^{t/5}.

This form says that every 5 minutes, the excess temperature is multiplied by about 3/4.

 Prediction

The predicted temperature after 30 minutes is

T(30)=22+68\left(\frac34\right)^6.

Since

\left(\frac34\right)^6\approx0.178,

we get

T(30)\approx22+68(0.178)\approx34.1^\circ\text{C}.

 Computing task

The two-point model uses only the first two measurements. A better model should use all the data.

Let

E(t)=T(t)-22

be the excess temperature. If Newton’s law is a good model, then

E(t)=E(0)e^{-kt}.

Taking natural logarithms gives

\ln E(t)=\ln E(0)-kt.

Chapter review and applications

This chapter began with a simple change in perspective. Instead of being handed a function and asked to differentiate it, we were asked to build the function first.

A ladder slides. A box is folded. A cup cools. A population grows. A light ray chooses a path. In each case, the derivative did not appear at the beginning. It appeared after we translated the situation into mathematics.

That is the main skill of the chapter:

\text{real situation} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{mathematical model} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{derivative information} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{interpretation}.

The last step is as important as the first. A derivative answer without units, sign, domain, and meaning is not yet an answer to the problem.

 The chapter in one map

The chapter used derivatives in several different ways. The same derivative idea kept returning with different names.

\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{topic} \amp \textbf{main question} \amp \textbf{derivative role}\\ \hline \text{related rates} \amp \text{How fast is one quantity changing?} \amp \text{differentiate a relation}\\ \text{optimization} \amp \text{Which choice is best?} \amp \text{find and test candidates}\\ \text{linear approximation} \amp \text{How much does the output change?} \amp \Delta y\approx f'(x)\Delta x\\ \text{Newton's method} \amp \text{Where is a zero?} \amp \text{use tangent-line correction}\\ \text{exponential models} \amp \text{What grows at a rate proportional to itself?} \amp y'=ky\\ \text{logistic models} \amp \text{How does growth slow near a limit?} \amp P'=rP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{K}\right)\\ \text{least-time paths} \amp \text{Which path makes time stationary?} \amp \text{differentiate time or distance} \end{array}

A derivative answer must still pass three checks

\text{Does the sign make sense?}

\text{Do the units make sense?}

\text{Is the answer allowed by the domain of the model?}

These checks are not afterthoughts. They are part of the mathematics.

Why is the main skill of the chapter building the function first?

A ladder slides, a box is folded, a cup cools, a population grows. In your own words, why did the derivative appear after we translated the situation into mathematics, and why is that change of perspective the chapter’s central idea?

Real situation, then model, then derivative information, then interpretation. We were not handed a function and asked to differentiate it.

Formulas to remember

The formulas below are not separate tricks. Each is a compact version of an idea from the chapter.

\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{idea} \amp \textbf{formula}\\ \hline \text{linear approximation} \amp f(a+\Delta x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)\Delta x\\ \text{differential estimate} \amp dy=f'(x)\,dx\\ \text{Newton's method} \amp x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\\ \text{exponential growth or decay} \amp y'=ky,\qquad y(t)=y_0e^{kt}\\ \text{doubling time} \amp D=\dfrac{\ln2}{k}\quad(k>0)\\ \text{half-life} \amp H=-\dfrac{\ln2}{k}\quad(k<0)\\ \text{Newton's law of cooling} \amp T(t)=T_s+\bigl(T(0)-T_s\bigr)e^{-kt}\\ \text{logistic growth} \amp P'=rP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{K}\right)\\ \text{logistic solution} \amp P(t)=\dfrac{K}{1+\left(\dfrac{K-P_0}{P_0}\right)e^{-rt}} \end{array}

For related rates and optimization, the most important formulas are often not fixed in advance. The formula comes from the geometry or the constraint.

A ladder problem uses

x^2+y^2=L^2.

A cone problem uses

V=\frac13\pi r^2h

together with similar triangles. A box problem uses a volume formula and a physical domain. A can problem uses surface area and a fixed-volume constraint.

The hard part is not memorizing formulas. The hard part is choosing the right quantities and keeping the model honest.

 Skills: related rates and optimization

Related rates and optimization are the two main problem-solving skills of this chapter. They look similar because both begin with translation, but they ask different questions.

\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{problem type} \amp \textbf{what changes?} \amp \textbf{what is the goal?}\\ \hline \text{related rates} \amp \text{quantities change with time} \amp \text{find an unknown rate}\\ \text{optimization} \amp \text{a choice variable changes} \amp \text{maximize or minimize a quantity} \end{array}

Related rates checklist

1.Draw a picture, if geometry is involved.2.Name the changing quantities as functions of time.3.Write an equation relating the quantities.4.Differentiate with respect to time.5.Substitute values for the instant in question.6.Solve for the desired rate.7.Check sign and units.

The most common mistake is substituting the instant-specific numbers too early. The variables must remain variables until after the relation has been differentiated.

 Optimization checklist

1.Name the quantity to optimize.2.Name the variables.3.Write the objective function.4.Write the constraint.5.Use the constraint to get one variable.6.Find the physical domain.7.Find critical numbers and check endpoints.8.Translate the result back into the situation.

The most common mistake is finding a critical point and stopping. A critical point is a candidate, not a conclusion.

Related rates differentiate a relation. Optimization finds and tests candidates. Exponential and logistic models begin with a law for y'. In your own words, why is the derivative doing one job with several names, and how do you tell which question a problem is asking?

Ask whether the problem wants a rate, a best choice, a small-error estimate, a root, or a function obeying a rate law.

    30\pi\text{ cm}^3/\text{s}.

    How fast is the radius increasing when the radius is 5 cm?

    3\text{ ft/s}.

    How fast is the top sliding down when the bottom is 5 feet from the wall?

    x^3=10.

A basic can problem assumes that all material costs the same. Real containers are not always like that. The top and bottom may need thicker material. The side wall may be cheaper. The seams may matter.

This project keeps the model simple but makes the design question more realistic.

Design brief

A closed cylindrical container must hold a fixed volume

V_0

cubic centimeters. The side wall costs 1 unit per square centimeter. The top and bottom cost c units per square centimeter, where

c>0.

Find the radius and height that minimize material cost.

 Step 1: Build the cost function

The side area is

2\pi rh.

The top and bottom together have area

2\pi r^2.

Since the top and bottom cost c units per square centimeter, the material cost is

M=2\pi rh+2c\pi r^2.

The volume constraint is

\pi r^2h=V_0.

Solve the constraint for h:

h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}.

Substitute into the cost:

M(r) = 2\pi r\left(\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}\right)+2c\pi r^2.

Thus

M(r)=\frac{2V_0}{r}+2c\pi r^2, \qquad r>0.

 Step 2: Minimize

Differentiate:

M'(r)=-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}+4c\pi r.

Set M'(r)=0:

-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}+4c\pi r=0.

Multiply by r^2:

-2V_0+4c\pi r^3=0.

So

4c\pi r^3=2V_0,

and therefore

r^3=\frac{V_0}{2c\pi}.

Thus

r=\left(\frac{V_0}{2c\pi}\right)^{1/3}.

Now find the height:

h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}.

Since

V_0=2c\pi r^3,

we get

h=\frac{2c\pi r^3}{\pi r^2}=2cr.

Therefore the optimal shape satisfies

h=2cr.

When c=1, this gives

h=2r.

So the height equals the diameter, which matches the equal-cost can from Section .

 Step 3: Interpret the parameter <m>c</m>

The ratio

\frac{h}{r}=2c

shows how the design changes with material cost.

\begin{array}{c|c|c} c \amp h/r \amp \text{interpretation}\\ \hline 1 \amp 2 \amp \text{height equals diameter}\\ 2 \amp 4 \amp \text{top and bottom are expensive, so use smaller ends}\\ 4 \amp 8 \amp \text{ends are very expensive, so make the can tall and narrow} \end{array}

The formula tells a physical story. If the circular ends are expensive, the design tries to reduce their area by using a smaller radius. To keep the same volume, the height must increase.

Warning examples

The last few sections gave us strong tools:

\text{Fermat's theorem, Rolle's theorem, the Mean Value Theorem,}

\text{the first derivative test, the second derivative test, and l'Hospital's Rule.}

Each one has a boundary. A theorem is useful only when its hypotheses are true. This section collects the warning examples in one place, so the rules are easier to use and harder to misuse.

 Fermat’s theorem fails at an endpoint

Fermat’s theorem said:

\text{differentiable local extremum at an interior point} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f'(c)=0.

The phrase interior point matters.

Let

f(x)=x

on the interval

[0,1].

The function has an absolute minimum at

x=0

and an absolute maximum at

x=1.

But the derivative is

f'(x)=1.

There is no horizontal tangent.

There is no contradiction. Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint, the graph only has to be compared with points on one side. It can be best or worst without flattening out.

\text{Endpoint extrema do not have to satisfy } f'(c)=0.

That is why the closed interval method always checks endpoints separately.

Why can an endpoint extremum fail to have a horizontal tangent?

On [0,1], the function f(x)=x attains its max and min, but f' is never zero. In your own words, why is that compatible with Fermat’s theorem, and why does the closed interval method therefore check endpoints separately?

Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint the graph is compared with only one side, so it can be best or worst without flattening.

The Mean Value Theorem fails without continuity

The Mean Value Theorem said that if f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then some c\in(a,b) satisfies

f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.

Continuity on the whole closed interval matters.

Define

f(x)= \begin{cases} x, \amp 0\le x<1,\\ 0, \amp x=1. \end{cases}

on [0,1].

Then

f(0)=0, \qquad f(1)=0.

So the secant slope from 0 to 1 is

\frac{f(1)-f(0)}{1-0}=0.

But on the open interval (0,1),

f(x)=x,

so

f'(x)=1

for every x\in(0,1). There is no point c\in(0,1) with

f'(c)=0.

The graph climbs toward 1, then jumps down at the endpoint. The jump hides the climb from the endpoint calculation.

\text{The Mean Value Theorem needs continuity on }[a,b].

Why can the Mean Value Theorem fail without continuity or differentiability?

A jump on the closed interval, or a corner inside, can keep every existing tangent slope away from the secant slope. In your own words, why are continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b) not decorations, and what kind of escape does each hypothesis block?

Continuity keeps the graph from leaping over the needed height. Differentiability keeps a turn from happening at a corner instead of at a tangent.

The Mean Value Theorem fails without differentiability

The Mean Value Theorem also needs differentiability on the open interval.

Let

f(x)=|x|

on

[-1,1].

The function is continuous on [-1,1]. Its endpoint values are

f(-1)=1, \qquad f(1)=1.

So the secant slope is

\frac{f(1)-f(-1)}{1-(-1)} = \frac{1-1}{2} = 0.

If the Mean Value Theorem applied, there would be some c\in(-1,1) with

f'(c)=0.

But

f'(x)=-1 \quad\text{for }x<0,

and

f'(x)=1 \quad\text{for }x>0.

At x=0, the derivative does not exist. The graph turns at a corner.

The graph does return to the same height, but it turns too sharply. Rolle’s Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem do not promise a horizontal tangent unless the function is differentiable throughout the open interval.

\text{The Mean Value Theorem needs differentiability on }(a,b).

The second derivative test can be inconclusive

The second derivative test said:

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)>0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local minimum at }c,

and

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)<0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local maximum at }c.

But when

f''(c)=0,

the test says nothing.

Three different outcomes are possible.

A local minimum

Let

f(x)=x^4.

Then

f'(x)=4x^3, \qquad f''(x)=12x^2.

At x=0,

f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0.

The second derivative test gives no conclusion. But

x^4\ge0

for every x, so f has a local minimum at 0.

 A local maximum

Let

g(x)=-x^4.

Then

g'(x)=-4x^3, \qquad g''(x)=-12x^2.

At x=0,

g'(0)=0, \qquad g''(0)=0.

The test again gives no conclusion. But

-x^4\le0

for every x, so g has a local maximum at 0.

 No local extremum

Let

h(x)=x^3.

Then

h'(x)=3x^2, \qquad h''(x)=6x.

At x=0,

h'(0)=0, \qquad h''(0)=0.

But x^3 is increasing through 0. There is no local maximum or local minimum.

The moral is short:

f''(c)=0 \text{ means ``try another test.''}

Most often, we return to the first derivative test or to the definition of local maximum and local minimum.

 Why can the second derivative test stay silent?

If f'(c)=0 and f''(c)=0, the test gives no conclusion. In your own words, why can that same pair of facts describe a local min, a local max, or no extremum at all, and what extra evidence do we then need?

Look at the sign of f' on both sides, or compare the graphs of x^4, -x^4, and x^3 at the origin.

l’Hospital’s Rule cannot be used on every quotient

l’Hospital’s Rule is a rule for the indeterminate forms

\frac00 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{\infty}{\infty}.

The first question is always:

\text{What form does direct substitution produce?}

A quotient that is not indeterminate

Consider

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}.

Direct substitution gives

\frac{0^2+1}{0+1}=1.

So the limit is

1.

This is not a 0/0 form and not an \infty/\infty form.

If we incorrectly differentiate numerator and denominator, we get

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{2x}{1}=0,

which is wrong.

\text{Do not use l'Hospital's Rule when direct substitution already gives an ordinary number.}

A derivative quotient with no limit

Sometimes the original quotient has a limit, but the quotient of derivatives does not.

Consider

\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}.

The quotient is

\frac{x+\sin x}{x} = 1+\frac{\sin x}{x}.

Since

\left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right|\le \frac1x

for x>0, we get

\frac{\sin x}{x}\to0.

Therefore

\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}=1.

But the quotient of derivatives is

\frac{1+\cos x}{1}=1+\cos x,

which has no limit as x\to\infty.

There is no contradiction. l’Hospital’s Rule says that if the original quotient has the right indeterminate form and the derivative quotient has a limit, then the original limit has that same value. It does not say that the derivative quotient must always have a limit.

\text{If the derivative quotient does not settle, l'Hospital's Rule gives no conclusion.}

Why is l’Hospital’s Rule not a license for every quotient?

The rule applies only to certain indeterminate quotients, and only when the derivative quotient has a limit. In your own words, why can blindly differentiating a well-behaved quotient give the wrong answer, and why can a derivative quotient that refuses to settle leave the original limit still well-defined?

A theorem is a package: hypotheses imply a conclusion. Missing hypotheses mean the theorem is no longer the reason, even if luck later produces a true statement.

A theorem-use checklist

The warnings can be compressed into a practical checklist.

Warning examples

The last few sections gave us strong tools:

\text{Fermat's theorem, Rolle's theorem, the Mean Value Theorem,}

\text{the first derivative test, the second derivative test, and l'Hospital's Rule.}

Each one has a boundary. A theorem is useful only when its hypotheses are true. This section collects the warning examples in one place, so the rules are easier to use and harder to misuse.

 Fermat’s theorem fails at an endpoint

Fermat’s theorem said:

\text{differentiable local extremum at an interior point} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f'(c)=0.

The phrase interior point matters.

Let

f(x)=x

on the interval

[0,1].

The function has an absolute minimum at

x=0

and an absolute maximum at

x=1.

But the derivative is

f'(x)=1.

There is no horizontal tangent.

There is no contradiction. Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint, the graph only has to be compared with points on one side. It can be best or worst without flattening out.

\text{Endpoint extrema do not have to satisfy } f'(c)=0.

That is why the closed interval method always checks endpoints separately.

Why can an endpoint extremum fail to have a horizontal tangent?

On [0,1], the function f(x)=x attains its max and min, but f' is never zero. In your own words, why is that compatible with Fermat’s theorem, and why does the closed interval method therefore check endpoints separately?

Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint the graph is compared with only one side, so it can be best or worst without flattening.

The Mean Value Theorem fails without continuity

The Mean Value Theorem said that if f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then some c\in(a,b) satisfies

f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.

Continuity on the whole closed interval matters.

Define

f(x)= \begin{cases} x, \amp 0\le x<1,\\ 0, \amp x=1. \end{cases}

on [0,1].

Then

f(0)=0, \qquad f(1)=0.

So the secant slope from 0 to 1 is

\frac{f(1)-f(0)}{1-0}=0.

But on the open interval (0,1),

f(x)=x,

so

f'(x)=1

for every x\in(0,1). There is no point c\in(0,1) with

f'(c)=0.

The graph climbs toward 1, then jumps down at the endpoint. The jump hides the climb from the endpoint calculation.

\text{The Mean Value Theorem needs continuity on }[a,b].

Why can the Mean Value Theorem fail without continuity or differentiability?

A jump on the closed interval, or a corner inside, can keep every existing tangent slope away from the secant slope. In your own words, why are continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b) not decorations, and what kind of escape does each hypothesis block?

Continuity keeps the graph from leaping over the needed height. Differentiability keeps a turn from happening at a corner instead of at a tangent.

The Mean Value Theorem fails without differentiability

The Mean Value Theorem also needs differentiability on the open interval.

Let

f(x)=|x|

on

[-1,1].

The function is continuous on [-1,1]. Its endpoint values are

f(-1)=1, \qquad f(1)=1.

So the secant slope is

\frac{f(1)-f(-1)}{1-(-1)} = \frac{1-1}{2} = 0.

If the Mean Value Theorem applied, there would be some c\in(-1,1) with

f'(c)=0.

But

f'(x)=-1 \quad\text{for }x<0,

and

f'(x)=1 \quad\text{for }x>0.

At x=0, the derivative does not exist. The graph turns at a corner.

The graph does return to the same height, but it turns too sharply. Rolle’s Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem do not promise a horizontal tangent unless the function is differentiable throughout the open interval.

\text{The Mean Value Theorem needs differentiability on }(a,b).

The second derivative test can be inconclusive

The second derivative test said:

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)>0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local minimum at }c,

and

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)<0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local maximum at }c.

But when

f''(c)=0,

the test says nothing.

Three different outcomes are possible.

A local minimum

Let

f(x)=x^4.

Then

f'(x)=4x^3, \qquad f''(x)=12x^2.

At x=0,

f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0.

The second derivative test gives no conclusion. But

x^4\ge0

for every x, so f has a local minimum at 0.

 A local maximum

Let

g(x)=-x^4.

Then

g'(x)=-4x^3, \qquad g''(x)=-12x^2.

At x=0,

g'(0)=0, \qquad g''(0)=0.

The test again gives no conclusion. But

-x^4\le0

for every x, so g has a local maximum at 0.

 No local extremum

Let

h(x)=x^3.

Then

h'(x)=3x^2, \qquad h''(x)=6x.

At x=0,

h'(0)=0, \qquad h''(0)=0.

But x^3 is increasing through 0. There is no local maximum or local minimum.

The moral is short:

f''(c)=0 \text{ means ``try another test.''}

Most often, we return to the first derivative test or to the definition of local maximum and local minimum.

 Why can the second derivative test stay silent?

If f'(c)=0 and f''(c)=0, the test gives no conclusion. In your own words, why can that same pair of facts describe a local min, a local max, or no extremum at all, and what extra evidence do we then need?

Look at the sign of f' on both sides, or compare the graphs of x^4, -x^4, and x^3 at the origin.

l’Hospital’s Rule cannot be used on every quotient

l’Hospital’s Rule is a rule for the indeterminate forms

\frac00 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{\infty}{\infty}.

The first question is always:

\text{What form does direct substitution produce?}

A quotient that is not indeterminate

Consider

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}.

Direct substitution gives

\frac{0^2+1}{0+1}=1.

So the limit is

1.

This is not a 0/0 form and not an \infty/\infty form.

If we incorrectly differentiate numerator and denominator, we get

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{2x}{1}=0,

which is wrong.

\text{Do not use l'Hospital's Rule when direct substitution already gives an ordinary number.}

A derivative quotient with no limit

Sometimes the original quotient has a limit, but the quotient of derivatives does not.

Consider

\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}.

The quotient is

\frac{x+\sin x}{x} = 1+\frac{\sin x}{x}.

Since

\left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right|\le \frac1x

for x>0, we get

\frac{\sin x}{x}\to0.

Therefore

\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}=1.

But the quotient of derivatives is

\frac{1+\cos x}{1}=1+\cos x,

which has no limit as x\to\infty.

There is no contradiction. l’Hospital’s Rule says that if the original quotient has the right indeterminate form and the derivative quotient has a limit, then the original limit has that same value. It does not say that the derivative quotient must always have a limit.

\text{If the derivative quotient does not settle, l'Hospital's Rule gives no conclusion.}

Why is l’Hospital’s Rule not a license for every quotient?

The rule applies only to certain indeterminate quotients, and only when the derivative quotient has a limit. In your own words, why can blindly differentiating a well-behaved quotient give the wrong answer, and why can a derivative quotient that refuses to settle leave the original limit still well-defined?

A theorem is a package: hypotheses imply a conclusion. Missing hypotheses mean the theorem is no longer the reason, even if luck later produces a true statement.
