Chapter review and applications

This chapter began with a simple change in perspective. Instead of being handed a function and asked to differentiate it, we were asked to build the function first.

A ladder slides. A box is folded. A cup cools. A population grows. A light ray chooses a path. In each case, the derivative did not appear at the beginning. It appeared after we translated the situation into mathematics.

That is the main skill of the chapter:

\text{real situation} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{mathematical model} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{derivative information} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{interpretation}.

The last step is as important as the first. A derivative answer without units, sign, domain, and meaning is not yet an answer to the problem.

 The chapter in one map

The chapter used derivatives in several different ways. The same derivative idea kept returning with different names.

\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{topic} \amp \textbf{main question} \amp \textbf{derivative role}\\ \hline \text{related rates} \amp \text{How fast is one quantity changing?} \amp \text{differentiate a relation}\\ \text{optimization} \amp \text{Which choice is best?} \amp \text{find and test candidates}\\ \text{linear approximation} \amp \text{How much does the output change?} \amp \Delta y\approx f'(x)\Delta x\\ \text{Newton's method} \amp \text{Where is a zero?} \amp \text{use tangent-line correction}\\ \text{exponential models} \amp \text{What grows at a rate proportional to itself?} \amp y'=ky\\ \text{logistic models} \amp \text{How does growth slow near a limit?} \amp P'=rP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{K}\right)\\ \text{least-time paths} \amp \text{Which path makes time stationary?} \amp \text{differentiate time or distance} \end{array}

A derivative answer must still pass three checks

\text{Does the sign make sense?}

\text{Do the units make sense?}

A closed cylindrical container must hold a fixed volume

V_0

h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}.

-2V_0+4c\pi r^3=0.

So

4c\pi r^3=2V_0,

r^3=\frac{V_0}{2c\pi}.

r=\left(\frac{V_0}{2c\pi}\right)^{1/3}.

Now find the height:

h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}.

V_0=2c\pi r^3,

When c=1, this gives

 Project: model cooling data

Chapter 2 used cooling coffee as an example of data that should not be modeled by a line forever. This chapter gives the derivative law behind the better model.

Newton’s law of cooling says

T'=-k(T-T_s), \qquad k>0,

where T_s is the surrounding temperature. The solution is

T(t)=T_s+\bigl(T(0)-T_s\bigr)e^{-kt}.

The quantity that decays exponentially is not T itself. It is the excess temperature

T-T_s.

Data

A cup of coffee sits in a room whose temperature is

22^\circ\text{C}.

The measured temperatures are:

\begin{array}{c|cccccc} t\text{ (minutes)} \amp 0 \amp 5 \amp 10 \amp 15 \amp 20 \amp 25\\ \hline T(t)\text{ }(^\circ\text{C}) \amp 90 \amp 73 \amp 60 \amp 51 \amp 44 \amp 39 \end{array}

 A first model from two points

Since

T_s=22

and

T(0)=90,

the model has the form

T(t)=22+68e^{-kt}.

Use T(5)=73:

73=22+68e^{-5k}.

Thus

51=68e^{-5k},

so

e^{-5k}=\frac{51}{68}=\frac34.

Therefore

k=-\frac15\ln\left(\frac34\right).

Numerically,

k\approx0.0575.

So a two-point model is

T(t)=22+68e^{-0.0575t}.

Equivalently,

T(t)=22+68\left(\frac34\right)^{t/5}.

This form says that every 5 minutes, the excess temperature is multiplied by about 3/4.

 Prediction

The predicted temperature after 30 minutes is

T(30)=22+68\left(\frac34\right)^6.

Since

\left(\frac34\right)^6\approx0.178,

we get

T(30)\approx22+68(0.178)\approx34.1^\circ\text{C}.

The two-point model uses only the first two measurements. A better model should use all the data.

Let

E(t)=T(t)-22

be the excess temperature. If Newton’s law is a good model, then

E(t)=E(0)e^{-kt}.

Taking natural logarithms gives

\ln E(t)=\ln E(0)-kt.

So the points

\bigl(t,\ln(T(t)-22)\bigr)

should lie approximately on a line with slope -k.

Complete the following tasks.

  1. Compute the excess temperatures E(t)=T(t)-22.

  2. Compute \ln E(t) for each measured time.

  3. Plot the points

    (t,\ln E(t)).

    Do they look approximately linear?

  4. Estimate the slope of the best-fitting line. Then estimate

    k=-\text{slope}.

  5. Build the model

    T(t)=22+Ae^{-kt}.

    You may take A=68, or estimate A from your fitted line.

  6. Use your model to predict T(30), T(45), and T(60).

  7. Compute residuals:

    \text{residual} = \text{measured temperature} - \text{model temperature}.

    Are the residuals small? Do they show a pattern?

  8. Compare the cooling model with the linear model through the first and last data points. Which model gives a more reasonable prediction after 2 hours? Explain.

A model is not only a formula that fits numbers. It should also respect the behavior of the situation. A cooling object should approach room temperature, not pass below it because a line keeps decreasing forever.

    y'=ky,

    P'=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)

Why must a derivative answer still pass three checks?

Sign, units, and domain are listed as part of the mathematics, not as afterthoughts. In your own words, why can a correctly computed derivative still fail to answer the original problem if one of those checks is skipped?

A number without direction, units, or feasibility is not yet an answer to a related-rates, optimization, or modeling question.

Where this points

This chapter showed how much can be done with a derivative.

A derivative can relate changing quantities. It can find a best choice. It can estimate error. It can turn a tangent line into a root-finding method. It can express a physical law such as

T'=-k(T-T_s)

or

P'=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right).

But a derivative is still local. It tells how fast something is changing at an instant.

Many questions ask for the accumulated result of those changes.

If velocity is known at every instant, how far did the object travel?

If a force changes with position, how much work was done?

If density varies along a rod, what is the rod’s total mass?

If a rate law tells how a quantity changes, how much total change has occurred over an interval?

Those questions return us to the dashboard from the beginning of the book. The speedometer gives rate. The odometer gives accumulation.

The next chapter builds the second great operation of calculus: adding up infinitely many small changes.

T(30)\approx22+68(0.178)\approx34.1^\circ\text{C}.

 Computing task

The two-point model uses only the first two measurements. A better model should use all the data.

Let

E(t)=T(t)-22

be the excess temperature. If Newton’s law is a good model, then

E(t)=E(0)e^{-kt}.

Taking natural logarithms gives

\ln E(t)=\ln E(0)-kt.

So the points

\bigl(t,\ln(T(t)-22)\bigr)

should lie approximately on a line with slope -k.

Complete the following tasks.

  1. Compute the excess temperatures E(t)=T(t)-22.

  2. Compute \ln E(t) for each measured time.

  3. Plot the points

    (t,\ln E(t)).

    Do they look approximately linear?

  4. Estimate the slope of the best-fitting line. Then estimate

    k=-\text{slope}.

  5. Build the model

    T(t)=22+Ae^{-kt}.

    You may take A=68, or estimate A from your fitted line.

  6. Use your model to predict T(30), T(45), and T(60).

  7. Compute residuals:

    \text{residual} = \text{measured temperature} - \text{model temperature}.

    Are the residuals small? Do they show a pattern?

  8. Compare the cooling model with the linear model through the first and last data points. Which model gives a more reasonable prediction after 2 hours? Explain.

What the project tests

A model is not only a formula that fits numbers. It should also respect the behavior of the situation. A cooling object should approach room temperature, not pass below it because a line keeps decreasing forever.

 Why is a model a promise with conditions?

Exponential growth promises a constant relative rate. Logistic growth adds a fixed carrying capacity. In your own words, why must we check whether that promise matches the situation before trusting a formula, and what goes wrong if the conditions are invisible in the early data?

A formula can be mathematically correct and still be the wrong story. Early exponential-looking data may hide a later ceiling.

Concept checks

  1. In a related rates problem, why should we usually differentiate before substituting the values for the instant in question?

  2. In an optimization problem, why is the physical domain part of the model?

  3. A critical point of an objective function lies outside the physical domain. What should you do with it?

  4. Explain the difference between absolute error and relative error.

  5. Why does Newton’s method require f'(x_n)\neq0?

  6. Give one reason Newton’s method can fail even when a root exists.

  7. In the equation

    y'=ky,

    what does k measure?

  8. Why is

    P'=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)

    approximately exponential when P\ll K?

  9. In the logistic model, why is the growth fastest at P=K/2?

  10. Reflection minimizes distance, but refraction minimizes time. Why are these not the same problem when the speed changes?

Why must a derivative answer still pass three checks?

Sign, units, and domain are listed as part of the mathematics, not as afterthoughts. In your own words, why can a correctly computed derivative still fail to answer the original problem if one of those checks is skipped?

A number without direction, units, or feasibility is not yet an answer to a related-rates, optimization, or modeling question.

Where this points

This chapter showed how much can be done with a derivative.

A derivative can relate changing quantities. It can find a best choice. It can estimate error. It can turn a tangent line into a root-finding method. It can express a physical law such as

T'=-k(T-T_s)

or

P'=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right).

But a derivative is still local. It tells how fast something is changing at an instant.

Many questions ask for the accumulated result of those changes.

If velocity is known at every instant, how far did the object travel?

If a force changes with position, how much work was done?

If density varies along a rod, what is the rod’s total mass?

If a rate law tells how a quantity changes, how much total change has occurred over an interval?

Those questions return us to the dashboard from the beginning of the book. The speedometer gives rate. The odometer gives accumulation.

The next chapter builds the second great operation of calculus: adding up infinitely many small changes.

That observation grew into a much larger picture. The derivative gives more than instantaneous rate. It gives shape, turning, bending, bounds, and sometimes limits.

Here is the main dictionary.

\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{calculus evidence} \amp \textbf{graph information}\\ \hline f'(x)>0 \amp f \text{ is increasing}\\ f'(x)<0 \amp f \text{ is decreasing}\\ f'(c)=0 \text{ or } f'(c)\text{ undefined} \amp c \text{ is a critical number candidate}\\ f' \text{ changes } + \text{ to } - \amp \text{local maximum}\\ f' \text{ changes } - \text{ to } + \amp \text{local minimum}\\ f''(x)>0 \amp f \text{ is concave up}\\ f''(x)<0 \amp f \text{ is concave down}\\ f'' \text{ changes sign at } c \amp (c,f(c)) \text{ is an inflection point}\\ f'(c)=0,\ f''(c)>0 \amp \text{local minimum}\\ f'(c)=0,\ f''(c)<0 \amp \text{local maximum} \end{array}

The Mean Value Theorem supplies the bridge from local derivative information to whole-interval information:

f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}

for some

c\in(a,b),

provided f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b).

That bridge proves the first derivative sign rule. It also proves that a function with zero derivative on an interval is constant there.

l’Hospital’s Rule is another derivative bridge. For certain indeterminate quotients, the limiting ratio of two functions can be found from the limiting ratio of their derivatives:

\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x\to a}\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)},

when the hypotheses of the rule are satisfied.

The chapter’s map translates signs of f' and f'' into rising, falling, concavity, extrema, and inflection. In your own words, why is that dictionary more than a list of tests, and what single idea lets local rate information describe the shape of a graph?

The first derivative is about direction of change; the second is about how that direction itself is changing. Sign charts are a way of reading those stories across intervals.

A complete review example

Sketch the graph of

\begin{array}{c|ccc} \text{interval} \amp (-\infty,0) \amp (0,2) \amp (2,\infty)\\ \hline f'(x) \amp + \amp - \amp +\\ f \amp \text{increasing} \amp \text{decreasing} \amp \text{increasing} \end{array}

The values are

f(0)=0,

and

f(2)=\frac13(8)-4=\frac83-\frac{12}{3}=-\frac43.

Now compute the second derivative:

f''(x)=2x-2.

The sign chart for f'' is

\begin{array}{c|cc} \text{interval} \amp (-\infty,1) \amp (1,\infty)\\ \hline f''(x) \amp - \amp +\\ f \amp \text{concave down} \amp \text{concave up} \end{array}

The concavity changes at x=1. Therefore there is an inflection point at

\left(1,f(1)\right) = \left(1,\frac13-1\right) = \left(1,-\frac23\right).

The graph must rise to (0,0), fall to \left(2,-\frac43\right), then rise again. It bends downward before x=1 and upward after x=1.

This example is small, but the workflow is the same for harder functions:

\text{domain, intercepts, asymptotes, } f', f'', \text{ sign charts, then sketch.}

A derivative at a point is local. Claims such as increasing on an interval or constant on an interval compare values. In your own words, why does the Mean Value Theorem make that leap, and what hypotheses must travel with it?

  1. A function with positive derivative is increasing.

    Suppose f is continuous on an interval I, differentiable at the interior points of I, and

    f'(x)>0

  2. A zero derivative forces a constant function.

  2. Find a function with a local minimum at x=0 where the derivative does not exist at 0.

  3. Find a continuous function on [-1,1] that is not differentiable on (-1,1), and for which Rolle’s conclusion fails.

  4. Find a function that is differentiable on (0,1) but not continuous on [0,1], and for which the Mean Value Theorem conclusion fails.

Why are critical numbers and zeros of <m>f''</m> candidates rather than conclusions?

f'(c)=0 need not be an extremum, and f''(c)=0 need not be an inflection point. In your own words, what extra evidence turns a candidate into a conclusion, and why is that warning the same idea in two different disguises?

Look for an actual change: a sign change of f' for extrema, a sign change of f'' for inflection.

Project: reconstruct a trip from acceleration data

A derivative gives rate of change. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:

a(t)=v'(t).

Velocity is the derivative of position:

v(t)=s'(t).

So acceleration is two derivative steps away from position:

s(t) \longrightarrow v(t) \longrightarrow a(t).

This project asks you to walk backward from acceleration data to velocity and position. The exact method belongs to integration, but a finite-step reconstruction already shows the idea.

Suppose a small cart moves along a track. Its acceleration is measured once every second:

\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc} t\text{ (seconds)} \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \amp 3 \amp 4 \amp 5 \amp 6 \amp 7 \amp 8\\ \hline a(t)\text{ (m/s}^2\text{)} \amp 3 \amp 2 \amp 1 \amp 0 \amp -1 \amp -2 \amp -3 \amp -2 \amp -1 \end{array}

Assume

v(0)=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad s(0)=0.

For this project, treat the acceleration as constant on each one-second interval, using the left endpoint value. Thus on the interval from t=k to t=k+1, use

a(t)\approx a(k).

With \Delta t=1, update velocity by

v_{k+1}=v_k+a_k\Delta t.

Then update position in one of two ways.

The rough update is

s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t.

The constant-acceleration update is

s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t+\frac12a_k(\Delta t)^2.

Tasks

  1. Make a table with columns

    k,\quad t_k,\quad a_k,\quad v_k,\quad s_k.

    Use the constant-acceleration update for s_k.

  2. Graph the acceleration data.

  3. Graph the reconstructed velocity.

  4. Graph the reconstructed position.

  5. During which time interval is the cart speeding up? During which time interval is it slowing down? Explain using the signs of v and a.

  6. When is the velocity largest? How can you see this from the acceleration data?

  7. When does the position appear largest? How can you see this from the velocity data?

  8. Repeat the reconstruction with the rough update

    s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t.

    Compare the two position graphs.

  9. Write one paragraph explaining why recovering position from acceleration is an accumulation problem.

  10. Write one paragraph predicting how the next part of calculus should make this finite reconstruction exact.

Use a spreadsheet or a short program to repeat the reconstruction with a smaller time step. For example, try

\Delta t=0.5

using linearly interpolated acceleration data. Compare the graph with the one-second reconstruction.

Fermat, Rolle, the Mean Value Theorem, the second derivative test, and l’Hospital’s Rule each fail when a hypothesis is dropped. In your own words, why is checking hypotheses part of using the theorem, rather than an optional courtesy after the conclusion is written?

If the hypotheses are missing, the conclusion may still be true by luck. But the theorem is no longer the reason.

Discovery problems

  1. How many roots can a derivative control?

    Suppose f is differentiable on an interval and f'(x)>0 throughout the interval. Prove that f(x)=0 has at most one solution.

  2. Two zeros force a zero derivative.

    Suppose f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and

    f(a)=f(b)=0.

    Prove that there is some c\in(a,b) such that

    f'(c)=0.

    Then explain why this is exactly Rolle’s Theorem in a special case.

  3. Three zeros force a zero second derivative.

    Suppose f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and has three zeros in the interval. Assume f'' exists where needed. Prove that there is some point c where

    f''(c)=0.

    Hint: apply Rolle’s Theorem more than once.

  4. A polynomial root-counting fact.

    Use the previous problem to explain why a quadratic polynomial cannot have three distinct real roots unless it is the zero polynomial.

  5. A tangent parallel to a chord.

    Pick a smooth function f and two points a<b. Draw the secant line through

    (a,f(a)) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (b,f(b)).

    Find a point c where the tangent is parallel to that secant. Then verify your picture algebraically.

  6. A horizontal inflection point.

    Find a function f such that

    f'(0)=0,

    but 0 is not a local maximum or local minimum. Explain why your example has a horizontal tangent without a turning point.

  7. A graph from a derivative only.

    Suppose f'(x)=x^2-1 and f(0)=2. Without finding a formula for f(x), decide where f is increasing and decreasing and where it has local extrema. Then, if you know antiderivatives already, find f(x) and check your prediction.

  8. A limit without l’Hospital.

    Evaluate

    \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin(3x)}{x}

    using the standard limit

    \lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin u}{u}=1.

    Then evaluate it again with l’Hospital’s Rule. Compare the two methods.

 Where this points

This chapter taught us how to read a graph from its derivatives. That is already useful: we can locate peaks, valleys, flat points, bends, and asymptotes.

But many real questions do not start by asking for a graph. They ask for a choice.

\text{What shape gives the largest volume?}

\text{What route takes the least time?}

\text{What price gives the greatest profit?}

\text{How fast is one quantity changing when another quantity is changing?}

Those questions still use derivatives, but now the graph is only part of the story. The next chapter turns shape information into decisions: related rates, optimization, and models.

    \begin{array}{c|ccc} \text{interval} \amp (-\infty,1) \amp (1,4) \amp (4,\infty)\\ \hline g''(x) \amp + \amp - \amp + \end{array}

    and g is continuous everywhere. Identify all inflection points forced by the chart.

 Extrema and closed interval practice

  1. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of

    f(x)=x^3-3x+2

    on

    [-2,3].

  2. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of

    g(x)=x+\frac4x

    on

    [1,6].

  3. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of

    h(x)=\sqrt{x}(4-x)

    on

    [0,4].

  4. Let

    p(x)=x^4-8x^2+3.

    Find all local extrema and all absolute extrema on

    [-3,3].

  5. Explain why the function

    f(x)=\frac1x

    has no absolute maximum or minimum on

    (0,1).

    Which hypothesis of the Extreme Value Theorem is missing?

  6. Explain why the function

    f(x)=x

    has no absolute maximum on

    [0,\infty).

    Which hypothesis of the Extreme Value Theorem is missing?

 Mean Value Theorem practice

  1. Verify the hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem for

    f(x)=x^2

    on

    [1,4].

    Find all numbers c\in(1,4) satisfying

    f'(c)=\frac{f(4)-f(1)}{4-1}.

  2. Verify the hypotheses of Rolle’s Theorem for

    f(x)=x^2-4x+3

    on

    [1,3].

    Find the number c promised by the theorem.

  3. Let

    f(x)=\sqrt{x}

    on

    [1,9].

    Find the number c promised by the Mean Value Theorem.

  4. Show that the Mean Value Theorem cannot be applied to

    f(x)=|x|

    on

    [-1,1].

    Then explain why the conclusion fails.

  5. Show that the Mean Value Theorem cannot be applied to

    f(x)= \begin{cases} x, \amp 0\le x<1,\\ 0, \amp x=1 \end{cases}

    on

    [0,1].

    Then explain why the conclusion fails.

  6. A car travels 150 miles in 3 hours. Assume its position is continuous and differentiable during the trip. What does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee about its instantaneous velocity?

  7. Suppose a runner’s position s(t), in meters, is differentiable on [0,10], with

    s(0)=0, \qquad s(10)=80.

    What instantaneous velocity is guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem?

Why is the Mean Value Theorem the bridge from local rates to whole-interval facts?

A derivative at a point is local. Claims such as increasing on an interval or constant on an interval compare values. In your own words, why does the Mean Value Theorem make that leap, and what hypotheses must travel with it?

Some instantaneous rate equals the average rate. If every instantaneous rate is positive, or zero, the corresponding net change is forced.

Proof practice with the Mean Value Theorem

  1. A function with positive derivative is increasing.

    Suppose f is continuous on an interval I, differentiable at the interior points of I, and

    f'(x)>0

    throughout the interior of I. Use the Mean Value Theorem to prove that f is increasing on I.

  2. A zero derivative forces a constant function.

    Suppose

    f'(x)=0

    for every x in an interval I. Use the Mean Value Theorem to prove that f is constant on I.

  3. Equal derivatives differ by a constant.

    Suppose

    f'(x)=g'(x)

    for every x in an interval I. Prove that

    f(x)-g(x)

    is constant on I.

  4. A derivative bound controls total change.

    Suppose |f'(x)|\le M for all x\in[a,b]. Prove that

    |f(b)-f(a)|\le M|b-a|.

  5. Sine changes no faster than its input.

    Use the previous problem with f(x)=\sin x to prove that

    |\sin b-\sin a|\le |b-a|

    for all real numbers a and b.

  6. A uniqueness proof.

    Show that the equation

    x+\cos x=0

    has exactly one solution in the interval [-1,0].

    Hint: use the Intermediate Value Theorem for existence, and the Mean Value Theorem for uniqueness.

  7. A useful logarithm inequality.

    Use the Mean Value Theorem on

    f(x)=\ln x

    to prove that, for x>0,

    \ln x \le x-1.

    When does equality occur?

For each limit, decide first whether l’Hospital’s Rule is legal. Then evaluate the limit, if it exists.

  1. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{2x}-1}{x}.

  2. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}.

  3. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}.

  4. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x-x}{x^3}.

  5. \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln x}{\sqrt{x}}.

  6. \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x^3}{e^x}.

  7. \lim_{x\to0^+}x\ln x.

  8. \lim_{x\to0^+}x^x.

  9. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}.

    Explain why l’Hospital’s Rule is not legal.

  10. \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}.

    Evaluate the limit without l’Hospital’s Rule. Then explain why differentiating the numerator and denominator gives no useful conclusion.

  1. Find a function with a critical number at x=0 but no local extremum at 0.

  2. Find a function with a local minimum at x=0 where the derivative does not exist at 0.

  3. Find a continuous function on [-1,1] that is not differentiable on (-1,1), and for which Rolle’s conclusion fails.

  4. Find a function that is differentiable on (0,1) but not continuous on [0,1], and for which the Mean Value Theorem conclusion fails.

  5. Find a function with

    f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0,

    that has a local maximum at 0.

  6. Find a function with

    f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0,

    that has no local extremum at 0.

  7. Give an example of a quotient where direct substitution gives a real number, but differentiating numerator and denominator gives the wrong limit.

  8. Give an example of a quotient where the original limit exists but the quotient of derivatives has no limit.

Why are critical numbers and zeros of <m>f''</m> candidates rather than conclusions?

f'(c)=0 need not be an extremum, and f''(c)=0 need not be an inflection point. In your own words, what extra evidence turns a candidate into a conclusion, and why is that warning the same idea in two different disguises?

Look for an actual change: a sign change of f' for extrema, a sign change of f'' for inflection.

Project: reconstruct a trip from acceleration data

A derivative gives rate of change. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:

a(t)=v'(t).

Velocity is the derivative of position:

v(t)=s'(t).

So acceleration is two derivative steps away from position:

s(t) \longrightarrow v(t) \longrightarrow a(t).

This project asks you to walk backward from acceleration data to velocity and position. The exact method belongs to integration, but a finite-step reconstruction already shows the idea.

Suppose a small cart moves along a track. Its acceleration is measured once every second:

\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc} t\text{ (seconds)} \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \amp 3 \amp 4 \amp 5 \amp 6 \amp 7 \amp 8\\ \hline a(t)\text{ (m/s}^2\text{)} \amp 3 \amp 2 \amp 1 \amp 0 \amp -1 \amp -2 \amp -3 \amp -2 \amp -1 \end{array}

Assume

v(0)=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad s(0)=0.

For this project, treat the acceleration as constant on each one-second interval, using the left endpoint value. Thus on the interval from t=k to t=k+1, use

a(t)\approx a(k).

With \Delta t=1, update velocity by

v_{k+1}=v_k+a_k\Delta t.

Then update position in one of two ways.

The rough update is

s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t.

The constant-acceleration update is

s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t+\frac12a_k(\Delta t)^2.

Tasks

  1. Make a table with columns

    k,\quad t_k,\quad a_k,\quad v_k,\quad s_k.

    Use the constant-acceleration update for s_k.

  2. Graph the acceleration data.

  3. Graph the reconstructed velocity.

  4. Graph the reconstructed position.

  5. During which time interval is the cart speeding up? During which time interval is it slowing down? Explain using the signs of v and a.

  6. When is the velocity largest? How can you see this from the acceleration data?

  7. When does the position appear largest? How can you see this from the velocity data?

  8. Repeat the reconstruction with the rough update

    s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t.

    Compare the two position graphs.

  9. Write one paragraph explaining why recovering position from acceleration is an accumulation problem.

  10. Write one paragraph predicting how the next part of calculus should make this finite reconstruction exact.

 Optional computing extension

Use a spreadsheet or a short program to repeat the reconstruction with a smaller time step. For example, try

\Delta t=0.5

using linearly interpolated acceleration data. Compare the graph with the one-second reconstruction.

 Why must every theorem in this chapter be used as a hypotheses-to-conclusion package?

Fermat, Rolle, the Mean Value Theorem, the second derivative test, and l’Hospital’s Rule each fail when a hypothesis is dropped. In your own words, why is checking hypotheses part of using the theorem, rather than an optional courtesy after the conclusion is written?

If the hypotheses are missing, the conclusion may still be true by luck. But the theorem is no longer the reason.

Discovery problems

  1. How many roots can a derivative control?

    Suppose f is differentiable on an interval and f'(x)>0 throughout the interval. Prove that f(x)=0 has at most one solution.

  2. Two zeros force a zero derivative.

    Suppose f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and

    f(a)=f(b)=0.

    Prove that there is some c\in(a,b) such that

    f'(c)=0.

    Then explain why this is exactly Rolle’s Theorem in a special case.

  3. Three zeros force a zero second derivative.

    Suppose f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and has three zeros in the interval. Assume f'' exists where needed. Prove that there is some point c where

    f''(c)=0.

    Hint: apply Rolle’s Theorem more than once.

  4. A polynomial root-counting fact.

    Use the previous problem to explain why a quadratic polynomial cannot have three distinct real roots unless it is the zero polynomial.

  5. A tangent parallel to a chord.

    Pick a smooth function f and two points a<b. Draw the secant line through

    (a,f(a)) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (b,f(b)).

    Find a point c where the tangent is parallel to that secant. Then verify your picture algebraically.

  6. A horizontal inflection point.

    Find a function f such that

    f'(0)=0,

    but 0 is not a local maximum or local minimum. Explain why your example has a horizontal tangent without a turning point.

  7. A graph from a derivative only.

    Suppose f'(x)=x^2-1 and f(0)=2. Without finding a formula for f(x), decide where f is increasing and decreasing and where it has local extrema. Then, if you know antiderivatives already, find f(x) and check your prediction.

  8. A limit without l’Hospital.

    Evaluate

    \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin(3x)}{x}

    using the standard limit

    \lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin u}{u}=1.

    Then evaluate it again with l’Hospital’s Rule. Compare the two methods.

 Where this points

This chapter taught us how to read a graph from its derivatives. That is already useful: we can locate peaks, valleys, flat points, bends, and asymptotes.

But many real questions do not start by asking for a graph. They ask for a choice.

\text{What shape gives the largest volume?}

\text{What route takes the least time?}

\text{What price gives the greatest profit?}

\text{How fast is one quantity changing when another quantity is changing?}

Those questions still use derivatives, but now the graph is only part of the story. The next chapter turns shape information into decisions: related rates, optimization, and models.

Chapter 4 defined the derivative:

f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

That definition gave meaning, but it was too slow for everyday use.

Chapter 5 built a working language. We learned how derivatives behave under algebra, composition, implicit relations, inverse functions, and the elementary functions. The point was not to memorize a long table. The point was to read structure.

Why does the way a function is built determine the derivative rule?

Chapter 5 has one main story: how a function is built determines how its derivative is built. In your own words, why are a sum, a product, a quotient, a composition, and an inverse different constructions, and why is reading the structure the first step rather than a race to symbols?

Each construction changes for a different reason. The table of elementary derivatives is useful only when paired with the matching rule.

Derivative table

The main elementary derivative formulas from this chapter are collected below. Each formula is valid on intervals where the function is defined and differentiable.

\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{function} \amp \textbf{derivative}\\ \hline c \amp 0\\ x \amp 1\\ x^r \amp rx^{r-1}\\ e^x \amp e^x\\ a^x \amp (\ln a)a^x,\quad a>0\\ \ln x \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x>0\\ \ln|x| \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x\neq0\\ \sin x \amp \cos x\\ \cos x \amp -\sin x\\ \tan x \amp \sec^2x\\ \sec x \amp \sec x\tan x\\ \csc x \amp -\csc x\cot x\\ \cot x \amp -\csc^2x\\ \arcsin x \amp \dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arccos x \amp -\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arctan x \amp \dfrac1{1+x^2}\\ \sinh x \amp \cosh x\\ \cosh x \amp \sinh x\\ \tanh x \amp \operatorname{sech}^2x \end{array}

The table is only useful when paired with the rules:

(af+bg)'\amp=af'+bg', (fg)'\amp=f'g+fg', \left(\frac fg\right)'\amp=\frac{gf'-fg'}{g^2}, (f(g(x)))'\amp=f'(g(x))g'(x).

Most real derivative calculations use both a table formula and a rule.

 Worked mixed examples Example

Differentiate

F(x)=e^{-x}\cos(2x)+\ln(1+x^2).

The first term is a product:

e^{-x}\cos(2x).

Differentiate each factor:

\frac{d}{dx}e^{-x}=-e^{-x},

and

\frac{d}{dx}\cos(2x)=-2\sin(2x).

So

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = (-e^{-x})\cos(2x)+e^{-x}(-2\sin(2x)).

Thus

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x).

The logarithmic term uses the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\ln(1+x^2)=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

Therefore

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

We can factor the first two terms if desired:

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\bigl(\cos(2x)+2\sin(2x)\bigr) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

 Example

Differentiate

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

This function has a variable exponent. Since the base is always positive,

x^2+1>0,

logarithmic differentiation is safe.

Take natural logarithms:

\ln y=\sin x\ln(x^2+1).

Differentiate both sides:

\frac{y'}{y} = \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \sin x\cdot\frac{2x}{x^2+1}.

Multiply by y:

y' = y\left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

Substitute back

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

Thus

y' = (x^2+1)^{\sin x} \left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

This example uses several ideas at once: logarithms, product rule, chain rule, and the fact that x^2+1 is positive.

 Example

Find dy/dx if

x^2y+\sin y=e^x.

Here y is treated as a function of x. Differentiate both sides with respect to x.

For x^2y, use the product rule:

\frac{d}{dx}(x^2y)=2xy+x^2y'.

For \sin y, use the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\sin y=\cos y\,y'.

For e^x,

\frac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x.

Therefore

2xy+x^2y'+\cos y\,y'=e^x.

Collect the y'-terms:

(x^2+\cos y)y'=e^x-2xy.

So

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{e^x-2xy}{x^2+\cos y}.

The denominator warns us: if

x^2+\cos y=0,

then this equation does not determine a finite value of dy/dx. The algebra may be pointing to a vertical tangent or to a place where the curve is not a single differentiable branch y(x).

Why do implicit and inverse derivatives reverse two different things?

Implicit differentiation treats y as changing because x changes, even with no formula y=f(x). The inverse rule reverses a graph and therefore reverses slope. In your own words, why are those two ideas related to the chain rule, yet not the same task?

One starts from a relation and solves for dy/dx. The other starts from a reversible function and takes the reciprocal slope at the matching point.

Chapter 5 has one main story: how a function is built determines how its derivative is built. In your own words, why are a sum, a product, a quotient, a composition, and an inverse different constructions, and why is reading the structure the first step rather than a race to symbols?

Each construction changes for a different reason. The table of elementary derivatives is useful only when paired with the matching rule.

Derivative table

The main elementary derivative formulas from this chapter are collected below. Each formula is valid on intervals where the function is defined and differentiable.

\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{function} \amp \textbf{derivative}\\ \hline c \amp 0\\ x \amp 1\\ x^r \amp rx^{r-1}\\ e^x \amp e^x\\ a^x \amp (\ln a)a^x,\quad a>0\\ \ln x \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x>0\\ \ln|x| \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x\neq0\\ \sin x \amp \cos x\\ \cos x \amp -\sin x\\ \tan x \amp \sec^2x\\ \sec x \amp \sec x\tan x\\ \csc x \amp -\csc x\cot x\\ \cot x \amp -\csc^2x\\ \arcsin x \amp \dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arccos x \amp -\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arctan x \amp \dfrac1{1+x^2}\\ \sinh x \amp \cosh x\\ \cosh x \amp \sinh x\\ \tanh x \amp \operatorname{sech}^2x \end{array}

 Worked mixed examples Example

Differentiate

F(x)=e^{-x}\cos(2x)+\ln(1+x^2).

The first term is a product:

e^{-x}\cos(2x).

Differentiate each factor:

\frac{d}{dx}e^{-x}=-e^{-x},

and

\frac{d}{dx}\cos(2x)=-2\sin(2x).

So

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = (-e^{-x})\cos(2x)+e^{-x}(-2\sin(2x)).

Thus

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x).

The logarithmic term uses the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\ln(1+x^2)=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

Therefore

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

We can factor the first two terms if desired:

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\bigl(\cos(2x)+2\sin(2x)\bigr) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

 Example

Differentiate

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

This function has a variable exponent. Since the base is always positive,

x^2+1>0,

logarithmic differentiation is safe.

Take natural logarithms:

\ln y=\sin x\ln(x^2+1).

Differentiate both sides:

\frac{y'}{y} = \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \sin x\cdot\frac{2x}{x^2+1}.

Multiply by y:

y' = y\left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

Substitute back

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

Thus

y' = (x^2+1)^{\sin x} \left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

This example uses several ideas at once: logarithms, product rule, chain rule, and the fact that x^2+1 is positive.

 Example

Find dy/dx if

x^2y+\sin y=e^x.

Here y is treated as a function of x. Differentiate both sides with respect to x.

For x^2y, use the product rule:

\frac{d}{dx}(x^2y)=2xy+x^2y'.

For \sin y, use the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\sin y=\cos y\,y'.

For e^x,

\frac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x.

Therefore

2xy+x^2y'+\cos y\,y'=e^x.

Collect the y'-terms:

(x^2+\cos y)y'=e^x-2xy.

So

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{e^x-2xy}{x^2+\cos y}.

The denominator warns us: if

x^2+\cos y=0,

then this equation does not determine a finite value of dy/dx. The algebra may be pointing to a vertical tangent or to a place where the curve is not a single differentiable branch y(x).

Warning examples

This chapter has given us speed. We no longer need to return to the limit definition every time we differentiate. We have rules.

That speed is useful, but it also creates a danger. A rule that is remembered only as a symbol can be used in the wrong place.

The safest way to use derivative rules is to keep asking:

\text{How was this function built?}

A sum, a product, a quotient, a composition, and an inverse are different constructions. Their derivatives are different because their changes are different.

 The product rule is not <m>(fg)'=f'g'</m>

A common mistake is to guess that the derivative of a product is the product of the derivatives:

(fg)' \stackrel{\text{wrong}}{=} f'g'.

This is false.

Take the simplest possible example:

f(x)=x, \qquad g(x)=x.

Then

f(x)g(x)=x^2.

So

(fg)'(x)=2x.

But

f'(x)g'(x)=1\cdot1=1.

These are not the same. For example, at x=3,

(fg)'(3)=6, \qquad f'(3)g'(3)=1.

The correct rule is

(fg)'=f'g+fg'.

This rule has a geometric picture visualization. If a rectangle has side lengths f(x) and g(x), then its area is

A(x)=f(x)g(x).

When x changes a little, both sides may change. The new area comes from two first-order strips:

f'(x)g(x)\Delta x \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(x)g'(x)\Delta x.

That is why two terms appear.

For exact finite changes, write \Delta f=f(x+\Delta x)-f(x) and \Delta g=g(x+\Delta x)-g(x). Then

\Delta(fg) = (f+\Delta f)(g+\Delta g)-fg.

Expanding,

\Delta(fg)=f\,\Delta g+g\,\Delta f+\Delta f\,\Delta g.

For differentiable factors, \Delta f\,\Delta g divided by \Delta x approaches zero. Dividing the exact identity by \Delta x and passing to the limit gives

(fg)'=fg'+gf'.

The false rule f'g' forgets the original sizes f and g. But the original sizes matter. A small change in the width of a large rectangle adds more area than the same change in the width of a small rectangle.

Another quick test

Let

f(x)=x^2, \qquad g(x)=\sin x.

Then

(fg)'=2x\sin x+x^2\cos x.

But

f'g'=(2x)(\cos x)=2x\cos x.

The false rule loses the term 2x\sin x and changes the other term. It is not a small error. It is a different derivative.

Product warning

Do not multiply derivatives. Differentiate the product by letting each factor change once:

(fg)'=f'g+fg'.

Why is the derivative of a product not the product of the derivatives?

The false rule (fg)'=f'g' forgets the original sizes of the factors. In your own words, why do those sizes matter, and what do the two first-order strips record that the false rule throws away?

A small change in the width of a large rectangle adds more area than the same change in a small rectangle. Each factor must change once, weighted by the other factor.

The chain rule needs the order of composition

The chain rule is a rule for functions built in layers. The order of the layers matters.

Let

f(u)=\sin u, \qquad g(x)=x^2.

There are two different composites:

f(g(x))=\sin(x^2),

and

g(f(x))=(\sin x)^2.

They use the same two functions, but in different orders.

Differentiate the first one:

\frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2) = \cos(x^2)\cdot 2x.

So

\frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2)=2x\cos(x^2).

Differentiate the second one:

\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x)^2 = 2\sin x\cdot\cos x.

So

\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x)^2=2\sin x\cos x.

These are not the same derivative because the original functions are not the same function.

The chain rule says

\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x))=f'(g(x))g'(x).

The outside derivative is evaluated at the inside value. That detail is easy to miss.

For

y=\sin(x^2),

the outside function is

f(u)=\sin u.

Its derivative is

f'(u)=\cos u.

At the current inside value

u=x^2,

this becomes

\cos(x^2).

Then we multiply by the inside derivative

\frac{d}{dx}(x^2)=2x.

So the derivative is

2x\cos(x^2).

A wrong answer and why it is wrong

For

y=\sin(x^2),

a common wrong answer is

2\sin x\cos x.

But that is the derivative of

(\sin x)^2,

not of

\sin(x^2).

The mistake changed the order of construction.

before:
Optimization problems

The previous chapter taught us how to find high and low points of a function. Optimization turns that skill into a method for solving word problems.

A real question rarely arrives as

\text{maximize } f(x).

It arrives as a sentence:

\text{Build the largest box from this sheet of cardboard.}

\text{Use the least metal for this can.}

\text{Enclose the most area with this much fence.}

The first task is not calculus. The first task is translation.

\text{situation} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{function} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{derivative} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{decision}.

 Translating a word problem into a function

A farmer has 200 meters of fencing and wants to enclose a rectangular field along a straight river. The river forms one side of the rectangle, so fencing is needed only for the other three sides.

What dimensions give the largest area?

Let

x=\text{the width perpendicular to the river}

and

y=\text{the length parallel to the river}.

The fencing is used for two widths and one length:

2x+y=200.

The area is

A=xy.

We want to maximize A, but right now A uses two variables. Use the constraint

2x+y=200

to solve for y:

y=200-2x.

Then

A(x)=x(200-2x)=200x-2x^2.

Now the problem is a one-variable calculus problem.

The physical domain is

0\le x\le 100.

If x=0, the rectangle has no width. If x=100, then y=0. Both give area 0. For 0<x<100, the rectangle has positive area.

Differentiate:

A'(x)=200-4x.

Set the derivative equal to 0:

200-4x=0.

Thus

x=50.

Then

y=200-2(50)=100.

Since A''(x)=-4<0, the area is concave down; also A(0)=A(100)=0 and A(50)=5000. Thus the absolute maximum area occurs when

x=50,\qquad y=100.

The farmer should build a field 50 meters wide and 100 meters long.

The optimization translation

objectivethe quantity to maximize or minimizeconstraintthe condition that limits the choicesdomainthe physically meaningful values of the variable

In the fencing problem, the objective was area, the constraint was the amount of fencing, and the domain came from requiring nonnegative side lengths.

Why is the first task of optimization translation, not calculus?

A real question arrives as a sentence about a box, a fence, or a can, not as maximize f(x). In your own words, why must we first name the objective, the constraint, and the domain, and why is that translation already most of the mathematics?

The derivative can only act on a function. Until the situation has been written as a function of one variable, there is nothing to differentiate.

Constraints in one variable

Many optimization problems begin with several quantities. The constraint is what lets us reduce to one variable.

The general pattern is:

\text{objective } Q=Q(x,y)

together with

\text{constraint relating }x\text{ and }y.

Use the constraint to write

y=\text{a formula in }x.

Then

Q=Q(x)

becomes a one-variable function.

Optimization workflow

  1. Identify the quantity to optimize.

  2. Name the variables.

  3. Write the objective function.

  4. Write the constraint.

  5. Use the constraint to get one variable.

  6. Find the physical domain.

  7. Use derivatives and endpoint checks.

  8. Translate the answer back into the problem.

The domain is not optional. It is part of the model.

A critical number outside the physical domain is not a possible solution. An endpoint inside the domain may be the best solution.

Why does a constraint reduce an optimization problem to one variable?

Many problems begin with two quantities linked by a restriction, such as a fixed amount of fencing. In your own words, why do we use that restriction to eliminate a variable, and what would go wrong if we differentiated an objective that still contained two independent inputs?

The constraint is what makes the choices depend on one another. After substituting, the objective becomes an ordinary one-variable function.

Geometry: boxes, fences, cans, and light paths

Geometry problems are good training because the constraints are visible.

the largest open box from a square sheet

A square sheet of cardboard is 12 inches by 12 inches. Equal squares of side length x are cut from the four corners. The sides are folded up to make an open box.

What value of x gives the largest volume?

After cutting, the base has side length

12-2x.

The height is

x.

So the volume is

V(x)=x(12-2x)^2.

The physical domain is

0\le x\le 6.

At x=0, no box is formed. At x=6, the base has side length 0. Both endpoints give volume 0.

Differentiate:

V(x)=x(12-2x)^2.

Using the product and chain rules,

V'(x) = (12-2x)^2+x\cdot 2(12-2x)(-2).

Factor:

V'(x) = (12-2x)\bigl((12-2x)-4x\bigr).

Thus

V'(x) = (12-2x)(12-6x).

The critical numbers are

x=6 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=2.

The number x=6 is an endpoint. The interior critical number is x=2.

Check the volumes:

V(0)=0,

V(2)=2(12-4)^2=2(8)^2=128,

V(6)=0.

Therefore the largest volume occurs at

x=2

inches. The box dimensions are

8\text{ in}\times 8\text{ in}\times 2\text{ in}.

 the least material for a closed can

A closed cylindrical can must hold volume V_0. What shape uses the least surface area?

Let

r=\text{radius}

and

h=\text{height}.

The volume constraint is

\pi r^2h=V_0.

The surface area of a closed cylinder is

S=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh.

Use the constraint to solve for h:

h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}.

Substitute into S:

S(r) = 2\pi r^2+2\pi r\left(\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}\right).

So

S(r)=2\pi r^2+\frac{2V_0}{r}, \qquad r>0.

Differentiate:

S'(r)=4\pi r-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}.

Set S'(r)=0:

4\pi r-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}=0.

Multiply by r^2:

4\pi r^3-2V_0=0.

Thus

2\pi r^3=V_0.

Now compute the corresponding height:

h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}.

Since V_0=2\pi r^3,

h=\frac{2\pi r^3}{\pi r^2}=2r.

Therefore the least-material closed can satisfies

h=2r.

The height equals the diameter.

A second derivative check confirms this critical point is a minimum:

S''(r)=4\pi+\frac{4V_0}{r^3}>0.

So S is concave up at every positive r. The critical point is the least surface area.

 the shortest reflected path

A point A is located a units above a straight mirror, and a point B is located b units above the same mirror. Their horizontal separation is L. A light ray travels from A to the mirror and then to B. Where should it hit the mirror to make the total distance as small as possible?

Place the mirror on the x-axis. Let

A=(0,a), \qquad B=(L,b),

and let the reflection point be

P=(x,0).

The total distance is

D(x)=\sqrt{x^2+a^2}+\sqrt{(L-x)^2+b^2}.

The physical domain is

0\le x\le L.

Differentiate:

D'(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} - \frac{L-x}{\sqrt{(L-x)^2+b^2}}.

At the shortest path, an interior critical point must satisfy

\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} = \frac{L-x}{\sqrt{(L-x)^2+b^2}}.

Both sides are positive, so square:

\frac{x^2}{x^2+a^2} = \frac{(L-x)^2}{(L-x)^2+b^2}.

Cross-multiply:

x^2\bigl((L-x)^2+b^2\bigr) = (L-x)^2(x^2+a^2).

Cancel the matching term x^2(L-x)^2:

b^2x^2=a^2(L-x)^2.

Taking positive square roots gives

bx=a(L-x).

Therefore

(a+b)x=aL,

so

x=\frac{aL}{a+b}.

Here a,b,L>0. The second derivative is D''(x)=a^2/(x^2+a^2)^{3/2}+b^2/((L-x)^2+b^2)^{3/2}>0, and the critical point lies in (0,L), so it is the unique absolute minimum. This condition is the familiar reflection rule: the incoming and outgoing angles are equal. The derivative has found the law of reflection from a shortest-path principle.

 Endpoint checks and physical feasibility

Optimization problems are not finished when we find a critical number.

A critical number is a candidate. It may give a maximum, a minimum, neither, or it may not be physically allowed.

The correct conclusion depends on the domain.

Closed interval method for applications

If the objective function is continuous on a closed interval, then:

  1. Find the critical numbers inside the interval.

  2. Evaluate the objective function at those critical numbers.

  3. Evaluate the objective function at the endpoints.

  4. Compare the values.

In the open-box problem, the domain was

0\le x\le 6.

The endpoints gave

V(0)=0, \qquad V(6)=0.

The interior critical point gave

V(2)=128.

So x=2 gave the absolute maximum.

But endpoints do not always lose. If a problem asks for a minimum, an endpoint may win. If a domain is open, the best value may not be attained at all. If a critical point lies outside the physical domain, it is irrelevant.

Warning example: a critical point outside the domain

Suppose a company models profit from selling q units by

P(q)=-q^2+40q-300.

The derivative is

P'(q)=-2q+40.

The critical point is

q=20.

If the company can produce any number of units between 0 and 50, then q=20 is a real candidate. But if a contract requires

30\le q\le 50,

then q=20 is not physically allowed. On the interval [30,50],

P'(q)=-2q+40<0.

So P is decreasing throughout the allowed interval. The maximum allowed profit occurs at the endpoint

q=30.

The derivative found the best point for the wrong domain.

The domain is part of the problem

A formula alone does not know what choices are possible. The domain tells the formula which choices are allowed.

Related rates asked how fast quantities change together. Optimization asked which choice is best. Both depended on building a model and then reading a derivative.

But real measurements are rarely exact. A radius may be 3 cm only to the nearest millimeter. A length may have a small error. The next question is not the best exact choice, but how sensitive an answer is to small changes.

 Why is the domain part of the problem, not an afterthought?

A critical number may give a max, a min, neither, or a value that is not physically allowed. In your own words, why must we check endpoints and feasibility, and why can the derivative find the best point for the wrong domain?

A formula alone does not know what choices are possible. Endpoints can win, and a critical point outside the allowed interval is irrelevant.

S(r)=2\pi r^2+\frac{2V_0}{r}, \qquad r>0.

Differentiate:

S'(r)=4\pi r-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}.

Set S'(r)=0:

4\pi r-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}=0.

Multiply by r^2:

4\pi r^3-2V_0=0.

Thus

2\pi r^3=V_0.

Now compute the corresponding height:

h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}.

Since V_0=2\pi r^3,

h=\frac{2\pi r^3}{\pi r^2}=2r.

Therefore the least-material closed can satisfies

h=2r.

The height equals the diameter.

A second derivative check confirms this critical point is a minimum:

S''(r)=4\pi+\frac{4V_0}{r^3}>0.

So S is concave up at every positive r. The critical point is the least surface area.

 the shortest reflected path

A point A is located a units above a straight mirror, and a point B is located b units above the same mirror. Their horizontal separation is L. A light ray travels from A to the mirror and then to B. Where should it hit the mirror to make the total distance as small as possible?

Place the mirror on the x-axis. Let

A=(0,a), \qquad B=(L,b),

and let the reflection point be

P=(x,0).

The total distance is

D(x)=\sqrt{x^2+a^2}+\sqrt{(L-x)^2+b^2}.

The physical domain is

0\le x\le L.

Differentiate:

D'(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} - \frac{L-x}{\sqrt{(L-x)^2+b^2}}.

At the shortest path, an interior critical point must satisfy

\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} = \frac{L-x}{\sqrt{(L-x)^2+b^2}}.

Both sides are positive, so square:

\frac{x^2}{x^2+a^2} = \frac{(L-x)^2}{(L-x)^2+b^2}.

Cross-multiply:

x^2\bigl((L-x)^2+b^2\bigr) = (L-x)^2(x^2+a^2).

Cancel the matching term x^2(L-x)^2:

b^2x^2=a^2(L-x)^2.

Taking positive square roots gives

bx=a(L-x).

Therefore

(a+b)x=aL,

so

x=\frac{aL}{a+b}.

Here a,b,L>0. The second derivative is D''(x)=a^2/(x^2+a^2)^{3/2}+b^2/((L-x)^2+b^2)^{3/2}>0, and the critical point lies in (0,L), so it is the unique absolute minimum. This condition is the familiar reflection rule: the incoming and outgoing angles are equal. The derivative has found the law of reflection from a shortest-path principle.

 Endpoint checks and physical feasibility

Optimization problems are not finished when we find a critical number.

A critical number is a candidate. It may give a maximum, a minimum, neither, or it may not be physically allowed.

The correct conclusion depends on the domain.

Closed interval method for applications

If the objective function is continuous on a closed interval, then:

  1. Find the critical numbers inside the interval.

  2. Evaluate the objective function at those critical numbers.

  3. Evaluate the objective function at the endpoints.

  4. Compare the values.

In the open-box problem, the domain was

0\le x\le 6.

The endpoints gave

V(0)=0, \qquad V(6)=0.

The interior critical point gave

V(2)=128.

So x=2 gave the absolute maximum.

But endpoints do not always lose. If a problem asks for a minimum, an endpoint may win. If a domain is open, the best value may not be attained at all. If a critical point lies outside the physical domain, it is irrelevant.

Warning example: a critical point outside the domain

Suppose a company models profit from selling q units by

P(q)=-q^2+40q-300.

The derivative is

P'(q)=-2q+40.

The critical point is

q=20.

If the company can produce any number of units between 0 and 50, then q=20 is a real candidate. But if a contract requires

30\le q\le 50,

then q=20 is not physically allowed. On the interval [30,50],

P'(q)=-2q+40<0.

So P is decreasing throughout the allowed interval. The maximum allowed profit occurs at the endpoint

q=30.

The derivative found the best point for the wrong domain.

The domain is part of the problem

A formula alone does not know what choices are possible. The domain tells the formula which choices are allowed.

Related rates asked how fast quantities change together. Optimization asked which choice is best. Both depended on building a model and then reading a derivative.

But real measurements are rarely exact. A radius may be 3 cm only to the nearest millimeter. A length may have a small error. The next question is not the best exact choice, but how sensitive an answer is to small changes.

 Why is the domain part of the problem, not an afterthought?

A critical number may give a max, a min, neither, or a value that is not physically allowed. In your own words, why must we check endpoints and feasibility, and why can the derivative find the best point for the wrong domain?

A formula alone does not know what choices are possible. Endpoints can win, and a critical point outside the allowed interval is irrelevant.

surface area of a sphere

Rotate the upper semicircle

x=R\cos t, \qquad y=R\sin t, \qquad 0\le t\le\pi,

around the x-axis. This produces a sphere of radius R.

We already know the speed:

\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2+ \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2} = R.

Therefore

S= 2\pi\int_0^\pi (R\sin t)(R)\,dt.

So

S=2\pi R^2\int_0^\pi \sin t\,dt.

Since

\int_0^\pi \sin t\,dt=2,

we get

S=4\pi R^2.

The familiar surface area of a sphere is again an accumulated band area.

Vibrations and second-order equations

Chapter already introduced second-order equations through vibrating systems. A spring gave us

y''+\omega^2y=0.

At that time, sine and cosine solved the equation because their second derivatives return negative copies of themselves.

Complex numbers explain the deeper reason:

\text{oscillation is the shadow of rotation.}

A point rotating in the complex plane has a horizontal shadow \cos(\omega t) and a vertical shadow \sin(\omega t). Those shadows move back and forth. The spring motion is one such shadow.

 The spring equation

Picture a mass m>0 attached to a spring on a frictionless horizontal track.

Let

y(t)=\text{displacement from equilibrium at time }t.

The equilibrium position is

y=0.

Positive y means the mass is displaced to the right. Negative y means the mass is displaced to the left.

Hooke’s law says that the spring force is proportional to displacement and points back toward equilibrium:

F_{\text{spring}}=-ky, \qquad k>0.

Newton’s second law says

F=ma.

Here acceleration is the second derivative:

a=y''.

Thus

my''=-ky.

Rearrange:

my''+ky=0.

Divide by m:

y''+\frac{k}{m}y=0.

It is customary to write

\omega^2=\frac{k}{m}, \qquad \omega>0.

Then the equation becomes

y''+\omega^2y=0.

This is the simple harmonic oscillator.

The equation says

y''=-\omega^2y.

So the acceleration always points opposite the displacement. When the mass is to the right, acceleration points left. When the mass is to the left, acceleration points right.

That is what makes the motion reverse.

A second-order equation needs two initial conditions. To know how the mass will move, we need both its initial position and its initial velocity:

y(0)=y_0, \qquad y'(0)=v_0.

Position alone is not enough. If the mass is at y=1, it could be moving right, moving left, or momentarily stopped. Those motions have different futures.

Why is a spring a second-order equation?

Newton’s law plus Hooke’s law produce y''+\omega^2 y=0. In your own words, why does a restoring force become a statement about the second derivative, and why is position alone not enough to determine the future motion?

Force determines acceleration, which is y''. The same position can be moving right, moving left, or stopped, so the initial velocity is a second piece of data.

Sine and cosine as natural motions

The complex function

z(t)=e^{i\omega t}

satisfies

Fourier series preview

A single spring gives one clean frequency:

\cos(\omega t) \qquad\text{or}\qquad \sin(\omega t).

But real periodic motion is rarely one pure wave. A violin string, an electrical signal, a heartbeat, a tide table, and a repeating temperature pattern all contain mixtures.

Taylor series built functions from powers:

1,\ x,\ x^2,\ x^3,\ldots.

Fourier series build periodic functions from waves:

1,\ \cos t,\ \sin t,\ \cos(2t),\ \sin(2t),\ \cos(3t),\ \sin(3t),\ldots.

This section is a preview. The full convergence theory belongs to a later course. But the main idea is already visible with the calculus we know:

\text{Fourier series use integrals to measure how much of each wave is present.}

Building a periodic function from waves

A function f is periodic with period 2\pi if

f(t+2\pi)=f(t)

for every t.

The basic waves

\cos(nt) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sin(nt)

are all 2\pi-periodic when n is a positive integer. The integer n counts how many full oscillations occur during one interval of length 2\pi.

A finite mixture of these waves has the form

P_N(t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{N} \bigl(a_n\cos(nt)+b_n\sin(nt)\bigr).

This is called a trigonometric polynomial. It is a finite Fourier approximation.

Fourier idea

For a 2\pi-periodic function f, try to write

f(t) \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \bigl(a_n\cos(nt)+b_n\sin(nt)\bigr).

The coefficients a_n and b_n measure how much of each cosine and sine wave is present.

The symbol

\sim

is being used carefully. It means “has Fourier series.” It does not automatically mean that the series converges everywhere to f(t). Convergence is part of the deeper theory.

Still, the guiding picture is simple:

\text{complicated periodic motion can often be approximated by adding simple waves.}

This is why Fourier series belong after vibrations. One oscillator gives one wave. Many oscillators, or one complicated periodic signal, give a mixture.

Why do Fourier series use waves instead of powers?

Taylor series build functions from powers near a center. Fourier series build periodic functions from sines and cosines over a cycle. In your own words, why is that a different question, and why does the symbol \sim warn that having a Fourier series is not automatically the same as equaling it everywhere?

A repeating shape asks which frequencies are present, not how the function looks near one point. Convergence of the wave series is a separate, deeper issue, especially at jumps.

Orthogonality of sine and cosine, geometrically

To find the coefficients in a Fourier series, we need a way to measure how much one function points in the direction of another.

For ordinary vectors, the dot product measures alignment. Perpendicular vectors have dot product zero.

For functions on [-\pi,\pi], the analogous dot product is an integral:

\langle f,g\rangle = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)g(t)\,dt.

If

\langle f,g\rangle=0,

we say the functions are orthogonal on [-\pi,\pi].

This language is geometric. The functions are being treated like vectors, but with infinitely many coordinates.

Why do integrals measure how much of each wave is present?

On [-\pi,\pi], the inner product of two functions is an integral, and distinct sine and cosine waves are orthogonal. In your own words, why is that the analogue of a dot product, and why does orthogonality let you extract one coefficient without the others interfering?

Perpendicular vectors have dot product zero, so projection onto one direction ignores the others. Integrating a function against one wave is the same idea: the other waves contribute signed area zero over a full period.

Example

The functions \sin t and \sin(2t) are orthogonal on [-\pi,\pi], because

\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin t\sin(2t)\,dt=0.

Use the product-to-sum identity

\sin A\sin B = \frac12\bigl(\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)\bigr).

With A=t and B=2t,

\sin t\sin(2t) = \frac12\bigl(\cos t-\cos(3t)\bigr).

Therefore

\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin t\sin(2t)\,dt = \frac12\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos t\,dt - \frac12\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos(3t)\,dt.

Both integrals are zero over a full symmetric period. Hence

\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin t\sin(2t)\,dt=0.

The same cancellation happens systematically. If m and n are positive integers, then

\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos(mt)\cos(nt)\,dt=0 \qquad\text{when }m\neq n,

\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin(mt)\sin(nt)\,dt=0 \qquad\text{when }m\neq n,

and

\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin(mt)\cos(nt)\,dt=0

for all m,n.

The only time a sine or cosine wave has nonzero dot product with itself is when the frequencies match:

\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2(nt)\,dt=\pi, \qquad n\ge1,

The one-dimensional Stokes theorem

The Fundamental Theorem told us that

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).

At first, this was an antiderivative rule. It let us evaluate integrals. But there is a deeper geometric reading:

\text{what accumulates inside an interval is measured by what happens on its boundary.}

In one dimension, the boundary of an interval consists of two endpoints. The right endpoint counts positively. The left endpoint counts negatively.

That signed boundary is the seed of Stokes’ theorem.

 Boundary of an interval

An interval is not just a set of points. When we write

\int_a^b f(x)\,dx,

we are traveling from a to b. The direction matters. Reversing the direction changes the sign:

\int_b^a f(x)\,dx=-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.

So the oriented interval from a to b has an oriented boundary.

\partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}.

This notation says:

\text{right endpoint} \quad - \quad \text{left endpoint}.

The endpoint b has sign +. The endpoint a has sign -.

This sign convention is not decoration. It is what makes intervals add correctly.

Suppose

a<c<b.

Then the interval [a,b] can be split into

[a,c] \qquad\text{and}\qquad [c,b].

Their boundaries are

\partial[a,c]=\{c\}-\{a\},

and

\partial[c,b]=\{b\}-\{c\}.

Add them:

\bigl(\{c\}-\{a\}\bigr)+\bigl(\{b\}-\{c\}\bigr)=\{b\}-\{a\}.

The interior point c cancels.

\text{interior boundaries cancel; only the outer boundary remains.}

This is the same cancellation that appeared in finite differences. If

a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b,

then

\bigl(F(x_1)-F(x_0)\bigr) + \bigl(F(x_2)-F(x_1)\bigr) + \cdots + \bigl(F(x_n)-F(x_{n-1})\bigr) = F(b)-F(a).

All the interior values cancel. The boundary values survive.

The Fundamental Theorem is the limiting version of this telescoping idea.

Why is the boundary of an interval two signed endpoints?

The oriented interval from a to b has boundary \{b\}-\{a\}. In your own words, why does direction matter, and why do those opposite signs make split intervals add correctly?

Traveling from a to b arrives at b and leaves a. If you split at an interior point, the extra interior endpoint is counted plus and then minus, so it cancels.

<m>\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)</m>

Let F be differentiable on [a,b], with F' continuous. Then the Fundamental Theorem gives

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).

We can now read the formula in boundary language:

F(b)-F(a) = \text{value of \(F\) on the signed boundary } \{b\}-\{a\}.

So

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx = \int_{\partial[a,b]} F.

The notation on the right is only a compact way to say

\int_{\partial[a,b]} F = F(b)-F(a).

It is not a new kind of ordinary integral yet. It is boundary bookkeeping.

Example

Let

F(x)=x^3.

Then

F'(x)=3x^2.

On the interval [1,3],

\int_1^3 3x^2\,dx = F(3)-F(1) = 27-1 = 26.

The integral of the derivative over the interval is determined entirely by the endpoint values of F.

 reversing the orientation

Again let

F(x)=x^3.

Then

\int_3^1 3x^2\,dx = F(1)-F(3) = 1-27 = -26.

The same interval with the opposite orientation has the opposite boundary:

\partial[3,1]=\{1\}-\{3\}.

So the sign changes exactly as it should.

 Warning: jumps are not ordinary derivatives

The theorem requires F to be differentiable on the interval. If F jumps, the ordinary derivative does not capture the jump.

Consider the step function

H(x)= \begin{cases} 0, \amp x<0,\\ 1, \amp x\ge0. \end{cases}

On [-1,1], the endpoint change is

H(1)-H(-1)=1-0=1.

But H is not differentiable at 0. Away from 0, it is constant, so its derivative is 0 where the derivative exists.

If we tried to integrate the ordinary derivative away from the jump, we would get

0,

not 1.

The missing change is concentrated at the jump. Ordinary single-variable calculus does not represent that jump as an ordinary derivative. This is why the differentiability hypothesis matters.

\text{The Fundamental Theorem applies to honest derivatives, not to hidden jumps.}

Why is the Fundamental Theorem a boundary theorem?

The identity \int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a) says that what accumulates inside is measured by the signed boundary. In your own words, why is that a geometric reading rather than only an antiderivative rule, and why do hidden jumps refuse to be ordinary derivatives?

The interior contributions telescope, leaving only the ending value minus the starting value. A jump is not produced by a continuous derivative, so the theorem’s hypotheses are part of the geometry.

The FTC as a boundary theorem

The differential notation makes the boundary pattern clearer.

For a differentiable function F, define

dF=F'(x)\,dx.

At this point, dF is a compact name for the integrand F'(x)\,dx. It is the small change in F predicted by the derivative:

F(x+dx)-F(x)\approx F'(x)\,dx.

With this notation, the Fundamental Theorem becomes

\int_{[a,b]} dF=F(b)-F(a).

Using boundary notation,

\int_{[a,b]} dF=\int_{\partial[a,b]} F.

This is the one-dimensional Stokes theorem.

The one-dimensional Stokes theorem

If F is differentiable on [a,b] and F' is continuous, then

\int_{[a,b]} dF=\int_{\partial[a,b]} F.

In ordinary calculus notation, this says

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).

The theorem has the same structure as the finite telescoping sum:

\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(F(x_j)-F(x_{j-1})\bigr)=F(b)-F(a).

The integral version replaces finite changes by infinitely many small changes:

dF=F'(x)\,dx.

Then the interior cancellations become continuous. Only the boundary remains.

Exact integrands

An integrand of the form

F'(x)\,dx=dF

is called an exact differential.

When an integrand is exact, its integral depends only on the boundary:

\int_a^b dF=F(b)-F(a).

This is exactly what an antiderivative does. Finding an antiderivative is finding a function F whose differential is the integrand.

 What does it mean for an integrand to be exact?

An integrand of the form dF=F'(x)\,dx is exact, and its integral depends only on the boundary. In your own words, why is finding an antiderivative the same as recognizing an exact differential, and why does that make interior cancellations the whole story?

If every small piece is a change in F, adding the pieces is telescoping. Only the two ends survive, which is exactly what an antiderivative computes.

Example

The integrand

2x\,dx

is exact because

2x\,dx=d(x^2).

Therefore

\int_a^b 2x\,dx = x^2\Big|_a^b = b^2-a^2.

The integrand

\cos x\,dx

is exact because

\cos x\,dx=d(\sin x).

Therefore

\int_a^b \cos x\,dx = \sin b-\sin a.

In one-variable calculus, every continuous integrand f(x)\,dx has an antiderivative locally, because we can define an accumulation function

A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt.

Then the Fundamental Theorem says

dA=f(x)\,dx.

In higher dimensions, this becomes a real question: not every integrand is exact. That is one reason the boundary viewpoint becomes powerful.

 Preview of line integrals and differential forms

The notation

f(x)\,dx

has been with us since the first integrals. It means more than “a function times a symbol.” It is an object designed to be accumulated along an oriented interval.

The dx carries direction. When the direction reverses, dx reverses:

\int_b^a f(x)\,dx=-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.

Substitution also fits this view. If

x=g(u),

then the small step changes by

dx=g'(u)\,du.

So the integrand changes as

f(x)\,dx = f(g(u))g'(u)\,du.

This is not symbol pushing. It is changing the measuring stick.

The same habit prepares line integrals.

In one variable, a path along the line can be written as

x=x(t), \qquad \alpha\le t\le \beta.

Then

dx=x'(t)\,dt.

So the integral of f(x)\,dx along the path becomes

\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} f(x(t))x'(t)\,dt.

This is just substitution written as integration along a path.

In the plane, a curve has two changing coordinates:

x=x(t), \qquad y=y(t).

A natural integrand along such a curve has the form

P(x,y)\,dx+Q(x,y)\,dy.

Along the parametrized curve,

dx=x'(t)\,dt, \qquad dy=y'(t)\,dt.

So the line integral becomes

\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \Bigl(P(x(t),y(t))x'(t)+Q(x(t),y(t))y'(t)\Bigr)\,dt.

This is the next-course analogue of substitution.

Preview

A one-dimensional integrand f(x)\,dx is the simplest example of a differential form.

\text{right endpoint} \quad - \quad \text{left endpoint}.

The endpoint b has sign +. The endpoint a has sign -.

Conservation laws in one dimension

The last section rewrote the Fundamental Theorem as a boundary theorem:

\int_{[a,b]} dF=\int_{\partial[a,b]}F.

The interval contributes its two endpoints. The inside contributes a derivative. The same boundary idea explains one of the most important patterns in science:

\text{what is inside changes because something crosses the boundary or is created inside.}

That sentence is a conservation law.

 Density and flux on a line

Imagine a straight road. Cars move along it. At position x and time t, let

\rho(x,t)=\text{traffic density}

measured in

\text{cars per mile}.

The symbol \rho is the Greek letter rho. It is commonly used for density.

Density tells how much stuff is present per unit length. It does not yet say how fast the stuff is moving.

For motion we need another quantity. Let

q(x,t)=\text{traffic flux}

measured in

\text{cars per hour}.

The flux q(x,t) means the rate at which cars cross the point x, counted positive when they cross to the right.

Density and flux on a line quantity meaning units \rho(x,t) density at position x and time t cars/mile q(x,t) flux through position x at time t cars/hour

These two quantities are related, but they are not the same. A crowded traffic jam can have high density and small flux. A road with fewer cars moving quickly can have smaller density and larger flux.

The total number of cars in the road segment [a,b] at time t is

N(t)=\int_a^b \rho(x,t)\,dx.

This is an accumulation of density over length:

\frac{\text{cars}}{\text{mile}}\cdot \text{mile}=\text{cars}.

So the integral turns density into total amount.

Why are density and flux different quantities?

Density \rho measures how much is present per unit length. Flux q measures how fast stuff crosses a point. In your own words, why can a traffic jam have high density and small flux, and why do you need both quantities to write a conservation law?

Being crowded is not the same as moving. Conservation tracks how the amount inside changes, which requires both how much is there and how much is crossing the ends.

Accumulation inside an interval

Suppose no cars appear or disappear inside the interval [a,b]. There are no parking lots, no ramps, and no accidents removing cars from the road. Then the only way the number of cars inside can change is through the two endpoints.

Cars can enter through the left endpoint a. The rate of entry is

q(a,t).

Cars can leave through the right endpoint b. The rate of leaving is

q(b,t).

Therefore

\frac{dN}{dt}=q(a,t)-q(b,t).

Since

N(t)=\int_a^b \rho(x,t)\,dx,

we can write this as

\frac{d}{dt}\int_a^b \rho(x,t)\,dx = q(a,t)-q(b,t).

This is a one-dimensional conservation law.

Conservation law on an interval

If \rho(x,t) is the density of a conserved quantity and q(x,t) is the flux to the right, then, with no sources or sinks inside [a,b],

\frac{d}{dt}\int_a^b \rho(x,t)\,dx = q(a,t)-q(b,t).

In words:

\text{rate of change inside}=\text{inflow at left}-\text{outflow at right}.

The signs contain the orientation. Positive flux points to the right. At the left endpoint, rightward flux enters the interval. At the right endpoint, rightward flux leaves the interval.

Example

Suppose cars enter a road segment through a at

q(a,t)=1200

cars/hour and leave through b at

q(b,t)=950

cars/hour. Then

\frac{dN}{dt}=1200-950=250.

So the number of cars in the segment is increasing at

250\text{ cars/hour}.

Traffic is accumulating inside.

 Example

Suppose instead

q(a,t)=700, \qquad q(b,t)=1000.

Then

\frac{dN}{dt}=700-1000=-300.

The number of cars in the segment is decreasing at

300\text{ cars/hour}.

More cars leave than enter.

 Sign warning

Flux can be negative. Negative flux means motion to the left.

If

q(a,t)=-100

at the left endpoint, then cars are crossing a to the left. They are leaving the interval through the left endpoint. The formula still works:

\frac{dN}{dt}=q(a,t)-q(b,t).

The negative value of q(a,t) correctly decreases N(t).
