Warning examples

The last few sections gave us strong tools:

\text{Fermat's theorem, Rolle's theorem, the Mean Value Theorem,}

\text{the first derivative test, the second derivative test, and l'Hospital's Rule.}

Each one has a boundary. A theorem is useful only when its hypotheses are true. This section collects the warning examples in one place, so the rules are easier to use and harder to misuse.

 Fermat’s theorem fails at an endpoint

Fermat’s theorem said:

\text{differentiable local extremum at an interior point} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f'(c)=0.

The phrase interior point matters.

Let

f(x)=x

on the interval

[0,1].

The function has an absolute minimum at

x=0

and an absolute maximum at

x=1.

But the derivative is

f'(x)=1.

There is no horizontal tangent.

There is no contradiction. Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint, the graph only has to be compared with points on one side. It can be best or worst without flattening out.

\text{Endpoint extrema do not have to satisfy } f'(c)=0.

That is why the closed interval method always checks endpoints separately.

Why can an endpoint extremum fail to have a horizontal tangent?

On [0,1], the function f(x)=x attains its max and min, but f' is never zero. In your own words, why is that compatible with Fermat’s theorem, and why does the closed interval method therefore check endpoints separately?

Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint the graph is compared with only one side, so it can be best or worst without flattening.

The Mean Value Theorem fails without continuity

The Mean Value Theorem said that if f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then some c\in(a,b) satisfies

f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.

Continuity on the whole closed interval matters.

Define

f(x)= \begin{cases} x, \amp 0\le x<1,\\ 0, \amp x=1. \end{cases}

on [0,1].

Then

f(0)=0, \qquad f(1)=0.

So the secant slope from 0 to 1 is

\frac{f(1)-f(0)}{1-0}=0.

But on the open interval (0,1),

f(x)=x,

so

f'(x)=1

for every x\in(0,1). There is no point c\in(0,1) with

f'(c)=0.

The graph climbs toward 1, then jumps down at the endpoint. The jump hides the climb from the endpoint calculation.

\text{The Mean Value Theorem needs continuity on }[a,b].

Why can the Mean Value Theorem fail without continuity or differentiability?

A jump on the closed interval, or a corner inside, can keep every existing tangent slope away from the secant slope. In your own words, why are continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b) not decorations, and what kind of escape does each hypothesis block?

Continuity keeps the graph from leaping over the needed height. Differentiability keeps a turn from happening at a corner instead of at a tangent.

The Mean Value Theorem fails without differentiability

The Mean Value Theorem also needs differentiability on the open interval.

Let

f(x)=|x|

on

[-1,1].

The function is continuous on [-1,1]. Its endpoint values are

f(-1)=1, \qquad f(1)=1.

So the secant slope is

\frac{f(1)-f(-1)}{1-(-1)} = \frac{1-1}{2} = 0.

If the Mean Value Theorem applied, there would be some c\in(-1,1) with

f'(c)=0.

But

f'(x)=-1 \quad\text{for }x<0,

and

f'(x)=1 \quad\text{for }x>0.

At x=0, the derivative does not exist. The graph turns at a corner.

The graph does return to the same height, but it turns too sharply. Rolle’s Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem do not promise a horizontal tangent unless the function is differentiable throughout the open interval.

\text{The Mean Value Theorem needs differentiability on }(a,b).

The second derivative test can be inconclusive

The second derivative test said:

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)>0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local minimum at }c,

and

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)<0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local maximum at }c.

But when

f''(c)=0,

the test says nothing.

Three different outcomes are possible.

A local minimum

Let

f(x)=x^4.

Then

f'(x)=4x^3, \qquad f''(x)=12x^2.

At x=0,

f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0.

The second derivative test gives no conclusion. But

x^4\ge0

for every x, so f has a local minimum at 0.

 A local maximum

Let

g(x)=-x^4.

Then

g'(x)=-4x^3, \qquad g''(x)=-12x^2.

At x=0,

g'(0)=0, \qquad g''(0)=0.

The test again gives no conclusion. But

-x^4\le0

for every x, so g has a local maximum at 0.

 No local extremum

Let

h(x)=x^3.

Then

h'(x)=3x^2, \qquad h''(x)=6x.

At x=0,

h'(0)=0, \qquad h''(0)=0.

But x^3 is increasing through 0. There is no local maximum or local minimum.

The moral is short:

f''(c)=0 \text{ means ``try another test.''}

Most often, we return to the first derivative test or to the definition of local maximum and local minimum.

 Why can the second derivative test stay silent?

If f'(c)=0 and f''(c)=0, the test gives no conclusion. In your own words, why can that same pair of facts describe a local min, a local max, or no extremum at all, and what extra evidence do we then need?

Look at the sign of f' on both sides, or compare the graphs of x^4, -x^4, and x^3 at the origin.

l’Hospital’s Rule cannot be used on every quotient

l’Hospital’s Rule is a rule for the indeterminate forms

\frac00 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{\infty}{\infty}.

The first question is always:

\text{What form does direct substitution produce?}

A quotient that is not indeterminate

Consider

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}.

Direct substitution gives

\frac{0^2+1}{0+1}=1.

So the limit is

1.

This is not a 0/0 form and not an \infty/\infty form.

If we incorrectly differentiate numerator and denominator, we get

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{2x}{1}=0,

which is wrong.

\text{Do not use l'Hospital's Rule when direct substitution already gives an ordinary number.}

A derivative quotient with no limit

Sometimes the original quotient has a limit, but the quotient of derivatives does not.

Consider

\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}.

The quotient is

\frac{x+\sin x}{x} = 1+\frac{\sin x}{x}.

Since

\left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right|\le \frac1x

for x>0, we get

\frac{\sin x}{x}\to0.

Therefore

\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}=1.

But the quotient of derivatives is

\frac{1+\cos x}{1}=1+\cos x,

which has no limit as x\to\infty.

There is no contradiction. l’Hospital’s Rule says that if the original quotient has the right indeterminate form and the derivative quotient has a limit, then the original limit has that same value. It does not say that the derivative quotient must always have a limit.

\text{If the derivative quotient does not settle, l'Hospital's Rule gives no conclusion.}

The last few sections gave us strong tools:

\text{Fermat's theorem, Rolle's theorem, the Mean Value Theorem,}

\text{the first derivative test, the second derivative test, and l'Hospital's Rule.}

Each one has a boundary. A theorem is useful only when its hypotheses are true. This section collects the warning examples in one place, so the rules are easier to use and harder to misuse.

Fermat’s theorem said:

\text{differentiable local extremum at an interior point} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f'(c)=0.

The phrase interior point matters.

Let

f(x)=x

on the interval

[0,1].

The function has an absolute minimum at

x=0

and an absolute maximum at

x=1.

But the derivative is

f'(x)=1.

There is no horizontal tangent.

There is no contradiction. Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint, the graph only has to be compared with points on one side. It can be best or worst without flattening out.

\text{Endpoint extrema do not have to satisfy } f'(c)=0.

That is why the closed interval method always checks endpoints separately.

Why can an endpoint extremum fail to have a horizontal tangent?

On [0,1], the function f(x)=x attains its max and min, but f' is never zero. In your own words, why is that compatible with Fermat’s theorem, and why does the closed interval method therefore check endpoints separately?

Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint the graph is compared with only one side, so it can be best or worst without flattening.

The Mean Value Theorem fails without continuity

The Mean Value Theorem said that if f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then some c\in(a,b) satisfies

f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.

Continuity on the whole closed interval matters.

Define

f(x)= \begin{cases} x, \amp 0\le x<1,\\ 0, \amp x=1. \end{cases}

on [0,1].

Then

f(0)=0, \qquad f(1)=0.

So the secant slope from 0 to 1 is

\frac{f(1)-f(0)}{1-0}=0.

But on the open interval (0,1),

f(x)=x,

so

f'(x)=1

for every x\in(0,1). There is no point c\in(0,1) with

f'(c)=0.

The graph climbs toward 1, then jumps down at the endpoint. The jump hides the climb from the endpoint calculation.

\text{The Mean Value Theorem needs continuity on }[a,b].

Why can the Mean Value Theorem fail without continuity or differentiability?

A jump on the closed interval, or a corner inside, can keep every existing tangent slope away from the secant slope. In your own words, why are continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b) not decorations, and what kind of escape does each hypothesis block?

Continuity keeps the graph from leaping over the needed height. Differentiability keeps a turn from happening at a corner instead of at a tangent.

The Mean Value Theorem fails without differentiability

The Mean Value Theorem also needs differentiability on the open interval.

Let

f(x)=|x|

on

[-1,1].

The function is continuous on [-1,1]. Its endpoint values are

f(-1)=1, \qquad f(1)=1.

So the secant slope is

\frac{f(1)-f(-1)}{1-(-1)} = \frac{1-1}{2} = 0.

If the Mean Value Theorem applied, there would be some c\in(-1,1) with

f'(c)=0.

But

f'(x)=-1 \quad\text{for }x<0,

and

f'(x)=1 \quad\text{for }x>0.

At x=0, the derivative does not exist. The graph turns at a corner.

The graph does return to the same height, but it turns too sharply. Rolle’s Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem do not promise a horizontal tangent unless the function is differentiable throughout the open interval.

\text{The Mean Value Theorem needs differentiability on }(a,b).

The second derivative test said:

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)>0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local minimum at }c,

and

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)<0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local maximum at }c.

But when

f''(c)=0,

the test says nothing.

Three different outcomes are possible.

A local minimum

Let

f(x)=x^4.

Then

f'(x)=4x^3, \qquad f''(x)=12x^2.

At x=0,

f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0.

The second derivative test gives no conclusion. But

x^4\ge0

for every x, so f has a local minimum at 0.

 A local maximum

Let

g(x)=-x^4.

Then

g'(x)=-4x^3, \qquad g''(x)=-12x^2.

At x=0,

g'(0)=0, \qquad g''(0)=0.

The test again gives no conclusion. But

-x^4\le0

for every x, so g has a local maximum at 0.

 No local extremum

Let

h(x)=x^3.

Then

h'(x)=3x^2, \qquad h''(x)=6x.

At x=0,

h'(0)=0, \qquad h''(0)=0.

But x^3 is increasing through 0. There is no local maximum or local minimum.

The moral is short:

f''(c)=0 \text{ means ``try another test.''}

Most often, we return to the first derivative test or to the definition of local maximum and local minimum.

 Why can the second derivative test stay silent?

If f'(c)=0 and f''(c)=0, the test gives no conclusion. In your own words, why can that same pair of facts describe a local min, a local max, or no extremum at all, and what extra evidence do we then need?

Look at the sign of f' on both sides, or compare the graphs of x^4, -x^4, and x^3 at the origin.

l’Hospital’s Rule is a rule for the indeterminate forms

\frac00 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{\infty}{\infty}.

The first question is always:

\text{What form does direct substitution produce?}

A quotient that is not indeterminate

Consider

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}.

Direct substitution gives

\frac{0^2+1}{0+1}=1.

So the limit is

1.

This is not a 0/0 form and not an \infty/\infty form.

If we incorrectly differentiate numerator and denominator, we get

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{2x}{1}=0,

which is wrong.

\text{Do not use l'Hospital's Rule when direct substitution already gives an ordinary number.}

The quotient is

\frac{x+\sin x}{x} = 1+\frac{\sin x}{x}.

Since

\left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right|\le \frac1x

for x>0, we get

\frac{\sin x}{x}\to0.

Therefore

\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}=1.

\frac{1+\cos x}{1}=1+\cos x,

Chapter review and discovery problems

This chapter began with a simple observation:

f'(x)>0 \text{ means rising}, \qquad f'(x)<0 \text{ means falling}.

That observation grew into a much larger picture. The derivative gives more than instantaneous rate. It gives shape, turning, bending, bounds, and sometimes limits.

 The chapter’s map

Here is the main dictionary.

\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{calculus evidence} \amp \textbf{graph information}\\ \hline f'(x)>0 \amp f \text{ is increasing}\\ f'(x)<0 \amp f \text{ is decreasing}\\ f'(c)=0 \text{ or } f'(c)\text{ undefined} \amp c \text{ is a critical number candidate}\\ f' \text{ changes } + \text{ to } - \amp \text{local maximum}\\ f' \text{ changes } - \text{ to } + \amp \text{local minimum}\\ f''(x)>0 \amp f \text{ is concave up}\\ f''(x)<0 \amp f \text{ is concave down}\\ f'' \text{ changes sign at } c \amp (c,f(c)) \text{ is an inflection point}\\ f'(c)=0,\ f''(c)>0 \amp \text{local minimum}\\ f'(c)=0,\ f''(c)<0 \amp \text{local maximum} \end{array}

The Mean Value Theorem supplies the bridge from local derivative information to whole-interval information:

f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}

for some

c\in(a,b),

provided f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b).

That bridge proves the first derivative sign rule. It also proves that a function with zero derivative on an interval is constant there.

l’Hospital’s Rule is another derivative bridge. For certain indeterminate quotients, the limiting ratio of two functions can be found from the limiting ratio of their derivatives:

\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x\to a}\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)},

when the hypotheses of the rule are satisfied.

How does derivative evidence become graph information?

The chapter’s map translates signs of f' and f'' into rising, falling, concavity, extrema, and inflection. In your own words, why is that dictionary more than a list of tests, and what single idea lets local rate information describe the shape of a graph?

The first derivative is about direction of change; the second is about how that direction itself is changing. Sign charts are a way of reading those stories across intervals.

A complete review example

Sketch the graph of

f(x)=\frac13x^3-x^2

using derivatives.

First compute

f'(x)=x^2-2x=x(x-2).

The critical numbers are

x=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=2.

The sign chart for f' is

\begin{array}{c|ccc} \text{interval} \amp (-\infty,0) \amp (0,2) \amp (2,\infty)\\ \hline f'(x) \amp + \amp - \amp +\\ f \amp \text{increasing} \amp \text{decreasing} \amp \text{increasing} \end{array}

So f has a local maximum at x=0 and a local minimum at x=2.

The values are

f(0)=0,

and

f(2)=\frac13(8)-4=\frac83-\frac{12}{3}=-\frac43.

Now compute the second derivative:

f''(x)=2x-2.

The sign chart for f'' is

\begin{array}{c|cc} \text{interval} \amp (-\infty,1) \amp (1,\infty)\\ \hline f''(x) \amp - \amp +\\ f \amp \text{concave down} \amp \text{concave up} \end{array}

The concavity changes at x=1. Therefore there is an inflection point at

\left(1,f(1)\right) = \left(1,\frac13-1\right) = \left(1,-\frac23\right).

The graph must rise to (0,0), fall to \left(2,-\frac43\right), then rise again. It bends downward before x=1 and upward after x=1.

This example is small, but the workflow is the same for harder functions:

\text{domain, intercepts, asymptotes, } f', f'', \text{ sign charts, then sketch.}

 Concept checks

  1. Explain why a critical number is a candidate for a local extremum, not a guarantee.

  2. Give an example of a function with f'(0)=0 but no local maximum or local minimum at 0.

  3. Give an example of a function with a local minimum at 0 where f'(0) does not exist.

  4. Explain why endpoints must be checked when finding absolute extrema on a closed interval.

  5. State the hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem. For each hypothesis, give one sentence explaining why it is needed.

  6. Suppose f'(x)>0 for all x in an interval. Explain why f cannot take the same value twice in that interval.

  7. Suppose f''(x)>0 on an interval. What does that say about f'? What does it say about the graph of f?

  8. If f''(c)=0, what can you conclude about local extrema at c? What can you not conclude?

  9. Before applying l’Hospital’s Rule, what two checks should be made?

  10. Explain why

    \frac00

    is not a value of a limit.

 Skills: graph from derivatives

For each function below:

  1. Find the domain.

  2. Find intercepts, if reasonable.

  3. Find vertical, horizontal, or slant asymptotes, if any.

  4. Find critical numbers.

  5. Find increasing and decreasing intervals.

  6. Find local extrema.

  7. Find concavity intervals and inflection points.

  8. Sketch a graph consistent with all the evidence.

  1. f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1.

  2. f(x)=x^4-4x^2.

  3. f(x)=\frac{x}{x^2+1}.

  4. f(x)=\frac{x^2}{x-1}.

  5. f(x)=xe^{-x}.

  6. f(x)=\ln(x^2+1).

  7. f(x)=x+\frac1x, \qquad x\neq0.

  8. f(x)=\frac{x^3}{x^2-1}.

  9. The derivative of a function f has sign chart

    \begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{interval} \amp (-\infty,-2) \amp (-2,0) \amp (0,3) \amp (3,\infty)\\ \hline f'(x) \amp - \amp + \amp + \amp - \end{array}

    and f is continuous everywhere. Identify all local extrema forced by the chart.

  10. The second derivative of a function g has sign chart

    \begin{array}{c|ccc} \text{interval} \amp (-\infty,1) \amp (1,4) \amp (4,\infty)\\ \hline g''(x) \amp + \amp - \amp + \end{array}

    and g is continuous everywhere. Identify all inflection points forced by the chart.

 Extrema and closed interval practice

  1. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of

    f(x)=x^3-3x+2

    on

    [-2,3].

  2. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of

    g(x)=x+\frac4x

    on

    [1,6].

  3. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of

    h(x)=\sqrt{x}(4-x)

    on

    [0,4].

  4. Let

    p(x)=x^4-8x^2+3.

    Find all local extrema and all absolute extrema on

    [-3,3].

  5. Explain why the function

    f(x)=\frac1x

    has no absolute maximum or minimum on

    (0,1).

    Which hypothesis of the Extreme Value Theorem is missing?

  6. Explain why the function

    f(x)=x

    has no absolute maximum on

    [0,\infty).

    Which hypothesis of the Extreme Value Theorem is missing?

 Mean Value Theorem practice

  1. Verify the hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem for

    f(x)=x^2

    on

    [1,4].

    Find all numbers c\in(1,4) satisfying

    f'(c)=\frac{f(4)-f(1)}{4-1}.

  2. Verify the hypotheses of Rolle’s Theorem for

    f(x)=x^2-4x+3

    on

    [1,3].

    Find the number c promised by the theorem.

  3. Let

    f(x)=\sqrt{x}

    on

    [1,9].

    Find the number c promised by the Mean Value Theorem.

  4. Show that the Mean Value Theorem cannot be applied to

    f(x)=|x|

    on

    [-1,1].

    Then explain why the conclusion fails.

  5. Show that the Mean Value Theorem cannot be applied to

    f(x)= \begin{cases} x, \amp 0\le x<1,\\ 0, \amp x=1 \end{cases}

    on

    [0,1].

    Then explain why the conclusion fails.

  6. A car travels 150 miles in 3 hours. Assume its position is continuous and differentiable during the trip. What does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee about its instantaneous velocity?

  7. Suppose a runner’s position s(t), in meters, is differentiable on [0,10], with

    s(0)=0, \qquad s(10)=80.

    What instantaneous velocity is guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem?

Why is the Mean Value Theorem the bridge from local rates to whole-interval facts?

A derivative at a point is local. Claims such as increasing on an interval or constant on an interval compare values. In your own words, why does the Mean Value Theorem make that leap, and what hypotheses must travel with it?

Some instantaneous rate equals the average rate. If every instantaneous rate is positive, or zero, the corresponding net change is forced.

Proof practice with the Mean Value Theorem

  1. A function with positive derivative is increasing.

    Suppose f is continuous on an interval I, differentiable at the interior points of I, and

    f'(x)>0

    throughout the interior of I. Use the Mean Value Theorem to prove that f is increasing on I.

  2. A zero derivative forces a constant function.

    Suppose

    f'(x)=0

    for every x in an interval I. Use the Mean Value Theorem to prove that f is constant on I.

  3. Equal derivatives differ by a constant.

    Suppose

    f'(x)=g'(x)

    for every x in an interval I. Prove that

    f(x)-g(x)

    is constant on I.

  4. A derivative bound controls total change.

    Suppose |f'(x)|\le M for all x\in[a,b]. Prove that

    |f(b)-f(a)|\le M|b-a|.

  5. Sine changes no faster than its input.

    Use the previous problem with f(x)=\sin x to prove that

    |\sin b-\sin a|\le |b-a|

    for all real numbers a and b.

  6. A uniqueness proof.

    Show that the equation

    x+\cos x=0

    has exactly one solution in the interval [-1,0].

    Hint: use the Intermediate Value Theorem for existence, and the Mean Value Theorem for uniqueness.

  7. A useful logarithm inequality.

    Use the Mean Value Theorem on

    f(x)=\ln x

    to prove that, for x>0,

    \ln x \le x-1.

    When does equality occur?

 l’Hospital’s Rule practice

For each limit, decide first whether l’Hospital’s Rule is legal. Then evaluate the limit, if it exists.

  1. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{2x}-1}{x}.

  2. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}.

  3. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}.

  4. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x-x}{x^3}.

  5. \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln x}{\sqrt{x}}.

  6. \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x^3}{e^x}.

  7. \lim_{x\to0^+}x\ln x.

  8. \lim_{x\to0^+}x^x.

  9. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}.

    Explain why l’Hospital’s Rule is not legal.

  10. \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}.

    Evaluate the limit without l’Hospital’s Rule. Then explain why differentiating the numerator and denominator gives no useful conclusion.

 Counterexample problems

  1. Find a function with a critical number at x=0 but no local extremum at 0.

  2. Find a function with a local minimum at x=0 where the derivative does not exist at 0.

  3. Find a continuous function on [-1,1] that is not differentiable on (-1,1), and for which Rolle’s conclusion fails.

  4. Find a function that is differentiable on (0,1) but not continuous on [0,1], and for which the Mean Value Theorem conclusion fails.

  5. Find a function with

    f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0,

    that has a local maximum at 0.

  6. Find a function with

    f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0,

    that has no local extremum at 0.

  7. Give an example of a quotient where direct substitution gives a real number, but differentiating numerator and denominator gives the wrong limit.

  8. Give an example of a quotient where the original limit exists but the quotient of derivatives has no limit.

Why are critical numbers and zeros of <m>f''</m> candidates rather than conclusions?

f'(c)=0 need not be an extremum, and f''(c)=0 need not be an inflection point. In your own words, what extra evidence turns a candidate into a conclusion, and why is that warning the same idea in two different disguises?

Look for an actual change: a sign change of f' for extrema, a sign change of f'' for inflection.

Project: reconstruct a trip from acceleration data

A derivative gives rate of change. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:

a(t)=v'(t).

Velocity is the derivative of position:

v(t)=s'(t).

So acceleration is two derivative steps away from position:

s(t) \longrightarrow v(t) \longrightarrow a(t).

This project asks you to walk backward from acceleration data to velocity and position. The exact method belongs to integration, but a finite-step reconstruction already shows the idea.

Suppose a small cart moves along a track. Its acceleration is measured once every second:

\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc} t\text{ (seconds)} \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \amp 3 \amp 4 \amp 5 \amp 6 \amp 7 \amp 8\\ \hline a(t)\text{ (m/s}^2\text{)} \amp 3 \amp 2 \amp 1 \amp 0 \amp -1 \amp -2 \amp -3 \amp -2 \amp -1 \end{array}

Assume

v(0)=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad s(0)=0.

For this project, treat the acceleration as constant on each one-second interval, using the left endpoint value. Thus on the interval from t=k to t=k+1, use

a(t)\approx a(k).

With \Delta t=1, update velocity by

v_{k+1}=v_k+a_k\Delta t.

Then update position in one of two ways.

The rough update is

s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t.

The constant-acceleration update is

s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t+\frac12a_k(\Delta t)^2.

Tasks

  1. Make a table with columns

    k,\quad t_k,\quad a_k,\quad v_k,\quad s_k.

    Use the constant-acceleration update for s_k.

  2. Graph the acceleration data.

  3. Graph the reconstructed velocity.

  4. Graph the reconstructed position.

  5. During which time interval is the cart speeding up? During which time interval is it slowing down? Explain using the signs of v and a.

  6. When is the velocity largest? How can you see this from the acceleration data?

  7. When does the position appear largest? How can you see this from the velocity data?

  8. Repeat the reconstruction with the rough update

    s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t.

    Compare the two position graphs.

  9. Write one paragraph explaining why recovering position from acceleration is an accumulation problem.

  10. Write one paragraph predicting how the next part of calculus should make this finite reconstruction exact.

 Optional computing extension

Use a spreadsheet or a short program to repeat the reconstruction with a smaller time step. For example, try

\Delta t=0.5

using linearly interpolated acceleration data. Compare the graph with the one-second reconstruction.

 Why must every theorem in this chapter be used as a hypotheses-to-conclusion package?

Fermat, Rolle, the Mean Value Theorem, the second derivative test, and l’Hospital’s Rule each fail when a hypothesis is dropped. In your own words, why is checking hypotheses part of using the theorem, rather than an optional courtesy after the conclusion is written?

If the hypotheses are missing, the conclusion may still be true by luck. But the theorem is no longer the reason.

Discovery problems

  1. How many roots can a derivative control?

    Suppose f is differentiable on an interval and f'(x)>0 throughout the interval. Prove that f(x)=0 has at most one solution.

  2. Two zeros force a zero derivative.

    Suppose f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and

    f(a)=f(b)=0.

    Prove that there is some c\in(a,b) such that

    f'(c)=0.

    Then explain why this is exactly Rolle’s Theorem in a special case.

  3. Three zeros force a zero second derivative.

    Suppose f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and has three zeros in the interval. Assume f'' exists where needed. Prove that there is some point c where

    f''(c)=0.

    Hint: apply Rolle’s Theorem more than once.

  4. A polynomial root-counting fact.

    Use the previous problem to explain why a quadratic polynomial cannot have three distinct real roots unless it is the zero polynomial.

  5. A tangent parallel to a chord.

    Pick a smooth function f and two points a<b. Draw the secant line through

    (a,f(a)) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (b,f(b)).

    Find a point c where the tangent is parallel to that secant. Then verify your picture algebraically.

  6. A horizontal inflection point.

    Find a function f such that

    f'(0)=0,

    but 0 is not a local maximum or local minimum. Explain why your example has a horizontal tangent without a turning point.

  7. A graph from a derivative only.

    Suppose f'(x)=x^2-1 and f(0)=2. Without finding a formula for f(x), decide where f is increasing and decreasing and where it has local extrema. Then, if you know antiderivatives already, find f(x) and check your prediction.

  8. A limit without l’Hospital.

    Evaluate

    \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin(3x)}{x}

    using the standard limit

    \lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin u}{u}=1.

    Then evaluate it again with l’Hospital’s Rule. Compare the two methods.

 Where this points

This chapter taught us how to read a graph from its derivatives. That is already useful: we can locate peaks, valleys, flat points, bends, and asymptotes.

But many real questions do not start by asking for a graph. They ask for a choice.

\text{What shape gives the largest volume?}

\text{What route takes the least time?}

\text{What price gives the greatest profit?}

\text{How fast is one quantity changing when another quantity is changing?}

Those questions still use derivatives, but now the graph is only part of the story. The next chapter turns shape information into decisions: related rates, optimization, and models.

Chapter review and discovery problems

This chapter began with a simple observation:

f'(x)>0 \text{ means rising}, \qquad f'(x)<0 \text{ means falling}.

That observation grew into a much larger picture. The derivative gives more than instantaneous rate. It gives shape, turning, bending, bounds, and sometimes limits.

 The chapter’s map

Here is the main dictionary.

\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{calculus evidence} \amp \textbf{graph information}\\ \hline f'(x)>0 \amp f \text{ is increasing}\\ f'(x)<0 \amp f \text{ is decreasing}\\ f'(c)=0 \text{ or } f'(c)\text{ undefined} \amp c \text{ is a critical number candidate}\\ f' \text{ changes } + \text{ to } - \amp \text{local maximum}\\ f' \text{ changes } - \text{ to } + \amp \text{local minimum}\\ f''(x)>0 \amp f \text{ is concave up}\\ f''(x)<0 \amp f \text{ is concave down}\\ f'' \text{ changes sign at } c \amp (c,f(c)) \text{ is an inflection point}\\ f'(c)=0,\ f''(c)>0 \amp \text{local minimum}\\ f'(c)=0,\ f''(c)<0 \amp \text{local maximum} \end{array}

The Mean Value Theorem supplies the bridge from local derivative information to whole-interval information:

f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}

for some

c\in(a,b),

provided f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b).

That bridge proves the first derivative sign rule. It also proves that a function with zero derivative on an interval is constant there.

l’Hospital’s Rule is another derivative bridge. For certain indeterminate quotients, the limiting ratio of two functions can be found from the limiting ratio of their derivatives:

\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x\to a}\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)},

when the hypotheses of the rule are satisfied.

How does derivative evidence become graph information?

The chapter’s map translates signs of f' and f'' into rising, falling, concavity, extrema, and inflection. In your own words, why is that dictionary more than a list of tests, and what single idea lets local rate information describe the shape of a graph?

The first derivative is about direction of change; the second is about how that direction itself is changing. Sign charts are a way of reading those stories across intervals.

A complete review example

Sketch the graph of

f(x)=\frac13x^3-x^2

using derivatives.

First compute

f'(x)=x^2-2x=x(x-2).

The critical numbers are

x=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=2.

The sign chart for f' is

\begin{array}{c|ccc} \text{interval} \amp (-\infty,0) \amp (0,2) \amp (2,\infty)\\ \hline f'(x) \amp + \amp - \amp +\\ f \amp \text{increasing} \amp \text{decreasing} \amp \text{increasing} \end{array}

So f has a local maximum at x=0 and a local minimum at x=2.

The values are

f(0)=0,

and

f(2)=\frac13(8)-4=\frac83-\frac{12}{3}=-\frac43.

Now compute the second derivative:

f''(x)=2x-2.

The sign chart for f'' is

\begin{array}{c|cc} \text{interval} \amp (-\infty,1) \amp (1,\infty)\\ \hline f''(x) \amp - \amp +\\ f \amp \text{concave down} \amp \text{concave up} \end{array}

The concavity changes at x=1. Therefore there is an inflection point at

\left(1,f(1)\right) = \left(1,\frac13-1\right) = \left(1,-\frac23\right).

The graph must rise to (0,0), fall to \left(2,-\frac43\right), then rise again. It bends downward before x=1 and upward after x=1.

This example is small, but the workflow is the same for harder functions:

\text{domain, intercepts, asymptotes, } f', f'', \text{ sign charts, then sketch.}

 Concept checks

  1. Explain why a critical number is a candidate for a local extremum, not a guarantee.

  2. Give an example of a function with f'(0)=0 but no local maximum or local minimum at 0.

  3. Give an example of a function with a local minimum at 0 where f'(0) does not exist.

  4. Explain why endpoints must be checked when finding absolute extrema on a closed interval.

  5. State the hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem. For each hypothesis, give one sentence explaining why it is needed.

  6. Suppose f'(x)>0 for all x in an interval. Explain why f cannot take the same value twice in that interval.

  7. Suppose f''(x)>0 on an interval. What does that say about f'? What does it say about the graph of f?

  8. If f''(c)=0, what can you conclude about local extrema at c? What can you not conclude?

  9. Before applying l’Hospital’s Rule, what two checks should be made?

  10. Explain why

    \frac00

    is not a value of a limit.

 Skills: graph from derivatives

For each function below:

  1. Find the domain.

  2. Find intercepts, if reasonable.

  3. Find vertical, horizontal, or slant asymptotes, if any.

  4. Find critical numbers.

  5. Find increasing and decreasing intervals.

  6. Find local extrema.

  7. Find concavity intervals and inflection points.

  8. Sketch a graph consistent with all the evidence.

  1. f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1.

  2. f(x)=x^4-4x^2.

  3. f(x)=\frac{x}{x^2+1}.

  4. f(x)=\frac{x^2}{x-1}.

  5. f(x)=xe^{-x}.

  6. f(x)=\ln(x^2+1).

  7. f(x)=x+\frac1x, \qquad x\neq0.

  8. f(x)=\frac{x^3}{x^2-1}.

  9. The derivative of a function f has sign chart

    \begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{interval} \amp (-\infty,-2) \amp (-2,0) \amp (0,3) \amp (3,\infty)\\ \hline f'(x) \amp - \amp + \amp + \amp - \end{array}

    and f is continuous everywhere. Identify all local extrema forced by the chart.

  10. The second derivative of a function g has sign chart

    \begin{array}{c|ccc} \text{interval} \amp (-\infty,1) \amp (1,4) \amp (4,\infty)\\ \hline g''(x) \amp + \amp - \amp + \end{array}

    and g is continuous everywhere. Identify all inflection points forced by the chart.

 Extrema and closed interval practice

  1. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of

    f(x)=x^3-3x+2

    on

    [-2,3].

  2. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of

    g(x)=x+\frac4x

    on

    [1,6].

  3. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of

    h(x)=\sqrt{x}(4-x)

    on

    [0,4].

  4. Let

    p(x)=x^4-8x^2+3.

    Find all local extrema and all absolute extrema on

    [-3,3].

  5. Explain why the function

    f(x)=\frac1x

    has no absolute maximum or minimum on

    (0,1).

    Which hypothesis of the Extreme Value Theorem is missing?

  6. Explain why the function

    f(x)=x

    has no absolute maximum on

    [0,\infty).

    Which hypothesis of the Extreme Value Theorem is missing?

 Mean Value Theorem practice

  1. Verify the hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem for

    f(x)=x^2

    on

    [1,4].

    Find all numbers c\in(1,4) satisfying

    f'(c)=\frac{f(4)-f(1)}{4-1}.

  2. Verify the hypotheses of Rolle’s Theorem for

    f(x)=x^2-4x+3

    on

    [1,3].

    Find the number c promised by the theorem.

  3. Let

    f(x)=\sqrt{x}

    on

    [1,9].

    Find the number c promised by the Mean Value Theorem.

  4. Show that the Mean Value Theorem cannot be applied to

    f(x)=|x|

    on

    [-1,1].

    Then explain why the conclusion fails.

  5. Show that the Mean Value Theorem cannot be applied to

    f(x)= \begin{cases} x, \amp 0\le x<1,\\ 0, \amp x=1 \end{cases}

    on

    [0,1].

    Then explain why the conclusion fails.

  6. A car travels 150 miles in 3 hours. Assume its position is continuous and differentiable during the trip. What does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee about its instantaneous velocity?

  7. Suppose a runner’s position s(t), in meters, is differentiable on [0,10], with

    s(0)=0, \qquad s(10)=80.

    What instantaneous velocity is guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem?

Why is the Mean Value Theorem the bridge from local rates to whole-interval facts?

A derivative at a point is local. Claims such as increasing on an interval or constant on an interval compare values. In your own words, why does the Mean Value Theorem make that leap, and what hypotheses must travel with it?

Some instantaneous rate equals the average rate. If every instantaneous rate is positive, or zero, the corresponding net change is forced.

Proof practice with the Mean Value Theorem

  1. A function with positive derivative is increasing.

    Suppose f is continuous on an interval I, differentiable at the interior points of I, and

    f'(x)>0

    throughout the interior of I. Use the Mean Value Theorem to prove that f is increasing on I.

  2. A zero derivative forces a constant function.

    Suppose

    f'(x)=0

    for every x in an interval I. Use the Mean Value Theorem to prove that f is constant on I.

  3. Equal derivatives differ by a constant.

    Suppose

    f'(x)=g'(x)

    for every x in an interval I. Prove that

    f(x)-g(x)

    is constant on I.

  4. A derivative bound controls total change.

    Suppose |f'(x)|\le M for all x\in[a,b]. Prove that

    |f(b)-f(a)|\le M|b-a|.

  5. Sine changes no faster than its input.

    Use the previous problem with f(x)=\sin x to prove that

    |\sin b-\sin a|\le |b-a|

    for all real numbers a and b.

  6. A uniqueness proof.

    Show that the equation

    x+\cos x=0

    has exactly one solution in the interval [-1,0].

    Hint: use the Intermediate Value Theorem for existence, and the Mean Value Theorem for uniqueness.

  7. A useful logarithm inequality.

    Use the Mean Value Theorem on

    f(x)=\ln x

    to prove that, for x>0,

    \ln x \le x-1.

    When does equality occur?

 l’Hospital’s Rule practice

For each limit, decide first whether l’Hospital’s Rule is legal. Then evaluate the limit, if it exists.

  1. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{2x}-1}{x}.

  2. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}.

  3. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}.

  4. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x-x}{x^3}.

  5. \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln x}{\sqrt{x}}.

  6. \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x^3}{e^x}.

  7. \lim_{x\to0^+}x\ln x.

  8. \lim_{x\to0^+}x^x.

  9. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}.

    Explain why l’Hospital’s Rule is not legal.

  10. \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}.

    Evaluate the limit without l’Hospital’s Rule. Then explain why differentiating the numerator and denominator gives no useful conclusion.

 Counterexample problems

  1. Find a function with a critical number at x=0 but no local extremum at 0.

  2. Find a function with a local minimum at x=0 where the derivative does not exist at 0.

  3. Find a continuous function on [-1,1] that is not differentiable on (-1,1), and for which Rolle’s conclusion fails.

  4. Find a function that is differentiable on (0,1) but not continuous on [0,1], and for which the Mean Value Theorem conclusion fails.

  5. Find a function with

    f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0,

    that has a local maximum at 0.

  6. Find a function with

    f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0,

    that has no local extremum at 0.

  7. Give an example of a quotient where direct substitution gives a real number, but differentiating numerator and denominator gives the wrong limit.

  8. Give an example of a quotient where the original limit exists but the quotient of derivatives has no limit.

Why are critical numbers and zeros of <m>f''</m> candidates rather than conclusions?

f'(c)=0 need not be an extremum, and f''(c)=0 need not be an inflection point. In your own words, what extra evidence turns a candidate into a conclusion, and why is that warning the same idea in two different disguises?

Look for an actual change: a sign change of f' for extrema, a sign change of f'' for inflection.

Project: reconstruct a trip from acceleration data

A derivative gives rate of change. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:

a(t)=v'(t).

Velocity is the derivative of position:

v(t)=s'(t).

So acceleration is two derivative steps away from position:

s(t) \longrightarrow v(t) \longrightarrow a(t).

This project asks you to walk backward from acceleration data to velocity and position. The exact method belongs to integration, but a finite-step reconstruction already shows the idea.

Suppose a small cart moves along a track. Its acceleration is measured once every second:

\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc} t\text{ (seconds)} \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \amp 3 \amp 4 \amp 5 \amp 6 \amp 7 \amp 8\\ \hline a(t)\text{ (m/s}^2\text{)} \amp 3 \amp 2 \amp 1 \amp 0 \amp -1 \amp -2 \amp -3 \amp -2 \amp -1 \end{array}

Assume

v(0)=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad s(0)=0.

For this project, treat the acceleration as constant on each one-second interval, using the left endpoint value. Thus on the interval from t=k to t=k+1, use

a(t)\approx a(k).

With \Delta t=1, update velocity by

v_{k+1}=v_k+a_k\Delta t.

Then update position in one of two ways.

The rough update is

s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t.

The constant-acceleration update is

s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t+\frac12a_k(\Delta t)^2.

Tasks

  1. Make a table with columns

    k,\quad t_k,\quad a_k,\quad v_k,\quad s_k.

    Use the constant-acceleration update for s_k.

  2. Graph the acceleration data.

  3. Graph the reconstructed velocity.

  4. Graph the reconstructed position.

  5. During which time interval is the cart speeding up? During which time interval is it slowing down? Explain using the signs of v and a.

  6. When is the velocity largest? How can you see this from the acceleration data?

  7. When does the position appear largest? How can you see this from the velocity data?

  8. Repeat the reconstruction with the rough update

    s_{k+1}=s_k+v_k\Delta t.

    Compare the two position graphs.

  9. Write one paragraph explaining why recovering position from acceleration is an accumulation problem.

  10. Write one paragraph predicting how the next part of calculus should make this finite reconstruction exact.

 Optional computing extension

Use a spreadsheet or a short program to repeat the reconstruction with a smaller time step. For example, try

\Delta t=0.5

using linearly interpolated acceleration data. Compare the graph with the one-second reconstruction.

 Why must every theorem in this chapter be used as a hypotheses-to-conclusion package?

Fermat, Rolle, the Mean Value Theorem, the second derivative test, and l’Hospital’s Rule each fail when a hypothesis is dropped. In your own words, why is checking hypotheses part of using the theorem, rather than an optional courtesy after the conclusion is written?

If the hypotheses are missing, the conclusion may still be true by luck. But the theorem is no longer the reason.

Discovery problems

  1. How many roots can a derivative control?

    Suppose f is differentiable on an interval and f'(x)>0 throughout the interval. Prove that f(x)=0 has at most one solution.

  2. Two zeros force a zero derivative.

    Suppose f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and

    f(a)=f(b)=0.

    Prove that there is some c\in(a,b) such that

    f'(c)=0.

    Then explain why this is exactly Rolle’s Theorem in a special case.

  3. Three zeros force a zero second derivative.

    Suppose f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and has three zeros in the interval. Assume f'' exists where needed. Prove that there is some point c where

    f''(c)=0.

    Hint: apply Rolle’s Theorem more than once.

  4. A polynomial root-counting fact.

    Use the previous problem to explain why a quadratic polynomial cannot have three distinct real roots unless it is the zero polynomial.

  5. A tangent parallel to a chord.

    Pick a smooth function f and two points a<b. Draw the secant line through

    (a,f(a)) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (b,f(b)).

    Find a point c where the tangent is parallel to that secant. Then verify your picture algebraically.

  6. A horizontal inflection point.

    Find a function f such that

    f'(0)=0,

    but 0 is not a local maximum or local minimum. Explain why your example has a horizontal tangent without a turning point.

  7. A graph from a derivative only.

    Suppose f'(x)=x^2-1 and f(0)=2. Without finding a formula for f(x), decide where f is increasing and decreasing and where it has local extrema. Then, if you know antiderivatives already, find f(x) and check your prediction.

  8. A limit without l’Hospital.

    Evaluate

    \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin(3x)}{x}

    using the standard limit

    \lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin u}{u}=1.

    Then evaluate it again with l’Hospital’s Rule. Compare the two methods.

 Where this points

This chapter taught us how to read a graph from its derivatives. That is already useful: we can locate peaks, valleys, flat points, bends, and asymptotes.

But many real questions do not start by asking for a graph. They ask for a choice.

\text{What shape gives the largest volume?}

\text{What route takes the least time?}

\text{What price gives the greatest profit?}

\text{How fast is one quantity changing when another quantity is changing?}

Those questions still use derivatives, but now the graph is only part of the story. The next chapter turns shape information into decisions: related rates, optimization, and models.

Chapter review and discovery problems

Chapter 4 defined the derivative:

f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

That definition gave meaning, but it was too slow for everyday use.

Chapter 5 built a working language. We learned how derivatives behave under algebra, composition, implicit relations, inverse functions, and the elementary functions. The point was not to memorize a long table. The point was to read structure.

 Chapter map

The chapter has one main story:

\text{how a function is built} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{how its derivative is built}.

Chapter map construction derivative rule main idea sum and constant multiple (af+bg)'=af'+bg' derivatives are linear product (fg)'=f'g+fg' each factor changes once quotient \displaystyle \left(\frac fg\right)'=\frac{gf'-fg'}{g^2} quotient is product with a reciprocal composition (f\circ g)'=f'(g(x))g'(x) outside change times inside change implicit equation differentiate both sides y changes because x changes inverse \displaystyle (f^{-1})'(b)=\frac1{f'(a)} reversing a graph reverses slope logarithmic differentiation \displaystyle \frac{y'}y=(\ln y)' products become sums elementary functions tables below special functions have special rates
Why does the way a function is built determine the derivative rule?

Chapter 5 has one main story: how a function is built determines how its derivative is built. In your own words, why are a sum, a product, a quotient, a composition, and an inverse different constructions, and why is reading the structure the first step rather than a race to symbols?

Each construction changes for a different reason. The table of elementary derivatives is useful only when paired with the matching rule.

Derivative table

The main elementary derivative formulas from this chapter are collected below. Each formula is valid on intervals where the function is defined and differentiable.

\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{function} \amp \textbf{derivative}\\ \hline c \amp 0\\ x \amp 1\\ x^r \amp rx^{r-1}\\ e^x \amp e^x\\ a^x \amp (\ln a)a^x,\quad a>0\\ \ln x \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x>0\\ \ln|x| \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x\neq0\\ \sin x \amp \cos x\\ \cos x \amp -\sin x\\ \tan x \amp \sec^2x\\ \sec x \amp \sec x\tan x\\ \csc x \amp -\csc x\cot x\\ \cot x \amp -\csc^2x\\ \arcsin x \amp \dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arccos x \amp -\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arctan x \amp \dfrac1{1+x^2}\\ \sinh x \amp \cosh x\\ \cosh x \amp \sinh x\\ \tanh x \amp \operatorname{sech}^2x \end{array}

The table is only useful when paired with the rules:

(af+bg)'\amp=af'+bg', (fg)'\amp=f'g+fg', \left(\frac fg\right)'\amp=\frac{gf'-fg'}{g^2}, (f(g(x)))'\amp=f'(g(x))g'(x).

Most real derivative calculations use both a table formula and a rule.

 Worked mixed examples Example

Differentiate

F(x)=e^{-x}\cos(2x)+\ln(1+x^2).

The first term is a product:

e^{-x}\cos(2x).

Differentiate each factor:

\frac{d}{dx}e^{-x}=-e^{-x},

and

\frac{d}{dx}\cos(2x)=-2\sin(2x).

So

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = (-e^{-x})\cos(2x)+e^{-x}(-2\sin(2x)).

Thus

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x).

The logarithmic term uses the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\ln(1+x^2)=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

Therefore

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

We can factor the first two terms if desired:

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\bigl(\cos(2x)+2\sin(2x)\bigr) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

 Example

Differentiate

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

This function has a variable exponent. Since the base is always positive,

x^2+1>0,

logarithmic differentiation is safe.

Take natural logarithms:

\ln y=\sin x\ln(x^2+1).

Differentiate both sides:

\frac{y'}{y} = \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \sin x\cdot\frac{2x}{x^2+1}.

Multiply by y:

y' = y\left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

Substitute back

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

Thus

y' = (x^2+1)^{\sin x} \left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

This example uses several ideas at once: logarithms, product rule, chain rule, and the fact that x^2+1 is positive.

 Example

Find dy/dx if

x^2y+\sin y=e^x.

Here y is treated as a function of x. Differentiate both sides with respect to x.

For x^2y, use the product rule:

\frac{d}{dx}(x^2y)=2xy+x^2y'.

For \sin y, use the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\sin y=\cos y\,y'.

For e^x,

\frac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x.

Therefore

2xy+x^2y'+\cos y\,y'=e^x.

Collect the y'-terms:

(x^2+\cos y)y'=e^x-2xy.

So

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{e^x-2xy}{x^2+\cos y}.

The denominator warns us: if

x^2+\cos y=0,

then this equation does not determine a finite value of dy/dx. The algebra may be pointing to a vertical tangent or to a place where the curve is not a single differentiable branch y(x).

Find dy/dx. Then find the tangent slope at the given point when a point is provided.

  1. x^2+y^2=10.

Why do implicit and inverse derivatives reverse two different things?

Implicit differentiation treats y as changing because x changes, even with no formula y=f(x). The inverse rule reverses a graph and therefore reverses slope. In your own words, why are those two ideas related to the chain rule, yet not the same task?

One starts from a relation and solves for dy/dx. The other starts from a reversible function and takes the reciprocal slope at the matching point.

Concept check

Answer each question in complete sentences.

  1. Why does the product rule have two terms?

  2. In the chain rule

    (f(g(x)))'=f'(g(x))g'(x),

    why is f' evaluated at g(x) instead of at x?

  3. Why must angles be measured in radians for

    (\sin x)'=\cos x

    to be true without an extra constant?

  4. Why does implicit differentiation require the chain rule?

    (f^{-1})'(b)=\frac1{f'(a)}, \qquad b=f(a),

    why must the derivative of f be evaluated at a, not at b?

  6. Give an example of a function that has an inverse, but whose inverse is not differentiable at one point.

 Where the chapter points next

A derivative is more than a number to compute. It is information about shape.

For example, consider

f(x)=x^3-3x.

Its derivative is

f'(x)=3x^2-3=3(x-1)(x+1).

The derivative is positive when

x<-1

and when

x>1.

It is negative when

-1<x<1.

The graph rises, then falls, then rises again.

At

x=-1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=1,

the derivative is 0. The graph has horizontal tangents there. One is a high point nearby; the other is a low point nearby.

That observation opens the next part of the book.

Derivatives compute slopes. But slopes tell us when a function rises, when it falls, where it turns, and where it bends. The next chapter asks how much of a graph we can understand from its derivative.

Why is a computed derivative already information about shape?

The sign of f' tells where a graph rises or falls, and a zero of f' marks a horizontal tangent. In your own words, why was this chapter’s working language built not only to compute more derivatives, but to prepare for reading a graph from its slopes?

A derivative is local slope information. Collected point by point, those slopes begin to describe the whole curve.

\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{function} \amp \textbf{derivative}\\ \hline c \amp 0\\ x \amp 1\\ x^r \amp rx^{r-1}\\ e^x \amp e^x\\ a^x \amp (\ln a)a^x,\quad a>0\\ \ln x \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x>0\\ \ln|x| \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x\neq0\\ \sin x \amp \cos x\\ \cos x \amp -\sin x\\ \tan x \amp \sec^2x\\ \sec x \amp \sec x\tan x\\ \csc x \amp -\csc x\cot x\\ \cot x \amp -\csc^2x\\ \arcsin x \amp \dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arccos x \amp -\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arctan x \amp \dfrac1{1+x^2}\\ \sinh x \amp \cosh x\\ \cosh x \amp \sinh x\\ \tanh x \amp \operatorname{sech}^2x \end{array}

 Worked mixed examples Example

Differentiate

F(x)=e^{-x}\cos(2x)+\ln(1+x^2).

The first term is a product:

e^{-x}\cos(2x).

Differentiate each factor:

\frac{d}{dx}e^{-x}=-e^{-x},

and

\frac{d}{dx}\cos(2x)=-2\sin(2x).

So

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = (-e^{-x})\cos(2x)+e^{-x}(-2\sin(2x)).

Thus

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x).

The logarithmic term uses the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\ln(1+x^2)=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

Therefore

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

We can factor the first two terms if desired:

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\bigl(\cos(2x)+2\sin(2x)\bigr) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

 Example

Differentiate

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

This function has a variable exponent. Since the base is always positive,

x^2+1>0,

logarithmic differentiation is safe.

Take natural logarithms:

\ln y=\sin x\ln(x^2+1).

Differentiate both sides:

\frac{y'}{y} = \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \sin x\cdot\frac{2x}{x^2+1}.

Multiply by y:

y' = y\left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

Substitute back

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

Thus

y' = (x^2+1)^{\sin x} \left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

This example uses several ideas at once: logarithms, product rule, chain rule, and the fact that x^2+1 is positive.

 Example

Find dy/dx if

x^2y+\sin y=e^x.

Here y is treated as a function of x. Differentiate both sides with respect to x.

For x^2y, use the product rule:

\frac{d}{dx}(x^2y)=2xy+x^2y'.

For \sin y, use the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\sin y=\cos y\,y'.

For e^x,

\frac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x.

Therefore

2xy+x^2y'+\cos y\,y'=e^x.

Collect the y'-terms:

(x^2+\cos y)y'=e^x-2xy.

So

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{e^x-2xy}{x^2+\cos y}.

The denominator warns us: if

x^2+\cos y=0,

then this equation does not determine a finite value of dy/dx. The algebra may be pointing to a vertical tangent or to a place where the curve is not a single differentiable branch y(x).

The derivative is local linear approximation. That idea explains the chain rule better than symbol cancellation alone.

So the inside change is approximately

\Delta u \approx g'(a)h.

Near u=g(a), the outside function satisfies

f(u+\Delta u)\approx f(u)+f'(u)\Delta u.

Thus the outside change is approximately

\Delta y \approx f'(u)\Delta u.

Substitute the inside change:

\Delta y \approx f'(g(a))\bigl(g'(a)h\bigr).

\frac{\Delta y}{h} \approx f'(g(a))g'(a).

Letting h\to0 gives

u_0=g(a).

f(u_0+k) = f(u_0)+f'(u_0)k+k\varepsilon(k),

where we define \varepsilon(0)=0, and

\varepsilon(k)\to0 \qquad\text{as}\qquad k\to0.

k=g(a+h)-g(a).

Then

f(g(a+h)) = f(g(a))+f'(g(a))\bigl(g(a+h)-g(a)\bigr) + \bigl(g(a+h)-g(a)\bigr)\varepsilon(k).

Implicit differentiation

Many curves are not naturally written as

y=f(x).

A circle is easier to describe by

x^2+y^2=25

than by two separate formulas

y=\sqrt{25-x^2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad y=-\sqrt{25-x^2}.

The equation relates x and y without solving for y. Such an equation defines a curve implicitly.

The chain rule lets us find slopes on these curves directly.

The equation

x^2+y^2=25

does not describe one function y=f(x) on the whole circle. Most vertical lines through the circle meet it twice: once on the upper half and once on the lower half.

But near the point

(3,4),

the upper half of the circle can be treated as a function of x. As x changes a little, y changes in a definite way to keep the point on the circle.

We want the slope

\frac{dy}{dx}

at (3,4).

Solving for y is possible here:

y=\sqrt{25-x^2}

on the upper half. But differentiating the original equation is cleaner and teaches a method that works even when solving for y is unpleasant.

x^2+y^2=25.

Think of y as a function of x, even though we have not written its formula. Differentiate both sides with respect to x.

The derivative of x^2 is

2x.

\frac{d}{dx}(y^2)=2y\frac{dy}{dx}.

The derivative of 25 is 0. Therefore

2x+2y\frac{dy}{dx}=0.

2y\frac{dy}{dx}=-2x,

\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{y}.

The tangent line at (3,4) is

y-4=-\frac34(x-3).

Equivalently,

3x+4y=25.

Implicit differentiation turns an equation into slope information.

Derivatives of exponential and logarithmic functions

Sine and cosine return to themselves after differentiation, with a shift and a sign. Exponential functions are even more direct. The right exponential function returns exactly to itself.

That one fact explains why exponentials appear whenever the rate of change depends on the current amount.

Imagine a small colony of bacteria. If there are more bacteria, there are more bacteria able to divide. So the growth rate should depend on the current population.

A simple model says

P'(t)=kP(t),

where

P(t)

is the population at time t, and k is a constant.

If k>0, the population grows. If k<0, the quantity decays. The same equation appears in radioactive decay, continuous interest, and many first approximations to growth.

The equation

P'(t)=kP(t)

asks for a function whose derivative is a constant multiple of itself.

We already know one kind of candidate:

P(t)=a^t.

To see what its derivative looks like, use the definition:

\frac{d}{dt}a^t = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{a^{t+h}-a^t}{h}.

Using the exponent rule

a^{t+h}=a^t a^h,

we get

\frac{a^{t+h}-a^t}{h} = \frac{a^t a^h-a^t}{h} = a^t\frac{a^h-1}{h}.

Since a^t does not depend on h,

\frac{d}{dt}a^t = a^t\lim_{h\to0}\frac{a^h-1}{h}.

The limit

\lim_{h\to0}\frac{a^h-1}{h}

is the slope of the graph y=a^x at x=0. Call that number \lambda(a):

\lambda(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{a^h-1}{h}.

Then

\frac{d}{dx}a^x=\lambda(a)a^x.

Every exponential function has a derivative proportional to itself. The proportionality constant depends on the base.

The natural question is:

\text{Is there a base for which the proportionality constant is }1?

Yes. That base is e.

General power rule and hyperbolic functions

The power rule first appeared for positive integer powers:

\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}.

Then negative powers came from the reciprocal rule, and fractional-looking powers appeared through roots. But the formula is larger than all of those cases.

It works for any real exponent, as long as the function is defined and differentiable.

The logarithm gives the cleanest proof.

 The derivative of <m>x^r</m>

Suppose

y=x^\pi, \qquad x>0.

This is not a polynomial. The exponent is not an integer. For x>0, define a real power by x^r=e^{r\ln x}. The chain rule already shows that this function is differentiable. Logarithms then turn powers into products.

Take natural logarithms:

\ln y=\ln(x^\pi).

Using the logarithm rule,

\ln y=\pi\ln x.

Differentiate both sides with respect to x. The left side uses the chain rule:

\frac1y\frac{dy}{dx}=\pi\frac1x.

So

\frac{dy}{dx}=y\frac{\pi}{x}.

Since

y=x^\pi,

we get

\frac{dy}{dx}=x^\pi\frac{\pi}{x}.

Therefore

\frac{d}{dx}x^\pi=\pi x^{\pi-1}, \qquad x>0.

Nothing special about \pi was used. The same argument works for any real exponent.

General Power Rule

For any fixed real number r,

\frac{d}{dx}x^r=rx^{r-1}, \qquad x>0.

When x^r is defined on a larger domain, the same formula holds at points where the derivative exists. The logarithmic proof above applies directly on x>0.

Let

y=x^r, \qquad x>0.

Take logarithms:

\ln y=r\ln x.

Differentiate both sides:

\frac1y y'=\frac r x.

Multiply by y:

Warning examples

This chapter has given us speed. We no longer need to return to the limit definition every time we differentiate. We have rules.

That speed is useful, but it also creates a danger. A rule that is remembered only as a symbol can be used in the wrong place.

The safest way to use derivative rules is to keep asking:

\text{How was this function built?}

A sum, a product, a quotient, a composition, and an inverse are different constructions. Their derivatives are different because their changes are different.

 The product rule is not <m>(fg)'=f'g'</m>

A common mistake is to guess that the derivative of a product is the product of the derivatives:

(fg)' \stackrel{\text{wrong}}{=} f'g'.

This is false.

Take the simplest possible example:

f(x)=x, \qquad g(x)=x.

Then

f(x)g(x)=x^2.

So

(fg)'(x)=2x.

But

f'(x)g'(x)=1\cdot1=1.

These are not the same. For example, at x=3,

(fg)'(3)=6, \qquad f'(3)g'(3)=1.

The correct rule is

(fg)'=f'g+fg'.

This rule has a geometric picture visualization. If a rectangle has side lengths f(x) and g(x), then its area is

A(x)=f(x)g(x).

When x changes a little, both sides may change. The new area comes from two first-order strips:

f'(x)g(x)\Delta x \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(x)g'(x)\Delta x.

That is why two terms appear.

For exact finite changes, write \Delta f=f(x+\Delta x)-f(x) and \Delta g=g(x+\Delta x)-g(x). Then

\Delta(fg) = (f+\Delta f)(g+\Delta g)-fg.

Expanding,

\Delta(fg)=f\,\Delta g+g\,\Delta f+\Delta f\,\Delta g.

For differentiable factors, \Delta f\,\Delta g divided by \Delta x approaches zero. Dividing the exact identity by \Delta x and passing to the limit gives

(fg)'=fg'+gf'.

The false rule f'g' forgets the original sizes f and g. But the original sizes matter. A small change in the width of a large rectangle adds more area than the same change in the width of a small rectangle.

Another quick test

Let

f(x)=x^2, \qquad g(x)=\sin x.

Then

(fg)'=2x\sin x+x^2\cos x.

Average rate of change

A limit of average rates cannot be understood until the average rate itself is clear. So we begin with the ordinary slope between two points.

If f is a function and the input changes from a to b, then the output changes from f(a) to f(b). The average rate of change compares these two changes:

\frac{\text{change in output}}{\text{change in input}} = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.

This is the slope of the line through the two graph points

(a,f(a)) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (b,f(b)).

That line is called a secant line.

 Secant slope

On a straight line, one slope tells the whole story. On a curved graph, the slope between two points depends on which two points we choose.

Let

f(x)=x^2.

Between x=1 and x=3, the function changes from

f(1)=1

to

f(3)=9.

The average rate of change is

\frac{f(3)-f(1)}{3-1} = \frac{9-1}{2} = 4.

So over this interval the graph rises, on average, 4 units of output for each 1 unit of input.

The symbols \Delta x and \Delta y are useful here. The Greek letter \Delta means “change in.”

For the example above,

\Delta x=3-1=2,

and

\Delta y=f(3)-f(1)=9-1=8.

So

\text{secant slope} = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{8}{2} = 4.

Average rate of change

For a function f, the average rate of change from x=a to x=b, where a\neq b, is

\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.

Geometrically, this is the slope of the secant line through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)).

The order matters only through the signs. If we compute from b back to a, then both the numerator and denominator change sign:

\frac{f(a)-f(b)}{a-b} = \frac{-(f(b)-f(a))}{-(b-a)} = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.

So the secant slope is the same line slope either way.

Why is an average rate a secant slope rather than a local slope?

The average rate of change of f from a to b is the slope of the line through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)). In your own words, why does that number describe the whole interval at once, and why is it not the slope of the graph at every point in between?

A secant uses two points. On a curved graph, nearby pairs of points can produce different slopes.

Example

Find the average rate of change of

f(x)=x^2

from x=2 to x=5.

We compute

\frac{f(5)-f(2)}{5-2} = \frac{25-4}{3} = 7.

So on the interval [2,5], the function x^2 increases by an average of 7 output units per input unit.

Notice that this does not mean the graph has slope 7 everywhere between 2 and 5. Near x=2, the graph is less steep. Near x=5, it is steeper. The number 7 describes the whole interval at once.

 Average velocity

The same quotient appears in motion.

Let s(t) be the position of an object at time t. If s is measured in meters and t is measured in seconds, then

\frac{s(b)-s(a)}{b-a}

has units

\frac{\text{meters}}{\text{seconds}}.

That is a velocity.

Average velocity

If s(t) is position, then the average velocity from t=a to t=b is

\frac{s(b)-s(a)}{b-a}.

Example

Suppose a particle moves along a line with position

s(t)=t^2

meters after t seconds.

From t=2 to t=5, the average velocity is

\frac{s(5)-s(2)}{5-2} = \frac{25-4}{3} = 7.

So the average velocity over those 3 seconds is

7\text{ meters/second}.

From t=2 to t=3, the average velocity is

\frac{s(3)-s(2)}{3-2} = \frac{9-4}{1} = 5\text{ meters/second}.

From t=2 to t=2.1, the average velocity is

\frac{s(2.1)-s(2)}{2.1-2} = \frac{4.41-4}{0.1} = 4.1\text{ meters/second}.

The interval is getting shorter, and the average velocity is getting closer to the velocity at the instant t=2. That is the idea we will make precise in Section .

Average velocity uses signed change in position:

s(b)-s(a).

If an object moves forward and then backward, its displacement can be small even if it traveled a long distance.

For example, suppose a runner starts at 0 meters, runs to 100 meters, and then returns to 0 meters in 20 seconds. The average velocity over the full trip is

\frac{0-0}{20}=0\text{ meters/second}.

That does not mean the runner was standing still. It means the net change in position was 0. Average velocity measures net signed change per unit time.

 Why can average velocity be zero even if the object moved?

A runner who goes out and back in 20 seconds has average velocity 0. In your own words, why does that not mean the runner stood still, and what quantity is average velocity actually using?

Average velocity uses signed change in position. Distance traveled counts every step, forward or back.

A formula is not required. If we have a table, we can still compute average rates.

Recall the cooling coffee data from Chapter 2:

\begin{array}{c|cccccc} t\text{ (minutes)} \amp 0 \amp 5 \amp 10 \amp 15 \amp 20 \amp 25\\ \hline T(t)\text{ (degrees C)} \amp 90 \amp 73 \amp 60 \amp 51 \amp 44 \amp 39 \end{array}

The average rate of change of the coffee temperature from t=0 to t=5 is

\frac{T(5)-T(0)}{5-0} = \frac{73-90}{5} = -\frac{17}{5} = -3.4.

The units are degrees Celsius per minute. So during the first 5 minutes, the coffee cooled at an average rate of

The negative sign means the temperature decreased.

From t=15 to t=25, the average rate is

\frac{T(25)-T(15)}{25-15} = \frac{39-51}{10} = -1.2.

So between 15 and 25 minutes, the coffee cooled at an average rate of

A line through two points has one slope. Changing the order of the two points does not change the line.

The units of an average rate come from the quotient:

\frac{\text{output units}}{\text{input units}}.

That simple rule prevents many mistakes.

\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{function} \amp \textbf{average rate} \amp \textbf{units}\\ \hline s(t)=\text{position} \amp \dfrac{s(b)-s(a)}{b-a} \amp \text{meters/second}\\ T(t)=\text{temperature} \amp \dfrac{T(b)-T(a)}{b-a} \amp ^\circ\text{C/minute}\\ C(q)=\text{cost} \amp \dfrac{C(b)-C(a)}{b-a} \amp \text{dollars/item}\\ P(t)=\text{population} \amp \dfrac{P(b)-P(a)}{b-a} \amp \text{people/year} \end{array}

The units also explain the meaning of the sign.

If

\frac{T(5)-T(0)}{5-0}=-3.4,

then the coffee temperature is decreasing by an average of 3.4^\circ\text{C} per minute.

If

\frac{P(2030)-P(2020)}{2030-2020}=15000,

then the population is increasing by an average of 15{,}000 people per year.

If

\frac{C(101)-C(100)}{101-100}=8.25,

then producing the 101st item increased the cost by 8.25 dollars compared with producing 100 items. This is an average over one item, and in many cost models it is close to what economists call marginal cost.

An average rate of change is always a comparison:

\frac{\text{how much the output changed}}{\text{how much the input changed}}.

The units tell what kind of comparison it is.

Average rates are useful, but they still describe an interval. A speedometer does not report the average velocity over the last hour. It reports what is happening now.

To get that number from position, we must make the interval shrink.

An average rate always has the form output units per input unit, and its value depends on which two data points we compare. In your own words, why do the units tell the meaning of the comparison, and why can a table give average rates without giving an exact instantaneous rate?

A quotient inherits units from numerator and denominator. A table only supplies certain points, so any rate computed from it still belongs to an interval.

Instantaneous rate of change

Average velocity looks across an interval. Instantaneous velocity looks at one time.

That sounds impossible at first. If there is only one time, there is no change in time, and a quotient like

\frac{\text{change in position}}{\text{change in time}}

would have denominator 0.

The way out is not to divide by 0. The way out is to divide by a nonzero time change h, and then let h approach 0.

Let

s(t)=t^2

be position in meters after t seconds. We want the velocity at t=2.

The average velocity from t=2 to t=2+h is

\frac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{(2+h)-2} = \frac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h}, \qquad h\neq0.

Compute:

\frac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h} = \frac{(2+h)^2-4}{h} = \frac{4+4h+h^2-4}{h} = \frac{4h+h^2}{h}.

Since h\neq0,

\frac{4h+h^2}{h}=4+h.

So the average velocity over the interval from 2 to 2+h is

4+h.

Now let h get close to 0:

\begin{array}{c|cccccc} h \amp -0.1 \amp -0.01 \amp -0.001 \amp 0.001 \amp 0.01 \amp 0.1\\ \hline 4+h \amp 3.9 \amp 3.99 \amp 3.999 \amp 4.001 \amp 4.01 \amp 4.1 \end{array}

4\text{ meters/second}.

\text{instantaneous rate}= \lim_{\text{interval width}\to0} \text{average rate}.

The difference quotient \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} is an average rate. In your own words, why must h approach 0 rather than be set equal to 0, and what idea does the resulting limit name?

Setting h=0 divides by zero. The instantaneous rate is the value the averages settle toward, not a value obtained by plugging in.

Now we name the limiting average rate.

Let f be a function defined at a and near a. The derivative of f at a, written f'(a), is

f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},

provided this limit exists as a finite number.

If the limit exists, we say that f is differentiable at a.

The quotient

\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}

is the average rate of change from a to a+h. The derivative is the limit of these average rates as the second point moves toward the first.

There is another form of the same definition. Put

x=a+h.

Then

h=x-a.

As h\to0, we have x\to a. The quotient becomes

\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}.

So

f'(a)=\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a},

when the limit exists.

The derivative as a function

Section gave the derivative at one point. For example,

f(x)=x^2

has

f'(2)=4.

That number is the slope of one tangent line. But a curve has many points, and the slope usually changes from point to point. If the point moves, the derivative moves with it.

So the derivative is not only a number. It is also a new function.

 From one tangent slope to many

The calculation for f(x)=x^2 at x=2 did not really depend on the number 2. Let us repeat it at a general point a.

Let

f(x)=x^2.

Then

f'(a) = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

Substitute the formula:

f'(a) = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{(a+h)^2-a^2}{h}.

Expand:

(a+h)^2=a^2+2ah+h^2.

Therefore

\frac{(a+h)^2-a^2}{h} = \frac{2ah+h^2}{h}.

Since h\neq0,

\frac{2ah+h^2}{h}=2a+h.

Now take the limit:

f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}(2a+h)=2a.

So the tangent slope at x=a is

2a.

If we let the input point be called x, we write

f'(x)=2x.

This new function f' gives the slope of the graph of f at each point where the derivative exists.

\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x \amp -2 \amp -1 \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 2\\ \hline f(x)=x^2 \amp 4 \amp 1 \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 4\\ f'(x)=2x \amp -4 \amp -2 \amp 0 \amp 2 \amp 4 \end{array}

The original function f(x)=x^2 gives heights. The derivative function f'(x)=2x gives slopes.

Derivative function

The derivative function of f is

f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h},

defined at every x where this limit exists.

The domain of f' may be smaller than the domain of f. For example,

f(x)=|x|

is defined for every real number x. But at x=0,

\lim_{h\to0}\frac{|h|}{h}

does not exist, because the left and right limiting slopes disagree. For x<0, the graph is the line y=-x, so the slope is -1. For x>0, the graph is the line y=x, so the slope is 1. Thus

f'(x)= \begin{cases} -1, \amp x<0,\\ 1, \amp x>0, \end{cases}

and f'(0) does not exist.

A derivative function records where slopes exist. It also records where they fail to exist.

Why may the domain of <m>f'</m> be smaller than the domain of <m>f</m>?

The function f(x)=|x| is defined for every real x, but f'(0) does not exist. In your own words, why can a derivative function omit points that the original function includes?

f' is defined only where the limiting slope exists. Existence of a height is a weaker demand than existence of a single nearby slope.

Let

f(x)=x^3.

Then

f'(x) = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{(x+h)^3-x^3}{h}.

Expand:

(x+h)^3=x^3+3x^2h+3xh^2+h^3.

So

\frac{(x+h)^3-x^3}{h} = \frac{3x^2h+3xh^2+h^3}{h}.

Since h\neq0,

\frac{3x^2h+3xh^2+h^3}{h} = 3x^2+3xh+h^2.

Therefore

f'(x) = \lim_{h\to0}(3x^2+3xh+h^2) = 3x^2.

So

\frac{d}{dx}x^3=3x^2.

The derivative is important enough to have several notations. Each notation emphasizes a different part of the same idea.

If

y=f(x),

then the following notations all refer to the derivative:

\begin{array}{c|l} \textbf{notation} \amp \textbf{meaning}\\ \hline f'(x) \amp \text{the derivative function of }f\\ \dfrac{dy}{dx} \amp \text{the rate of change of }y\text{ with respect to }x\\ \dfrac{d}{dx}f(x) \amp \text{the result of differentiating }f(x)\text{ with respect to }x\\ D_x f(x) \amp \text{another compact notation for the same operation} \end{array}

For example, if

y=x^2,

then

f'(x)=2x,

and we may also write

\frac{dy}{dx}=2x,

or

\frac{d}{dx}(x^2)=2x,

D_x(x^2)=2x.

At a particular point x=a, we write

\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=a}=f'(a).

\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=3}=6.

\frac{ds}{dt}

has units

\frac{\text{meters}}{\text{seconds}}.

So

v(t)=s'(t)=\frac{ds}{dt}

is velocity.

\frac{dT}{dt}

has units

\frac{^\circ\text{C}}{\text{minute}}.

So \dfrac{dT}{dt} measures how quickly the temperature is changing.
