Inverse trigonometric functions

An inverse function reverses input and output. But sine and cosine repeat, so they do not have inverses on the whole real line.

For example,

\sin 0=0, \qquad \sin \pi=0, \qquad \sin(2\pi)=0.

If we tried to invert sine on all real numbers, the output 0 would have many possible inputs. That is not a function.

The repair is familiar: restrict the domain before taking the inverse.

 Why restrictions are needed

A function has an inverse only when it is one-to-one on the domain we choose.

The sine function is one-to-one on

\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right].

On that interval, it increases from -1 to 1. So we define \arcsin x as the inverse of sine on this restricted interval.

Arcsine

For -1\le x\le1,

y=\arcsin x

means

\sin y=x \qquad\text{and}\qquad -\frac{\pi}{2}\le y\le\frac{\pi}{2}.

Thus \arcsin x is the angle in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right] whose sine is x.

The range condition is part of the definition.

For example,

\arcsin\left(\frac12\right)=\frac{\pi}{6},

not

\frac{5\pi}{6},

even though

\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\frac12.

The angle \frac{5\pi}{6} is not in the chosen range for arcsine.

 Arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent

The three main inverse trigonometric functions are:

Arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent function meaning domain range y=\arcsin x \sin y=x [-1,1] \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] y=\arccos x \cos y=x [-1,1] [0,\pi] y=\arctan x \tan y=x \mathbb R \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)

The ranges are chosen so that each restricted trigonometric function is one-to-one.

Example

Evaluate

\arccos\left(-\frac12\right).

We need the angle y in

[0,\pi]

such that

\cos y=-\frac12.

That angle is

\frac{2\pi}{3}.

Therefore

\arccos\left(-\frac12\right)=\frac{2\pi}{3}.

Example

Evaluate

\arctan(-1).

We need the angle y in

\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)

such that

\tan y=-1.

That angle is

-\frac{\pi}{4}.

So

\arctan(-1)=-\frac{\pi}{4}.

Notation warning

The notation

\sin^{-1}x

usually means

\arcsin x,

not

\frac1{\sin x}.

To avoid confusion, this book uses \arcsin x, \arccos x, and \arctan x.

The inverse identities work in two directions, but with domains and ranges attached.

For -1\le x\le1,

\sin(\arcsin x)=x.

For every y in

\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right],

\arcsin(\sin y)=y.

The second identity is not true for every real y. For example,

\arcsin(\sin \pi)=\arcsin(0)=0,

not \pi.

The inverse returns the angle in its chosen range.

Simplify

\cos(\arcsin x), \qquad -1\le x\le1.

Let

\theta=\arcsin x.

Then

\sin\theta=x

and

-\frac{\pi}{2}\le \theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}.

On this interval,

\cos\theta\ge0.

Using

\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1,

we get

x^2+\cos^2\theta=1.

Thus

\cos^2\theta=1-x^2.

Since \cos\theta\ge0,

\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-x^2}.

Therefore

\cos(\arcsin x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}.

The positive square root is not optional. It comes from the chosen range of arcsine.

Simplify

\sin(\arctan x).

Let

\theta=\arctan x.

Then

\tan\theta=x=\frac{x}{1}.

For x>0, use a right triangle with opposite side x, adjacent side 1, and hypotenuse

\sqrt{x^2+1}.

Since \arctan x lies in

\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right),

the adjacent side is positive, and this triangle represents the angle correctly.

Thus

\sin\theta=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}.

Therefore

\sin(\arctan x)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}.

At x=0, both sides are zero. For x<0, use the oddness of sine and arctangent to obtain the same formula.

These triangle translations appear often in integration, especially in trigonometric substitution.

Inverse trigonometric functions

An inverse function reverses input and output. But sine and cosine repeat, so they do not have inverses on the whole real line.

For example,

\sin 0=0, \qquad \sin \pi=0, \qquad \sin(2\pi)=0.

If we tried to invert sine on all real numbers, the output 0 would have many possible inputs. That is not a function.

The repair is familiar: restrict the domain before taking the inverse.

 Why restrictions are needed

A function has an inverse only when it is one-to-one on the domain we choose.

The sine function is one-to-one on

\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right].

On that interval, it increases from -1 to 1. So we define \arcsin x as the inverse of sine on this restricted interval.

Arcsine

For -1\le x\le1,

y=\arcsin x

means

\sin y=x \qquad\text{and}\qquad -\frac{\pi}{2}\le y\le\frac{\pi}{2}.

Thus \arcsin x is the angle in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right] whose sine is x.

The range condition is part of the definition.

For example,

\arcsin\left(\frac12\right)=\frac{\pi}{6},

not

\frac{5\pi}{6},

even though

\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\frac12.

The angle \frac{5\pi}{6} is not in the chosen range for arcsine.

The three main inverse trigonometric functions are:

The ranges are chosen so that each restricted trigonometric function is one-to-one.

\arccos\left(-\frac12\right).

We need the angle y in

such that

\cos y=-\frac12.

That angle is

\frac{2\pi}{3}.

Therefore

\arccos\left(-\frac12\right)=\frac{2\pi}{3}.

Evaluate

\arctan(-1).

We need the angle y in

\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)

such that

\tan y=-1.

That angle is

-\frac{\pi}{4}.

So

\arctan(-1)=-\frac{\pi}{4}.

\sin^{-1}x

usually means

\arcsin x,

not

\frac1{\sin x}.

Lines

The first graph in calculus is often a line. Constant velocity gives a line. A tangent approximation gives a line. Newton’s method follows a line. The Mean Value Theorem compares a tangent slope with a secant slope.

So lines deserve to be completely familiar.

 Slope

A nonvertical line has a constant steepness. That steepness is its slope.

If a line passes through two distinct points

(x_1,y_1) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (x_2,y_2),

with x_1\neq x_2, then its slope is

m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}.

In words,

\text{slope}=\frac{\text{change in }y}{\text{change in }x} = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}.

Example

Find the slope of the line through

(1,1) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (5,4).

The change in y is

4-1=3.

The change in x is

5-1=4.

Therefore

m=\frac34.

The line rises 3 units for every 4 units it moves to the right.

 Example

Find the slope of the line through

(2,5) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (6,-3).

We compute

m=\frac{-3-5}{6-2}=\frac{-8}{4}=-2.

The negative sign means the line falls as x increases.

 Vertical lines

A vertical line has no slope, because its run is 0. The slope formula would require division by 0.

A vertical line has equation

x=a.

A horizontal line has slope 0 and equation

y=b.

 Point-slope form

If a line has slope m and passes through the point

(x_1,y_1),

then every point (x,y) on the line satisfies

\frac{y-y_1}{x-x_1}=m

when x\neq x_1. Multiplying by x-x_1 gives the most useful form:

y-y_1=m(x-x_1).

This is called the point-slope form of a line.

It is the same form used for tangent lines in calculus:

y-f(a)=f'(a)(x-a).

Example

Find an equation of the line through

(2,-1)

with slope

m=\frac32.

Use point-slope form:

y-(-1)=\frac32(x-2).

Thus

y+1=\frac32(x-2).

If we solve for y,

y+1=\frac32x-3,

so

y=\frac32x-4.

Slope-intercept form

If a line has slope m and crosses the y-axis at

(0,b),

then point-slope form gives

y-b=m(x-0).

So

y=mx+b.

This is the slope-intercept form. The number b is the y-intercept.

Example

The line

y=-2x+5

has slope

m=-2

and y-intercept

b=5.

So it crosses the y-axis at

(0,5).

It falls 2 units for every 1 unit it moves to the right.

 Line through two points

To find a line through two points:

\text{first find the slope, then use point-slope form.}

Example

Find an equation of the line through

(1,4) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (5,-2).

First compute the slope:

m=\frac{-2-4}{5-1}=\frac{-6}{4}=-\frac32.

Use point-slope form with (1,4):

y-4=-\frac32(x-1).

This is already a good equation. If we want slope-intercept form,

y-4=-\frac32x+\frac32,

so

y=-\frac32x+\frac{11}{2}.

General form

Every line can be written in the form

Ax+By+C=0,

where A, B, and C are constants, and A and B are not both 0.

If B\neq0, then we can solve for y:

By=-Ax-C,

so

y=-\frac ABx-\frac CB.

Therefore the slope is

m=-\frac AB

and the y-intercept is

b=-\frac CB.

If B=0, the equation becomes

Ax+C=0,

so

x=-\frac CA.

That is a vertical line.

Example

Find the slope and intercepts of

3x-5y=15.

Solve for y:

-5y=15-3x.

Thus

y=\frac35x-3.

So the slope is

\frac35

and the y-intercept is

(0,-3).

To find the x-intercept, set y=0:

3x=15,

so

x=5.

Thus the x-intercept is

(5,0).

 Parallel and perpendicular lines

Slope detects parallel and perpendicular lines.

Parallel lines

Two nonvertical lines are parallel exactly when they have the same slope.

 Perpendicular lines

Two nonvertical lines with slopes m_1 and m_2 are perpendicular exactly when

m_1m_2=-1.

Equivalently,

m_2=-\frac1{m_1}.

A vertical line is perpendicular to a horizontal line.

Example

Find the line through

(-1,2)

parallel to

2x-3y=6.

First solve the given line for y:

-3y=6-2x,

so

y=\frac23x-2.

The slope is

m=\frac23.

A parallel line has the same slope. Using point-slope form,

y-2=\frac23(x+1).

Thus

y=\frac23x+\frac83.

Example

Find the line through

(4,-1)

perpendicular to

y=-4x+7.

The given line has slope

-4.

A perpendicular line has slope

\frac14,

because

(-4)\left(\frac14\right)=-1.

Thus

y+1=\frac14(x-4).

So

y=\frac14x-2.

Circles

A circle is a distance condition.

Choose a center

(h,k)

and a radius r>0. A point (x,y) lies on the circle if its distance from (h,k) is exactly r.

That sentence becomes an equation.

 Equation of a circle

The distance from (x,y) to (h,k) is

\sqrt{(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2}.

So the circle condition is

\sqrt{(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2}=r.

Squaring both sides gives

(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2.

This is the standard equation of a circle with center (h,k) and radius r.

If the center is the origin, the equation becomes

x^2+y^2=r^2.

Example

Find an equation of the circle with center

(2,-3)

and radius

5.

Use the standard form:

(x-2)^2+(y-(-3))^2=5^2.

Thus

(x-2)^2+(y+3)^2=25.

Completing the square

A circle is not always written in standard form. Completing the square reveals the center and radius.

Example

Show that

x^2+y^2-6x+4y-12=0

is a circle, and find its center and radius.

Group the x-terms and y-terms:

x^2-6x+y^2+4y=12.

Complete the square in each variable:

x^2-6x=(x-3)^2-9,

and

y^2+4y=(y+2)^2-4.

Substitute:

(x-3)^2-9+(y+2)^2-4=12.

Thus

(x-3)^2+(y+2)^2=25.

So the center is

(3,-2)

and the radius is

5.

 Disks and circle inequalities

A circle is the boundary. A disk is the filled-in region.

The equation

(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2

means distance exactly r from (h,k).

The inequality

(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2<r^2

means distance less than r. This is the inside of the circle, without the boundary.

The inequality

(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2\le r^2

means the inside together with the boundary.

Disks and circle inequalities condition region (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2 circle (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2<r^2 inside, boundary excluded (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2\le r^2 inside, boundary included (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2>r^2 outside, boundary excluded
Example

Describe the region

(x-1)^2+(y+3)^2\le 9.

The center is

(1,-3),

and the radius is

3.

Because the inequality is \le, the region is the closed disk: all points whose distance from (1,-3) is at most 3.

Parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas

Lines and circles are not the only curves that appear in calculus. Parabolas are the basic graphs of quadratic functions. Ellipses appear in planetary motion and optimization. Hyperbolas appear in reciprocal functions, asymptotes, and polar coordinates.

These curves are called conic sections, or simply conics, because they can be obtained by slicing a cone with a plane. For our purposes, the most important skill is algebraic recognition.

\text{Which squared terms appear?} \qquad \text{What are their signs?} \qquad \text{Can we complete the square?}

 Parabolas

A vertical parabola, with a\ne0, has vertex form

y=a(x-h)^2+k.

Its vertex is

(h,k).

If a>0, it opens upward. If a<0, it opens downward.

A horizontal parabola has form

x=a(y-k)^2+h.

If a>0, it opens to the right. If a<0, it opens to the left.

Example

Describe the graph of

y=2(x-1)^2-3.

The vertex is

(1,-3).

Since a=2>0, the parabola opens upward. Compared with

y=x^2,

it is shifted right 1, shifted down 3, and vertically stretched by a factor of 2.

 Example

Rewrite

y=x^2-6x+5

in vertex form.

Complete the square:

x^2-6x=(x-3)^2-9.

Therefore

y=(x-3)^2-9+5.

So

y=(x-3)^2-4.

The vertex is

(3,-4).

 Focus and directrix form

A parabola can also be defined as a distance condition: points equidistant from a fixed point and a fixed line.

For a vertical parabola with vertex (h,k) and p\ne0,

(x-h)^2=4p(y-k)

has focus

(h,k+p)

and directrix

y=k-p.

The number p gives the signed distance from the vertex to the focus. If p>0, the parabola opens upward. If p<0, it opens downward.

For a horizontal parabola,

(y-k)^2=4p(x-h)

has focus

(h+p,k)

and directrix

x=h-p.

Example

Find the focus and directrix of

x^2=8y.

Compare with

x^2=4py.

So

4p=8, \qquad p=2.

The vertex is the origin. Therefore the focus is

(0,2)

and the directrix is

y=-2.

 Ellipses

An ellipse is an oval. With a,b>0, its standard equation is

\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}+\frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1.

The center is

(h,k).

The horizontal semi-axis length is a. The vertical semi-axis length is b. The full width is 2a, and the full height is 2b.

Example

Describe the ellipse

\frac{(x+2)^2}{16}+\frac{(y-1)^2}{9}=1.

The center is

(-2,1).

The horizontal semi-axis length is

4,

because 16=4^2. The vertical semi-axis length is

3,

because 9=3^2.

So the ellipse has width 8 and height 6.

 Hyperbolas

A hyperbola has two branches and two asymptotes. In its standard forms below, a,b>0.

A horizontal hyperbola has standard form

\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}-\frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1.

It opens left and right. Its center is (h,k). Its vertices are

(h-a,k) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (h+a,k).

Its asymptotes are

y-k=\pm\frac ba(x-h).

A vertical hyperbola has standard form

\frac{(y-k)^2}{a^2}-\frac{(x-h)^2}{b^2}=1.

It opens up and down. Its vertices are

(h,k-a) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (h,k+a).

Its asymptotes are

y-k=\pm\frac ab(x-h).

Example

Describe

\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{4}=1.

This is a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin. Here

a=3, \qquad b=2.

The vertices are

(-3,0) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (3,0).

The asymptotes are

y=\pm\frac23x.

completing the square for a hyperbola

Put

9y^2-18y-4x^2-4x=28

in standard form.

Group terms:

9(y^2-2y)-4(x^2+x)=28.

Complete the square inside each group:

y^2-2y=(y-1)^2-1,

and

x^2+x=\left(x+\frac12\right)^2-\frac14.

Substitute:

9\bigl((y-1)^2-1\bigr) - 4\left(\left(x+\frac12\right)^2-\frac14\right) = 28.

Expand the constants:

9(y-1)^2-9 - 4\left(x+\frac12\right)^2 +1 = 28.

So

9(y-1)^2-4\left(x+\frac12\right)^2=36.

Divide by 36:

\frac{(y-1)^2}{4} - \frac{\left(x+\frac12\right)^2}{9} = 1.

This is a vertical hyperbola with center

\left(-\frac12,1\right).

Since a=2 and b=3, the vertices are

\left(-\frac12,1-2\right) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \left(-\frac12,1+2\right).

Thus the vertices are

\left(-\frac12,-1\right) \quad\text{and}\quad \left(-\frac12,3\right).

The asymptotes are

y-1=\pm\frac23\left(x+\frac12\right).

Parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas

Lines and circles are not the only curves that appear in calculus. Parabolas are the basic graphs of quadratic functions. Ellipses appear in planetary motion and optimization. Hyperbolas appear in reciprocal functions, asymptotes, and polar coordinates.

These curves are called conic sections, or simply conics, because they can be obtained by slicing a cone with a plane. For our purposes, the most important skill is algebraic recognition.

\text{Which squared terms appear?} \qquad \text{What are their signs?} \qquad \text{Can we complete the square?}

 Parabolas

A vertical parabola, with a\ne0, has vertex form

y=a(x-h)^2+k.

Its vertex is

(h,k).

If a>0, it opens upward. If a<0, it opens downward.

A horizontal parabola has form

x=a(y-k)^2+h.

If a>0, it opens to the right. If a<0, it opens to the left.

Example

Describe the graph of

y=2(x-1)^2-3.

The vertex is

(1,-3).

Since a=2>0, the parabola opens upward. Compared with

y=x^2,

it is shifted right 1, shifted down 3, and vertically stretched by a factor of 2.

 Example

Rewrite

y=x^2-6x+5

in vertex form.

Complete the square:

x^2-6x=(x-3)^2-9.

Therefore

y=(x-3)^2-9+5.

So

y=(x-3)^2-4.

The vertex is

(3,-4).

 Focus and directrix form

A parabola can also be defined as a distance condition: points equidistant from a fixed point and a fixed line.

For a vertical parabola with vertex (h,k) and p\ne0,

(x-h)^2=4p(y-k)

has focus

(h,k+p)

and directrix

y=k-p.

The number p gives the signed distance from the vertex to the focus. If p>0, the parabola opens upward. If p<0, it opens downward.

For a horizontal parabola,

(y-k)^2=4p(x-h)

has focus

(h+p,k)

and directrix

x=h-p.

Example

Find the focus and directrix of

x^2=8y.

Compare with

x^2=4py.

So

4p=8, \qquad p=2.

The vertex is the origin. Therefore the focus is

(0,2)

and the directrix is

y=-2.

 Ellipses

An ellipse is an oval. With a,b>0, its standard equation is

\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}+\frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1.

The center is

(h,k).

The horizontal semi-axis length is a. The vertical semi-axis length is b. The full width is 2a, and the full height is 2b.

Example

Describe the ellipse

\frac{(x+2)^2}{16}+\frac{(y-1)^2}{9}=1.

The center is

(-2,1).

The horizontal semi-axis length is

4,

because 16=4^2. The vertical semi-axis length is

3,

because 9=3^2.

So the ellipse has width 8 and height 6.

 Hyperbolas

A hyperbola has two branches and two asymptotes. In its standard forms below, a,b>0.

A horizontal hyperbola has standard form

\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}-\frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1.

It opens left and right. Its center is (h,k). Its vertices are

(h-a,k) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (h+a,k).

Its asymptotes are

y-k=\pm\frac ba(x-h).

A vertical hyperbola has standard form

\frac{(y-k)^2}{a^2}-\frac{(x-h)^2}{b^2}=1.

It opens up and down. Its vertices are

(h,k-a) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (h,k+a).

Its asymptotes are

y-k=\pm\frac ab(x-h).

Example

Describe

\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{4}=1.

This is a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin. Here

a=3, \qquad b=2.

The vertices are

(-3,0) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (3,0).

The asymptotes are

y=\pm\frac23x.

Put

in standard form.

and

x^2+x=\left(x+\frac12\right)^2-\frac14.

Substitute:

Expand the constants:

So

9(y-1)^2-4\left(x+\frac12\right)^2=36.

Divide by 36:

\frac{(y-1)^2}{4} - \frac{\left(x+\frac12\right)^2}{9} = 1.

This is a vertical hyperbola with center

\left(-\frac12,1\right).

Since a=2 and b=3, the vertices are

\left(-\frac12,1-2\right) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \left(-\frac12,1+2\right).

Thus the vertices are

\left(-\frac12,-1\right) \quad\text{and}\quad \left(-\frac12,3\right).

The asymptotes are

y-1=\pm\frac23\left(x+\frac12\right).

Distance and midpoint formulas

Distance turns coordinate geometry into measurement. The distance formula is just the Pythagorean Theorem written with coordinates.

 Distance between two points

Let

P_1=(x_1,y_1) \qquad\text{and}\qquad P_2=(x_2,y_2).

The horizontal change from P_1 to P_2 is

x_2-x_1.

The vertical change is

y_2-y_1.

These are the legs of a right triangle. Therefore the distance between the points is

d(P_1,P_2) = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}.

Example

Find the distance between

(-2,3) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (4,-5).

Use the formula:

d=\sqrt{(4-(-2))^2+(-5-3)^2}.

So

d=\sqrt{6^2+(-8)^2} = \sqrt{36+64} = \sqrt{100} = 10.

 Midpoint of a segment

The midpoint is halfway in the x-direction and halfway in the y-direction.

If

P_1=(x_1,y_1) \qquad\text{and}\qquad P_2=(x_2,y_2),

then the midpoint is

M= \left( \frac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1+y_2}{2} \right).

Example

Find the midpoint of the segment joining

(-2,3) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (4,-5).

Average the x-coordinates:

\frac{-2+4}{2}=1.

Average the y-coordinates:

\frac{3+(-5)}{2}=-1.

So the midpoint is

(1,-1).

A locus example: perpendicular bisectors

A locus is a set of points satisfying a condition.

For example, the perpendicular bisector of a segment is the set of all points equidistant from the segment’s endpoints.

Example

Find the set of points (x,y) equidistant from

A=(0,0)

and

B=(4,2).

Equidistant means

d((x,y),A)=d((x,y),B).

Using squared distances avoids square roots:

x^2+y^2=(x-4)^2+(y-2)^2.

Expand the right side:

x^2+y^2=x^2-8x+16+y^2-4y+4.

Cancel x^2+y^2 from both sides:

0=-8x-4y+20.

Thus

8x+4y=20.

Divide by 4:

2x+y=5.

This line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment from A to B.

 Why squared distances are allowed

Distance is nonnegative. If two distances are equal, then their squares are equal. Conversely, if two nonnegative distances have equal squares, then the distances are equal.

Scaling and shifting graphs

Many graphs in calculus come from simpler graphs by shifting, stretching, and reflecting.

If we understand the parent graph, transformations let us sketch the new graph quickly. More importantly, they tell us how the formula changes the geometry.

 Vertical and horizontal shifts

Let y=f(x).

The graph of

y=f(x)+k

is the graph of y=f(x) shifted vertically by k.

If k>0, the graph moves up. If k<0, it moves down.

The graph of

y=f(x-h)

is the graph of y=f(x) shifted horizontally by h.

If h>0, the graph moves right. If h<0, it moves left.

Vertical and horizontal shifts new function effect on graph of y=f(x) f(x)+k shift up by k if k>0, down if k<0 f(x-h) shift right by h if h>0, left if h<0
Example

Start with

f(x)=x^2.

Then

g(x)=(x-3)^2-1

is the graph of x^2 shifted right 3 and down 1. Its vertex is

(3,-1).

 Vertical scaling and reflection

The graph of

y=af(x)

is a vertical scaling of the graph of y=f(x).

If

|a|>1,

the graph stretches vertically.

If

0<|a|<1,

the graph compresses vertically.

If

a<0,

the graph is also reflected across the x-axis.

Example

Start with

f(x)=\sqrt{x}.

Then

g(x)=-2\sqrt{x}

is reflected across the x-axis and stretched vertically by 2. Its domain is still

[0,\infty),

but its range is

(-\infty,0].

 Horizontal scaling and reflection

The graph of

y=f(cx)

is a horizontal scaling of the graph of y=f(x).

If

|c|>1,

the graph compresses horizontally by a factor of |c|.

If

0<|c|<1,

the graph stretches horizontally by a factor of 1/|c|.

If

c<0,

the graph is also reflected across the y-axis.

This direction can feel backwards. The reason is that the input is being changed before f acts.

For example,

f(2x)

reaches the old input 1 when

2x=1,

so

x=\frac12.

Everything happens in half the horizontal distance. The graph is compressed.

Horizontal scaling and reflection new function effect on graph of y=f(x) af(x), a>1 vertical stretch by a af(x), 0<a<1 vertical compression by a -f(x) reflection across the x-axis f(cx), c>1 horizontal compression by c f(cx), 0<c<1 horizontal stretch by 1/c f(-x) reflection across the y-axis
Example

Compare

y=\sin x

and

y=\sin(2x).

The graph of \sin(2x) completes a full oscillation when

2x=2\pi,

so

x=\pi.

Thus its period is

\pi,

half the period of \sin x. The graph is horizontally compressed by 2.

 Transformations and domains

Transformations also affect domains and ranges.

Example

Find the domain and range of

g(x)=\sqrt{x-2}+1.

The square root requires

x-2\ge0.

So

x\ge2.

Thus the domain is

[2,\infty).

Since

\sqrt{x-2}\ge0,

we have

\sqrt{x-2}+1\ge1.

Thus the range is

[1,\infty).

The graph of y=\sqrt{x} has been shifted right 2 and up 1.

Transformations are not limited to functions. They also apply to equations.

For example, the unit circle

x^2+y^2=1

becomes an ellipse if we stretch horizontally by 3 and vertically by 2.

A point on the stretched curve has the form

x=3u, \qquad y=2v,

where

u^2+v^2=1.

So

u=\frac{x}{3}, \qquad v=\frac{y}{2}.

Substitute into the unit circle equation:

\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)^2+\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)^2=1.

Thus the stretched curve is

\frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1.

If we then shift the ellipse up by 1, replace y by y-1:

\frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{(y-1)^2}{4}=1.

This is an ellipse centered at

(0,1)

with horizontal semi-axis 3 and vertical semi-axis 2.

Transformation warning

For graph transformations, the input changes in the opposite-looking direction. The expression x-h shifts right by h, not left.

A reliable check is to track a familiar point. If the old graph starts at (0,0), then y=\sqrt{x-2}+1 starts at (2,1).

Factoring and completing the square

Factoring turns addition into multiplication. That is why it is so useful in calculus. Multiplication can cancel. Multiplication has signs we can track. Multiplication reveals zeros.

 Common factors

The first question in factoring is always:

\text{Is there a common factor?}

For example,

6x^3-9x^2=3x^2(2x-3).

The common factor 3x^2 was present in both terms.

Example

Factor

4x^4-8x^3+12x^2.

Each term contains 4x^2, so

4x^4-8x^3+12x^2 = 4x^2(x^2-2x+3).

The quadratic x^2-2x+3 does not factor over the real numbers, because its discriminant is

(-2)^2-4(1)(3)=4-12=-8<0.

So the real factorization is

4x^4-8x^3+12x^2=4x^2(x^2-2x+3).

Special products

Some patterns appear often enough that they should become automatic.

Special products name identity Difference of squares \displaystyle a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b) Perfect square \displaystyle a^2+2ab+b^2=(a+b)^2 Perfect square \displaystyle a^2-2ab+b^2=(a-b)^2 Difference of cubes \displaystyle a^3-b^3=(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2) Sum of cubes \displaystyle a^3+b^3=(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)
Example

Factor

x^2-9.

This is a difference of squares:

x^2-9=x^2-3^2=(x-3)(x+3).

 Example

Factor

4x^2+12x+9.

This is a perfect square:

4x^2+12x+9=(2x)^2+2(2x)(3)+3^2.

Therefore

4x^2+12x+9=(2x+3)^2.

Factoring quadratics

A quadratic has the form

ax^2+bx+c.

When a=1, factoring asks for two numbers whose product is c and whose sum is b.

Example

Factor

x^2+5x+6.

We need two numbers with product 6 and sum 5. They are 2 and 3. Thus

x^2+5x+6=(x+2)(x+3).

Example

Factor

x^2-x-12.

We need two numbers with product -12 and sum -1. They are -4 and 3. Thus

x^2-x-12=(x-4)(x+3).

When the leading coefficient is not 1, one reliable method is grouping.

 Example

Factor

6x^2+x-2.

First multiply the leading coefficient and constant term:

6(-2)=-12.

We need two numbers with product -12 and sum 1. They are 4 and -3. Rewrite the middle term:

6x^2+x-2=6x^2+4x-3x-2.

Group:

6x^2+4x-3x-2 = 2x(3x+2)-1(3x+2).

Now factor out the common binomial:

6x^2+x-2=(3x+2)(2x-1).

Why factoring matters in limits

A common calculus move is to simplify a difference quotient.

Example

Simplify

\frac{(2+h)^2-4}{h}, \qquad h\neq0.

Expand:

(2+h)^2-4=4+4h+h^2-4=4h+h^2.

Factor:

4h+h^2=h(4+h).

Therefore

\frac{(2+h)^2-4}{h} = \frac{h(4+h)}{h}.

Since h\neq0,

\frac{(2+h)^2-4}{h}=4+h.

The cancellation is legal because h\neq0. That condition matters. The original fraction is undefined at h=0, but the simplified expression 4+h shows what the fraction approaches as h gets close to 0.

 Completing the square

Factoring is not always possible. Completing the square is often the next best move.

The pattern is

x^2+bx = \left(x+\frac b2\right)^2-\left(\frac b2\right)^2.

So

x^2+bx+c = \left(x+\frac b2\right)^2+c-\left(\frac b2\right)^2.

Example

Complete the square:

x^2-6x+10.

Half of -6 is -3. Square it:

(-3)^2=9.

Add and subtract 9:

x^2-6x+10 = (x^2-6x+9)+1.

Therefore

x^2-6x+10=(x-3)^2+1.

This form immediately tells us that

x^2-6x+10\ge1

for every real x, because (x-3)^2\ge0.

 Example

Complete the square for

2x^2+8x-5.

First factor out the leading coefficient from the quadratic and linear terms:

2x^2+8x-5=2(x^2+4x)-5.

Complete the square inside the parentheses. Half of 4 is 2, and 2^2=4:

x^2+4x=(x+2)^2-4.

Thus

2(x^2+4x)-5 = 2\bigl((x+2)^2-4\bigr)-5.

So

2x^2+8x-5=2(x+2)^2-13.

This form tells us that the minimum value is -13, reached at x=-2.

 Quadratic formula

Completing the square also gives the quadratic formula. For

ax^2+bx+c=0, \qquad a\neq0,

the solutions are

x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}.

The expression

b^2-4ac

is called the discriminant. It tells how many real roots the quadratic has.

Quadratic formula discriminant real roots b^2-4ac>0 two distinct real roots b^2-4ac=0 one repeated real root b^2-4ac<0 no real roots
Example

Solve

Factoring and completing the square

Factoring turns addition into multiplication. That is why it is so useful in calculus. Multiplication can cancel. Multiplication has signs we can track. Multiplication reveals zeros.

 Common factors

The first question in factoring is always:

\text{Is there a common factor?}

For example,

6x^3-9x^2=3x^2(2x-3).

The common factor 3x^2 was present in both terms.

Example

Factor

4x^4-8x^3+12x^2.

Each term contains 4x^2, so

4x^4-8x^3+12x^2 = 4x^2(x^2-2x+3).

The quadratic x^2-2x+3 does not factor over the real numbers, because its discriminant is

(-2)^2-4(1)(3)=4-12=-8<0.

So the real factorization is

4x^4-8x^3+12x^2=4x^2(x^2-2x+3).

Special products

Some patterns appear often enough that they should become automatic.

Special products name identity Difference of squares \displaystyle a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b) Perfect square \displaystyle a^2+2ab+b^2=(a+b)^2 Perfect square \displaystyle a^2-2ab+b^2=(a-b)^2 Difference of cubes \displaystyle a^3-b^3=(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2) Sum of cubes \displaystyle a^3+b^3=(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)
Example

Factor

x^2-9.

This is a difference of squares:

x^2-9=x^2-3^2=(x-3)(x+3).

 Example

Factor

4x^2+12x+9.

This is a perfect square:

4x^2+12x+9=(2x)^2+2(2x)(3)+3^2.

Therefore

4x^2+12x+9=(2x+3)^2.

Factoring quadratics

A quadratic has the form

ax^2+bx+c.

When a=1, factoring asks for two numbers whose product is c and whose sum is b.

Example

Factor

x^2+5x+6.

We need two numbers with product 6 and sum 5. They are 2 and 3. Thus

x^2+5x+6=(x+2)(x+3).

Example

Factor

x^2-x-12.

We need two numbers with product -12 and sum -1. They are -4 and 3. Thus

x^2-x-12=(x-4)(x+3).

When the leading coefficient is not 1, one reliable method is grouping.

 Example

Factor

6x^2+x-2.

First multiply the leading coefficient and constant term:

6(-2)=-12.

We need two numbers with product -12 and sum 1. They are 4 and -3. Rewrite the middle term:

6x^2+x-2=6x^2+4x-3x-2.

Group:

6x^2+4x-3x-2 = 2x(3x+2)-1(3x+2).

Now factor out the common binomial:

6x^2+x-2=(3x+2)(2x-1).

Why factoring matters in limits

A common calculus move is to simplify a difference quotient.

Example

Simplify

\frac{(2+h)^2-4}{h}, \qquad h\neq0.

Expand:

(2+h)^2-4=4+4h+h^2-4=4h+h^2.

Factor:

4h+h^2=h(4+h).

Therefore

\frac{(2+h)^2-4}{h} = \frac{h(4+h)}{h}.

Since h\neq0,

\frac{(2+h)^2-4}{h}=4+h.

The cancellation is legal because h\neq0. That condition matters. The original fraction is undefined at h=0, but the simplified expression 4+h shows what the fraction approaches as h gets close to 0.

Factoring is not always possible. Completing the square is often the next best move.

The pattern is

x^2+bx = \left(x+\frac b2\right)^2-\left(\frac b2\right)^2.

So

x^2+bx+c = \left(x+\frac b2\right)^2+c-\left(\frac b2\right)^2.

Example

Complete the square:

x^2-6x+10.

Half of -6 is -3. Square it:

(-3)^2=9.

Add and subtract 9:

x^2-6x+10 = (x^2-6x+9)+1.

Therefore

x^2-6x+10=(x-3)^2+1.

This form immediately tells us that

x^2-6x+10\ge1

for every real x, because (x-3)^2\ge0.

Complete the square for

2x^2+8x-5.

First factor out the leading coefficient from the quadratic and linear terms:

2x^2+8x-5=2(x^2+4x)-5.

Complete the square inside the parentheses. Half of 4 is 2, and 2^2=4:

x^2+4x=(x+2)^2-4.

Thus

2(x^2+4x)-5 = 2\bigl((x+2)^2-4\bigr)-5.

So

2x^2+8x-5=2(x+2)^2-13.

This form tells us that the minimum value is -13, reached at x=-2.

Completing the square also gives the quadratic formula. For

ax^2+bx+c=0, \qquad a\neq0,

the solutions are

x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}.

The expression

b^2-4ac

is called the discriminant. It tells how many real roots the quadratic has.

Quadratic formula discriminant real roots b^2-4ac>0 two distinct real roots b^2-4ac=0 one repeated real root b^2-4ac<0 no real roots

Solve

Inequalities and absolute values

Calculus uses inequalities to control error.

A limit proof says: make the input error small enough so that the output error is below a chosen bound. An approximation theorem says: the remainder is no larger than a certain expression. A convergence test says: compare one quantity with another.

So inequalities are not only algebraic chores. They are the grammar of control.

 Rules for inequalities

The safe rules are:

Rules for inequalities operation rule Add the same number If a<b, then a+c<b+c. Subtract the same number If a<b, then a-c<b-c. Multiply by a positive number If a<b and c>0, then ac<bc. Multiply by a negative number If a<b and c<0, then ac>bc. Take reciprocals of positives If 0<a<b, then \dfrac1a>\dfrac1b.

The most common mistake is forgetting to reverse the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.

Example

Solve

-3x+5<11.

Subtract 5:

-3x<6.

Divide by -3. Because -3 is negative, reverse the inequality:

x>-2.

Sign charts

For polynomial and rational inequalities, factoring and sign charts are usually safer than expanding.

Example

Solve

x^2-x-6>0.

Factor:

x^2-x-6=(x-3)(x+2).

The critical numbers are

x=-2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=3.

They split the real line into three intervals:

(-\infty,-2), \qquad (-2,3), \qquad (3,\infty).

Test one point in each interval.

Example interval x+2 x-3 (x+2)(x-3) (-\infty,-2) - - + (-2,3) + - - (3,\infty) + + +

We need the product to be positive, so

x<-2 \quad\text{or}\quad x>3.

In interval notation,

(-\infty,-2)\cup(3,\infty).

Because the inequality is strict, the endpoints are not included.

 Example

Solve

\frac{x+1}{x-2}\le0.

The numerator is zero at x=-1. The denominator is zero at x=2, where the expression is undefined.

These numbers split the line into

(-\infty,-1), \qquad (-1,2), \qquad (2,\infty).

Example interval x+1 x-2 \dfrac{x+1}{x-2} (-\infty,-1) - - + (-1,2) + - - (2,\infty) + + +

We need the expression to be less than or equal to 0. It is negative on (-1,2), and it is zero at x=-1. It is undefined at x=2.

Therefore

[-1,2).

Absolute value as distance

The absolute value |x| is the distance from x to 0. More generally,

|x-a|

is the distance from x to a.

This gives the most important translations:

|x-a|<r \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a-r<x<a+r, \qquad r>0,

and

|x-a|\le r \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a-r\le x\le a+r.

Example

Solve

|x-4|<0.2.

This means that x is within 0.2 of 4. Therefore

4-0.2<x<4+0.2.

So

3.8<x<4.2.

Example

Solve

|2x+1|\le5.

Translate to a compound inequality:

-5\le2x+1\le5.

Subtract 1:

-6\le2x\le4.

Divide by 2:

-3\le x\le2.

Absolute value and limits

The notation in limits uses absolute value because limits are about distance.

For example,

|x-2|<0.01

means that x is within 0.01 of 2.

If

f(x)=3x+1,

then the distance from f(x) to 7 is

|f(x)-7| = |3x+1-7| = |3x-6| = 3|x-2|.

So if we want

|f(x)-7|<0.03,

it is enough to require

3|x-2|<0.03.

That is,

|x-2|<0.01.

This is the algebraic heart of a simple epsilon-delta proof. The absolute value measures the input error and the output error.

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus The Fundamental Theorem

Chapter built the integral as accumulated signed change:

\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.

At first this integral was a number. It accumulated from one fixed endpoint to another.

That small change turns the integral into a function. The surprise is that this new function has a derivative, and its derivative is the function we started with.

\text{accumulate } f \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{differentiate the accumulation} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f.

This is the first half of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

What Integrals Measure Applications of Integration

In Chapter , the foundational slice was a rectangle:

\text{height}\cdot\text{width}.

Moving forward, the geometry of the slice will adapt to the problem. For the area between curves, the slice is a vertical strip. For the volume of a solid, the slice is a thin cross-section.

Geometry is only the beginning. Integrals can just as easily accumulate mass, mechanical work, fluid pressure, or probability. In every new application, the formula and units of the slice will change. But while the definition of the slice varies wildly from problem to problem, the underlying architecture of the calculus does not. Every application relies on the exact same sequence:

\text{isolate a differential slice, approximate its contribution, and integrate to accumulate the total.}

The one-dimensional Stokes theorem

The Fundamental Theorem told us that

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).

At first, this was an antiderivative rule. It let us evaluate integrals. But there is a deeper geometric reading:

\text{what accumulates inside an interval is measured by what happens on its boundary.}

In one dimension, the boundary of an interval consists of two endpoints. The right endpoint counts positively. The left endpoint counts negatively.

That signed boundary is the seed of Stokes’ theorem.

 Boundary of an interval

An interval is not just a set of points. When we write

\int_a^b f(x)\,dx,

we are traveling from a to b. The direction matters. Reversing the direction changes the sign:

\int_b^a f(x)\,dx=-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.

So the oriented interval from a to b has an oriented boundary.

\partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}.

This notation says:

\text{right endpoint} \quad - \quad \text{left endpoint}.

The endpoint b has sign +. The endpoint a has sign -.

This sign convention is not decoration. It is what makes intervals add correctly.

Suppose

a<c<b.

Then the interval [a,b] can be split into

[a,c] \qquad\text{and}\qquad [c,b].

Their boundaries are

\partial[a,c]=\{c\}-\{a\},

and

\partial[c,b]=\{b\}-\{c\}.

Add them:

\bigl(\{c\}-\{a\}\bigr)+\bigl(\{b\}-\{c\}\bigr)=\{b\}-\{a\}.

The interior point c cancels.

\text{interior boundaries cancel; only the outer boundary remains.}

This is the same cancellation that appeared in finite differences. If

a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b,

then

\bigl(F(x_1)-F(x_0)\bigr) + \bigl(F(x_2)-F(x_1)\bigr) + \cdots + \bigl(F(x_n)-F(x_{n-1})\bigr) = F(b)-F(a).

All the interior values cancel. The boundary values survive.

The Fundamental Theorem is the limiting version of this telescoping idea.

Why is the boundary of an interval two signed endpoints?

The oriented interval from a to b has boundary \{b\}-\{a\}. In your own words, why does direction matter, and why do those opposite signs make split intervals add correctly?

Traveling from a to b arrives at b and leaves a. If you split at an interior point, the extra interior endpoint is counted plus and then minus, so it cancels.

<m>\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)</m>

Let F be differentiable on [a,b], with F' continuous. Then the Fundamental Theorem gives

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).

We can now read the formula in boundary language:

F(b)-F(a) = \text{value of \(F\) on the signed boundary } \{b\}-\{a\}.

So

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx = \int_{\partial[a,b]} F.

The notation on the right is only a compact way to say

\int_{\partial[a,b]} F = F(b)-F(a).

It is not a new kind of ordinary integral yet. It is boundary bookkeeping.

Example

Let

F(x)=x^3.

Then

F'(x)=3x^2.

On the interval [1,3],

\int_1^3 3x^2\,dx = F(3)-F(1) = 27-1 = 26.

The integral of the derivative over the interval is determined entirely by the endpoint values of F.

 reversing the orientation

Again let

F(x)=x^3.

Then

\int_3^1 3x^2\,dx = F(1)-F(3) = 1-27 = -26.

The same interval with the opposite orientation has the opposite boundary:

\partial[3,1]=\{1\}-\{3\}.

So the sign changes exactly as it should.

 Warning: jumps are not ordinary derivatives

The theorem requires F to be differentiable on the interval. If F jumps, the ordinary derivative does not capture the jump.

Consider the step function

H(x)= \begin{cases} 0, \amp x<0,\\ 1, \amp x\ge0. \end{cases}

On [-1,1], the endpoint change is

H(1)-H(-1)=1-0=1.

But H is not differentiable at 0. Away from 0, it is constant, so its derivative is 0 where the derivative exists.

If we tried to integrate the ordinary derivative away from the jump, we would get

0,

not 1.

The missing change is concentrated at the jump. Ordinary single-variable calculus does not represent that jump as an ordinary derivative. This is why the differentiability hypothesis matters.

\text{The Fundamental Theorem applies to honest derivatives, not to hidden jumps.}

Why is the Fundamental Theorem a boundary theorem?

The identity \int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a) says that what accumulates inside is measured by the signed boundary. In your own words, why is that a geometric reading rather than only an antiderivative rule, and why do hidden jumps refuse to be ordinary derivatives?

The interior contributions telescope, leaving only the ending value minus the starting value. A jump is not produced by a continuous derivative, so the theorem’s hypotheses are part of the geometry.

The FTC as a boundary theorem

The differential notation makes the boundary pattern clearer.

For a differentiable function F, define

dF=F'(x)\,dx.

At this point, dF is a compact name for the integrand F'(x)\,dx. It is the small change in F predicted by the derivative:

F(x+dx)-F(x)\approx F'(x)\,dx.

With this notation, the Fundamental Theorem becomes

\int_{[a,b]} dF=F(b)-F(a).

Using boundary notation,

\int_{[a,b]} dF=\int_{\partial[a,b]} F.

This is the one-dimensional Stokes theorem.

The one-dimensional Stokes theorem

If F is differentiable on [a,b] and F' is continuous, then

\int_{[a,b]} dF=\int_{\partial[a,b]} F.

In ordinary calculus notation, this says

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).

The theorem has the same structure as the finite telescoping sum:

\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(F(x_j)-F(x_{j-1})\bigr)=F(b)-F(a).

The integral version replaces finite changes by infinitely many small changes:

dF=F'(x)\,dx.

Then the interior cancellations become continuous. Only the boundary remains.

Exact integrands

An integrand of the form

F'(x)\,dx=dF

is called an exact differential.

When an integrand is exact, its integral depends only on the boundary:

\int_a^b dF=F(b)-F(a).

This is exactly what an antiderivative does. Finding an antiderivative is finding a function F whose differential is the integrand.

 What does it mean for an integrand to be exact?

An integrand of the form dF=F'(x)\,dx is exact, and its integral depends only on the boundary. In your own words, why is finding an antiderivative the same as recognizing an exact differential, and why does that make interior cancellations the whole story?

If every small piece is a change in F, adding the pieces is telescoping. Only the two ends survive, which is exactly what an antiderivative computes.

Example

The integrand

2x\,dx

is exact because

2x\,dx=d(x^2).

Therefore

\int_a^b 2x\,dx = x^2\Big|_a^b = b^2-a^2.

The integrand

\cos x\,dx

is exact because

\cos x\,dx=d(\sin x).

Therefore

\int_a^b \cos x\,dx = \sin b-\sin a.

In one-variable calculus, every continuous integrand f(x)\,dx has an antiderivative locally, because we can define an accumulation function

A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt.

Then the Fundamental Theorem says

dA=f(x)\,dx.

In higher dimensions, this becomes a real question: not every integrand is exact. That is one reason the boundary viewpoint becomes powerful.

 Preview of line integrals and differential forms

The notation

f(x)\,dx

has been with us since the first integrals. It means more than “a function times a symbol.” It is an object designed to be accumulated along an oriented interval.

The dx carries direction. When the direction reverses, dx reverses:

\int_b^a f(x)\,dx=-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.

Substitution also fits this view. If

x=g(u),

then the small step changes by

dx=g'(u)\,du.

So the integrand changes as

f(x)\,dx = f(g(u))g'(u)\,du.

This is not symbol pushing. It is changing the measuring stick.

The same habit prepares line integrals.

In one variable, a path along the line can be written as

x=x(t), \qquad \alpha\le t\le \beta.

Then

dx=x'(t)\,dt.

So the integral of f(x)\,dx along the path becomes

\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} f(x(t))x'(t)\,dt.

This is just substitution written as integration along a path.

In the plane, a curve has two changing coordinates:

x=x(t), \qquad y=y(t).

A natural integrand along such a curve has the form

P(x,y)\,dx+Q(x,y)\,dy.

Along the parametrized curve,

dx=x'(t)\,dt, \qquad dy=y'(t)\,dt.

So the line integral becomes

\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} \Bigl(P(x(t),y(t))x'(t)+Q(x(t),y(t))y'(t)\Bigr)\,dt.

This is the next-course analogue of substitution.

Preview

A one-dimensional integrand f(x)\,dx is the simplest example of a differential form.

A plane integrand

P\,dx+Q\,dy

is accumulated along a curve.

If it happens to equal

d\Phi

for some potential function \Phi, then its integral depends only on the boundary:

\int_C d\Phi=\Phi(\text{end})-\Phi(\text{start}).

That last formula is the same boundary theorem again. The interval has become a curve. The endpoints are still the boundary.

Stokes’ theorem in higher dimensions says the same kind of thing in larger geometry:

\text{integral of a derivative over a region} = \text{integral of the original object over the boundary.}

Single-variable calculus has carried this pattern all along:

\int_{[a,b]} dF=\int_{\partial[a,b]} F.

The next bridge uses the same boundary idea for conservation. If a quantity inside an interval changes, then something must be created inside or must cross the boundary.

Why does <m>dx</m> carry direction?

Reversing limits changes the sign of an integral, and substitution replaces dx by g'(u)\,du. In your own words, why is f(x)\,dx already the simplest differential form, and how does that habit prepare line integrals in the plane?

The symbol dx is an oriented measuring stick, not mere decoration. Along a plane curve the same idea produces P\,dx+Q\,dy, with each coordinate contributing its own directed step.

[a,c] \qquad\text{and}\qquad [c,b].

Their boundaries are

\partial[a,c]=\{c\}-\{a\},

and

\partial[c,b]=\{b\}-\{c\}.

Add them:

\bigl(\{c\}-\{a\}\bigr)+\bigl(\{b\}-\{c\}\bigr)=\{b\}-\{a\}.

The interior point c cancels.

This is the same cancellation that appeared in finite differences. If

a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b,

then

\bigl(F(x_1)-F(x_0)\bigr) + \bigl(F(x_2)-F(x_1)\bigr) + \cdots + \bigl(F(x_n)-F(x_{n-1})\bigr) = F(b)-F(a).

All the interior values cancel. The boundary values survive.

<m>\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)</m>

Let F be differentiable on [a,b], with F' continuous. Then the Fundamental Theorem gives

So

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx = \int_{\partial[a,b]} F.

The notation on the right is only a compact way to say

\int_{\partial[a,b]} F = F(b)-F(a).

It is not a new kind of ordinary integral yet. It is boundary bookkeeping.

Example

Let

F(x)=x^3.

Then

F'(x)=3x^2.

On the interval [1,3],

The integral of the derivative over the interval is determined entirely by the endpoint values of F.

 reversing the orientation

Again let

F(x)=x^3.

Then

\int_3^1 3x^2\,dx = F(1)-F(3) = 1-27 = -26.

The same interval with the opposite orientation has the opposite boundary:

\partial[3,1]=\{1\}-\{3\}.

So the sign changes exactly as it should.

 Warning: jumps are not ordinary derivatives

The theorem requires F to be differentiable on the interval. If F jumps, the ordinary derivative does not capture the jump.

Consider the step function

H(x)= \begin{cases} 0, \amp x<0,\\ 1, \amp x\ge0. \end{cases}

On [-1,1], the endpoint change is

But H is not differentiable at 0. Away from 0, it is constant, so its derivative is 0 where the derivative exists.

If we tried to integrate the ordinary derivative away from the jump, we would get

0,

not 1.

The identity \int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a) says that what accumulates inside is measured by the signed boundary. In your own words, why is that a geometric reading rather than only an antiderivative rule, and why do hidden jumps refuse to be ordinary derivatives?

The interior contributions telescope, leaving only the ending value minus the starting value. A jump is not produced by a continuous derivative, so the theorem’s hypotheses are part of the geometry.

The differential notation makes the boundary pattern clearer.

For a differentiable function F, define

Then the interior cancellations become continuous. Only the boundary remains.

is called an exact differential.

An integrand of the form dF=F'(x)\,dx is exact, and its integral depends only on the boundary. In your own words, why is finding an antiderivative the same as recognizing an exact differential, and why does that make interior cancellations the whole story?

is exact because

Therefore

Therefore

Conservation laws in one dimension

The last section rewrote the Fundamental Theorem as a boundary theorem:

\int_{[a,b]} dF=\int_{\partial[a,b]}F.

The interval contributes its two endpoints. The inside contributes a derivative. The same boundary idea explains one of the most important patterns in science:

\text{what is inside changes because something crosses the boundary or is created inside.}

That sentence is a conservation law.

 Density and flux on a line

Imagine a straight road. Cars move along it. At position x and time t, let

\rho(x,t)=\text{traffic density}

measured in

\text{cars per mile}.

The symbol \rho is the Greek letter rho. It is commonly used for density.

Density tells how much stuff is present per unit length. It does not yet say how fast the stuff is moving.

For motion we need another quantity. Let

q(x,t)=\text{traffic flux}

measured in

\text{cars per hour}.

The flux q(x,t) means the rate at which cars cross the point x, counted positive when they cross to the right.

Density and flux on a line quantity meaning units \rho(x,t) density at position x and time t cars/mile q(x,t) flux through position x at time t cars/hour

These two quantities are related, but they are not the same. A crowded traffic jam can have high density and small flux. A road with fewer cars moving quickly can have smaller density and larger flux.

The total number of cars in the road segment [a,b] at time t is

N(t)=\int_a^b \rho(x,t)\,dx.

This is an accumulation of density over length:

\frac{\text{cars}}{\text{mile}}\cdot \text{mile}=\text{cars}.

So the integral turns density into total amount.

Why are density and flux different quantities?

Density \rho measures how much is present per unit length. Flux q measures how fast stuff crosses a point. In your own words, why can a traffic jam have high density and small flux, and why do you need both quantities to write a conservation law?

Being crowded is not the same as moving. Conservation tracks how the amount inside changes, which requires both how much is there and how much is crossing the ends.

Accumulation inside an interval

Suppose no cars appear or disappear inside the interval [a,b]. There are no parking lots, no ramps, and no accidents removing cars from the road. Then the only way the number of cars inside can change is through the two endpoints.

Cars can enter through the left endpoint a. The rate of entry is

q(a,t).

Cars can leave through the right endpoint b. The rate of leaving is

q(b,t).

Therefore

\frac{dN}{dt}=q(a,t)-q(b,t).

Since

N(t)=\int_a^b \rho(x,t)\,dx,

we can write this as

\frac{d}{dt}\int_a^b \rho(x,t)\,dx = q(a,t)-q(b,t).

This is a one-dimensional conservation law.

Conservation law on an interval

If \rho(x,t) is the density of a conserved quantity and q(x,t) is the flux to the right, then, with no sources or sinks inside [a,b],

\frac{d}{dt}\int_a^b \rho(x,t)\,dx = q(a,t)-q(b,t).

In words:

\text{rate of change inside}=\text{inflow at left}-\text{outflow at right}.

The signs contain the orientation. Positive flux points to the right. At the left endpoint, rightward flux enters the interval. At the right endpoint, rightward flux leaves the interval.

Example

Suppose cars enter a road segment through a at

q(a,t)=1200

cars/hour and leave through b at

q(b,t)=950

cars/hour. Then

\frac{dN}{dt}=1200-950=250.

So the number of cars in the segment is increasing at

250\text{ cars/hour}.

Traffic is accumulating inside.

 Example

Suppose instead

q(a,t)=700, \qquad q(b,t)=1000.

Then

\frac{dN}{dt}=700-1000=-300.

The number of cars in the segment is decreasing at

300\text{ cars/hour}.

More cars leave than enter.

 Sign warning

Flux can be negative. Negative flux means motion to the left.

If

q(a,t)=-100

at the left endpoint, then cars are crossing a to the left. They are leaving the interval through the left endpoint. The formula still works:

\frac{dN}{dt}=q(a,t)-q(b,t).

The negative value of q(a,t) correctly decreases N(t).

 Why is the rate of change inside equal to inflow minus outflow?

With no sources or sinks, \frac{d}{dt}\int_a^b \rho\,dx=q(a,t)-q(b,t). In your own words, why do the signs match the orientation of the interval, and why is this the same boundary idea as the Fundamental Theorem?

Positive flux points to the right, so it enters at the left endpoint and leaves at the right. The interior changes because of what happens on the signed boundary.

What crosses the boundary changes what is inside

The conservation law can be written with the outward boundary in mind.

The interval [a,b] has two outward directions:

\text{left endpoint }a: \text{ outward direction is left},

\text{right endpoint }b: \text{ outward direction is right}.

Since q is positive to the right, the outward flux is

-q(a,t)

at the left endpoint and

q(b,t)

at the right endpoint.

So the total outward flux is

q(b,t)-q(a,t).

The amount inside decreases when outward flux is positive:

\frac{d}{dt}\int_a^b \rho(x,t)\,dx = -\bigl(q(b,t)-q(a,t)\bigr).

This is the same formula as before:

-\bigl(q(b,t)-q(a,t)\bigr)=q(a,t)-q(b,t).

The boundary form is useful because it generalizes.

\text{change inside}=-\text{net outward flow through the boundary}.

Sources and sinks

The formula above assumes that nothing is created or destroyed inside the interval. That assumption matters.

Suppose cars can enter through an on-ramp inside [a,b]. Let

s(x,t)=\text{source rate density}

measured in

\text{cars per mile per hour}.

Then the total rate of creation inside the interval is

\int_a^b s(x,t)\,dx.

The conservation law becomes

\frac{d}{dt}\int_a^b \rho(x,t)\,dx = q(a,t)-q(b,t)+\int_a^b s(x,t)\,dx.

If s>0, cars are being added. If s<0, cars are being removed.

Warning

Boundary flux alone explains the change inside only when there are no sources or sinks inside the interval.

If material is created or destroyed inside, the source term must be included.

This is the same kind of honesty we used throughout calculus. A theorem’s hypotheses are not decoration. They say exactly what the formula is allowed to ignore.

 Why must sources and sinks be named separately?

Boundary flux alone explains the change inside only when nothing is created or destroyed in the interval. In your own words, why is that hypothesis part of the conservation law, and how does a source term restore honesty when cars appear from an on-ramp?

A theorem cannot ignore what it has not been told about. If material is created inside, the accounting must include an interior integral of the source rate.

Preview of divergence in multivariable calculus

The conservation law on every interval contains a local law.

Start with the no-source case:

\frac{d}{dt}\int_a^b \rho(x,t)\,dx = q(a,t)-q(b,t).

If \rho and q are smooth enough, we may read the left side as

\int_a^b \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}(x,t)\,dx.

The notation

\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}

means: differentiate \rho(x,t) with respect to t, while holding x fixed. This is multivariable notation, but the idea is familiar.

The right side can be rewritten using the Fundamental Theorem:

q(a,t)-q(b,t) = -\bigl(q(b,t)-q(a,t)\bigr) = -\int_a^b \frac{\partial q}{\partial x}(x,t)\,dx.

Therefore

\int_a^b \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}(x,t)\,dx = -\int_a^b \frac{\partial q}{\partial x}(x,t)\,dx.

Bring everything to one side:

\int_a^b \left( \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial q}{\partial x} \right) dx=0.

If this holds for every interval [a,b], then the integrand must be zero:

\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial q}{\partial x} = 0.

This is the local form of conservation in one dimension.

One-dimensional conservation law, local form

With no sources or sinks,

\rho_t+q_x=0.

With source term s,

\rho_t+q_x=s.

Here

\rho_t=\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}, \qquad q_x=\frac{\partial q}{\partial x}.

What does q_x mean physically?

Look at a tiny interval from x to x+\Delta x. The flux entering from the left is approximately

q(x,t),

and the flux leaving to the right is approximately

q(x+\Delta x,t).

The net outward flux is

q(x+\Delta x,t)-q(x,t).

Divide by the length \Delta x:

\frac{q(x+\Delta x,t)-q(x,t)}{\Delta x}.

As \Delta x\to0, this approaches

q_x(x,t).

So q_x measures local net outward flow per unit length.

If

q_x>0,

more is leaving a tiny interval than entering it, so density tends to decrease. If

q_x<0,

more is entering than leaving, so density tends to increase.

In multivariable calculus, the flux becomes a vector field. Instead of moving only left or right, material can flow in many directions. The derivative q_x becomes divergence:

\nabla\cdot \mathbf{q}.

The conservation law becomes

\rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}=s.

The idea is the same as the one-dimensional version:

\text{local change in density} + \text{local net outward flow} = \text{local creation}.

This is why the boundary viewpoint matters. The Fundamental Theorem, flux through endpoints, conservation laws, and divergence are not separate tricks. They are stages of one story:

\text{inside} \quad \longleftrightarrow \quad \text{boundary}.

There is one final bridge. Calculus has optimized numbers: shortest distance, largest area, greatest profit. But physics and geometry often ask for the best path. That means optimizing a whole function.

Why does an interval law become a local law?

If the conservation identity holds on every interval, the integrand \rho_t+q_x must vanish. In your own words, why does that local equation deserve the name divergence, and what does it say about how interior change is produced by nearby flux imbalance?

A continuous integrand whose integral vanishes on every interval must be zero: a nonzero value would retain its sign on a small interval. The term q_x measures how flux changes along the line, the one-dimensional divergence.

\eta(a)=\eta(b)=0.

For this to be zero for every allowed wiggle \eta, the coefficient of \eta must be zero:

\frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{y'}{\sqrt{1+(y')^2}} \right) =0.

is constant. This forces y' itself to be constant. Therefore

for some constant m, and hence

The book began with two instruments on a dashboard. One measured accumulated distance. The other measured instantaneous change.

Since then, the same two ideas have appeared in many forms:

\text{derivatives measure local change}, \qquad \text{integrals accumulate small pieces}.

Taylor polynomials turned local derivative information into approximations. Differential equations turned laws of change into unknown functions. Parametric curves let motion draw geometry. Fourier ideas built periodic motion from waves. The one-dimensional Stokes theorem revealed the Fundamental Theorem as a boundary theorem.

These final projects ask you to use the whole story.

Each project below can be done alone or with a small group. A good solution should include clear calculations, graphs when they help, and a short written explanation of what the calculations mean.

 Model, solve, and test a cooling law

Newton’s law of cooling was one of our first differential equation models:

T'=-k(T-T_s).

It says that the rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference between the object and its surroundings.

This project asks you to build the model from data, solve it, and then test whether it deserves to be trusted.

Project question

A cup of coffee is placed in a room whose temperature is

T_s=22^\circ\text{C}.

The coffee temperature is recorded every 5 minutes.

Project question t (minutes) 0 5 10 15 20 25 30 T(t) (^\circ\text{C}) 86 71 59 50 43 38 34

Does Newton’s law of cooling give a reasonable model for this data?

 Part A: solve the model

Start from

T'=-k(T-T_s).

Let

u=T-T_s.

Then

u'=T',

so the differential equation becomes

u'=-ku.

Therefore

u(t)=Ce^{-kt}.

Since

u(t)=T(t)-T_s,

the temperature model is

T(t)=T_s+Ce^{-kt}.

Using the initial temperature T(0)=86, find C.

 Part B: estimate the cooling constant

Use the first and last data points to estimate k. Since

T(t)-T_s=Ce^{-kt},

we have

\frac{T(t_2)-T_s}{T(t_1)-T_s} = e^{-k(t_2-t_1)}.

Taking logarithms gives

k = -\frac{1}{t_2-t_1} \ln \left( \frac{T(t_2)-T_s}{T(t_1)-T_s} \right).

Using t_1=0 and t_2=30,

k \approx -\frac1{30} \ln \left( \frac{34-22}{86-22} \right).

Compute this value. Then write the complete model

T(t)=22+Ce^{-kt}.

 Part C: linearize the data

The model predicts

T(t)-T_s=Ce^{-kt}.

Taking logarithms gives

\ln(T(t)-T_s)=\ln C-kt.

So if Newton’s law is a good model, the points

\bigl(t,\ln(T(t)-22)\bigr)

should lie approximately on a line.

Make a table of

\ln(T(t)-22)

for the data. Plot these transformed points. Estimate the slope of the line and compare it with -k.

 Part D: test the model

For each recorded time t_j, compute the model prediction

T_{\text{model}}(t_j)=22+Ce^{-kt_j}.

Then compute the residual

R_j=T_{\text{data}}(t_j)-T_{\text{model}}(t_j).

Record your results in a table.

Part D: test the model time t_j data T_{\text{data}}(t_j) model T_{\text{model}}(t_j) residual R_j

Plot the residuals. A good model should not show a strong pattern in the residuals. If the residuals are all positive early and all negative later, the model is missing something systematic.

 Part E: interpret the result

Write a short conclusion answering these questions.

  1. What value of k did you find, and what are its units?

  2. According to your model, when will the coffee reach 40^\circ\text{C}?

  3. Does the transformed logarithm plot look approximately linear?

  4. Are the residuals small compared with the temperature changes?

  5. What physical effects might make the model imperfect?

A model is not good because it has a formula. A model is good when it explains the data well enough for the question being asked.

 Why must a model be solved and then tested?

The cooling project asks you to solve Newton’s law, estimate a constant from data, and then check whether the model deserves trust. In your own words, why is solving a differential equation not the end of the scientific story, and what does a mismatch with data force you to admit?

A solved formula is only as good as the law and the measurements that produced it. Testing asks whether the local rule actually shapes the observed global behavior.

Approximate a difficult integral three ways

Some integrals exist clearly but do not have elementary antiderivatives. The integral

I=\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx

is one of the most important examples.

The function

e^{-x^2}

is continuous and positive on [0,1], so the integral exists. But no elementary function has derivative e^{-x^2}. The Fundamental Theorem still tells us what an antiderivative would do, but it does not supply one from our usual list.

So we approximate.

Project question

Approximate

I=\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx

using three numerical methods, compare the answers, and give an error discussion.

 Part A: midpoint rule

Divide [0,1] into n equal subintervals of width

\Delta x=\frac1n.

The midpoint rule is

M_n = \Delta x \sum_{j=1}^{n} f\left(\frac{x_{j-1}+x_j}{2}\right),

where

f(x)=e^{-x^2}.

Compute M_n for

n=4,\quad 8,\quad 16,\quad 32.

 Part B: trapezoidal rule

The trapezoidal rule is

T_n = \frac{\Delta x}{2} \left[ f(x_0)+2f(x_1)+2f(x_2)+\cdots+2f(x_{n-1})+f(x_n) \right].

Compute T_n for

n=4,\quad 8,\quad 16,\quad 32.

 Part C: Simpson’s rule

For even n, Simpson’s rule is

S_n = \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) +\cdots+ 2f(x_{n-2}) + 4f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n) \right].

Compute S_n for

n=4,\quad 8,\quad 16,\quad 32.

 Part D: organize the results

Make a table.

Part D: organize the results \boldsymbol{n} \boldsymbol{M_n} \boldsymbol{T_n} \boldsymbol{S_n} 4 8 16 32

Which column appears to settle fastest?

 Part E: use error bounds

For

f(x)=e^{-x^2}

on [0,1], you may use the bounds

|f''(x)|\le 2

and

|f^{(4)}(x)|\le 12.

The midpoint and trapezoidal error estimates are

|E_M| \le \frac{K(b-a)^3}{24n^2}

and

|E_T| \le \frac{K(b-a)^3}{12n^2},

where

|f''(x)|\le K.

Simpson’s rule has the error estimate

|E_S| \le \frac{K(b-a)^5}{180n^4},

where

|f^{(4)}(x)|\le K.

Use these formulas to give guaranteed error bounds for M_{32}, T_{32}, and S_{32}.

 Optional extension: Taylor series method

Use the Taylor series

e^{-x^2} = 1-x^2+\frac{x^4}{2!}-\frac{x^6}{3!} +\frac{x^8}{4!}-\cdots.

Integrate term by term on [0,1]:

\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx = 1-\frac13+\frac{1}{2!\,5} -\frac{1}{3!\,7} +\frac{1}{4!\,9} -\cdots.

Compare this series approximation with your numerical approximations.

 Final report

Your report should include:

  1. the three approximation tables;

  2. at least one graph of y=e^{-x^2} on [0,1];

  3. a comparison of midpoint, trapezoidal, and Simpson approximations;

  4. a clear error statement for your best approximation;

  5. a paragraph explaining why numerical integration is needed here.

A decimal answer without an error statement is unfinished calculus.

 Why is an approximation incomplete without an error bound?

The integral and Taylor-calculator projects compare several numerical methods and insist on a stopping rule. In your own words, why can three different approximations of the same integral still be unfinished work until their errors are controlled?

More digits are not a guarantee. An error bound turns a computation into a promise, which is the same remainder idea that made Taylor series into algorithms.

Build a Taylor-series calculator

A calculator evaluates functions so quickly that it is easy to forget the question:

\text{How does the calculator know the value?}

For many functions, one answer is Taylor series. The calculator does not store every value of \sin x, e^x, or \cos x. It uses algorithms, and Taylor polynomials are one of the first algorithms we can understand.

Project question

Build a Taylor-series calculator for one or more elementary functions, and test its accuracy.

Choose at least one of the following functions.

Build a Taylor-series calculator function series centered at 0 natural domain for project e^x \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n!} -3\le x\le3 \sin x \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!} -\pi\le x\le\pi \cos x \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!} -\pi\le x\le\pi \ln(1+x) \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n+1}\frac{x^n}{n} -1<x\le1 \arctan x \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{2n+1} -1\le x\le1
Part A: write the partial sums

For your chosen function, define the N-th Taylor approximation.

For example, for \sin x,

S_N(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} (-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}.

For \cos x,

C_N(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} (-1)^n\frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!}.

 Part B: avoid recomputing factorials

A practical calculator should not recompute every factorial from scratch. Use a recurrence for the terms.

For e^x, if

a_n=\frac{x^n}{n!},

then

a_{n+1}=a_n\frac{x}{n+1}.

For \sin x, if

a_n=(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},

then

a_{n+1} = -a_n \frac{x^2}{(2n+2)(2n+3)}.

For \cos x, if

a_n=(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!},

then

a_{n+1} = -a_n \frac{x^2}{(2n+1)(2n+2)}.

Use a similar recurrence for your chosen series.

 Part C: choose a stopping rule

Pick a tolerance such as

10^{-4},\qquad 10^{-6},\qquad \text{or}\qquad 10^{-8}.

For alternating series with decreasing term sizes, the alternating series estimate gives

|\text{error}|\le \text{first omitted term}.

That applies cleanly to many values of \sin x, \cos x, \ln(1+x), and \arctan x, but only when the term sizes are decreasing.

For e^x, use the Lagrange remainder estimate:

|R_N(x)| \le \frac{e^B |x|^{N+1}}{(N+1)!}

when

|x|\le B.

On the interval [-3,3], you may use B=3.

 Part D: test the calculator

Choose at least 8 input values in the interval. For each one, record:

  1. the Taylor approximation;

  2. the number of terms used;

  3. the value from a calculator or computer;

  4. the absolute error.

Use a table.

Part D: test the calculator \boldsymbol{x} Taylor approximation terms used reference value absolute error
Part E: graph the error

Let P_N(x) be your Taylor approximation. Plot

E_N(x)=|f(x)-P_N(x)|

on the interval. Make several plots using different values of N.

Explain where the approximation is best and where it is worst.

 Warning: small terms are not always enough

A common mistake is to stop when the next term is small, without knowing whether the tail is controlled. For alternating series with decreasing terms, that is justified. For other series, it may not be.

A calculator must be fast, but it must also be honest.

 Analyze a parametric curve from motion data

Parametric equations describe a moving point:

x=x(t), \qquad y=y(t).

Real motion data often comes as sampled positions, not exact formulas. This project asks you to recover velocity, speed, distance traveled, and qualitative shape from a table.

Project question

A small robot moves in the plane. Its position is recorded every 0.5 seconds.

Project question t 0 0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0 2.5 3.0 3.5 4.0 x(t) 0.0 0.8 1.4 1.8 2.0 1.9 1.6 1.1 0.5 y(t) 0.0 0.3 0.8 1.5 2.3 3.0 3.5 3.8 3.9

Analyze the motion.

 Part A: plot the path

Plot the points

(x(t_j),y(t_j)).

Connect consecutive points with line segments. Add arrows to show the direction of increasing t.

Describe the shape of the path. Is it nearly straight, curved, looping, or bending sharply?

 Part B: estimate velocity components

At an interior time t_j, estimate the velocity components using centered differences:

x'(t_j)\approx \frac{x(t_{j+1})-x(t_{j-1})}{t_{j+1}-t_{j-1}},

y'(t_j)\approx \frac{y(t_{j+1})-y(t_{j-1})}{t_{j+1}-t_{j-1}}.

Since the time step is 0.5, the denominator is

t_{j+1}-t_{j-1}=1.

Estimate

x'(t),\qquad y'(t)

at

t=0.5,\ 1.0,\ 1.5,\ 2.0,\ 2.5,\ 3.0,\ 3.5.

 Part C: estimate speed

The speed is the length of the velocity vector:

v(t)=\sqrt{(x'(t))^2+(y'(t))^2}.

Make a table of estimated speeds.

Part C: estimate speed \boldsymbol{t} \boldsymbol{x'(t)} \boldsymbol{y'(t)} \boldsymbol{v(t)} 0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0 2.5 3.0 3.5

When is the robot moving fastest? When is it moving slowest?

 Part D: estimate total distance traveled

The robot’s total distance traveled is approximately the sum of the chord lengths between successive recorded positions:

L \approx \sum_{j=0}^{7} \sqrt{ \bigl(x(t_{j+1})-x(t_j)\bigr)^2 + \bigl(y(t_{j+1})-y(t_j)\bigr)^2 }.

Compute this estimate.

This is the data version of the arc length formula

L=\int_a^b \sqrt{ \left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2 } \,dt.

 Part E: estimate acceleration

At an interior time, use second differences:

x''(t_j) \approx \frac{x(t_{j+1})-2x(t_j)+x(t_{j-1})}{(\Delta t)^2},

y''(t_j) \approx \frac{y(t_{j+1})-2y(t_j)+y(t_{j-1})}{(\Delta t)^2},

where

\Delta t=0.5.

Estimate acceleration at several times. Mark on your path where the direction of motion seems to change most strongly.

 Part F: write a motion report

Your report should answer:

  1. What is the approximate total distance traveled?

  2. How is this different from the straight-line distance between the first and last points?

  3. Where is the speed largest?

  4. Where does the path bend most noticeably?

  5. How do finite differences imitate derivatives?

  6. What information would improve your estimates?

Motion data turns the derivative from a formula into a measurement problem.

 Explain the FTC as the first boundary theorem

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a).

For most of the book, this was the theorem that connected antiderivatives and definite integrals. In Section , we gave it a second meaning:

\int_{[a,b]} dF=\int_{\partial[a,b]}F.

The derivative is accumulated over the interval. The original function is evaluated on the boundary.

Project question

Write a short explanation of the Fundamental Theorem as the one-dimensional version of a boundary theorem.

 Part A: start with finite differences

Let

a=x_0<x_1<x_2<\cdots<x_n=b.

Show that

\bigl(F(x_1)-F(x_0)\bigr) + \bigl(F(x_2)-F(x_1)\bigr) +\cdots+ \bigl(F(x_n)-F(x_{n-1})\bigr) = F(b)-F(a).

Explain the cancellation in words:

\text{interior values cancel; boundary values remain.}

Part B: pass from finite differences to the integral

Use the idea

F(x_j)-F(x_{j-1}) \approx F'(x_j^*)\Delta x

to explain why the telescoping sum becomes

\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)

in the limit.

You do not need to give a fully rigorous proof. The goal is to explain the idea clearly.

 Part C: explain orientation

Draw an oriented interval from a to b. Label the left endpoint with a minus sign and the right endpoint with a plus sign.

Then explain the notation

\partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}.

Use this to explain why

\int_{\partial[a,b]}F=F(b)-F(a).

Also explain why reversing the interval reverses the sign:

\int_b^a F'(x)\,dx=F(a)-F(b).

 Part D: include examples

Your explanation should include at least two ordinary calculus examples.

For example,

F(x)=x^2

gives

dF=2x\,dx.

Therefore

\int_1^4 2x\,dx = F(4)-F(1) = 16-1 = 15.

Also include an example with a trigonometric function, such as

F(x)=\sin x.

Then

dF=\cos x\,dx,

so

\int_0^\pi \cos x\,dx = \sin\pi-\sin0 = 0.

Explain why the signed positive and negative parts cancel.

 Part E: connect to the road ahead

End your report by explaining at least one of the following bridges.

  1. In line integrals, the interval becomes a curve, but the boundary is still the two endpoints.

  2. In Green’s theorem, a region in the plane has a boundary curve.

  3. In the Divergence Theorem, a solid has a boundary surface.

  4. In conservation laws, the amount inside changes because something crosses the boundary or is created inside.

The exact higher-dimensional theorems belong to multivariable calculus. But the pattern already appears in one dimension:

\text{integral of a derivative over a region} = \text{integral of the original quantity over the boundary.}

Why is the Fundamental Theorem the first boundary theorem?

One project asks you to explain the FTC as a telescoping finite-difference statement that becomes an integral of a derivative. In your own words, why do interior cancellations leave only the boundary, and why does that viewpoint point toward Green, Stokes, and the Divergence Theorem?

Adding consecutive changes cancels everything except the last value minus the first. In higher dimensions the same pattern remains: what happens inside is measured by what happens on the oriented boundary.

Closing note: what calculus has taught us

This book has followed one thread through many forms.

A derivative began as a velocity:

v(t)=s'(t).

Then it became a tangent slope, a local linear approximation, a sensitivity, an optimizer, and a law of change.

An integral began as accumulated distance:

\int_a^b v(t)\,dt.

Then it became area, mass, work, probability, numerical approximation, and a boundary principle.

A Taylor polynomial began as a local approximation:

f(x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)+\frac{f''(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2+\cdots.

Then it became a gateway to infinite series, Euler’s formula, and waves.

The same ideas now point outward.

Closing note: what calculus has taught us single-variable idea where it leads next derivative partial derivatives, gradients, differential equations integral double integrals, triple integrals, line integrals, surface integrals FTC Green’s theorem, Stokes’ theorem, Divergence Theorem Taylor series approximation theory, numerical methods, complex analysis Fourier preview waves, signal processing, heat flow, quantum mechanics conservation laws fluid flow, electromagnetism, continuum mechanics least action mechanics, geometry, optimization over functions

The subject is larger than this book. But the central pattern is already here:

\text{calculus measures change, accumulates change, and explains how local rules shape global behavior.}

That pattern is worth carrying forward.

What pattern has calculus been teaching all along?

The book began with a speedometer and an odometer and ended with series, waves, conservation, and paths. In your own words, why are derivatives, integrals, remainders, and boundary terms one language rather than four subjects, and what does it mean that local rules shape global behavior?

Instantaneous change and accumulated change undo each other. Approximations become trustworthy through error. Models and conservation laws turn a local derivative statement into a global picture. That is the pattern to carry forward.

Build a Taylor-series calculator for one or more elementary functions, and test its accuracy.

Choose at least one of the following functions.

Build a Taylor-series calculator function series centered at 0 natural domain for project e^x \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n!} -3\le x\le3 \sin x \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!} -\pi\le x\le\pi \cos x \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!} -\pi\le x\le\pi \ln(1+x) \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n+1}\frac{x^n}{n} -1<x\le1 \arctan x \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{2n+1} -1\le x\le1
Part A: write the partial sums

For your chosen function, define the N-th Taylor approximation.

For example, for \sin x,

S_N(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} (-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}.

For \cos x,

C_N(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} (-1)^n\frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!}.

 Part B: avoid recomputing factorials

A practical calculator should not recompute every factorial from scratch. Use a recurrence for the terms.

For e^x, if

a_n=\frac{x^n}{n!},

then

a_{n+1}=a_n\frac{x}{n+1}.

For \sin x, if

a_n=(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},

then

a_{n+1} = -a_n \frac{x^2}{(2n+2)(2n+3)}.

For \cos x, if

a_n=(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!},

then

a_{n+1} = -a_n \frac{x^2}{(2n+1)(2n+2)}.

Use a similar recurrence for your chosen series.

Pick a tolerance such as

10^{-4},\qquad 10^{-6},\qquad \text{or}\qquad 10^{-8}.

For alternating series with decreasing term sizes, the alternating series estimate gives

|\text{error}|\le \text{first omitted term}.

That applies cleanly to many values of \sin x, \cos x, \ln(1+x), and \arctan x, but only when the term sizes are decreasing.

For e^x, use the Lagrange remainder estimate:

|R_N(x)| \le \frac{e^B |x|^{N+1}}{(N+1)!}

when

|x|\le B.

Choose at least 8 input values in the interval. For each one, record:

  1. the Taylor approximation;

  2. the number of terms used;

  3. the value from a calculator or computer;

Use a table.

Part E: graph the error

E_N(x)=|f(x)-P_N(x)|

A common mistake is to stop when the next term is small, without knowing whether the tail is controlled. For alternating series with decreasing terms, that is justified. For other series, it may not be.
