Chapter review and applications

This chapter began with a simple change in perspective. Instead of being handed a function and asked to differentiate it, we were asked to build the function first.

A ladder slides. A box is folded. A cup cools. A population grows. A light ray chooses a path. In each case, the derivative did not appear at the beginning. It appeared after we translated the situation into mathematics.

That is the main skill of the chapter:

real situation \longrightarrow mathematical model \longrightarrow derivative information \longrightarrow interpretation.

The last step is as important as the first. A derivative answer without units, sign, domain, and meaning is not yet an answer to the problem.

 The chapter in one map

The chapter used derivatives in several different ways. The same derivative idea kept returning with different names.

Models and calculus

topic

main question

derivative role

related rates

How fast is one quantity changing?

differentiate a relation

optimization

Which choice is best?

find and test candidates

linear approximation

How much does the output change?

\Delta y\approx f'(x)\Delta x

Newton's method

Where is a zero?

use tangent-line correction

exponential models

What grows at a rate proportional to itself?

y'=ky

logistic models

How does growth slow near a limit?

P'=rP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{K}\right)

least-time paths

Which path makes time stationary?

differentiate time or distance

A derivative answer must still pass three checks

\text{Does the sign make sense?}

\text{Do the units make sense?}

\text{Is the answer allowed by the domain of the model?}

These checks are not afterthoughts. They are part of the mathematics.

Why is the main skill of the chapter building the function first?

A ladder slides, a box is folded, a cup cools, a population grows. In your own words, why did the derivative appear after we translated the situation into mathematics, and why is that change of perspective the chapter’s central idea?

Real situation, then model, then derivative information, then interpretation. We were not handed a function and asked to differentiate it.

Formulas to remember

The formulas below are not separate tricks. Each is a compact version of an idea from the chapter.

\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{idea} \amp \textbf{formula}\\ \hline \text{linear approximation} \amp f(a+\Delta x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)\Delta x\\ \text{differential estimate} \amp dy=f'(x)\,dx\\ \text{Newton's method} \amp x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\\ \text{exponential growth or decay} \amp y'=ky,\qquad y(t)=y_0e^{kt}\\ \text{doubling time} \amp D=\dfrac{\ln2}{k}\quad(k>0)\\ \text{half-life} \amp H=-\dfrac{\ln2}{k}\quad(k<0)\\ \text{Newton's law of cooling} \amp T(t)=T_s+\bigl(T(0)-T_s\bigr)e^{-kt}\\ \text{logistic growth} \amp P'=rP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{K}\right)\\ \text{logistic solution} \amp P(t)=\dfrac{K}{1+\left(\dfrac{K-P_0}{P_0}\right)e^{-rt}} \end{array}

For related rates and optimization, the most important formulas are often not fixed in advance. The formula comes from the geometry or the constraint.

A ladder problem uses

x^2+y^2=L^2.

A cone problem uses

V=\frac13\pi r^2h

together with similar triangles. A box problem uses a volume formula and a physical domain. A can problem uses surface area and a fixed-volume constraint.

The hard part is not memorizing formulas. The hard part is choosing the right quantities and keeping the model honest.

 Skills: related rates and optimization

Related rates and optimization are the two main problem-solving skills of this chapter. They look similar because both begin with translation, but they ask different questions.

Related rates and optimization

problem type

what changes?

what is the goal?

related rates

quantities change with time

find an unknown rate

optimization

a choice variable changes

maximize or minimize a quantity

Related rates checklist

  1. Draw a picture, if geometry is involved.

  2. Name the changing quantities as functions of time.

  3. Write an equation relating the quantities.

  4. Differentiate with respect to time.

  5. Substitute values for the instant in question.

  6. Solve for the desired rate.

  7. Check sign and units.

The most common mistake is substituting the instant-specific numbers too early. The variables must remain variables until after the relation has been differentiated.

 Optimization checklist

  1. Name the quantity to optimize.

  2. Name the variables.

  3. Write the objective function.

  4. Write the constraint.

  5. Use the constraint to get one variable.

  6. Find the physical domain.

  7. Find critical numbers and check endpoints.

  8. Translate the result back into the situation.

The most common mistake is finding a critical point and stopping. A critical point is a candidate, not a conclusion.

 Why do related rates, optimization, and models use the same derivative differently?

Related rates differentiate a relation. Optimization finds and tests candidates. Exponential and logistic models begin with a law for y'. In your own words, why is the derivative doing one job with several names, and how do you tell which question a problem is asking?

Ask whether the problem wants a rate, a best choice, a small-error estimate, a root, or a function obeying a rate law.

Review problems

The problems below are meant to mix the chapter’s ideas. For each one, write a complete solution with units and a sentence interpreting the answer.

  1. Inflating sphere. Air is pumped into a spherical balloon at a constant rate of

    30\pi\text{ cm}^3/\text{s}.

    How fast is the radius increasing when the radius is 5 cm?

  2. Sliding ladder. A 13-foot ladder leans against a wall. The bottom slides away from the wall at

    3\text{ ft/s}.

    How fast is the top sliding down when the bottom is 5 feet from the wall?

  3. Water in a cone. An inverted cone has height 10 feet and radius 5 feet at the top. Water is flowing in at

    3\text{ ft}^3/\text{min}.

    How fast is the water level rising when the water height is 4 feet?

  4. Two cars. One car travels east from an intersection at 40 mph. Another travels north from the same intersection at 30 mph. How fast is the distance between the cars increasing 2 hours later?

  5. Largest rectangle under a parabola. A rectangle has its base on the x-axis and its upper two vertices on the graph

    y=12-x^2.

    Assume the rectangle is symmetric about the y-axis. What dimensions give the largest area?

  6. Open box. A 20-inch by 30-inch sheet of cardboard has equal squares of side length x cut from its corners. The sides are folded up to make an open box. What value of x gives the largest volume?

  7. Fence along a river. A farmer has 300 meters of fencing and wants to make a rectangular field along a river, using the river as one side. What dimensions maximize the area?

  8. Least material can. A closed cylindrical can must hold

    1000\text{ cm}^3.

    Ignoring seams and thickness, find the radius and height that minimize surface area.

  9. Newton’s method. Use Newton’s method to approximate the positive solution of

    x^3=10.

    Start with x_0=2. Compute x_1, x_2, and x_3.

  10. Cooling model. A metal object is heated to 100^\circ\text{C} and placed in a room at 20^\circ\text{C}. After 5 minutes, its temperature is 70^\circ\text{C}. Assuming Newton’s law of cooling, estimate its temperature after 15 minutes.

  11. Logistic growth. A population satisfies

    P'=0.6P\left(1-\frac{P}{800}\right), \qquad P(0)=100.

    Find P(t). When does the population reach 400?

  12. A warning problem. A model for profit is

    P(q)=-q^2+60q-500.

    A factory is allowed to produce only

    40\le q\le 80

    units. Find the production level that maximizes profit on the allowed domain. Explain why the unconstrained critical point is not the answer.

 Project: design a least-material container

A basic can problem assumes that all material costs the same. Real containers are not always like that. The top and bottom may need thicker material. The side wall may be cheaper. The seams may matter.

This project keeps the model simple but makes the design question more realistic.

Design brief

A closed cylindrical container must hold a fixed volume

V_0

cubic centimeters. The side wall costs 1 unit per square centimeter. The top and bottom cost c units per square centimeter, where

c>0.

Find the radius and height that minimize material cost.

 Step 1: Build the cost function

The side area is

2\pi rh.

The top and bottom together have area

2\pi r^2.

Since the top and bottom cost c units per square centimeter, the material cost is

M=2\pi rh+2c\pi r^2.

The volume constraint is

\pi r^2h=V_0.

Solve the constraint for h:

h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}.

Substitute into the cost:

M(r) = 2\pi r\left(\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}\right)+2c\pi r^2.

Thus

M(r)=\frac{2V_0}{r}+2c\pi r^2, \qquad r>0.

 Step 2: Minimize

Differentiate:

M'(r)=-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}+4c\pi r.

Set M'(r)=0:

-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}+4c\pi r=0.

Multiply by r^2:

-2V_0+4c\pi r^3=0.

So

4c\pi r^3=2V_0,

and therefore

r^3=\frac{V_0}{2c\pi}.

Thus

r=\left(\frac{V_0}{2c\pi}\right)^{1/3}.

Now find the height:

h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}.

Since

V_0=2c\pi r^3,

we get

h=\frac{2c\pi r^3}{\pi r^2}=2cr.

Therefore the optimal shape satisfies

h=2cr.

When c=1, this gives

h=2r.

So the height equals the diameter, which matches the equal-cost can from Section .

 Step 3: Interpret the parameter <m>c</m>

The ratio

\frac{h}{r}=2c

shows how the design changes with material cost.

\begin{array}{c|c|c} c \amp h/r \amp \text{interpretation}\\ \hline 1 \amp 2 \amp \text{height equals diameter}\\ 2 \amp 4 \amp \text{top and bottom are expensive, so use smaller ends}\\ 4 \amp 8 \amp \text{ends are very expensive, so make the can tall and narrow} \end{array}

The formula tells a physical story. If the circular ends are expensive, the design tries to reduce their area by using a smaller radius. To keep the same volume, the height must increase.

 Report questions

Write a short report answering these questions.

  1. Derive the cost function M(r) from the geometry and the volume constraint.

  2. Prove that the critical point gives an absolute minimum. One way is to use

    M''(r)=\frac{4V_0}{r^3}+4c\pi>0.

    Another way is to examine what happens to M(r) as r\to0^+ and as r\to\infty.

  3. For

    V_0=1000\text{ cm}^3

    compute the optimal r and h for

    c=1,\qquad c=2,\qquad c=4.

  4. Make a graph of M(r) for each value of c. Mark the minimizing radius.

  5. Explain, in words, why increasing c makes the optimal container taller and narrower.

  6. Extension. Suppose the container has no top. If the bottom costs c units per square centimeter and the side costs 1, build and minimize the new cost function.

 Project: model cooling data

Chapter 2 used cooling coffee as an example of data that should not be modeled by a line forever. This chapter gives the derivative law behind the better model.

Newton’s law of cooling says

T'=-k(T-T_s), \qquad k>0,

where T_s is the surrounding temperature. The solution is

T(t)=T_s+\bigl(T(0)-T_s\bigr)e^{-kt}.

The quantity that decays exponentially is not T itself. It is the excess temperature

T-T_s.

Data

A cup of coffee sits in a room whose temperature is

22^\circ\text{C}.

The measured temperatures are:

\begin{array}{c|cccccc} t\text{ (minutes)} \amp 0 \amp 5 \amp 10 \amp 15 \amp 20 \amp 25\\ \hline T(t)\text{ }(^\circ\text{C}) \amp 90 \amp 73 \amp 60 \amp 51 \amp 44 \amp 39 \end{array}

 A first model from two points

Since

T_s=22

and

T(0)=90,

the model has the form

T(t)=22+68e^{-kt}.

Use T(5)=73:

73=22+68e^{-5k}.

Thus

51=68e^{-5k},

so

e^{-5k}=\frac{51}{68}=\frac34.

Therefore

k=-\frac15\ln\left(\frac34\right).

Numerically,

k\approx0.0575.

So a two-point model is

T(t)=22+68e^{-0.0575t}.

Equivalently,

T(t)=22+68\left(\frac34\right)^{t/5}.

This form says that every 5 minutes, the excess temperature is multiplied by about 3/4.

 Prediction

The predicted temperature after 30 minutes is

T(30)=22+68\left(\frac34\right)^6.

Since

\left(\frac34\right)^6\approx0.178,

we get

T(30)\approx22+68(0.178)\approx34.1^\circ\text{C}.

 Computing task

The two-point model uses only the first two measurements. A better model should use all the data.

Let

E(t)=T(t)-22

be the excess temperature. If Newton’s law is a good model, then

E(t)=E(0)e^{-kt}.

Taking natural logarithms gives

\ln E(t)=\ln E(0)-kt.

So the points

\bigl(t,\ln(T(t)-22)\bigr)

should lie approximately on a line with slope -k.

Complete the following tasks.

  1. Compute the excess temperatures E(t)=T(t)-22.

  2. Compute \ln E(t) for each measured time.

  3. Plot the points

    (t,\ln E(t)).

    Do they look approximately linear?

  4. Estimate the slope of the best-fitting line. Then estimate

    k=-\text{slope}.

  5. Build the model

    T(t)=22+Ae^{-kt}.

    You may take A=68, or estimate A from your fitted line.

  6. Use your model to predict T(30), T(45), and T(60).

  7. Compute residuals:

    \text{residual} = \text{measured temperature} - \text{model temperature}.

    Are the residuals small? Do they show a pattern?

  8. Compare the cooling model with the linear model through the first and last data points. Which model gives a more reasonable prediction after 2 hours? Explain.

What the project tests

A model is not only a formula that fits numbers. It should also respect the behavior of the situation. A cooling object should approach room temperature, not pass below it because a line keeps decreasing forever.

 Why is a model a promise with conditions?

Exponential growth promises a constant relative rate. Logistic growth adds a fixed carrying capacity. In your own words, why must we check whether that promise matches the situation before trusting a formula, and what goes wrong if the conditions are invisible in the early data?

A formula can be mathematically correct and still be the wrong story. Early exponential-looking data may hide a later ceiling.

Concept checks

  1. In a related rates problem, why should we usually differentiate before substituting the values for the instant in question?

  2. In an optimization problem, why is the physical domain part of the model?

  3. A critical point of an objective function lies outside the physical domain. What should you do with it?

  4. Explain the difference between absolute error and relative error.

  5. Why does Newton’s method require f'(x_n)\neq0?

  6. Give one reason Newton’s method can fail even when a root exists.

  7. In the equation

    y'=ky,

    what does k measure?

  8. Why is

    P'=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)

    approximately exponential when P\ll K?

  9. In the logistic model, why is the growth fastest at P=K/2?

  10. Reflection minimizes distance, but refraction minimizes time. Why are these not the same problem when the speed changes?

Why must a derivative answer still pass three checks?

Sign, units, and domain are listed as part of the mathematics, not as afterthoughts. In your own words, why can a correctly computed derivative still fail to answer the original problem if one of those checks is skipped?

A number without direction, units, or feasibility is not yet an answer to a related-rates, optimization, or modeling question.

Where this points

This chapter showed how much can be done with a derivative.

A derivative can relate changing quantities. It can find a best choice. It can estimate error. It can turn a tangent line into a root-finding method. It can express a physical law such as

T'=-k(T-T_s)

or

P'=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right).

But a derivative is still local. It tells how fast something is changing at an instant.

Many questions ask for the accumulated result of those changes.

If velocity is known at every instant, how far did the object travel?

If a force changes with position, how much work was done?

If density varies along a rod, what is the rod’s total mass?

If a rate law tells how a quantity changes, how much total change has occurred over an interval?

Those questions return us to the dashboard from the beginning of the book. The speedometer gives rate. The odometer gives accumulation.

The next chapter builds the second great operation of calculus: adding up infinitely many small changes.

Warning examples

The last few sections gave us strong tools:

\text{Fermat's theorem, Rolle's theorem, the Mean Value Theorem,}

\text{the first derivative test, the second derivative test, and l'Hospital's Rule.}

Each one has a boundary. A theorem is useful only when its hypotheses are true. This section collects the warning examples in one place, so the rules are easier to use and harder to misuse.

 Fermat’s theorem fails at an endpoint

Fermat’s theorem said:

differentiable local extremum at an interior point \Longrightarrow f'(c)=0.

The phrase interior point matters.

Let

f(x)=x

on the interval

[0,1].

The function has an absolute minimum at

x=0

and an absolute maximum at

x=1.

But the derivative is

f'(x)=1.

There is no horizontal tangent.

There is no contradiction. Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint, the graph only has to be compared with points on one side. It can be best or worst without flattening out.

\text{Endpoint extrema do not have to satisfy } f'(c)=0.

That is why the closed interval method always checks endpoints separately.

Why can an endpoint extremum fail to have a horizontal tangent?

On [0,1], the function f(x)=x attains its max and min, but f' is never zero. In your own words, why is that compatible with Fermat’s theorem, and why does the closed interval method therefore check endpoints separately?

Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint the graph is compared with only one side, so it can be best or worst without flattening.

The Mean Value Theorem fails without continuity

The Mean Value Theorem said that if f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then some c\in(a,b) satisfies

f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.

Continuity on the whole closed interval matters.

Define

f(x)= \begin{cases} x, \amp 0\le x<1,\\ 0, \amp x=1. \end{cases}

on [0,1].

Then

f(0)=0, \qquad f(1)=0.

So the secant slope from 0 to 1 is

\frac{f(1)-f(0)}{1-0}=0.

But on the open interval (0,1),

f(x)=x,

so

f'(x)=1

for every x\in(0,1). There is no point c\in(0,1) with

f'(c)=0.

The graph climbs toward 1, then jumps down at the endpoint. The jump hides the climb from the endpoint calculation.

\text{The Mean Value Theorem needs continuity on }[a,b].

Why can the Mean Value Theorem fail without continuity or differentiability?

A jump on the closed interval, or a corner inside, can keep every existing tangent slope away from the secant slope. In your own words, why are continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b) not decorations, and what kind of escape does each hypothesis block?

Continuity keeps the graph from leaping over the needed height. Differentiability keeps a turn from happening at a corner instead of at a tangent.

The Mean Value Theorem fails without differentiability

The Mean Value Theorem also needs differentiability on the open interval.

Let

f(x)=|x|

on

[-1,1].

The function is continuous on [-1,1]. Its endpoint values are

f(-1)=1, \qquad f(1)=1.

So the secant slope is

\frac{f(1)-f(-1)}{1-(-1)} = \frac{1-1}{2} = 0.

If the Mean Value Theorem applied, there would be some c\in(-1,1) with

f'(c)=0.

But

f'(x)=-1 \quad\text{for }x<0,

and

f'(x)=1 \quad\text{for }x>0.

At x=0, the derivative does not exist. The graph turns at a corner.

The graph does return to the same height, but it turns too sharply. Rolle’s Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem do not promise a horizontal tangent unless the function is differentiable throughout the open interval.

\text{The Mean Value Theorem needs differentiability on }(a,b).

The second derivative test can be inconclusive

The second derivative test said:

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)>0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local minimum at }c,

and

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)<0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local maximum at }c.

But when

f''(c)=0,

the test says nothing.

Three different outcomes are possible.

A local minimum

Let

f(x)=x^4.

Then

f'(x)=4x^3, \qquad f''(x)=12x^2.

At x=0,

f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0.

The second derivative test gives no conclusion. But

x^4\ge0

for every x, so f has a local minimum at 0.

 A local maximum

Let

g(x)=-x^4.

Then

g'(x)=-4x^3, \qquad g''(x)=-12x^2.

At x=0,

g'(0)=0, \qquad g''(0)=0.

The test again gives no conclusion. But

-x^4\le0

for every x, so g has a local maximum at 0.

 No local extremum

Let

h(x)=x^3.

Then

h'(x)=3x^2, \qquad h''(x)=6x.

At x=0,

h'(0)=0, \qquad h''(0)=0.

But x^3 is increasing through 0. There is no local maximum or local minimum.

The moral is short:

f''(c)=0 \text{ means ``try another test.''}

Most often, we return to the first derivative test or to the definition of local maximum and local minimum.

 Why can the second derivative test stay silent?

If f'(c)=0 and f''(c)=0, the test gives no conclusion. In your own words, why can that same pair of facts describe a local min, a local max, or no extremum at all, and what extra evidence do we then need?

Look at the sign of f' on both sides, or compare the graphs of x^4, -x^4, and x^3 at the origin.

l’Hospital’s Rule cannot be used on every quotient

l’Hospital’s Rule is a rule for the indeterminate forms

\frac00 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{\infty}{\infty}.

The first question is always:

\text{What form does direct substitution produce?}

A quotient that is not indeterminate

Consider

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}.

Direct substitution gives

\frac{0^2+1}{0+1}=1.

So the limit is

1.

This is not a 0/0 form and not an \infty/\infty form.

If we incorrectly differentiate numerator and denominator, we get

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{2x}{1}=0,

which is wrong.

Do not use l'Hospital's Rule when direct substitution already gives an ordinary number.

 A derivative quotient with no limit

Sometimes the original quotient has a limit, but the quotient of derivatives does not.

Consider

\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}.

The quotient is

\frac{x+\sin x}{x} = 1+\frac{\sin x}{x}.

Since

\left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right|\le \frac1x

for x>0, we get

\frac{\sin x}{x}\to0.

Therefore

\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}=1.

But the quotient of derivatives is

\frac{1+\cos x}{1}=1+\cos x,

which has no limit as x\to\infty.

There is no contradiction. l’Hospital’s Rule says that if the original quotient has the right indeterminate form and the derivative quotient has a limit, then the original limit has that same value. It does not say that the derivative quotient must always have a limit.

If the derivative quotient does not settle, l'Hospital's Rule gives no conclusion.

 Why is l’Hospital’s Rule not a license for every quotient?

The rule applies only to certain indeterminate quotients, and only when the derivative quotient has a limit. In your own words, why can blindly differentiating a well-behaved quotient give the wrong answer, and why can a derivative quotient that refuses to settle leave the original limit still well-defined?

A theorem is a package: hypotheses imply a conclusion. Missing hypotheses mean the theorem is no longer the reason, even if luck later produces a true statement.

A theorem-use checklist

The warnings can be compressed into a practical checklist.

A theorem-use checklist tool check before using it Fermat's theorem Is the extremum at an interior point? Is the function differentiable there? Mean Value Theorem Is the function continuous on [a,b]? Is it differentiable on (a,b)? first derivative test Does f' actually change sign around the critical number? second derivative test Is f'(c)=0? Is f''(c) positive or negative, not zero? l'Hospital's Rule Is the quotient really 0/0 or \infty/\infty? Does the derivative quotient have a limit?

A theorem is not only a conclusion. It is a package:

\text{hypotheses} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{conclusion}.

If the hypotheses are missing, the conclusion may still be true by luck. But the theorem is no longer the reason.

These warnings prepare the chapter review. We now gather the ideas into one working map: how to read shape from derivatives, how to prove global facts from the Mean Value Theorem, and how to tell when a tempting shortcut is legal.

f'(c)=0.

But

f'(x)=-1 \quad\text{for }x<0,

and

f'(x)=1 \quad\text{for }x>0.

At x=0, the derivative does not exist. The graph turns at a corner.

The graph does return to the same height, but it turns too sharply. Rolle’s Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem do not promise a horizontal tangent unless the function is differentiable throughout the open interval.

\text{The Mean Value Theorem needs differentiability on }(a,b).

The second derivative test can be inconclusive

The second derivative test said:

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)>0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local minimum at }c,

and

f'(c)=0,\quad f''(c)<0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{local maximum at }c.

But when

f''(c)=0,

the test says nothing.

Three different outcomes are possible.

A local minimum

Let

f(x)=x^4.

Then

f'(x)=4x^3, \qquad f''(x)=12x^2.

At x=0,

f'(0)=0, \qquad f''(0)=0.

The second derivative test gives no conclusion. But

x^4\ge0

for every x, so f has a local minimum at 0.

 A local maximum

Let

g(x)=-x^4.

Then

g'(x)=-4x^3, \qquad g''(x)=-12x^2.

At x=0,

g'(0)=0, \qquad g''(0)=0.

The test again gives no conclusion. But

-x^4\le0

for every x, so g has a local maximum at 0.

 No local extremum

Let

h(x)=x^3.

Then

h'(x)=3x^2, \qquad h''(x)=6x.

At x=0,

h'(0)=0, \qquad h''(0)=0.

But x^3 is increasing through 0. There is no local maximum or local minimum.

The moral is short:

f''(c)=0 \text{ means ``try another test.''}

Most often, we return to the first derivative test or to the definition of local maximum and local minimum.

 Why can the second derivative test stay silent?

If f'(c)=0 and f''(c)=0, the test gives no conclusion. In your own words, why can that same pair of facts describe a local min, a local max, or no extremum at all, and what extra evidence do we then need?

Look at the sign of f' on both sides, or compare the graphs of x^4, -x^4, and x^3 at the origin.

l’Hospital’s Rule cannot be used on every quotient

l’Hospital’s Rule is a rule for the indeterminate forms

\frac00 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{\infty}{\infty}.

The first question is always:

\text{What form does direct substitution produce?}

A quotient that is not indeterminate

Consider

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}.

Direct substitution gives

\frac{0^2+1}{0+1}=1.

So the limit is

1.

This is not a 0/0 form and not an \infty/\infty form.

If we incorrectly differentiate numerator and denominator, we get

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{2x}{1}=0,

which is wrong.

Do not use l'Hospital's Rule when direct substitution already gives an ordinary number.

 A derivative quotient with no limit

Sometimes the original quotient has a limit, but the quotient of derivatives does not.

Consider

\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}.

The quotient is

\frac{x+\sin x}{x} = 1+\frac{\sin x}{x}.

Since

\left|\frac{\sin x}{x}\right|\le \frac1x

for x>0, we get

\frac{\sin x}{x}\to0.

Therefore

\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x+\sin x}{x}=1.

But the quotient of derivatives is

\frac{1+\cos x}{1}=1+\cos x,

which has no limit as x\to\infty.

There is no contradiction. l’Hospital’s Rule says that if the original quotient has the right indeterminate form and the derivative quotient has a limit, then the original limit has that same value. It does not say that the derivative quotient must always have a limit.

If the derivative quotient does not settle, l'Hospital's Rule gives no conclusion.

 Why is l’Hospital’s Rule not a license for every quotient?

The rule applies only to certain indeterminate quotients, and only when the derivative quotient has a limit. In your own words, why can blindly differentiating a well-behaved quotient give the wrong answer, and why can a derivative quotient that refuses to settle leave the original limit still well-defined?

A theorem is a package: hypotheses imply a conclusion. Missing hypotheses mean the theorem is no longer the reason, even if luck later produces a true statement.

A theorem-use checklist

The warnings can be compressed into a practical checklist.

A theorem-use checklist

tool

check before using it

Fermat's theorem

Is the extremum at an interior point? Is the function differentiable there?

Mean Value Theorem

Is the function continuous on [a,b]? Is it differentiable on (a,b)?

first derivative test

Does f' actually change sign around the critical number?

second derivative test

Is f'(c)=0? Is f''(c) positive or negative, not zero?

l'Hospital's Rule

Is the quotient really 0/0 or \infty/\infty? Does the derivative quotient have a limit?

A theorem is not only a conclusion. It is a package:

\text{hypotheses} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{conclusion}.

If the hypotheses are missing, the conclusion may still be true by luck. But the theorem is no longer the reason.

These warnings prepare the chapter review. We now gather the ideas into one working map: how to read shape from derivatives, how to prove global facts from the Mean Value Theorem, and how to tell when a tempting shortcut is legal.

f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

That definition gave meaning, but it was too slow for everyday use.

Chapter 5 built a working language. We learned how derivatives behave under algebra, composition, implicit relations, inverse functions, and the elementary functions. The point was not to memorize a long table. The point was to read structure.

The chapter has one main story:

\text{how a function is built} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{how its derivative is built}.

Why does the way a function is built determine the derivative rule?

Chapter 5 has one main story: how a function is built determines how its derivative is built. In your own words, why are a sum, a product, a quotient, a composition, and an inverse different constructions, and why is reading the structure the first step rather than a race to symbols?

Each construction changes for a different reason. The table of elementary derivatives is useful only when paired with the matching rule.

Derivative table

The main elementary derivative formulas from this chapter are collected below. Each formula is valid on intervals where the function is defined and differentiable.

\begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{function} \amp \textbf{derivative}\\ \hline c \amp 0\\ x \amp 1\\ x^r \amp rx^{r-1}\\ e^x \amp e^x\\ a^x \amp (\ln a)a^x,\quad a>0\\ \ln x \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x>0\\ \ln|x| \amp \dfrac1x,\quad x\neq0\\ \sin x \amp \cos x\\ \cos x \amp -\sin x\\ \tan x \amp \sec^2x\\ \sec x \amp \sec x\tan x\\ \csc x \amp -\csc x\cot x\\ \cot x \amp -\csc^2x\\ \arcsin x \amp \dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arccos x \amp -\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\\ \arctan x \amp \dfrac1{1+x^2}\\ \sinh x \amp \cosh x\\ \cosh x \amp \sinh x\\ \tanh x \amp \operatorname{sech}^2x \end{array}

The table is only useful when paired with the rules:

(af+bg)'\amp=af'+bg', (fg)'\amp=f'g+fg', \left(\frac fg\right)'\amp=\frac{gf'-fg'}{g^2}, (f(g(x)))'\amp=f'(g(x))g'(x).

Most real derivative calculations use both a table formula and a rule.

 Worked mixed examples Example

Differentiate

F(x)=e^{-x}\cos(2x)+\ln(1+x^2).

The first term is a product:

e^{-x}\cos(2x).

Differentiate each factor:

\frac{d}{dx}e^{-x}=-e^{-x},

and

\frac{d}{dx}\cos(2x)=-2\sin(2x).

So

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = (-e^{-x})\cos(2x)+e^{-x}(-2\sin(2x)).

Thus

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x).

The logarithmic term uses the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\ln(1+x^2)=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

Therefore

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

We can factor the first two terms if desired:

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\bigl(\cos(2x)+2\sin(2x)\bigr) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

 Example

Differentiate

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

This function has a variable exponent. Since the base is always positive,

x^2+1>0,

logarithmic differentiation is safe.

Take natural logarithms:

\ln y=\sin x\ln(x^2+1).

Differentiate both sides:

\frac{y'}{y} = \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \sin x\cdot\frac{2x}{x^2+1}.

Multiply by y:

y' = y\left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

Substitute back

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

Thus

y' = (x^2+1)^{\sin x} \left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

This example uses several ideas at once: logarithms, product rule, chain rule, and the fact that x^2+1 is positive.

 Example

Find dy/dx if

x^2y+\sin y=e^x.

Here y is treated as a function of x. Differentiate both sides with respect to x.

For x^2y, use the product rule:

\frac{d}{dx}(x^2y)=2xy+x^2y'.

For \sin y, use the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\sin y=\cos y\,y'.

For e^x,

\frac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x.

Therefore

2xy+x^2y'+\cos y\,y'=e^x.

Collect the y'-terms:

(x^2+\cos y)y'=e^x-2xy.

So

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{e^x-2xy}{x^2+\cos y}.

The denominator warns us: if

x^2+\cos y=0,

then this equation does not determine a finite value of dy/dx. The algebra may be pointing to a vertical tangent or to a place where the curve is not a single differentiable branch y(x).

 Implicit differentiation practice

Find dy/dx. Then find the tangent slope at the given point when a point is provided.

  1. x^2+y^2=10.

  2. x^2+xy+y^2=7.

  3. y^3+xy=10, \qquad (1,2).

  4. x^2y+\sin y=e^x.

  5. e^{xy}+y^2=x+2.

  6. \ln(x+y)=xy.

  7. \sin(xy)=x-y.

  8. x^3+y^3=6xy.

  9. Find y'' for the circle

    x^2+y^2=25.

  10. For

    x^2+y^2=25,

    find all points on the circle where the tangent line is horizontal. Then find all points where the tangent line is vertical.

Why do implicit and inverse derivatives reverse two different things?

Implicit differentiation treats y as changing because x changes, even with no formula y=f(x). The inverse rule reverses a graph and therefore reverses slope. In your own words, why are those two ideas related to the chain rule, yet not the same task?

One starts from a relation and solves for dy/dx. The other starts from a reversible function and takes the reciprocal slope at the matching point.

Concept check

Answer each question in complete sentences.

  1. Why does the product rule have two terms?

  2. In the chain rule

    (f(g(x)))'=f'(g(x))g'(x),

    why is f' evaluated at g(x) instead of at x?

  3. Why must angles be measured in radians for

    (\sin x)'=\cos x

    to be true without an extra constant?

  4. Why does implicit differentiation require the chain rule?

  5. In the inverse derivative formula

    (f^{-1})'(b)=\frac1{f'(a)}, \qquad b=f(a),

    why must the derivative of f be evaluated at a, not at b?

  6. Give an example of a function that has an inverse, but whose inverse is not differentiable at one point.

  7. Explain why logarithmic differentiation is useful for

    y=x^x.

  8. The formulas

    (\sinh x)'=\cosh x \qquad\text{and}\qquad (\cosh x)'=\sinh x

    look similar to the sine and cosine formulas. Where does the sign difference appear?

 True or false

Decide whether each statement is true or false. If it is false, give a correction or a counterexample.

  1. (fg)'=f'g'

    for all differentiable functions f and g.

  2. (f+g)'=f'+g'

    for all differentiable functions f and g.

  3. \frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2)=2x\cos(x^2).

  4. \frac{d}{dx}(\sin x)^2=2x\cos(x^2).

  5. \frac{d}{dx}\ln|x|=\frac1x

    for x\neq0.

  6. \frac{d}{dx}a^x=xa^{x-1}

    for every positive constant a.

  7. \frac{d}{dx}x^a=ax^{a-1}

    for a fixed real number a, at least for x>0.

  8. If f'(a)=0, then f cannot have an inverse.

  9. If f has an inverse and f'(a)=0, then the formula

    (f^{-1})'(f(a))=\frac1{f'(a)}

    cannot be used.

  10. The derivative of \arctan x exists for every real x.

 Proof practice

These problems ask you to justify the rules, not only use them.

  1. Product rule from the definition. Suppose f and g are differentiable at x. Starting from

    \frac{f(x+h)g(x+h)-f(x)g(x)}{h},

    add and subtract

    f(x+h)g(x)

    in the numerator. Use this to prove

    (fg)'(x)=f'(x)g(x)+f(x)g'(x).

  2. Reciprocal rule from the product rule. Let

    q(x)=\frac1{g(x)},

    where g(x)\neq0. Since

    g(x)q(x)=1,

    differentiate both sides and solve for q'(x). Prove

    \left(\frac1g\right)'=-\frac{g'}{g^2}.

  3. Quotient rule from product and reciprocal rules. Write

    \frac{f}{g}=f\cdot\frac1g.

    Use the product rule and reciprocal rule to prove

    \left(\frac fg\right)'=\frac{gf'-fg'}{g^2}.

  4. Chain rule using local linearity. Suppose

    u=g(x), \qquad y=f(u).

    Use the approximations

    g(x+h)=g(x)+g'(x)h+\text{small error}

    and

    f(u+k)=f(u)+f'(u)k+\text{small error}

    to explain why

    \frac{d}{dx}f(g(x))=f'(g(x))g'(x).

  5. Inverse derivative formula. Let g=f^{-1}. Starting from

    f(g(x))=x,

    differentiate both sides using the chain rule. Solve for g'(x) and obtain

    (f^{-1})'(x)=\frac1{f'(f^{-1}(x))}.

    What condition is needed to divide?

  6. Derivative of \ln x from the inverse rule. Use the fact that \ln x is the inverse of e^x to prove

    \frac{d}{dx}\ln x=\frac1x.

  7. General power rule. For x>0, let

    y=x^r,

    where r is a fixed real number. Take logarithms and differentiate implicitly to prove

    \frac{d}{dx}x^r=rx^{r-1}.

 Project: derivative formulas from numerical experiments

A derivative is a limit. Numerical experiments can suggest what the limit is before we prove it.

For a small positive number h, define the symmetric difference quotient

D_h f(a)=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a-h)}{2h}.

This often gives a better numerical estimate of f'(a) than the one-sided quotient

\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

The goal of this project is to rediscover several derivative formulas from data.

Step 1: choose step sizes

Use

h=10^{-1},\ 10^{-2},\ 10^{-3},\ 10^{-4},\ 10^{-5},\ 10^{-6}.

For each function and each point a, compute

D_h f(a).

Organize your results in a table.

\begin{array}{c|cccccc} h \amp 10^{-1} \amp 10^{-2} \amp 10^{-3} \amp 10^{-4} \amp 10^{-5} \amp 10^{-6}\\ \hline D_h f(a) \amp \amp \amp \amp \amp \amp \end{array}

 Step 2: test powers

Use

f(x)=x^2,\qquad f(x)=x^3,\qquad f(x)=\sqrt{x}.

Test at

a=1,\quad a=2,\quad a=4.

Use the numerical estimates to guess the formulas for

(x^2)',\qquad (x^3)',\qquad (\sqrt{x})'.

Compare your guesses with the power rule.

 Step 3: test trigonometric functions

Use radians. Compute numerical derivatives for

f(x)=\sin x \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(x)=\cos x

at

a=0,\quad \frac{\pi}{6},\quad \frac{\pi}{4},\quad \frac{\pi}{3},\quad \frac{\pi}{2}.

Compare the numerical derivative of \sin x with \cos x. Compare the numerical derivative of \cos x with -\sin x.

Then repeat the experiment using degrees by defining

S(x)=\sin(x^\circ)=\sin\left(\frac{\pi x}{180}\right).

Estimate S'(30). Explain why the extra factor

\frac{\pi}{180}

appears.

 Step 4: test exponentials

For

f(x)=a^x,

the derivative should be proportional to a^x. Estimate

\frac{D_h f(0)}{f(0)}

for

a=2,\quad a=3,\quad a=10.

Since f(0)=1, this is just the estimated slope at 0. Compare the results with

\ln2,\qquad \ln3,\qquad \ln10.

Now test

f(x)=e^x.

Estimate D_h f(a) at

a=-1,\quad 0,\quad 1,\quad 2.

Compare with e^a.

 Step 5: test logarithms

Use

f(x)=\ln x.

Estimate f'(a) at

a=1,\quad 2,\quad 5,\quad 10.

Compare with

\frac1a.

Try step sizes smaller than 10^{-6}, such as

10^{-8},\quad 10^{-10},\quad 10^{-12}.

Do the estimates always improve? Explain what you see.

Your report should answer three questions:

  1. Which derivative formulas did your data suggest?

  2. Where did the numerical evidence become unreliable?

  3. Why is a proof still needed after a convincing table of values?

 Discovery problems

  1. A hidden product rule. Let

    A(x)=(x+1)(x+2)(x+3).

    Differentiate A(x) in two ways:

    \text{first by expanding,}

    and

    \text{then by applying the product rule twice.}

    Show that the two answers agree.

  2. A pattern for logarithmic derivatives. Let

    P(x)=(x-a_1)(x-a_2)\cdots(x-a_n).

    Work on an interval where all factors are nonzero. Take the logarithm of the absolute value, using \ln|P(x)|=\sum_{j=1}^n\ln|x-a_j|, and differentiate to show

    \frac{P'(x)}{P(x)} = \frac1{x-a_1}+\frac1{x-a_2}+\cdots+\frac1{x-a_n}.

    This formula is useful because it turns a product into a sum.

  3. A tangent to an inverse without finding the inverse. Let

    f(x)=x^5+x.

    Show that f is increasing. Find

    (f^{-1})'(2)

    without solving for f^{-1}(x).

  4. Two functions with the same value but different local behavior. Find two differentiable functions f and g such that

    f(0)=g(0)

    but

    f'(0)\neq g'(0).

    Explain in words what this means about their graphs near 0.

  5. Two functions with the same derivative at one point but different graphs. Find two differentiable functions f and g such that

    f'(0)=g'(0)

    but the graphs do not look the same near 0.

  6. A derivative that simplifies unexpectedly. Differentiate

    f(x)=\frac{1-\cos x}{\sin x}

    where it is defined. Then use trigonometric identities to simplify the derivative.

  7. A logarithmic identity through derivatives. Let

    F(x)=\ln(\sec x+\tan x).

    Differentiate F. On intervals where the functions are defined, show that

    F'(x)=\sec x.

    This identity will become useful when we integrate \sec x.

  8. A hyperbolic simplification. Differentiate

    f(x)=\ln(\cosh x).

    Express the answer using \tanh x.

  9. A variable base and variable exponent. For x>0, differentiate

    f(x)=x^{\ln x}.

    Hint: take logarithms first.

  10. A curve with no solved formula. The equation

    x^3+y^3=6xy

    defines a curve called the folium of Descartes. Use implicit differentiation to find dy/dx. Then find the slope at

    (3,3).

 Where the chapter points next

A derivative is more than a number to compute. It is information about shape.

For example, consider

f(x)=x^3-3x.

Its derivative is

f'(x)=3x^2-3=3(x-1)(x+1).

The derivative is positive when

x<-1

and when

x>1.

It is negative when

-1<x<1.

The graph rises, then falls, then rises again.

At

x=-1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=1,

the derivative is 0. The graph has horizontal tangents there. One is a high point nearby; the other is a low point nearby.

That observation opens the next part of the book.

Derivatives compute slopes. But slopes tell us when a function rises, when it falls, where it turns, and where it bends. The next chapter asks how much of a graph we can understand from its derivative.

Why is a computed derivative already information about shape?

The sign of f' tells where a graph rises or falls, and a zero of f' marks a horizontal tangent. In your own words, why was this chapter’s working language built not only to compute more derivatives, but to prepare for reading a graph from its slopes?

A derivative is local slope information. Collected point by point, those slopes begin to describe the whole curve.

(af+bg)'\amp=af'+bg', (fg)'\amp=f'g+fg', \left(\frac fg\right)'\amp=\frac{gf'-fg'}{g^2}, (f(g(x)))'\amp=f'(g(x))g'(x).

Most real derivative calculations use both a table formula and a rule.

 Worked mixed examples Example

Differentiate

F(x)=e^{-x}\cos(2x)+\ln(1+x^2).

The first term is a product:

e^{-x}\cos(2x).

Differentiate each factor:

\frac{d}{dx}e^{-x}=-e^{-x},

and

\frac{d}{dx}\cos(2x)=-2\sin(2x).

So

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = (-e^{-x})\cos(2x)+e^{-x}(-2\sin(2x)).

Thus

\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\cos(2x)\right) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x).

The logarithmic term uses the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\ln(1+x^2)=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

Therefore

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\cos(2x)-2e^{-x}\sin(2x) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

We can factor the first two terms if desired:

F'(x) = -e^{-x}\bigl(\cos(2x)+2\sin(2x)\bigr) + \frac{2x}{1+x^2}.

 Example

Differentiate

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

This function has a variable exponent. Since the base is always positive,

x^2+1>0,

logarithmic differentiation is safe.

Take natural logarithms:

\ln y=\sin x\ln(x^2+1).

Differentiate both sides:

\frac{y'}{y} = \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \sin x\cdot\frac{2x}{x^2+1}.

Multiply by y:

y' = y\left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

Substitute back

y=(x^2+1)^{\sin x}.

Thus

y' = (x^2+1)^{\sin x} \left( \cos x\ln(x^2+1) + \frac{2x\sin x}{x^2+1} \right).

This example uses several ideas at once: logarithms, product rule, chain rule, and the fact that x^2+1 is positive.

 Example

Find dy/dx if

x^2y+\sin y=e^x.

Here y is treated as a function of x. Differentiate both sides with respect to x.

For x^2y, use the product rule:

\frac{d}{dx}(x^2y)=2xy+x^2y'.

For \sin y, use the chain rule:

\frac{d}{dx}\sin y=\cos y\,y'.

For e^x,

\frac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x.

Therefore

2xy+x^2y'+\cos y\,y'=e^x.

Collect the y'-terms:

(x^2+\cos y)y'=e^x-2xy.

So

\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{e^x-2xy}{x^2+\cos y}.

The denominator warns us: if

x^2+\cos y=0,

then this equation does not determine a finite value of dy/dx. The algebra may be pointing to a vertical tangent or to a place where the curve is not a single differentiable branch y(x).

 Where the chapter points next

A derivative is more than a number to compute. It is information about shape.

For example, consider

f(x)=x^3-3x.

Its derivative is

f'(x)=3x^2-3=3(x-1)(x+1).

The derivative is positive when

x<-1

and when

x>1.

It is negative when

-1<x<1.

The graph rises, then falls, then rises again.

At

x=-1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=1,

the derivative is 0. The graph has horizontal tangents there. One is a high point nearby; the other is a low point nearby.

That observation opens the next part of the book.

Derivatives compute slopes. But slopes tell us when a function rises, when it falls, where it turns, and where it bends. The next chapter asks how much of a graph we can understand from its derivative.

Why is a computed derivative already information about shape?

The sign of f' tells where a graph rises or falls, and a zero of f' marks a horizontal tangent. In your own words, why was this chapter’s working language built not only to compute more derivatives, but to prepare for reading a graph from its slopes?

A derivative is local slope information. Collected point by point, those slopes begin to describe the whole curve.

Differentiability and continuity

Local linear approximation ended with the formula

f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+E(h), \qquad \frac{E(h)}{h}\to0.

This says that, near a, a differentiable function behaves like a line. A line cannot jump. So a differentiable function cannot jump either.

That is our first structural theorem about derivatives:

\text{differentiability is stronger than continuity.}

 Differentiability implies continuity

Recall what continuity at a means:

\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a).

In the h-notation, where x=a+h, this is

\lim_{h\to0}f(a+h)=f(a).

So continuity says that small input changes produce small output changes. Differentiability says more: small input changes produce output changes that are nearly linear.

A first example

Let

f(x)=x^2.

At a=3,

f(3+h)=(3+h)^2=9+6h+h^2.

So

f(3+h)-f(3)=6h+h^2.

As h\to0,

6h+h^2\to0.

Therefore

f(3+h)\to f(3).

The derivative at 3 is 6, but continuity only needs the weaker fact that the output change goes to 0.

The same idea works for every differentiable function.

Theorem

If f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a.

 Proof

Since f is differentiable at a, the limit

f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}

exists as a finite number.

For h\neq0, write

f(a+h)-f(a) = h\cdot \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

Now let h\to0. The first factor h approaches 0. The second factor approaches the finite number f'(a). Therefore the product approaches

0\cdot f'(a)=0.

Thus

\lim_{h\to0}\bigl(f(a+h)-f(a)\bigr)=0.

So

\lim_{h\to0}f(a+h)=f(a).

That is exactly continuity at a.

\text{differentiable at }a \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{continuous at }a.

The proof is short because the idea is simple. If

\frac{\text{output change}}{\text{input change}}

settles to a finite number, then the output change itself must go to 0 when the input change goes to 0.

 Why does differentiability force continuity?

If the difference quotient settles to a finite number, then f(a+h)-f(a) is that quotient times h. In your own words, why must the output change go to 0 as h\to 0, and why is this the claim that a differentiable function cannot jump?

A product of something approaching 0 and something approaching a finite number approaches 0. Continuity is exactly that output change going to 0.

Why the converse is false

The theorem has only one direction. Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does not imply differentiability.

Continuity says the graph has no break at the point. Differentiability says the graph has one limiting slope there. A graph can be unbroken and still have no single tangent slope.

The first warning example is

f(x)=|x|.

This function is continuous at 0, because

\lim_{x\to0}|x|=0=|0|.

But the derivative at 0 would be

f'(0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{|h|-0}{h} = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{|h|}{h}.

If h>0, then

\frac{|h|}{h}=1.

If h<0, then

\frac{|h|}{h}=-1.

The right-hand slopes approach 1. The left-hand slopes approach -1. There is no single limiting slope.

Therefore

f'(0)

does not exist.

|x|\text{ is continuous at }0,\text{ but not differentiable at }0.

The graph does not jump. It turns too sharply.

This example separates two ideas that are easy to confuse:

\text{continuity is about nearby heights,}

while

\text{differentiability is about nearby slopes.}

Why does continuity not promise a derivative?

Continuity is about nearby heights; differentiability is about nearby slopes. In your own words, why can a graph be unbroken and still fail to have a derivative, and how does |x| at 0 separate the two ideas?

Nearby values can match while the left and right limiting slopes disagree. A corner is continuous but not locally linear.

Corners, cusps, vertical tangents, and jumps

The derivative at a exists only if the difference quotient

\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}

approaches one finite number as h\to0. Several things can go wrong.

Corners, cusps, vertical tangents, and jumps graph feature what happens to slopes example corner left and right slopes are finite but unequal |x| cusp slopes become unbounded in opposite directions |x|^{2/3} vertical tangent slopes become unbounded \sqrt[3]{x} jump continuity already fails \begin{cases}0,\amp x<0\\ 1,\amp x\ge0\end{cases}
A corner

For

f(x)=|x|,

the function is continuous at 0. But the left and right slopes are

-1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad 1.

Since they disagree, the derivative does not exist.

 A cusp

Let

f(x)=|x|^{2/3}.

At 0, the function is continuous:

\lim_{x\to0}|x|^{2/3}=0=f(0).

But the difference quotient is

\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} = \frac{|h|^{2/3}}{h}.

If h>0, then

\frac{|h|^{2/3}}{h} = \frac{h^{2/3}}{h} = \frac{1}{h^{1/3}} \to+\infty.

If h<0, write h=-u, where u>0. Then

\frac{|h|^{2/3}}{h} = \frac{u^{2/3}}{-u} = -\frac{1}{u^{1/3}} \to-\infty.

The slopes do not approach a finite number. They shoot upward from one side and downward from the other.

 A vertical tangent

Let

g(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}.

Again,

g(x)\to0=g(0)

as x\to0, so g is continuous at 0.

The difference quotient at 0 is

\frac{g(h)-g(0)}{h} = \frac{\sqrt[3]{h}}{h} = \frac{1}{h^{2/3}}.

As h\to0, this grows without bound. It does not approach a finite slope. The graph has a vertical tangent line at the origin, but in our definition a derivative must be a finite number. Therefore

g'(0)

does not exist.

 A jump

Define

J(x)= \begin{cases} 0, \amp x<0,\\ 1, \amp x\ge0. \end{cases}

This function is not continuous at 0, because the left-hand values approach 0 while

J(0)=1.

Since differentiability implies continuity, J cannot be differentiable at 0.

We do not even need to inspect the slopes. The theorem already tells us that a jump prevents differentiability.

What continuity can and cannot promise

Continuity promises that the graph does not break.

It does not promise that the graph has a tangent slope.

 How can differentiability fail even when the graph does not jump?

Corners, cusps, and vertical tangents all prevent a finite two-sided derivative, while a jump already prevents continuity. In your own words, what happens to nearby slopes in each of the first three cases, and why does continuity rule out only the fourth?

A derivative requires one finite limiting slope. Finite-but-unequal, unbounded-in-opposite-directions, and unbounded-together are three different ways that demand can fail.

The absolute value as the first warning example

The function

f(x)=|x|

is the example to keep in mind because it is simple and honest. Nothing strange happens to the height. The function is continuous everywhere. The only problem is that at 0, the graph wants two different tangent lines:

y=-x \qquad\text{from the left,}

and

y=x \qquad\text{from the right.}

There is no single best linear approximation at the origin.

If we try to force a linear approximation

|h|\approx mh

near h=0, then the relative first-order error would be

\frac{|h|-mh}{h}.

For h>0,

\frac{|h|-mh}{h} = 1-m.

For h<0,

\frac{|h|-mh}{h} = -1-m.

For both sides to approach 0, we would need

1-m=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad -1-m=0.

That would require

m=1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad m=-1

at the same time. Impossible.

So the derivative fails for the same reason local linear approximation fails: there is no single slope that describes both sides.

 A note about endpoints

Our definition of f'(a) uses a two-sided limit:

f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

So f must be defined near a from both sides. If a is an endpoint of an interval, the ordinary two-sided derivative is not defined there.

For example,

f(x)=\sqrt{x}

is defined on

[0,\infty).

At x=0, we may study the right-hand quotient

\frac{\sqrt{h}-0}{h} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{h}}, \qquad h>0,

but there is no left side inside the domain. Later, endpoints will matter when we look for maximum and minimum values on closed intervals. At endpoints, one-sided behavior is useful, but it is not the same as the ordinary derivative.

The derivative is a strong demand. It gives continuity and a local linear model. The next question is practical: for the smooth functions we meet every day, how do we compute derivatives without returning to the limit definition each time?

Why is the ordinary derivative two-sided?

The definition of f'(a) uses a two-sided limit, so f must be defined near a from both sides. In your own words, why does that prevent an ordinary derivative of \sqrt{x} at 0, even though a right-hand quotient can still be studied?

At an endpoint there is no other side inside the domain. One-sided behavior is useful, but it is not the same as the two-sided derivative.

f(3+h)=(3+h)^2=9+6h+h^2.

So

f(3+h)-f(3)=6h+h^2.

As h\to0,

6h+h^2\to0.

Therefore

f(3+h)\to f(3).

The derivative at 3 is 6, but continuity only needs the weaker fact that the output change goes to 0.

The same idea works for every differentiable function.

Theorem

If f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a.

 Proof

Since f is differentiable at a, the limit

f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}

exists as a finite number.

For h\neq0, write

f(a+h)-f(a) = h\cdot \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

Now let h\to0. The first factor h approaches 0. The second factor approaches the finite number f'(a). Therefore the product approaches

0\cdot f'(a)=0.

Thus

\lim_{h\to0}\bigl(f(a+h)-f(a)\bigr)=0.

So

\lim_{h\to0}f(a+h)=f(a).

That is exactly continuity at a.

\text{differentiable at }a \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{continuous at }a.

The proof is short because the idea is simple. If

\frac{\text{output change}}{\text{input change}}

settles to a finite number, then the output change itself must go to 0 when the input change goes to 0.

 Why does differentiability force continuity?

If the difference quotient settles to a finite number, then f(a+h)-f(a) is that quotient times h. In your own words, why must the output change go to 0 as h\to 0, and why is this the claim that a differentiable function cannot jump?

A product of something approaching 0 and something approaching a finite number approaches 0. Continuity is exactly that output change going to 0.

Why the converse is false

The theorem has only one direction. Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does not imply differentiability.

Continuity says the graph has no break at the point. Differentiability says the graph has one limiting slope there. A graph can be unbroken and still have no single tangent slope.

The first warning example is

f(x)=|x|.

This function is continuous at 0, because

\lim_{x\to0}|x|=0=|0|.

But the derivative at 0 would be

f'(0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{|h|-0}{h} = \lim_{h\to0}\frac{|h|}{h}.

If h>0, then

\frac{|h|}{h}=1.

If h<0, then

\frac{|h|}{h}=-1.

The right-hand slopes approach 1. The left-hand slopes approach -1. There is no single limiting slope.

Therefore

f'(0)

does not exist.

|x|\text{ is continuous at }0,\text{ but not differentiable at }0.

The graph does not jump. It turns too sharply.

This example separates two ideas that are easy to confuse:

\text{continuity is about nearby heights,}

while

\text{differentiability is about nearby slopes.}

Why does continuity not promise a derivative?

Continuity is about nearby heights; differentiability is about nearby slopes. In your own words, why can a graph be unbroken and still fail to have a derivative, and how does |x| at 0 separate the two ideas?

Nearby values can match while the left and right limiting slopes disagree. A corner is continuous but not locally linear.

Corners, cusps, vertical tangents, and jumps

The derivative at a exists only if the difference quotient

\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}

approaches one finite number as h\to0. Several things can go wrong.

A corner

For

f(x)=|x|,

the function is continuous at 0. But the left and right slopes are

-1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad 1.

Since they disagree, the derivative does not exist.

 A cusp

Let

f(x)=|x|^{2/3}.

At 0, the function is continuous:

\lim_{x\to0}|x|^{2/3}=0=f(0).

But the difference quotient is

\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} = \frac{|h|^{2/3}}{h}.

If h>0, then

\frac{|h|^{2/3}}{h} = \frac{h^{2/3}}{h} = \frac{1}{h^{1/3}} \to+\infty.

If h<0, write h=-u, where u>0. Then

\frac{|h|^{2/3}}{h} = \frac{u^{2/3}}{-u} = -\frac{1}{u^{1/3}} \to-\infty.

The slopes do not approach a finite number. They shoot upward from one side and downward from the other.

 A vertical tangent

Let

g(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}.

Again,

g(x)\to0=g(0)

as x\to0, so g is continuous at 0.

The difference quotient at 0 is

\frac{g(h)-g(0)}{h} = \frac{\sqrt[3]{h}}{h} = \frac{1}{h^{2/3}}.

As h\to0, this grows without bound. It does not approach a finite slope. The graph has a vertical tangent line at the origin, but in our definition a derivative must be a finite number. Therefore

g'(0)

does not exist.

 A jump

Define

J(x)= \begin{cases} 0, \amp x<0,\\ 1, \amp x\ge0. \end{cases}

This function is not continuous at 0, because the left-hand values approach 0 while

J(0)=1.

Since differentiability implies continuity, J cannot be differentiable at 0.

We do not even need to inspect the slopes. The theorem already tells us that a jump prevents differentiability.

What continuity can and cannot promise

Continuity promises that the graph does not break.

It does not promise that the graph has a tangent slope.

 How can differentiability fail even when the graph does not jump?

Corners, cusps, and vertical tangents all prevent a finite two-sided derivative, while a jump already prevents continuity. In your own words, what happens to nearby slopes in each of the first three cases, and why does continuity rule out only the fourth?

A derivative requires one finite limiting slope. Finite-but-unequal, unbounded-in-opposite-directions, and unbounded-together are three different ways that demand can fail.

The absolute value as the first warning example

The function

f(x)=|x|

is the example to keep in mind because it is simple and honest. Nothing strange happens to the height. The function is continuous everywhere. The only problem is that at 0, the graph wants two different tangent lines:

y=-x \qquad\text{from the left,}

and

y=x \qquad\text{from the right.}

There is no single best linear approximation at the origin.

If we try to force a linear approximation

|h|\approx mh

near h=0, then the relative first-order error would be

\frac{|h|-mh}{h}.

For h>0,

\frac{|h|-mh}{h} = 1-m.

For h<0,

\frac{|h|-mh}{h} = -1-m.

For both sides to approach 0, we would need

1-m=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad -1-m=0.

That would require

m=1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad m=-1

at the same time. Impossible.

So the derivative fails for the same reason local linear approximation fails: there is no single slope that describes both sides.

Our definition of f'(a) uses a two-sided limit:

f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

So f must be defined near a from both sides. If a is an endpoint of an interval, the ordinary two-sided derivative is not defined there.

For example,

f(x)=\sqrt{x}

is defined on

[0,\infty).

At x=0, we may study the right-hand quotient

\frac{\sqrt{h}-0}{h} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{h}}, \qquad h>0,

but there is no left side inside the domain. Later, endpoints will matter when we look for maximum and minimum values on closed intervals. At endpoints, one-sided behavior is useful, but it is not the same as the ordinary derivative.

The derivative is a strong demand. It gives continuity and a local linear model. The next question is practical: for the smooth functions we meet every day, how do we compute derivatives without returning to the limit definition each time?

Why is the ordinary derivative two-sided?

The definition of f'(a) uses a two-sided limit, so f must be defined near a from both sides. In your own words, why does that prevent an ordinary derivative of \sqrt{x} at 0, even though a right-hand quotient can still be studied?

At an endpoint there is no other side inside the domain. One-sided behavior is useful, but it is not the same as the two-sided derivative.

Limits from motion and approximation

A speedometer gives an instantaneous reading. But if all we have is a position formula, we first see only average velocities over intervals. The limit is the act of shrinking the interval until the average rate settles toward one number.

 Average velocity as the interval shrinks

Let

s(t)=t^2

be the position of an object moving along a line, measured in meters after t seconds. We want the velocity at the instant t=2.

Over the interval from 2 to 2+h, the average velocity is

A(h)=\frac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h}, \qquad h\neq0.

Compute:

A(h) = \frac{(2+h)^2-2^2}{h} = \frac{4+4h+h^2-4}{h} = \frac{4h+h^2}{h}.

Since h\neq0, we may divide by h:

A(h)=4+h.

So the average velocity depends on the width h of the interval.

\begin{array}{c|cccccc} h \amp -0.1 \amp -0.01 \amp -0.001 \amp 0.001 \amp 0.01 \amp 0.1\\ \hline A(h)=4+h \amp 3.9 \amp 3.99 \amp 3.999 \amp 4.001 \amp 4.01 \amp 4.1 \end{array}

The closer h is to 0, the closer A(h) is to 4. This suggests that the instantaneous velocity at t=2 should be

4\text{ meters/second}.

The important point is not only the answer. The important point is how we got it:

\text{instantaneous velocity}=\text{limit of average velocities.}

The same calculation can be read geometrically. The average velocity over an interval is the slope of a secant line. As the second point moves toward t=2, the secant line approaches a tangent line.

This is why limits are needed before derivatives can be defined. A tangent slope is not usually found from two separated points. It is found by letting one point approach another.

Why is instantaneous velocity a limit of averages?

For s(t)=t^2, the average velocity over an interval of width h is 4+h whenever h\neq0. In your own words, why is that average not yet a speedometer reading, and why should shrinking the interval be a better clue to the velocity at the instant t=2?

An average still spreads a change over a whole window. The speedometer asks about one instant inside that window. Geometrically, secant slopes are trying to settle toward a tangent slope.

Decimal approximations to a number

Limits do not belong only to motion. They also appear whenever approximations close in on a target.

Chapter 2 used nested intervals to trap \sqrt2:

1.4<\sqrt2<1.5,

1.41<\sqrt2<1.42,

1.414<\sqrt2<1.415.

The left endpoints

1.4,\quad 1.41,\quad 1.414,\quad 1.4142,\quad \ldots

approach \sqrt2 from below. The right endpoints approach it from above. Neither finite list equals the whole number \sqrt2, but the approximations can be made as close as desired.

A simpler example is

1.9,\quad 1.99,\quad 1.999,\quad 1.9999,\quad \ldots

These numbers approach 2. The error after n decimal places is a power of 10:

2-1.9=0.1,\qquad 2-1.99=0.01,\qquad 2-1.999=0.001.

The errors approach 0. So the approximations approach 2.

A limit is a target value for a process

A number can be approached by decimal approximations. A velocity can be approached by average velocities. A tangent slope can be approached by secant slopes.

The same idea appears in different clothing. The mathematics is the same: errors are forced to become small.

What is a limit a target for?

Decimal approximations approach a number, average velocities approach an instantaneous velocity, and secant slopes approach a tangent slope. In your own words, what do these processes have in common, and why is a limit a target value for a process rather than a value read off at the missing input?

Each process produces a sequence of errors that we try to force toward zero. The target is what the nearby values are heading toward, whether or not the process is allowed to use the exact center.

The informal meaning of a limit

Let f be a function. When we write

\lim_{x\to a} f(x)=L,

we mean:

\text{as \(x\) gets close to \(a\), the values \(f(x)\) get close to \(L\).}

The notation is read:

\text{the limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches \(a\) is \(L\).}

There is one detail that must be said early:

x\to a

does not mean x=a. It means x is close to a. In many limits, the value at x=a is not used at all.

Informal definition of a limit

We write

\lim_{x\to a} f(x)=L

if the values f(x) can be made as close to L as desired by taking x sufficiently close to a, with x\neq a.

This definition is still informal because the phrases “as close as desired” and “sufficiently close” have not yet been made precise. Section will do that. For now, the informal definition is enough to compute and interpret many limits.

Why is a limit near <m>a</m> not the same as the value at <m>a</m>?

The notation x\to a does not mean x=a. In your own words, why can a function have a limit at a even if f(a) is missing or has been placed somewhere else, and what extra agreement will later be called continuity?

A limit watches nearby outputs. The actual assigned height at the point is a separate piece of data. Continuity is the calm case where those two numbers match.

a limit from a formula

Find

\lim_{x\to 3}(2x+5).

If x is close to 3, then 2x+5 is close to

2(3)+5=11.

So

\lim_{x\to 3}(2x+5)=11.

Here nothing strange happens at x=3. We can find the limit by direct substitution.

 the value at the point may not matter

Define

F(x)= \begin{cases} 2x+1, \amp x\neq1,\\ -1, \amp x=1. \end{cases}

Near x=1, but not at x=1, the function behaves like

2x+1.

As x\to1,

2x+1\to3.

Therefore

\lim_{x\to1}F(x)=3,

even though

F(1)=-1.

This example is important enough to remember:

\text{A limit near \(a\) is not the same thing as the value at \(a\).}

When the two do agree, we will have a special property called continuity.

 Limits from graphs and tables

A graph can suggest a limit. A table can suggest a limit. But both must be read with care.

What can a table or graph do for a limit?

A table of nearby values can suggest a limit, and a graph can suggest that no limit exists. In your own words, why is that evidence useful, and why is it still not a proof?

A table checks a few inputs. A graph depends on a window. Algebra will later prove what every nearby value is doing, not only the sampled ones.

a table that suggests a limit

Let

g(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}, \qquad x\neq1.

The formula is not defined at x=1, but we can still examine values near 1.

\begin{array}{c|cccccc} x \amp 0.9 \amp 0.99 \amp 0.999 \amp 1.001 \amp 1.01 \amp 1.1\\ \hline g(x) \amp 1.9 \amp 1.99 \amp 1.999 \amp 2.001 \amp 2.01 \amp 2.1 \end{array}

The values approach 2. So the table suggests

\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=2.

The table does not prove the limit. It gives evidence. Algebra will prove it in the next section.

 a graph that suggests no limit

Define

J(x)=\frac{|x|}{x}, \qquad x\neq0.

If x>0, then |x|=x, so

J(x)=1.

If x<0, then |x|=-x, so

J(x)=-1.

The values near 0 do not approach one common number. From the right they stay at 1. From the left they stay at -1.

Therefore

\lim_{x\to0}\frac{|x|}{x}

does not exist.

The moral is simple:

\text{A limit must have one target.}

A jump gives two competing targets, so the two-sided limit does not exist.

 What a limit can ignore

The limit

\lim_{x\to a}f(x)

ignores the value f(a). It watches what happens near a.

That means all three situations below are possible.

What a limit can ignore situation example what happens f(a) exists and equals the limit f(x)=x^2,\ a=2 \lim_{x\to2}f(x)=f(2)=4 f(a) exists but differs from the limit F(x)=\begin{cases}2x+1,\amp x\neq1\\ -1,\amp x=1\end{cases} \lim_{x\to1}F(x)=3,\ F(1)=-1 f(a) does not exist, but the limit exists g(x)=\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1},\ a=1 \lim_{x\to1}g(x)=2

The first situation is the calm one. The second and third are warning signs. They show why limits must come before continuity.

The next task is practical. Graphs and tables help us guess limits, but calculus needs reliable ways to calculate them. Algebra gives the first tools.

before:
Calculating limits

A table can point toward a limit, but a table only checks a few inputs. A graph can reveal the shape, but a graph depends on the viewing window. Algebra lets us prove what the nearby values are doing.

The first limits we can calculate are the ones where nearby behavior is preserved by arithmetic.

 A first limit law from an example

Suppose

f(x)=x^2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad g(x)=3x-1.

As x\to2,

f(x)\to4 \qquad\text{and}\qquad g(x)\to5.

Now look at their sum:

f(x)+g(x)=x^2+3x-1.

As x\to2, this approaches

4+5=9.

So

\lim_{x\to2}(x^2+3x-1)=9.

The limit of the sum is the sum of the limits.

The same thing happens for products:

f(x)g(x)=x^2(3x-1).

As x\to2, this approaches

4\cdot5=20.

So

\lim_{x\to2}x^2(3x-1)=20.

The nearby behavior of the pieces controls the nearby behavior of the expression built from them.

 Limit laws

The example suggests the general rules.

Limit laws

Suppose

\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L \qquad\text{and}\qquad \lim_{x\to a}g(x)=M.

Then:

\lim_{x\to a}\bigl(f(x)+g(x)\bigr)=L+M,

\lim_{x\to a}\bigl(f(x)-g(x)\bigr)=L-M,

\lim_{x\to a}\bigl(cf(x)\bigr)=cL \qquad\text{for any constant }c,

\lim_{x\to a}\bigl(f(x)g(x)\bigr)=LM,

and, if M\neq0,

\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\frac{L}{M}.

The condition M\neq0 in the quotient law is not decoration. Division by a quantity approaching 0 can behave wildly.

Why the sum law is believable

If f(x) is close to L, and g(x) is close to M, then

f(x)+g(x)

should be close to

L+M.

The error is controlled by

\bigl|(f(x)+g(x))-(L+M)\bigr| = \bigl|(f(x)-L)+(g(x)-M)\bigr|.

Using the triangle inequality,

\bigl|(f(x)-L)+(g(x)-M)\bigr| \le |f(x)-L|+|g(x)-M|.

So if both errors on the right are small, the error on the left is small. This is the whole idea. The precise \varepsilon-\delta proof will come later.

 Warning: the quotient law needs a nonzero limiting denominator

Consider

\frac{1}{x}.

Continuity

The precise definition of a limit gave us a way to control nearby values. It said:

x\text{ close to }a \quad \Longrightarrow \quad f(x)\text{ close to }L.

But a limit still does not have to care about the value at the point. A function may have a hole, a wrong value, or no value at all, and still have a limit nearby.

Continuity is the calm case. It is the case where the nearby behavior and the actual value agree.

 Continuity at a point

Recall the function

F(x)= \begin{cases} 2x+1, \amp x\neq1,\\ -1, \amp x=1. \end{cases}

Near x=1, but not at x=1, the function follows the line

y=2x+1.

So

\lim_{x\to1}F(x)=3.

But

F(1)=-1.

The limit exists, but it does not equal the actual value. The graph has the nearby behavior of the line y=2x+1, except that the point at x=1 has been placed somewhere else.

This function is not continuous at x=1.

Continuity at a point

A function f is continuous at a if

\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a).

Equivalently, three things must happen:

\begin{array}{ll} 1. \amp f(a)\text{ is defined},\\ 2. \amp \displaystyle \lim_{x\to a}f(x)\text{ exists},\\ 3. \amp \displaystyle \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a). \end{array}

The third condition is the heart of the definition. Nearby values must approach the actual value.

Continuity means: nearby inputs give nearby outputs, including at the point itself.

a polynomial is continuous at a point

Let

f(x)=x^2.

At x=2,

f(2)=4.

Also,

\lim_{x\to2}x^2=4.

Therefore

\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=f(2),

so f is continuous at 2.

In fact, the same reasoning works at every point. If a is any real number, then

\lim_{x\to a}x^2=a^2=f(a).

So x^2 is continuous everywhere.

 The <m>\varepsilon</m>-<m>\delta</m> version

The limit definition gives a precise version of continuity.

A function f is continuous at a if, for every \varepsilon>0, there is a \delta>0 such that whenever x is in the domain of f and

|x-a|<\delta,

we have

|f(x)-f(a)|<\varepsilon.

There is no need to exclude x=a here. If x=a, then

|f(x)-f(a)|=|f(a)-f(a)|=0,

which is already less than every positive \varepsilon.

So the limit definition uses a punctured interval:

0<|x-a|<\delta,

while continuity uses the full interval:

|x-a|<\delta.

 What three things must happen for continuity at a point?

Continuity at a means \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a). In your own words, why does that one equation hide three requirements, and what goes wrong if the nearby limit exists but the actual value is missing or wrong?

Check separately that the function value exists, that the nearby values have a limit, and that the value equals that limit. A hole removes the function value; relocating a point can leave the limit unchanged while breaking agreement with the value.

 Holes and continuous extensions

Consider again

g(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}, \qquad x\neq1.

For x\neq1,

g(x)=x+1.

Thus

\lim_{x\to1}g(x)=2.

But g(1) is not defined, because the original formula gives division by 0. So g is not continuous at 1.

The failure is small. The graph only has a missing point. We can repair it by defining a new function

\widetilde g(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}, \amp x\neq1,\\ 2, \amp x=1. \end{cases}

Now

\lim_{x\to1}\widetilde g(x)=2

and

\widetilde g(1)=2.

Therefore \widetilde g is continuous at 1.

A discontinuity like this is called removable. The limit tells us exactly what value to insert.

Removable discontinuity

A function has a removable discontinuity at a if the limit

\lim_{x\to a}f(x)

exists, but the function is not continuous at a because f(a) is missing or has the wrong value.

The word “removable” does not mean the original function was continuous. It means we can make it continuous by changing the value at one point.

When can a hole be repaired?

The function \frac{x^2-1}{x-1} is not continuous at x=1 because the value is missing, yet defining the missing height to be 2 produces a continuous extension. In your own words, what makes a discontinuity removable, and why can a jump or a vertical asymptote not be repaired by filling in one point?

Repair is possible only when nearby values already agree on a finite target. A jump has two targets. An infinite discontinuity has no finite target at all.

Continuity on an interval

A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of that interval.

For an open interval (a,b), this means continuity at each point

a<x<b.

For a closed interval [a,b], the endpoints need one-sided versions:

\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=f(a)

at the left endpoint, and

\lim_{x\to b^-}f(x)=f(b)

at the right endpoint.

Continuity on a closed interval

A function f is continuous on [a,b] if

f\text{ is continuous at every point of }(a,b),

\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=f(a),

and

\lim_{x\to b^-}f(x)=f(b).

The one-sided conditions are natural. At the left endpoint a, points of the interval approach a only from the right. At the right endpoint b, points of the interval approach b only from the left.

Why do endpoints of a closed interval use one-sided continuity?

Continuity on [a,b] asks for ordinary continuity inside (a,b), but only a right-hand match at a and a left-hand match at b. In your own words, why are those one-sided conditions the natural ones at the ends of a closed interval?

If the inner limit fails, when can the composition still have a limit?

The function |x|/x has no two-sided limit at 0. Neither does the identity of that function. Its square does. When does an inner jump remain after composition? When does it disappear?

Why is continuity easy to build from old continuous pieces?

Sums, products, and (when the denominator is nonzero) quotients of continuous functions are continuous, and so is a composition f\circ g when g is continuous at a and f is continuous at g(a). Three common discontinuities

Continuity can fail in several ways. The three most common early failures are removable discontinuities, jump discontinuities, and infinite discontinuities.

\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{type} \amp \textbf{what happens} \amp \textbf{example}\\ \hline \text{removable} \amp \text{limit exists, but value is missing or wrong} \amp \displaystyle \frac{x^2-1}{x-1}\text{ at }x=1\\ \text{jump} \amp \text{left and right limits disagree} \amp \displaystyle \frac{|x|}{x}\text{ at }x=0\\ \text{infinite} \amp \text{values grow without bound} \amp \displaystyle \frac{1}{(x-2)^2}\text{ at }x=2 \end{array}

The names are not just vocabulary. They tell us what kind of repair, if any, is possible.

A removable discontinuity can be fixed by changing one value.

A jump cannot be fixed by changing one value, because the two sides approach different targets.

An infinite discontinuity cannot be fixed by changing one value, because nearby values do not stay near any finite number.

 A continuity checklist

When checking continuity at a, ask:

A continuity checklist question meaning Is f(a) defined? If not, the function is not continuous at a. Does \lim_{x\to a}f(x) exist? If the two sides disagree or the values do not settle, the function is not continuous at a. Does the limit equal f(a)? If not, the nearby behavior and the actual value disagree.

For familiar formulas, continuity often lets us substitute directly. For piecewise functions, endpoints between pieces must be checked. For quotients, denominators must be watched. For roots and logarithms, the domain must be respected.

Continuity is still a local idea: it describes what happens near one point. But it has surprising global consequences. A continuous graph cannot jump over a height, and on a closed finite interval it cannot avoid having a highest and lowest point.

Those two facts are the next payoff.
