\lim_{x\to0}f(s(x))

does not exist either.

Now square the same inner function:

\bigl(s(x)\bigr)^2=1 \qquad\text{for }x\neq0.

\lim_{x\to0}\bigl(s(x)\bigr)^2=1,

Three common discontinuities

\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{type} \amp \textbf{what happens} \amp \textbf{example}\\ \hline \text{removable} \amp \text{limit exists, but value is missing or wrong} \amp \displaystyle \frac{x^2-1}{x-1}\text{ at }x=1\\ \text{jump} \amp \text{left and right limits disagree} \amp \displaystyle \frac{|x|}{x}\text{ at }x=0\\ \text{infinite} \amp \text{values grow without bound} \amp \displaystyle \frac{1}{(x-2)^2}\text{ at }x=2 \end{array}

The names are not just vocabulary. They tell us what kind of repair, if any, is possible.

A removable discontinuity can be fixed by changing one value.

A jump cannot be fixed by changing one value, because the two sides approach different targets.

An infinite discontinuity cannot be fixed by changing one value, because nearby values do not stay near any finite number.

 A continuity checklist

When checking continuity at a, ask:

A continuity checklist

question

meaning

Is f(a) defined?

If not, the function is not continuous at a.

Does \lim_{x\to a}f(x) exist?

If the two sides disagree or the values do not settle, the function is not continuous at a.

Does the limit equal f(a)?

If not, the nearby behavior and the actual value disagree.

For familiar formulas, continuity often lets us substitute directly. For piecewise functions, endpoints between pieces must be checked. For quotients, denominators must be watched. For roots and logarithms, the domain must be respected.

Continuity is still a local idea: it describes what happens near one point. But it has surprising global consequences. A continuous graph cannot jump over a height, and on a closed finite interval it cannot avoid having a highest and lowest point.

Those two facts are the next payoff.

Two theorems about continuous functions

Continuity began as a local condition:

x\text{ close to }a \quad \Longrightarrow \quad f(x)\text{ close to }f(a).

But local calm forces global behavior. If a continuous graph starts below a horizontal line and ends above it, it must cross that line somewhere. If a continuous graph lives on a closed finite interval, it must reach a highest point and a lowest point.

These facts sound obvious from a picture. Their hypotheses are where the mathematics lives.

 Intermediate values

Suppose the temperature outside is 50^\circF at sunrise and 74^\circF at noon. If the temperature changes continuously, then at some time between sunrise and noon it must have been 60^\circF.

It cannot move from 50 to 74 without passing through the values in between.

The same idea solves equations.

finding a root without a formula

Let

p(x)=x^3-x-1.

Then

p(1)=1-1-1=-1

and

p(2)=8-2-1=5.

The value of p(x) changes from negative to positive on the interval [1,2]. Since p is a polynomial, it is continuous. Therefore the graph must cross the x-axis somewhere between 1 and 2.

So there is a number c\in(1,2) such that

p(c)=0.

In other words,

c^3-c-1=0.

We have proved that the equation has a solution in (1,2), even though we have not found an exact formula for c.

This example is the Intermediate Value Theorem in miniature.

 Intermediate Value Theorem

Suppose f is continuous on the closed interval [a,b]. If N is any number between f(a) and f(b), then there is at least one number c\in[a,b] such that

f(c)=N.

If

f(a)<N<f(b),

then the theorem says that f hits the value N somewhere between a and b. The same is true if

f(b)<N<f(a).

The graph may wiggle many times. It may hit the value N more than once. The theorem promises at least one hit, not exactly one.

Root form of the theorem

A common special case is N=0.

If f is continuous on [a,b] and

f(a)<0<f(b),

or

f(b)<0<f(a),

then there is a number c\in(a,b) such that

f(c)=0.

This is the form used to prove that equations have solutions.

 What does the Intermediate Value Theorem promise, and what does it refuse to compute?

If a continuous function on [a,b] changes from negative to positive, it must hit zero somewhere in between. In your own words, why does continuity force that crossing, and why is the theorem an existence statement rather than a formula for the root?

A continuous graph cannot jump over a height. The theorem promises at least one hit, not exactly one, and not an exact algebraic expression for the hitting point.

Bisection as a constructive proof idea

The Intermediate Value Theorem says a solution exists. Bisection shows how to trap one.

Return to

p(x)=x^3-x-1.

We know

p(1)<0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad p(2)>0.

Start with the interval

[1,2].

Cut it in half. The midpoint is

1.5.

Compute:

p(1.5)=1.5^3-1.5-1=0.875>0.

So a sign change occurs on

[1,1.5],

because

p(1)<0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad p(1.5)>0.

Cut again. The midpoint of [1,1.5] is

1.25.

Compute:

p(1.25)=1.25^3-1.25-1=-0.296875<0.

So a sign change occurs on

[1.25,1.5].

Continuing this process traps a root in smaller and smaller intervals.

\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \textbf{step} \amp \textbf{interval} \amp \textbf{midpoint} \amp \textbf{sign at midpoint}\\ \hline 0 \amp [1,2] \amp 1.5 \amp +\\ 1 \amp [1,1.5] \amp 1.25 \amp -\\ 2 \amp [1.25,1.5] \amp 1.375 \amp +\\ 3 \amp [1.25,1.375] \amp 1.3125 \amp - \end{array}

After each step, the interval is half as long as before. The intervals are nested:

[1,2]\supset[1,1.5]\supset[1.25,1.5]\supset[1.25,1.375]\supset\cdots.

The Nested Interval Principle traps one real number c in all these intervals. Continuity then forces

p(c)=0.

Idea of the proof of the Intermediate Value Theorem

For a target value N, apply bisection to

h(x)=f(x)-N.

If an endpoint or a midpoint has value zero, we have already found the desired point. Otherwise, if h(a) and h(b) have opposite signs, repeatedly keep the half interval where the sign change remains. The nested intervals shrink to a point c. Continuity prevents h(c) from being positive or negative, so

h(c)=0.

Therefore

f(c)=N.

This proof idea shows why the real line matters. Bisection produces smaller and smaller intervals. The real numbers guarantee that the intervals trap an actual point.

What the theorem does not say

The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees existence, not a formula. It tells us a root exists in (1,2), but it does not tell us the exact root.

Bisection gives approximations. If we keep cutting long enough, we can make the interval around the root as short as desired. This is one of the first reliable numerical methods in calculus.

 How does bisection turn existence into a trap?

Bisection repeatedly keeps the half-interval that still has a sign change. In your own words, why does that process trap a root, and why does completeness of the real line matter for the nested intervals it produces?

Each step preserves a sign change and halves the length. Nested closed intervals whose lengths shrink to zero trap one real number. Continuity then forces that trapped number to be a root.

Why continuity is required

The Intermediate Value Theorem fails without continuity.

Define

S(x)= \begin{cases} 0, \amp x<0,\\ 2, \amp x\ge0. \end{cases}

On the interval [-1,1],

S(-1)=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad S(1)=2.

The number 1 lies between 0 and 2. But there is no c\in[-1,1] such that

S(c)=1.

The function jumps from 0 to 2. It never takes the intermediate value 1.

The hypothesis of continuity is not decoration. It prevents jumping.

Why is the Intermediate Value Theorem a no-jump theorem?

A function that jumps from 0 to 2 can miss the intermediate value 1 even on a closed interval. In your own words, why is continuity not decoration, and what illegal move would it be to apply the theorem to a graph with a break?

The theorem’s machine needs a graph that cannot skip heights. If a hypothesis is missing, the output is no longer guaranteed.

Highest and lowest values

Continuity also gives a second global promise.

Suppose h(t) gives the height of a hiker above sea level at time t, for 0\le t\le4. If h is continuous, then during those four hours the hiker reaches a highest elevation and a lowest elevation.

The hiker cannot have a “least upper bound” of heights that is approached but never reached, as long as the time interval includes its endpoints and is finite.

A simple graph shows the idea.

Let

f(x)=x(2-x)

on the interval [0,2]. This function is continuous. Its values include

f(0)=0, \qquad f(1)=1, \qquad f(2)=0.

The absolute maximum value is

1,

attained at

x=1.

The absolute minimum value is

0,

attained at the endpoints

x=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=2.

The theorem says this always happens.

Extreme Value Theorem

If f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f attains an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on [a,b].

That is, there are numbers c,d\in[a,b] such that

f(c)\le f(x)\le f(d)

for every x\in[a,b].

The number f(d) is the absolute maximum value. The number f(c) is the absolute minimum value.

The theorem does not say where the maximum and minimum occur. They may occur at interior points, at endpoints, or at several points.

Example

The function

f(x)=x^3-3x

is continuous on [-2,2], so the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on [-2,2].

We do not yet have the derivative tools to find them efficiently. But we already know they exist.

This is how the theorem will be used later. Before optimizing a continuous function on a closed interval, we know that the best and worst values are really there.

 Why closed and bounded intervals matter

The Extreme Value Theorem has two interval hypotheses:

[a,b]\text{ is closed} \qquad\text{and}\qquad [a,b]\text{ is bounded}.

Both matter.

If the interval is not closed

Consider

f(x)=x

on the open interval

(0,1).

The values of f get close to 1, but never equal 1, because x=1 is not in the interval. So f has no absolute maximum on (0,1).

The values also get close to 0, but never equal 0, because x=0 is not in the interval. So f has no absolute minimum on (0,1).

The missing endpoints matter.

 If the interval is not bounded

Consider

f(x)=x

on the whole real line

(-\infty,\infty).

There is no largest value and no smallest value. The function can grow as large as we like and as negative as we like.

The function is continuous, but the interval is unbounded. The conclusion fails.

 If the function is not continuous

Even on a closed bounded interval, discontinuity can break the conclusion.

Define

K(x)= \begin{cases} x, \amp 0\le x<1,\\ 0, \amp x=1. \end{cases}

The domain is the closed interval [0,1], but K is not continuous at 1.

The values of K(x) get close to 1 as x\to1^-, but K(x) never equals 1. Also,

K(1)=0.

So K has no absolute maximum on [0,1].

\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{missing hypothesis} \amp \textbf{example} \amp \textbf{what fails}\\ \hline \text{closed interval} \amp f(x)=x\text{ on }(0,1) \amp \text{no maximum or minimum}\\ \text{bounded interval} \amp f(x)=x\text{ on }(-\infty,\infty) \amp \text{no maximum or minimum}\\ \text{continuity} \amp K(x)= \begin{cases} x,\amp 0\le x<1\\ 0,\amp x=1 \end{cases} \amp \text{no maximum} \end{array}

The theorem is strong because its hypotheses are strong.

 Why do closed and bounded intervals matter for highest and lowest values?

The Extreme Value Theorem says a continuous function on [a,b] reaches an absolute maximum and minimum. In your own words, why can the conclusion fail on an open interval, on an unbounded interval, or if continuity is dropped, even when the picture still looks calm?

Missing endpoints can be approached but never attained. An unbounded interval can let values escape to infinity. A jump can skip the would-be highest or lowest height. The theorem is strong because its hypotheses are strong.

Why these two theorems matter

The Intermediate Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem do not usually compute answers. They guarantee that answers exist.

Continuity gave us two promises: no skipped intermediate values, and actual highest and lowest values on closed finite intervals. The next section gathers the warning examples in one place. Warning examples

Continuity gave us two promises. The Intermediate Value Theorem says that a continuous graph cannot skip a height. The Extreme Value Theorem says that a continuous function on a closed finite interval reaches a highest and lowest value.

Those promises are strong because their hypotheses are strong. If we remove a hypothesis, the conclusion may fail.

This section gathers the warnings in one place. Each example is small, but each one protects a theorem from being used illegally.

 A function with no limit at a jump

A two-sided limit needs one target. A jump gives two targets.

Define

J(x)= \begin{cases} 0, \amp x<0,\\ 1, \amp x\ge 0. \end{cases}

As x\to0^-, the values of J(x) are always 0. So

\lim_{x\to0^-}J(x)=0.

As x\to0^+, the values of J(x) are always 1. So

\lim_{x\to0^+}J(x)=1.

The one-sided limits disagree. Therefore

\lim_{x\to0}J(x)

does not exist.

Changing the value at x=0 cannot repair the two-sided limit. The problem is not the point itself. The problem is that the nearby values on the two sides head toward different numbers.

\text{A two-sided limit is about agreement from both sides.}

Why can changing the value at a jump never repair a two-sided limit?

At a jump, the left-hand and right-hand limits disagree. In your own words, why is the problem not the point itself, and why does a two-sided limit demand agreement from both sides?

Nearby values on the two sides are already heading toward different numbers. Relabeling the single center point cannot make those two neighborhoods share a target.

A limit that is infinite, not finite

A different kind of failure happens when the values do not settle near any finite number.

Consider

f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2}, \qquad x\neq0.

As x gets close to 0, the denominator x^2 gets close to 0, but stays positive. The quotient grows larger and larger.

\begin{array}{c|cccccc} x \amp -0.1 \amp -0.01 \amp -0.001 \amp 0.001 \amp 0.01 \amp 0.1\\ \hline \dfrac1{x^2} \amp 100 \amp 10{,}000 \amp 1{,}000{,}000 \amp 1{,}000{,}000 \amp 10{,}000 \amp 100 \end{array}

We write

\lim_{x\to0}\frac1{x^2}=\infty.

This notation does not mean that the function has a finite limit. It means the values grow beyond every fixed positive bound.

There is no real number L such that

\lim_{x\to0}\frac1{x^2}=L.

A removable discontinuity can be repaired by filling in one value. Infinite divergent behavior cannot. No choice of f(0) can keep the nearby values close to a finite number.

\infty\text{ describes unbounded behavior. It is not a real-number target.}

Why is <m>\infty</m> not a real-number target?

The values of \frac1{x^2} grow beyond every fixed positive bound as x\to0. In your own words, why is that infinite behavior not a finite limit, and why can no choice of a value at the missing point keep the nearby outputs close to a real number L?

A finite limit requires outputs to settle inside some \varepsilon-window around a real target. Unbounded growth refuses every such window. Filling one point cannot cage an exploding neighborhood.

The Intermediate Value Theorem fails without continuity

The Intermediate Value Theorem said:

continuous graph+endpoint values \Longrightarrow all intermediate values are hit.

The word continuous cannot be removed.

Define

S(x)= \begin{cases} 0, \amp x<0,\\ 2, \amp x\ge0. \end{cases}

On the interval [-1,1],

S(-1)=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad S(1)=2.

The number 1 lies between 0 and 2. If we tried to use the Intermediate Value Theorem, we might expect some c\in[-1,1] such that

S(c)=1.

But no such c exists. The function takes only the values 0 and 2. It jumps over 1.

The theorem fails because S is not continuous at 0.

\text{The Intermediate Value Theorem is a no-jump theorem.}

What illegal use of the Intermediate Value Theorem do the warnings protect against?

The Intermediate Value Theorem is a no-jump theorem: continuous graph plus endpoint values imply that intermediate heights are hit. In your own words, why does dropping continuity let a function skip a height, and what should you check before using the theorem to prove that an equation has a solution?

A theorem is a machine with conditions. If the graph can jump, an intermediate value is no longer guaranteed. Check continuity on the closed interval first.

The Extreme Value Theorem fails on an open interval

The Extreme Value Theorem said:

continuous on [a,b] \Longrightarrow absolute maximum and minimum are reached.

The closed interval [a,b] includes its endpoints. If the endpoints are missing, the conclusion can fail.

Consider

f(x)=x

on the open interval

(0,1).

The function is continuous at every point of its domain. Its values get close to 1, but never equal 1, because x=1 is not in the interval.

So f has no absolute maximum on (0,1).

The values also get close to 0, but never equal 0, because x=0 is not in the interval.

So f has no absolute minimum on (0,1).

The problem is not the formula. The formula f(x)=x is perfectly continuous. The problem is the domain. The endpoints are missing.

\text{For the Extreme Value Theorem, endpoints matter.}

Which Extreme Value Theorem hypotheses can quietly fail?

On an open interval, f(x)=x approaches its apparent highest and lowest values without reaching them. On [0,\infty), the same formula has no largest value. In your own words, why do both closed and bounded matter, and what does it mean to say that a theorem’s output is no longer guaranteed when a condition is missing?

Endpoints can be the place where a max or min is attained. An interval that stretches forever can let values escape. The examples are reminders of what the theorem actually says, not exceptions to it.

The Extreme Value Theorem fails on an unbounded interval

A closed interval is not enough if it stretches forever.

Consider

f(x)=x

on

[0,\infty).

The function is continuous on its domain. The interval includes its left endpoint 0, so f has an absolute minimum:

f(0)=0.

But f has no absolute maximum. Given any value f(x)=x, we can choose a larger input, such as x+1, and get

f(x+1)=x+1>f(x).

So no largest value exists.

A physical version is also common. Recall the cooling model

T(t)=70+\frac{90}{t+1}, \qquad t\ge0.

The interval [0,\infty) is unbounded. The temperature starts at

T(0)=160,

and approaches 70 as t\to\infty. It never reaches 70 for any finite t, because

\frac{90}{t+1}>0.

So this continuous function has an absolute maximum on [0,\infty), but no absolute minimum.

\text{A function can approach a best value forever without reaching it.}

The word “bounded” in the Extreme Value Theorem prevents this escape to infinity.

 A map of the warnings

The examples above are not exceptions to the theorems. They are reminders of what the theorems actually say.

A map of the warnings claim we want missing hypothesis what breaks \lim_{x\to a}f(x) exists left and right sides agree jump gives two targets finite limit exists values stay bounded near a vertical asymptote IVT conclusion continuity intermediate value can be skipped EVT conclusion closed interval endpoint value may not be reached EVT conclusion bounded interval largest or smallest value may escape to infinity

A theorem is a machine with conditions. If a condition is missing, the output is no longer guaranteed.

Limits and continuity have now given us a careful language for functions of a real variable x. But some limiting processes arrive as lists:

1,\quad \frac12,\quad \frac13,\quad \frac14,\quad \ldots

or

1.4,\quad 1.41,\quad 1.414,\quad 1.4142,\quad \ldots

The input is no longer every nearby real number. The input is the whole-number step n. That leads to sequences.

Chapter review and discovery problems

This chapter began with one small calculation:

\frac{(2+h)^2-2^2}{h}=4+h, \qquad h\neq0.

The forbidden value h=0 did not stop us from seeing what happens as h gets close to 0. That idea became the language of limits. Limits then gave us continuity, one-sided behavior, infinite behavior, asymptotes, sequences, and two existence theorems.

Before we use limits to define derivatives, it is worth pausing to see the whole map.

 The chapter in one picture

A limit is the central idea. The other ideas in the chapter are different ways of asking what a limit is doing.

The most important habit is not memorizing a table of limit forms. It is asking:

\text{What is the input doing, and what target is the output approaching?}

What one idea sits at the center of the chapter?

The chapter began with a forbidden value h=0 that did not stop us from seeing what happens as h gets close to 0. In your own words, what does a limit watch, and why can continuity, one-sided behavior, asymptotes, and sequences all be seen as different ways of asking the same nearby-target question?

A limit is a controlled approach to a target. Sometimes the input is a real number, sometimes a whole-number index, sometimes only one side, and sometimes the target is infinite rather than finite.

A decision guide for limits and continuity

When you face a limit problem, begin with the simplest test. Then move only as far as the problem requires.

A decision guide for limits and continuity what you see what to try direct substitution gives a real number Use continuity or the limit laws. direct substitution gives \dfrac00 Factor, cancel, expand, combine fractions, or rationalize. Then try again. left and right sides behave differently Compute one-sided limits. A two-sided limit exists only if they agree. denominator approaches 0 without cancellation Check signs from the left and right. The limit may be \infty, -\infty, or may fail to exist. x\to\infty or x\to-\infty Divide by the largest power, or compare leading terms. an oscillating factor is multiplied by something small Try the squeeze principle. a theorem about continuous functions is tempting Check the hypotheses first: continuity, closed interval, bounded interval, and the right endpoint information. a sequence appears Use the \varepsilon-N definition, algebraic limit laws, or monotone bounded convergence.

The warning examples in Section should stay close by. Most mistakes come from using a true theorem without checking the conditions that make it true.

 Review problems

The problems below are grouped by purpose. Some are computational. Some ask for explanations. Some ask for proof. In the proof problems, the goal is not speed. The goal is control.

A. Concept checks

  1. Explain the difference between

    \lim_{x\to a}f(x) \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(a).

    Give an example where the limit exists but does not equal the function value.

  2. Explain why the condition

    0<|x-a|<\delta

    appears in the definition of a limit.

  3. What does the statement

    \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=\infty

    mean? Why is this not convergence to a real number?

  4. A table gives values of f(x) near x=3, and the values appear to approach 8. Why is the table useful? Why is it not, by itself, a proof?

  5. State the two-sided limit test using left-hand and right-hand limits.

  6. In your own words, explain what continuity at a means.

  7. Why can a removable discontinuity be repaired by changing one value, but a jump discontinuity cannot?

  8. State the Intermediate Value Theorem. Name its main hypothesis.

  9. State the Extreme Value Theorem. Explain why both words “closed” and “bounded” matter in the interval hypothesis.

  10. Explain the difference between convergence of a sequence and convergence of a series. Use the words terms and partial sums.

B. Skills: compute and interpret limits

Compute each limit if it exists as a finite real number. If no finite two-sided limit exists, explain why. When appropriate, give one-sided limits.

  1. Polynomial and rational limits.

    \lim_{x\to4}(3x^2-5x+1), \qquad \lim_{x\to-2}\frac{x^2+1}{x-3},

    \lim_{x\to0}\frac{5x^3-2x+7}{x^2+1}, \qquad \lim_{x\to3}\frac{x^2-9}{x+1}.

  2. Removable discontinuities.

    \lim_{x\to3}\frac{x^2-9}{x-3}, \qquad \lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^3-8}{x-2},

    \lim_{x\to4}\frac{\sqrt{x+5}-3}{x-4}, \qquad \lim_{x\to2}\frac{\frac1x-\frac12}{x-2}.

  3. Squeeze principle.

    \lim_{x\to0}x\sin\frac1x, \qquad \lim_{x\to0}x^2\cos\frac1{x^2},

    \lim_{x\to0}|x|\sin\frac1x.

    For each one, write the inequalities that trap the function.

  4. One-sided limits for a piecewise function. Let

    F(x)= \begin{cases} x^2+2, \amp x<1,\\ 4, \amp x=1,\\ 3x, \amp x>1. \end{cases}

    Find

    \lim_{x\to1^-}F(x), \qquad \lim_{x\to1^+}F(x), \qquad \lim_{x\to1}F(x), \qquad F(1).

    Is F continuous at 1?

  5. Another piecewise function. Let

    G(x)= \begin{cases} 2x+1, \amp x<2,\\ 5, \amp x=2,\\ x^2-1, \amp x>2. \end{cases}

    Find the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, two-sided limit, and function value at x=2. Is this a removable discontinuity, a jump discontinuity, or neither?

  6. Infinite limits.

    \lim_{x\to3^-}\frac1{x-3}, \qquad \lim_{x\to3^+}\frac1{x-3},

    \lim_{x\to3}\frac1{(x-3)^2}, \qquad \lim_{x\to2^-}\frac{x+2}{x^2-4}, \qquad \lim_{x\to2^+}\frac{x+2}{x^2-4}.

    For each function, identify any vertical asymptote.

  7. Limits at infinity.

    \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{5x^2-x+1}{2x^2+3}, \qquad \lim_{x\to-\infty}\frac{5x^2-x+1}{2x^2+3},

    \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{3x+7}{x^2+1}, \qquad \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x^2+1}{x-1}.

    For the last function, decide whether there is a horizontal asymptote or a slant asymptote.

  8. Slant asymptote. Write

    \frac{x^2+3x}{x+1}

    in the form

    mx+b+\frac{r}{x+1}.

    Then find the slant asymptote as x\to\infty and as x\to-\infty.

  9. Sequence limits.

    \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{3n+1}{2n-5}, \qquad \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1-\frac1n\right),

    \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n^2+4}{5n^2-n}, \qquad \lim_{n\to\infty}(-1)^n.

    Classify each sequence as convergent or divergent.

  10. Monotone bounded sequences. For each sequence, decide whether it is increasing, decreasing, bounded above, bounded below, and convergent.

    a_n=1-\frac1n, \qquad b_n=\frac1n, \qquad c_n=n, \qquad d_n=(-1)^n.

C. Reading limits from a graph

Use Figure for the next problem.

  1. Find

    \lim_{x\to-1^-}f(x), \qquad \lim_{x\to-1^+}f(x), \qquad \lim_{x\to-1}f(x), \qquad f(-1).

  2. Find

    \lim_{x\to1^-}f(x), \qquad \lim_{x\to1^+}f(x), \qquad \lim_{x\to1}f(x), \qquad f(1).

  3. At which points shown in the graph is f discontinuous? Classify each discontinuity as removable, jump, or neither.

  4. Could changing only f(-1) make the function continuous at -1? Explain.

  5. Could changing only f(1) make the function continuous at 1? Explain.

D. Continuity and theorem use

  1. Find the value of c that makes the function continuous at x=2:

    H(x)= \begin{cases} x^2+c, \amp x<2,\\ 3x-1, \amp x\ge2. \end{cases}

  2. Find the value of c that makes the function continuous at x=2:

    K(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^2-4}{x-2}, \amp x\neq2,\\ c, \amp x=2. \end{cases}

  3. Find all points where the function is discontinuous:

    R(x)=\frac{x+1}{x^2-1}.

    For each discontinuity, decide whether it is removable or infinite.

  4. Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that the equation

    x^3+x-3=0

    has a solution in (1,2).

  5. Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that the equation

    x^5+x-1=0

    has a solution in (0,1).

  6. Let

    f(x)=x^4-4x+1.

    Explain why f must attain an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on [-2,3]. You do not need to find them.

  7. The function

    f(x)=\frac1x

    is continuous on (0,1). Does the Extreme Value Theorem guarantee an absolute maximum and minimum on (0,1)? Explain exactly which hypothesis is missing.

  8. A function f is continuous on [0,4], with

    f(0)=-2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(4)=7.

    What values must f take somewhere on [0,4]? What values might it take, but are not guaranteed by this information alone?

  9. A function g is defined on [0,4], with

    g(0)=-2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad g(4)=7.

    But g is not continuous. Can we conclude that g(c)=0 for some c\in[0,4]? Give an example or explain why not.

  10. Give an example of a continuous function on an unbounded interval that has no absolute maximum.

E. Proof practice with <m>\varepsilon</m>, <m>\delta</m>, and <m>N</m>

These problems are about writing precise arguments. Do not begin by saying “it is obvious from the graph.” Begin with the error you must control.

  1. Prove from the definition that

    \lim_{x\to3}(2x+5)=11.

  2. Prove from the definition that

    \lim_{x\to a}(mx+b)=ma+b,

    where m and b are constants.

  3. Prove from the definition that

    \lim_{x\to2}x^2=4.

    Hint: factor

    |x^2-4|=|x-2||x+2|.

    First make |x+2| bounded by requiring |x-2|<1.

  4. Prove from the definition that

    \lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=2.

    Remember that the definition already assumes x\neq1.

  5. Prove that

    \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n=0.

    Use the precise definition of sequence convergence.

  6. Prove that

    \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{2n+1}{n+3}=2.

    Hint:

    \left|\frac{2n+1}{n+3}-2\right| = \frac5{n+3}.

  7. For the sequence

    a_n=1-\frac1n,

    prove directly that a_n\to1.

  8. Show that the sequence

    b_n=(-1)^n

    does not converge. Hint: if it converged to L, the even terms and odd terms would both have to approach L.

  9. Let \varepsilon=10^{-4}. Find a value of N such that

    n\ge N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left|\frac1n-0\right|<10^{-4}.

  10. Let

    a_n=\frac{n}{n+1}.

    Find a value of N such that

    n\ge N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad |a_n-1|<0.001.

What should you check before forcing a two-sided finite limit?

Direct substitution, the form \frac00, disagreeing sides, and unbounded growth are different pictures. In your own words, how do you decide whether to substitute, rewrite, split into one-sided limits, or refuse a finite two-sided claim?

First check whether continuity justifies direct substitution. The form \frac00 is a question. Different one-sided limits block a two-sided limit. Growth without bound is infinite behavior, not a real-number target.

 Project: bisection method for a root

The Intermediate Value Theorem proves that roots exist. Bisection turns that proof into a numerical method.

Use

p(x)=x^3-x-1.

We know

p(1)=-1<0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad p(2)=5>0.

Since p is continuous, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees at least one root in (1,2).

The method

Begin with

[L_0,R_0]=[1,2].

At each step, compute the midpoint

M_k=\frac{L_k+R_k}{2}.

Then choose the half interval where the sign change remains:

[L_{k+1},R_{k+1}] = \begin{cases} [L_k,M_k], \amp p(L_k)\text{ and }p(M_k)\text{ have opposite signs},\\ [M_k,R_k], \amp p(M_k)\text{ and }p(R_k)\text{ have opposite signs}. \end{cases}

If p(M_k)=0, the midpoint is the exact root and the process stops.

 Part 1: complete the table

Use exact arithmetic or decimal approximations. Keep at least six decimal places in the midpoint and in p(M_k).

\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} k \amp L_k \amp R_k \amp M_k \amp p(M_k) \amp \text{next interval}\\ \hline 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \amp 1.5 \amp 0.875 \amp [1,1.5]\\ 1 \amp 1 \amp 1.5 \amp 1.25 \amp -0.296875 \amp [1.25,1.5]\\ 2 \amp \amp \amp \amp \amp\\ 3 \amp \amp \amp \amp \amp\\ 4 \amp \amp \amp \amp \amp\\ 5 \amp \amp \amp \amp \amp\\ 6 \amp \amp \amp \amp \amp\\ 7 \amp \amp \amp \amp \amp \end{array}

 Part 2: error control

After N completed bisections, what is the length of the interval that still contains the root?

Start with length

R_0-L_0=1.

After one bisection, the length is

\frac12.

After two bisections, the length is

\frac14.

Find a formula for the length after N bisections.

 Part 3: midpoint estimate

If the root c lies inside [L_N,R_N], and we report the midpoint

M_N=\frac{L_N+R_N}{2},

show that

|M_N-c|\le \frac{R_N-L_N}{2}.

Chapter review and discovery problems

This chapter began with one small calculation:

\frac{(2+h)^2-2^2}{h}=4+h, \qquad h\neq0.

The forbidden value h=0 did not stop us from seeing what happens as h gets close to 0. That idea became the language of limits. Limits then gave us continuity, one-sided behavior, infinite behavior, asymptotes, sequences, and two existence theorems.

Before we use limits to define derivatives, it is worth pausing to see the whole map.

 The chapter in one picture

A limit is the central idea. The other ideas in the chapter are different ways of asking what a limit is doing.

The most important habit is not memorizing a table of limit forms. It is asking:

\text{What is the input doing, and what target is the output approaching?}

What one idea sits at the center of the chapter?

The chapter began with a forbidden value h=0 that did not stop us from seeing what happens as h gets close to 0. In your own words, what does a limit watch, and why can continuity, one-sided behavior, asymptotes, and sequences all be seen as different ways of asking the same nearby-target question?

A limit is a controlled approach to a target. Sometimes the input is a real number, sometimes a whole-number index, sometimes only one side, and sometimes the target is infinite rather than finite.

A decision guide for limits and continuity

When you face a limit problem, begin with the simplest test. Then move only as far as the problem requires.

A decision guide for limits and continuity

what you see

what to try

direct substitution gives a real number

Use continuity or the limit laws.

direct substitution gives \dfrac00

Factor, cancel, expand, combine fractions, or rationalize. Then try again.

left and right sides behave differently

Compute one-sided limits. A two-sided limit exists only if they agree.

denominator approaches 0 without cancellation

Check signs from the left and right. The limit may be \infty, -\infty, or may fail to exist.

x\to\infty or x\to-\infty

Divide by the largest power, or compare leading terms.

an oscillating factor is multiplied by something small

Try the squeeze principle.

a theorem about continuous functions is tempting

Check the hypotheses first: continuity, closed interval, bounded interval, and the right endpoint information.

a sequence appears

Use the \varepsilon-N definition, algebraic limit laws, or monotone bounded convergence.

The warning examples in Section should stay close by. Most mistakes come from using a true theorem without checking the conditions that make it true.

 Review problems

The problems below are grouped by purpose. Some are computational. Some ask for explanations. Some ask for proof. In the proof problems, the goal is not speed. The goal is control.

A. Concept checks

  1. Explain the difference between

    \lim_{x\to a}f(x) \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(a).

    Give an example where the limit exists but does not equal the function value.

  2. Explain why the condition

    0<|x-a|<\delta

    appears in the definition of a limit.

  3. What does the statement

    \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=\infty

    mean? Why is this not convergence to a real number?

  4. A table gives values of f(x) near x=3, and the values appear to approach 8. Why is the table useful? Why is it not, by itself, a proof?

  5. State the two-sided limit test using left-hand and right-hand limits.

  6. In your own words, explain what continuity at a means.

  7. Why can a removable discontinuity be repaired by changing one value, but a jump discontinuity cannot?

  8. State the Intermediate Value Theorem. Name its main hypothesis.

  9. State the Extreme Value Theorem. Explain why both words “closed” and “bounded” matter in the interval hypothesis.

  10. Explain the difference between convergence of a sequence and convergence of a series. Use the words terms and partial sums.

B. Skills: compute and interpret limits

Compute each limit if it exists as a finite real number. If no finite two-sided limit exists, explain why. When appropriate, give one-sided limits.

  1. Polynomial and rational limits.

    \lim_{x\to4}(3x^2-5x+1), \qquad \lim_{x\to-2}\frac{x^2+1}{x-3},

    \lim_{x\to0}\frac{5x^3-2x+7}{x^2+1}, \qquad \lim_{x\to3}\frac{x^2-9}{x+1}.

  2. Removable discontinuities.

    \lim_{x\to3}\frac{x^2-9}{x-3}, \qquad \lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^3-8}{x-2},

    \lim_{x\to4}\frac{\sqrt{x+5}-3}{x-4}, \qquad \lim_{x\to2}\frac{\frac1x-\frac12}{x-2}.

  3. Squeeze principle.

    \lim_{x\to0}x\sin\frac1x, \qquad \lim_{x\to0}x^2\cos\frac1{x^2},

    \lim_{x\to0}|x|\sin\frac1x.

    For each one, write the inequalities that trap the function.

  4. One-sided limits for a piecewise function. Let

    F(x)= \begin{cases} x^2+2, \amp x<1,\\ 4, \amp x=1,\\ 3x, \amp x>1. \end{cases}

    Find

    \lim_{x\to1^-}F(x), \qquad \lim_{x\to1^+}F(x), \qquad \lim_{x\to1}F(x), \qquad F(1).

    Is F continuous at 1?

  5. Another piecewise function. Let

    G(x)= \begin{cases} 2x+1, \amp x<2,\\ 5, \amp x=2,\\ x^2-1, \amp x>2. \end{cases}

    Find the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, two-sided limit, and function value at x=2. Is this a removable discontinuity, a jump discontinuity, or neither?

  6. Infinite limits.

    \lim_{x\to3^-}\frac1{x-3}, \qquad \lim_{x\to3^+}\frac1{x-3},

    \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{5x^2-x+1}{2x^2+3}, \qquad \lim_{x\to-\infty}\frac{5x^2-x+1}{2x^2+3},

    Then find the slant asymptote as x\to\infty and as x\to-\infty.

Use Figure for the next problem.

  1. Find

    \lim_{x\to-1^-}f(x), \qquad \lim_{x\to-1^+}f(x), \qquad \lim_{x\to-1}f(x), \qquad f(-1).

  4. Could changing only f(-1) make the function continuous at -1? Explain.

  5. Could changing only f(1) make the function continuous at 1? Explain.

  1. Find the value of c that makes the function continuous at x=2:

    H(x)= \begin{cases} x^2+c, \amp x<2,\\ 3x-1, \amp x\ge2. \end{cases}

  2. Find the value of c that makes the function continuous at x=2:

    K(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^2-4}{x-2}, \amp x\neq2,\\ c, \amp x=2. \end{cases}

    has a solution in (0,1).

    f(x)=x^4-4x+1.

  7. The function

    f(x)=\frac1x

    is continuous on (0,1). Does the Extreme Value Theorem guarantee an absolute maximum and minimum on (0,1)? Explain exactly which hypothesis is missing.

  8. A function f is continuous on [0,4], with

    f(0)=-2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(4)=7.

  9. A function g is defined on [0,4], with

  2. Prove from the definition that

    \lim_{x\to a}(mx+b)=ma+b,

    where m and b are constants.

  3. Prove from the definition that

A catalog of essential functions

We can now build functions by formulas, graphs, tables, words, transformations, arithmetic, composition, and inverses. But calculus does not treat every function as a stranger.

Some families appear again and again. Lines describe constant rates. Polynomials describe smooth algebraic change. Rational functions show ratios and asymptotes. Trigonometric functions describe periodic motion. Exponential functions describe constant percentage change. Logarithms undo exponentials.

This catalog is not a list to memorize. It is a set of familiar shapes and stories.

 Linear functions and units

The distance function for constant velocity had the form

s(t)=s_0+vt.

This is a linear function.

In general, a linear function has the form

f(x)=mx+b.

The number m is the slope. It measures output change per unit input change:

m=\frac{\text{change in output}}{\text{change in input}}.

The number b is the value at input 0:

f(0)=b.

What is the signature of a linear function?

A linear function has the form f(x)=mx+b. In your own words, what does the constant average rate of change m remember, and why do the units of m already tell you how outputs change when inputs change?

Equal input steps produce equal output steps. The slope’s units are output units divided by input units, which is exactly the instruction change per unit change.

a cost model

Suppose a taxi ride costs 4 dollars to begin and 2.50 dollars per mile. If m is the number of miles, then

C(m)=4+2.50m.

The slope is

2.50\frac{\text{dollars}}{\text{mile}}.

The intercept is

4\text{ dollars}.

The units make the formula readable:

2.50\frac{\text{dollars}}{\text{mile}}\cdot m\text{ miles} = 2.50m\text{ dollars}.

A linear model says that equal changes in input produce equal changes in output.

 converting temperature

The Celsius-to-Fahrenheit function is

F(C)=\frac95 C+32.

The slope is

\frac95.

This says that increasing the Celsius temperature by 1^\circ increases the Fahrenheit temperature by

\frac95^\circ.

The intercept is 32, because

0^\circ\text{ C}=32^\circ\text{ F}.

The graph is a line, but the meaning is a conversion between two scales.

 Linear signature

A linear function has constant average rate of change:

\frac{f(x_2)-f(x_1)}{x_2-x_1}=m

for every x_1\neq x_2.

Later, the derivative of a linear function will simply be its slope.

 Powers and polynomials

Power functions have the form

f(x)=x^p.

The most familiar powers are

x,\qquad x^2,\qquad x^3,\qquad x^4.

They already appeared in the first chapter through finite differences. Squares grew with odd-number differences. Cubes grew faster.

Power functions describe scaling.

area and volume

The area of a circle of radius r is

A(r)=\pi r^2.

If the radius doubles, the area becomes

A(2r)=\pi(2r)^2=4\pi r^2=4A(r).

So doubling length multiplies area by 4.

The volume of a sphere of radius r is

V(r)=\frac43\pi r^3.

If the radius doubles, the volume becomes

V(2r)=\frac43\pi(2r)^3=8V(r).

So doubling length multiplies volume by 8.

This is the basic difference between square growth and cubic growth.

 Power-law scaling

For

f(x)=Cx^p,

for x>0 and k>0, multiplying the input by k multiplies the output by k^p:

f(kx)=C(kx)^p=k^pCx^p=k^p f(x).

A polynomial is a finite sum of power functions with nonnegative integer powers:

p(x)=a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0.

Here the coefficients

a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_n

are real numbers, and a_n\neq 0. The number n is the degree of the polynomial.

Examples

The function

p(x)=3x^4-2x^2+7x-1

is a polynomial of degree 4.

The function

q(x)=5x^2-9

is a polynomial of degree 2.

The function

r(x)=8

is a constant polynomial. Its degree is 0, as long as the constant is not 0.

Polynomials are defined for all real inputs. Their domains are

\mathbb R.

Their graphs have no breaks, holes, or vertical asymptotes. They may turn, cross the axis, or flatten, but they do not suddenly jump.

 Leading behavior

Far from the origin, the highest-power term usually dominates the shape. For

p(x)=2x^5-10x^2+3,

the term 2x^5 eventually becomes much larger in size than -10x^2 and 3. So for large positive or negative x, the graph behaves roughly like

y=2x^5.

This idea will become more precise when we study limits at infinity.

 Rational functions and asymptotic behavior

A rational function is a quotient of two polynomials:

r(x)=\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.

The denominator cannot be zero. Thus the natural domain is

\{x\in\mathbb R:q(x)\neq 0\}.

Example

The function

r(x)=\frac{x+1}{x^2-4}

is undefined when

x^2-4=0.

Since

x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2),

the forbidden inputs are

x=2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=-2.

So the natural domain is

(-\infty,-2)\cup(-2,2)\cup(2,\infty).

Rational functions often show behavior that polynomials do not: vertical asymptotes, horizontal asymptotes, and holes.

 average cost

Suppose producing x items costs

Models before calculus

The catalog gave us familiar function families. A model is the next step: we choose one of those families because a situation asks for it.

A model is not the same thing as reality. It is a mathematical story about reality. A good model respects units, captures the main pattern, and makes predictions we can test.

Definition

A mathematical model is a function, equation, graph, or table used to represent a real quantity.

A model should be judged by four questions:

\text{What assumptions does it make?}

\text{Do the units make sense?}

\text{How well does it fit the information we have?}

\text{Where should we not trust it?}

Calculus will later tell us how models change and how their effects accumulate. Before calculus begins, we should learn the main shapes that models can take.

 Linear growth

Suppose water is poured into a tank at a steady rate of 3 liters per minute. At the moment we start watching, the tank already contains 12 liters.

After t minutes, the amount of water is

W(t)=12+3t.

The number 12 is the starting amount. The number 3 is the rate of change.

\begin{array}{c|ccccc} t\text{ (minutes)} \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 2 \amp 3 \amp 4\\ \hline W(t)\text{ (liters)} \amp 12 \amp 15 \amp 18 \amp 21 \amp 24 \end{array}

Each time t increases by 1, the output increases by 3.

15-12=3,\qquad 18-15=3,\qquad 21-18=3.

This is the signature of a linear model: equal input changes produce equal output changes.

Linear model

A linear model has the form

y=b+mx.

The number b is the initial value, because

y(0)=b.

The number m is the constant rate of change:

m=\frac{\text{change in output}}{\text{change in input}}.

The units of m are output units divided by input units. In the water example,

m=3\frac{\text{liters}}{\text{minute}}.

 Hook: limits make near into mathematics

The last problem is the doorway to the next chapter.

For

s(t)=t^2,

the average velocity from t=2 to t=2+h is

4+h, \qquad h\neq0.

As h gets close to 0, the average velocity gets close to 4. Chapter 2 gave us the language to make that sentence sharper:

|(4+h)-4|=|h|.

So if we want the output error to be less than \varepsilon, we can demand

0<|h|<\varepsilon.

This is the shape of a limit. The input is allowed to approach a forbidden or special value. The output is forced into any desired error bound.

The next chapter gives this idea its name.

What is already the shape of a limit?

For s(t)=t^2, the average velocity from t=2 to t=2+h is 4+h with h\neq0, and the error from 4 is exactly |h|. In your own words, what promise is already visible here, and why is the input allowed to approach a forbidden value while the output is forced into any desired error bound?

The condition 0<|h|<\varepsilon keeps the step away from zero and still small enough. That is the measuring-tape language the next chapter will name.

The dashboard: speedometer and odometer

Look at two instruments on a car dashboard.

The odometer records distance. It tells how many miles the car has accumulated.

The speedometer records speed. It tells how fast the odometer reading is changing.

For the moment, imagine that the car moves only forward along a straight road. Then speed and velocity agree. Later, when the car can reverse direction, we will need signed velocity.

Let t denote time, measured in hours after the start of a trip. Let

d(t)

denote the number of miles traveled after t hours. Let

v(t)

denote the velocity at time t, measured in miles per hour.

The notation d(t) means: the distance depends on the time. When the input is a time t, the output is a distance d(t). We will soon give this kind of rule a name: a function. For now, the notation lets us keep track of the trip.

 Distance as accumulated motion

Suppose the odometer reads 18{,}246.3 miles at 9{:}00 and 18{,}346.3 miles at 11{:}00. During those two hours, the car has accumulated

18{,}346.3-18{,}246.3=100

miles.

The odometer does not say how the car traveled those 100 miles. The driver might have gone steadily. Or slowly at first and quickly later. The odometer remembers the total effect, not the moment-by-moment history.

If we reset the trip odometer at the start, then d(0)=0. After 2 hours in this example,

d(2)=100.

The distance function d(t) is a memory of the trip.

What does an odometer remember?

Two trips can produce the same odometer change even if one is steady and the other is stop-and-go. In your own words, what information does the final distance reading d(T) remember, and what information does it throw away? How does knowing the entire record d(t) give more information?

The final value d(T) is one running total. Different trips can have the same final total. The entire function d(t) records how that total changed throughout the trip; when differentiable, it determines speed.

Velocity as changing distance

Velocity measures how fast distance changes.

If the car travels 100 miles in 2 hours, then its average velocity over that time is

\frac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{change in time}} = \frac{100\text{ miles}}{2\text{ hours}} = 50\text{ miles/hour}.

Using d(t), this is

\frac{d(2)-d(0)}{2-0}.

This number is an average over an interval. It does not say that the car was moving at exactly 50 miles per hour at every instant. It only says that the total change, spread evenly over two hours, would be 50 miles per hour.

A speedometer asks a sharper question:

\text{How fast is the distance changing right now?}

That word “right now” is where calculus enters.

What does an average velocity hide?

If a car travels 100 miles in 2 hours, the average velocity is 50 miles per hour. In your own words, why is that number not yet a speedometer reading, and what extra question does the word right now add?

An average spreads a total change over a whole interval. A speedometer asks about one instant inside that interval.

Units already tell the story

The units point to the mathematics.

d(t) \quad \text{has units of miles},

while

v(t) \quad \text{has units of miles/hour}.

So velocity must be built from distance divided by time. That is why ratios like

\frac{d(b)-d(a)}{b-a}

will appear again and again.

The numerator measures change in distance. The denominator measures change in time. Their quotient measures change per unit time.

Units already tell the story symbol meaning units t time after the start hours d(t) distance traveled after t hours miles v(t) velocity at time t miles/hour

A good formula respects units. For example,

\text{miles/hour}\cdot \text{hours}=\text{miles}.

So multiplying velocity by time should produce a distance. This is exactly what happens when velocity is constant.

What do the units already tell you to do?

Distance is measured in miles and velocity in miles per hour. In your own words, why do those units force velocity to be a ratio of a change in distance to a change in time, and why does multiplying velocity by time return a distance?

Treat units as instructions: division by hours makes a rate; multiplication by hours undoes that division.

The first question: distance to velocity

Suppose we know the whole odometer record d(t). Can we recover the velocity v(t)?

For a long interval, we can compute only an average velocity. For example,

\frac{d(2)-d(0)}{2}

is the average velocity from time 0 to time 2.

To know the velocity near t=2, we should look closer:

\frac{d(2.1)-d(2)}{2.1-2}, \qquad \frac{d(2.01)-d(2)}{2.01-2}, \qquad \frac{d(2.001)-d(2)}{2.001-2}.

These fractions measure average velocity over shorter and shorter intervals beginning at t=2. If the numbers settle toward one value, that value should be the velocity at the instant t=2.

This is the first great problem of calculus:

\text{From distance, find velocity.}

Geometrically, this will become the problem of finding the slope of a tangent line.

How can a whole distance record produce a velocity at one instant?

Starting from a known function d(t), we look at fractions such as \frac{d(2.001)-d(2)}{2.001-2}. In your own words, what are those fractions measuring, and why should shorter and shorter time intervals be better clues to the velocity at t=2?

Each fraction is still an average, just over a smaller window. Ask what that window is trying to collapse onto.

The second question: velocity to distance

Now reverse the question.

Suppose we know the whole speedometer record v(t). Can we recover the distance d(t)?

If the velocity is 60 miles/hour for 2 hours, then the car travels

60\cdot 2=120

miles.

40\text{ miles/hour for } \frac12\text{ hour}

and then

60\text{ miles/hour for } \frac12\text{ hour}.

The distance traveled is

40\cdot \frac12 + 60\cdot \frac12 = 20+30 = 50

miles.

Each product

\text{velocity}\cdot \text{time}

gives distance for a small piece of the trip. Adding those pieces gives total distance.

This is the second great problem of calculus:

\text{From velocity, find distance.}

Geometrically, this will become the problem of finding area under a graph.

How can a velocity record rebuild distance?

If velocity is not constant, we break a trip into pieces and add products of the form velocity times time. In your own words, why does each such product give a piece of distance, and why does adding the pieces reconstruct the odometer change?

On a short piece where velocity hardly changes, the constant-velocity rule is a good local story. Accumulation is the act of adding those local stories.

The two questions are opposite in spirit.

\begin{array}{ccl} \text{distance} \amp \longrightarrow \amp \text{velocity}\\ d(t) \amp \longrightarrow \amp v(t) \end{array}

means: accumulate many small changes.

The first process will be called differentiation. The second will be called integration. The deepest early theorem in calculus will say that these two processes undo each other.

Why are the two dashboard questions inverses?

One question goes from distance to velocity; the other goes from velocity to distance. In your own words, why should these two processes undo each other, and what would go wrong in the story if they did not?

If you accumulate a rate of change, you should recover the original change. If you measure how fast an accumulated quantity is changing, you should recover the original rate.

For now, we test the story in the simplest case: constant velocity.

Forward, backward, and signed motion

Constant velocity gave us the first picture of calculus: slope on one graph and area on another. But we quietly assumed that the car only moved forward. The moment a car can reverse, the dashboard story needs one more idea.

Velocity has a sign.

Choose one direction on a straight road and call it positive. For example, east may be positive and west negative. A car moving east at 40 miles/hour has velocity

v=40.

A car moving west at the same speed has velocity

v=-40.

The speed is the size of the velocity:

\text{speed}=|v|.

So speed is never negative, but velocity can be negative. This sign is how calculus remembers direction.

 Positive and negative velocity

When motion can go backward, it is better to stop using d(t) for everything. The word “distance” usually means a nonnegative amount traveled. Instead, let

s(t)

denote the signed position of the car along the road at time t. We measure s(t) in miles from the starting point, with positive values in the chosen positive direction.

If s(0)=0, then:

s(t)>0

means the car is on the positive side of the starting point, while

s(t)<0

means the car is on the negative side.

The change

s(b)-s(a)

is called the displacement from time a to time b. Displacement is signed. It can be positive, negative, or zero.

What extra information does a sign on velocity carry?

Speed is never negative, but velocity can be. In your own words, what does a negative velocity tell you that a speedometer needle cannot, and why is that extra information needed to reconstruct position?

A speedometer reports how fast the odometer is ticking. It does not report whether the car is heading forward or backing up.

Example

Suppose a car moves as follows:

40\text{ miles/hour for }2\text{ hours},

then

-30\text{ miles/hour for }1\text{ hour}.

The first part moves the car

40\cdot 2=80

miles in the positive direction. The second part moves the car

-30\cdot 1=-30

miles in the negative direction.

So the displacement over the whole trip is

80+(-30)=50

miles.

The car ends 50 miles ahead of where it started.

 Displacement versus distance traveled

The odometer would tell a different story. The car actually drove 80 miles forward and then 30 miles backward. The total distance traveled is

80+30=110

miles.

So in this trip,

\text{displacement}=50\text{ miles},

but

\text{distance traveled}=110\text{ miles}.

These are not the same.

Displacement remembers direction

Forward motion counts positive. Backward motion counts negative.

\text{displacement}=s(b)-s(a).

Distance traveled ignores direction.

Forward and backward motion both add positive length.

\text{distance traveled}=\text{sum of the lengths of all pieces of motion}.

A person who walks 10 steps forward and 10 steps backward has displacement 0, but did not stand still. The distance traveled is 20 steps.

Why can displacement be smaller than distance traveled?

A car can travel many miles of road and still end near its starting point. In your own words, what is the difference between displacement and distance traveled, and which of the two is signed area designed to compute?

Forward and backward contributions can cancel. Absolute distance refuses to cancel.

Area below the time axis

Now look at the velocity graph. Positive velocity lies above the time axis. Negative velocity lies below it.

For the trip above,

v(t)= \begin{cases} 40, \amp 0\leq t<2,\\ -30, \amp 2<t\leq 3. \end{cases}

The signed position is

s(t)= \begin{cases} 40t, \amp 0\leq t\leq 2,\\ 80-30(t-2), \amp 2\leq t\leq 3. \end{cases}

At t=2, the simple model changes velocity instantly. We may leave v(2) undefined. That one instant has no width, so it does not affect any accumulated displacement in this step model. But it does leave a corner in the graph of s(t). Later, that corner will matter when we ask for instantaneous velocity.

The area above the time axis is a rectangle of height 40 and width 2:

40\cdot 2=80.

The area below the time axis is a rectangle of height 30 and width 1, but it counts negatively:

-30\cdot 1=-30.

Therefore the signed area under the velocity graph is

80-30=50.

This equals

s(3)-s(0)=50-0=50.

So the rule from constant velocity survives, but with a sign:

\text{change in signed position}=\text{signed area under the velocity graph}.

Why must area below the time axis count as negative?

On a velocity graph, a rectangle below the time axis has ordinary geometric area that is positive. In your own words, why does calculus assign that region a negative signed area anyway?

Signed area is not painting a wall. It is accumulating change, and backward motion decreases position.

A first piecewise-defined motion

A formula such as

v(t)= \begin{cases} 40, \amp 0\leq t<2,\\ -30, \amp 2<t\leq 3 \end{cases}

is called piecewise-defined. It gives different instructions on different pieces of the domain.

Piecewise-defined functions are not artificial. They describe many real situations:

Piecewise motionmotionpiecewise behaviora car stops at a red lightpositive velocity, then zero velocityan elevator goes up, stops, then goes downpositive, zero, negative velocitya thermostat turns heat on and offdifferent rules at different temperaturesa tax bracket changesdifferent rates on different income intervals

In a piecewise-constant velocity model, each time interval is easy. The velocity is constant on that interval, so displacement is

\text{velocity}\cdot \text{time}.

Then we add the pieces.

Example

Suppose a car has velocity

v(t)= \begin{cases} 50, \amp 0\leq t<1,\\ 0, \amp 1\leq t<2,\\ -20, \amp 2\leq t\leq 4. \end{cases}

The displacement from 0 to 4 is

50\cdot 1+0\cdot 1+(-20)\cdot 2 = 50+0-40 = 10.

The car ends 10 miles ahead of where it started.

The distance traveled is

|50|\cdot 1+|0|\cdot 1+|-20|\cdot 2 = 50+0+40 = 90.

The signed calculation tells where the car ends. The absolute-value calculation tells how much road the car has covered.

 What the sign prepares us for

Signed area is not ordinary geometric area. Ordinary geometric area is never negative. Signed area is different because it is designed to represent accumulated change.

If v(t)>0, the signed position increases.

If v(t)<0, the signed position decreases.

If v(t)=0, the signed position does not change.

That is why the graph of s(t) rises, falls, or stays flat according to the sign of v(t).

For piecewise-constant velocity, we can compute everything with rectangles. But the next idea is even simpler and deeper: if we know a list of signed positions at equally spaced times, then the changes between them contain all the information needed to recover the final position from the first one.

That is calculus before limits.

A first piecewise-defined motion

A formula such as

v(t)= \begin{cases} 40, \amp 0\leq t<2,\\ -30, \amp 2<t\leq 3 \end{cases}

is called piecewise-defined. It gives different instructions on different pieces of the domain.

Piecewise-defined functions are not artificial. They describe many real situations:

Piecewise motion

motion

piecewise behavior

a car stops at a red light

positive velocity, then zero velocity

an elevator goes up, stops, then goes down

positive, zero, negative velocity

a thermostat turns heat on and off

different rules at different temperatures

a tax bracket changes

different rates on different income intervals

In a piecewise-constant velocity model, each time interval is easy. The velocity is constant on that interval, so displacement is

\text{velocity}\cdot \text{time}.

Then we add the pieces.

Example

Suppose a car has velocity

v(t)= \begin{cases} 50, \amp 0\leq t<1,\\ 0, \amp 1\leq t<2,\\ -20, \amp 2\leq t\leq 4. \end{cases}

The displacement from 0 to 4 is

50\cdot 1+0\cdot 1+(-20)\cdot 2 = 50+0-40 = 10.

The car ends 10 miles ahead of where it started.

The distance traveled is

|50|\cdot 1+|0|\cdot 1+|-20|\cdot 2 = 50+0+40 = 90.

The signed calculation tells where the car ends. The absolute-value calculation tells how much road the car has covered.

 What the sign prepares us for

Signed area is not ordinary geometric area. Ordinary geometric area is never negative. Signed area is different because it is designed to represent accumulated change.

If v(t)>0, the signed position increases.

If v(t)<0, the signed position decreases.

If v(t)=0, the signed position does not change.

That is why the graph of s(t) rises, falls, or stays flat according to the sign of v(t).

For piecewise-constant velocity, we can compute everything with rectangles. But the next idea is even simpler and deeper: if we know a list of signed positions at equally spaced times, then the changes between them contain all the information needed to recover the final position from the first one.

That is calculus before limits.

A first map of the book

We have now met the four pictures that will guide the whole course:

\text{slope},\qquad \text{area},\qquad \text{difference},\qquad \text{sum}.

They do not represent four distinct topics. Instead, they are four perspectives of a single story: change and accumulation counteract each other.

 Derivative: from position to velocity

The derivative is the precise version of instantaneous rate of change.

Starting with signed position s(t), the derivative answers:

\text{How fast is }s(t)\text{ changing at this instant?}

The formula will be

s'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{s(a+h)-s(a)}{h},

when that limit exists.

The derivative is local. It studies what happens near one input a. On a graph, it gives the slope of the tangent line. In motion, it gives velocity. In an applied model, it gives sensitivity: how much the output changes when the input is nudged.

For s(t)=t^2, we found

s'(2)=4.

Later we will learn how to compute s'(t) for many functions without starting from the limit every time.

 Integral: from velocity to position

The integral is the precise version of accumulated signed change.

Starting with velocity v(t), the integral answers:

\text{How much signed position has accumulated over an interval?}

The notation will be

\int_a^b v(t)\,dt.

This means the signed accumulation of v(t) from t=a to t=b. If v(t) is above the time axis, it contributes positively. If v(t) is below the time axis, it contributes negatively.

The integral is global. It uses the whole interval, not just one instant. On a graph, it is signed area. In motion, it is displacement. In applications, it can represent accumulated mass, work, energy, probability, cost, or growth.

The central theorem of calculus will say that these two processes undo each other:

\text{differentiate to measure change,} \qquad \text{integrate to accumulate change.}

Approximation: how to work when exact formulas fail

Calculus gives exact definitions, but it also teaches controlled approximation.

The derivative begins with approximate slopes:

\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

The integral begins with approximate sums:

\sum f(x_j)\Delta x_j.

A tangent line gives a local approximation:

f(a+h)\approx f(a)+f'(a)h.

This simple formula will become one of the most useful ideas in the book. It says that a differentiable function looks almost linear when we zoom in far enough.

Later, the same idea will grow into Taylor polynomials:

\text{curved function} \approx \text{polynomial built from derivatives}.

Approximation is not a temporary trick before the exact answer arrives. In science, engineering, economics, and computation, approximation is often the answer we can actually use. The real question is:

\text{How close is it?}

Calculus gives ways to estimate that error.

 Differential equations: when the law gives the derivative

Sometimes a problem does not give the function directly. It gives a law for how the function changes.

For example, a population P(t) might grow at a rate proportional to its current size:

P'(t)=kP(t).

This equation does not tell us P(t) outright. It tells us the derivative of P. To solve the problem, we must find a function whose rate of change behaves in the required way.

A cooling cup of coffee can be modeled by

T'(t)=-k\bigl(T(t)-T_{\text{room}}\bigr).

The farther the coffee temperature is from room temperature, the faster it cools. Again, the law is written in the language of derivatives.

Equations involving derivatives are called differential equations. They are one of the main reasons calculus became the language of science.

The road in one picture

This map is only a beginning. Two phrases still need a careful foundation: h\to0 and \text{better and better approximations by sums}.

Common Taylor series

Taylor polynomials approximate functions near a chosen center. Taylor series continue that approximation indefinitely.

 Taylor polynomial and remainder

The Taylor polynomial of order N, with degree at most N, for f centered at a is

T_N(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n.

That is,

T_N(x) = f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)+\frac{f''(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2+\cdots+ \frac{f^{(N)}(a)}{N!}(x-a)^N.

Taylor’s theorem with Lagrange remainder says that, when f has continuous derivatives through order N+1 on an interval containing a and x,

f(x)=T_N(x)+R_N(x),

where

R_N(x) = \frac{f^{(N+1)}(\xi)}{(N+1)!}(x-a)^{N+1}

for some \xi between a and x.

Thus, if

|f^{(N+1)}(t)|\le M

between a and x, then

|R_N(x)|\le \frac{M}{(N+1)!}|x-a|^{N+1}.

This is the formula that turns a Taylor polynomial into a controlled approximation.

A series centered at a uses powers of x-a. To represent the same function at a new center, rewrite the function or recompute its Taylor coefficients; merely replacing x by x-a would shift the function itself.

we have

\frac1{1-x} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(x-a)^n}{(1-a)^{n+1}}.

Shifted series are useful when the function must be approximated near a point other than 0.

Numerical integration rules

Numerical integration approximates

I=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx

by replacing the graph with simple shapes.

Let a<b and let n be a positive integer. Set

\Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n}, \qquad x_j=a+j\Delta x, \qquad j=0,1,\ldots,n.

The midpoint of the j-th subinterval [x_{j-1},x_j] is

m_j=\frac{x_{j-1}+x_j}{2}.

Graphing windows

A graph on a screen is not the graph itself.

It is a sampled picture of part of the graph, drawn in a chosen rectangle:

x_{\min}\le x\le x_{\max}, \qquad y_{\min}\le y\le y_{\max}.

Anything outside that rectangle is invisible. Anything between sampled points may be missed. A good graphing window reveals structure. A poor window hides it.

 A window is a mathematical choice

Consider

f(x)=x^3-6x.

In the small window

-1\le x\le1, \qquad -6\le y\le6,

the graph looks mostly like a decreasing curve. In the wider window

-3\le x\le3, \qquad -12\le y\le12,

we see the full cubic shape: rising, falling, then rising again.

The function did not change. The picture changed.

Window habit

Before trusting a graph, change the window.

Try a smaller window, a larger window, and a window centered on important points: zeros, critical points, endpoints, and possible asymptotes.

 A graph can hide a hole

Technology often draws connected pixels. That can hide a missing point.

Consider

g(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}.

Algebraically,

x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1).

So for

x\neq1,

we have

g(x)=x+1.

But the original function is undefined at

x=1.

So the correct graph is the line

y=x+1

with a hole at

(1,2).

A graphing device may draw only the line and may not show the hole.

This is not a failure of technology. It is a reminder that a graphing tool cannot know which features matter unless we ask mathematically.

\text{The domain is part of the function.}

A graph can hide a sharp feature

A graphing device samples finitely many points. If important behavior occurs between sampled points, the plotted graph may miss it.

For example,

f(x)=\sin(100x)

oscillates rapidly. A coarse plot may connect sampled points in a way that looks much less oscillatory than the true function.

This matters in calculus because derivatives, roots, local extrema, asymptotes, and oscillations may all be small or narrow enough to be missed in a first plot.

 A graphing checklist

When using a graphing tool, ask these questions.

A graphing checklist question why it matters What is the domain? A plotted curve may hide holes or forbidden inputs. What window am I using? Important behavior may lie outside the viewing rectangle. Does the graph have asymptotes? Connecting across an asymptote can produce false lines. Have I zoomed in near zeros and critical points? Local behavior may be invisible at a large scale. Have I zoomed out? End behavior and global shape may be invisible at a small scale. Does algebra confirm the picture? Factoring, derivatives, and limits reveal features a plot may miss.
Graphing principle

A graph is evidence. It is not a proof.

Use it to form guesses. Use algebra, calculus, and domain information to check them.

Try a smaller window, a larger window, and a window centered on important points: zeros, critical points, endpoints, and possible asymptotes.

 A graph can hide a hole

Technology often draws connected pixels. That can hide a missing point.

Consider

g(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}.

Algebraically,

x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1).

So for

x\neq1,

we have

g(x)=x+1.

But the original function is undefined at

x=1.

So the correct graph is the line

y=x+1

with a hole at

(1,2).

A graphing device may draw only the line and may not show the hole.

This is not a failure of technology. It is a reminder that a graphing tool cannot know which features matter unless we ask mathematically.

\text{The domain is part of the function.}

A graph can hide a sharp feature

A graphing device samples finitely many points. If important behavior occurs between sampled points, the plotted graph may miss it.

For example,

f(x)=\sin(100x)

oscillates rapidly. A coarse plot may connect sampled points in a way that looks much less oscillatory than the true function.

This matters in calculus because derivatives, roots, local extrema, asymptotes, and oscillations may all be small or narrow enough to be missed in a first plot.

 A graphing checklist

When using a graphing tool, ask these questions.

A graphing checklist

question

why it matters

What is the domain?

A plotted curve may hide holes or forbidden inputs.

What window am I using?

Important behavior may lie outside the viewing rectangle.

Does the graph have asymptotes?

Connecting across an asymptote can produce false lines.

Have I zoomed in near zeros and critical points?

Local behavior may be invisible at a large scale.

Have I zoomed out?

End behavior and global shape may be invisible at a small scale.

Does algebra confirm the picture?

Factoring, derivatives, and limits reveal features a plot may miss.
Graphing principle

A graph is evidence. It is not a proof.

Use it to form guesses. Use algebra, calculus, and domain information to check them.

Numerical precision and roundoff

A real number can have infinitely many decimal places. A machine stores only finitely many digits.

That difference is small in many calculations and large in some.

Calculus cares about small errors, so we must know how numerical errors enter.

 Exact arithmetic and floating-point arithmetic

In exact mathematics,

\frac{1}{3}

is exactly one third.

In decimal floating-point arithmetic, it must be stored approximately:

0.333333333333\ldots

with only finitely many digits.

Similarly,

\sqrt2

is an exact number in mathematics, but a decimal approximation in a calculator.

A computer typically stores a number in scientific notation, roughly like

\pm d_1.d_2d_3\cdots d_k\times 10^m,

where only finitely many digits are kept. The exact storage system depends on the machine and software, but the main idea is universal:

\text{Most real numbers are rounded when stored.}

Roundoff error

Roundoff error is the error introduced when a real number is replaced by a nearby machine-representable number.

This does not make computation unreliable. It means computation must be interpreted with error in mind.

 Subtraction can magnify relative error

The most dangerous basic operation is often subtraction of nearly equal numbers.

Suppose a calculator stores the two numbers

1.0000001 \qquad\text{and}\qquad 1.0000000

with limited precision. Their difference is

0.0000001.

If each input has small rounding error, the difference may have a large relative error, because the true answer is very small.

This problem is called cancellation.

Calculus produces cancellation often. The difference quotient

\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}

subtracts two nearby function values when h is small. If h is too small on a computer, roundoff error can overwhelm the improvement we expected from taking a smaller interval.

a numerically unstable expression

Consider

Q(x)=\frac{\sqrt{1+x}-1}{x}

for x near 0.

Mathematically, rationalize:

\frac{\sqrt{1+x}-1}{x} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{1+x}+1}{\sqrt{1+x}+1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x}+1}, \qquad x\neq0.

So for x\neq0,

Q(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x}+1}.

As x\to0,

Q(x)\to \frac12.

The original form subtracts two nearby numbers:

\sqrt{1+x} \quad\text{and}\quad 1.

The rationalized form avoids that subtraction. Near x=0, it is usually more stable numerically.

\frac{\sqrt{1+x}-1}{x} \quad\text{and}\quad \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x}+1}

are algebraically equivalent for x\neq0, but not equally safe for numerical evaluation.

 Numerical algebra habit

Algebraic simplification is not only for exact answers. It can also make numerical answers more stable.

 Roundoff versus truncation

Many numerical methods have two different kinds of error.

Roundoff versus truncation error type meaning Truncation error The error from replacing an infinite or limiting process by a finite one. Roundoff error The error from storing and operating with finitely many digits.
derivative approximation

To approximate f'(a), we might use

\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.

If h is large, the secant slope may be a poor approximation to the tangent slope. That is truncation error.

If h is extremely small, then f(a+h) and f(a) may be almost equal as stored numbers. Their subtraction may lose important digits. That is roundoff error.

So making h smaller is not always better on a machine.

 Computing warning

In exact mathematics,

h\to0

is the right idea.

In floating-point computation, taking h too small can make the numerical result worse.

 Residuals and step sizes

When an algorithm produces an approximate answer, do not ask only:

\text{Did the program stop?}

Ask:

\text{Why did it stop?}

For root-finding, two common checks are:

|f(x_n)| \quad \text{and} \quad |x_n-x_{n-1}|.

The number |f(x_n)| is a residual. It tells how close the function value is to zero.

The number |x_n-x_{n-1}| is a step size. It tells how much the approximate root changed in the last step.

Both can matter.

A small step size alone does not prove that f(x_n) is small. An algorithm might be stuck.

A small residual alone does not always prove the root is known accurately. If the graph is very flat or very steep, residual size and input error can behave differently.

Numerical stopping habit

For iterative methods, record at least:

x_n,\qquad f(x_n),\qquad |x_n-x_{n-1}|.

A good computation leaves a trail.
