Polar equations of conics

The focus-directrix definition becomes especially simple in polar coordinates if we place the focus at the origin.

Let the focus be the pole. Let the directrix be the vertical line

x=d, \qquad d>0.

First use r\ge0 for a point P to the left of the directrix. Its distance to the focus is

r.

The Cartesian x-coordinate of P is

x=r\cos\theta.

So the distance from P to the directrix x=d, for points to the left of the directrix, is

d-r\cos\theta.

The focus-directrix condition is

r=e(d-r\cos\theta).

Solve for r:

r=ed-er\cos\theta.

Move the r-terms together:

r+er\cos\theta=ed.

Factor:

r(1+e\cos\theta)=ed.

Therefore

r=\frac{ed}{1+e\cos\theta}.

If we write

p=ed,

then

r=\frac{p}{1+e\cos\theta}.

For an ellipse or parabola, these nonnegative radii describe the whole conic. For a hyperbola they describe the branch to the left of the directrix. Allowing negative radii in the same algebraic polar formula also traces the other branch; there the focus distance is |r| and the directrix distance is |d-r\cos\theta|. The number p is called the semi-latus rectum. It is the radius when

\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}

or

\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2},

provided those points are on the curve.

Changing the position of the directrix changes the sign or replaces cosine by sine. The common polar forms are

r=\frac{p}{1\pm e\cos\theta}

and

r=\frac{p}{1\pm e\sin\theta}.

The same eccentricity test applies:

Polar equations of conics

eccentricity in polar equation

conic

0<e<1

ellipse

e=1

parabola

e>1

hyperbola
Why do polar coordinates put every conic in one equation?

With the focus at the pole, conics take the form r=p/(1+e\cos\theta). In your own words, why is that a natural language for the focus-directrix definition, and how does the single number e become visible in the formula?

Polar coordinates measure distance from the focus directly when r\ge0. In the standard focus form, after normalizing the constant denominator term to one, the absolute value of the cosine or sine coefficient is the eccentricity.

 identify a polar conic

Classify

r=\frac{6}{2+\cos\theta}.

First rewrite the denominator so that it has the form 1+e\cos\theta:

r = \frac{6}{2+\cos\theta} = \frac{3}{1+\frac12\cos\theta}.

Thus

p=3, \qquad e=\frac12.

Since

0<e<1,

the conic is an ellipse.

 a parabola in polar form

Consider

r=\frac{4}{1+\cos\theta}.

Here

e=1,

so the curve is a parabola.

We can also convert it to Cartesian form. Multiply both sides by the denominator:

r(1+\cos\theta)=4.

Since

r\cos\theta=x,

this becomes

r+x=4.

Thus

r=4-x.

Now use

r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.

So

\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=4-x.

Square both sides:

x^2+y^2=(4-x)^2.

Expand:

x^2+y^2=16-8x+x^2.

Cancel x^2:

y^2=16-8x.

So

y^2=-8(x-2).

This is a parabola opening left. Its focus is at the origin, exactly as the polar setup promised.

 classify several polar conics

Classify each curve.

r=\frac{10}{3+2\cos\theta}.

Rewrite:

r=\frac{10/3}{1+\frac23\cos\theta}.

So

e=\frac23.

This is an ellipse.

Next,

r=\frac{5}{1-\sin\theta}.

Here

e=1.

This is a parabola.

Finally,

r=\frac{7}{1-3\cos\theta}.

Here

e=3.

This is a hyperbola.

The classification comes from the coefficient of the sine or cosine after the constant term in the denominator has been made 1.

 Eccentricity

Eccentricity measures how far a conic is from being circular.

For ellipses,

e=\frac{c}{a},

where a is the semi-major axis and c is the distance from the center to either focus.

If

e=0,

then c=0, the foci coincide at the center, and the ellipse is a circle.

As e approaches 1, the ellipse becomes more stretched. It is still closed as long as

e<1.

At

e=1,

the conic becomes a parabola. It is no longer closed.

For

e>1,

the conic becomes a hyperbola, with two branches and asymptotes.

Eccentricity

eccentricity

curve

shape behavior

e=0

circle

perfectly round ellipse

0<e<1

ellipse

e=1

parabola

boundary between closed and open behavior

e>1

hyperbola

open branches with asymptotes

The polar form

r=\frac{p}{1+e\cos\theta}

makes eccentricity visible. The single number e decides whether the orbit closes, opens into a parabola, or splits into hyperbola branches.

That fact is more than geometry. It is one of the reasons polar coordinates are central in astronomy and mechanics. Planetary orbits are conics with the sun at a focus. The same polar equation that classifies conics will become an orbit equation.

The next optional project follows that thread. It asks why an ellipse is the natural curve for a planet, and why equal areas swept out by the radius vector correspond to equal times.

When is a Cartesian standard equation the better language?

Standard equations such as x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2=1 put a center at the origin, while polar form puts a focus at the pole. In your own words, why might you choose one description or the other?

Cartesian form is convenient for axes of symmetry and translations of the center. Polar form is convenient when the important point is a focus, as in an orbit.

Why the ratio matters

If

e=1,

then the point is equally far from the focus and the directrix. This gives a parabola.

If

0<e<1,

then

\operatorname{dist}(P,F)<\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell).

The focus distance is smaller than the directrix distance. The resulting curve closes up into an ellipse.

If

e>1,

then

\operatorname{dist}(P,F)>\operatorname{dist}(P,\ell).

The focus distance is larger than the directrix distance. The resulting curve opens into a hyperbola.

 What single comparison produces the whole conic family?

A conic is the set of points whose distance to a focus has a constant ratio to their distance to a directrix. In your own words, why does that one comparison unify parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas, and what role does the eccentricity e play?

For a nondegenerate focus-directrix conic, the positive ratio is e. The cases 0<e<1, e=1, and e>1 give ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola. A circle is the limiting case of an ellipse as eccentricity tends to zero.

 Standard equations

The focus-directrix definition gives the geometry. The standard equations give the algebra.

Parabolas

We already derived

x^2=4py.

This parabola has

\text{vertex }(0,0), \qquad \text{focus }(0,p), \qquad \text{directrix }y=-p.

It opens upward when p>0 and downward when p<0.

The sideways form is

y^2=4px.

This parabola has

\text{focus }(p,0), \qquad \text{directrix }x=-p.

It opens right when p>0 and left when p<0.

Example

Find the focus and directrix of

y^2=12x.

Compare with

y^2=4px.

So

4p=12, \qquad p=3.

Therefore the focus is

(3,0),

and the directrix is

x=-3.

Ellipses

An ellipse can be described as the set of points whose distances to two fixed foci have constant sum.

For the horizontal ellipse centered at the origin,

\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1, \qquad a\ge b>0.

The longer axis is along the x-axis. The vertices are

(\pm a,0),

and the endpoints of the shorter axis are

(0,\pm b).

The foci are

(\pm c,0),

where

c^2=a^2-b^2.

The eccentricity is

e=\frac{c}{a}.

Because c<a, an ellipse has

0\le e<1.

If a=b, then c=0, the two foci coincide at the center, and the ellipse is a circle.

 Example

Find the foci and eccentricity of

\frac{x^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{9}=1.

Here

a^2=25, \qquad b^2=9.

So

a=5, \qquad b=3.

Then

c^2=a^2-b^2=25-9=16,

so

c=4.

The foci are

(\pm4,0).

The eccentricity is

e=\frac{c}{a}=\frac45.

A hyperbola can be described as the set of points whose distances to two fixed foci have a constant positive absolute difference.

For the horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin, with a,b>0,

\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1.

The vertices are

(\pm a,0).

The foci are

(\pm c,0),

where

c^2=a^2+b^2.

The eccentricity is

e=\frac{c}{a}.

Because c>a, a hyperbola has

e>1.

The asymptotes are

y=\pm\frac{b}{a}x.

For ellipses, e=c/a. In your own words, why does e=0 recover a circle, why does e approaching 1 stretch the ellipse, and what changes when e crosses 1?

Find the foci and asymptotes of

\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{16}=1.

a^2=9, \qquad b^2=16,

a=3, \qquad b=4.

c^2=a^2+b^2=9+16=25,

so

c=5.

(\pm5,0).

y=\pm\frac{4}{3}x.

e=\frac{c}{a}=\frac53.

The focus-directrix definition becomes especially simple in polar coordinates if we place the focus at the origin.

Let the focus be the pole. Let the directrix be the vertical line

x=d, \qquad d>0.

First use r\ge0 for a point P to the left of the directrix. Its distance to the focus is

r.

The Cartesian x-coordinate of P is

x=r\cos\theta.

So the distance from P to the directrix x=d, for points to the left of the directrix, is

d-r\cos\theta.

The focus-directrix condition is

r=e(d-r\cos\theta).

Solve for r:

r=ed-er\cos\theta.

Move the r-terms together:

r+er\cos\theta=ed.

Factor:

r(1+e\cos\theta)=ed.

Therefore

r=\frac{ed}{1+e\cos\theta}.

If we write

p=ed,

then

r=\frac{p}{1+e\cos\theta}.

For an ellipse or parabola, these nonnegative radii describe the whole conic. For a hyperbola they describe the branch to the left of the directrix. Allowing negative radii in the same algebraic polar formula also traces the other branch; there the focus distance is |r| and the directrix distance is |d-r\cos\theta|. The number p is called the semi-latus rectum. It is the radius when

\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}

or

\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2},

provided those points are on the curve.

r=\frac{p}{1\pm e\cos\theta}

and

r=\frac{p}{1\pm e\sin\theta}.

Why do polar coordinates put every conic in one equation?

 identify a polar conic

Classify

r=\frac{6}{2+\cos\theta}.

Thus

p=3, \qquad e=\frac12.

Since

0<e<1,

the conic is an ellipse.

 a parabola in polar form

r=\frac{4}{1+\cos\theta}.

Here

e=1,

r\cos\theta=x,

this becomes

r=4-x.

Now use

r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.

So

r=\frac{10}{3+2\cos\theta}.

Eccentricity measures how far a conic is from being circular.

For ellipses,

e=\frac{c}{a},

where a is the semi-major axis and c is the distance from the center to either focus.

If

e=0,

then c=0, the foci coincide at the center, and the ellipse is a circle.

As e approaches 1, the ellipse becomes more stretched. It is still closed as long as

e<1.

At

e=1,

the conic becomes a parabola. It is no longer closed.

For

e>1,

the conic becomes a hyperbola, with two branches and asymptotes.

The polar form

r=\frac{p}{1+e\cos\theta}

makes eccentricity visible. The single number e decides whether the orbit closes, opens into a parabola, or splits into hyperbola branches.

That fact is more than geometry. It is one of the reasons polar coordinates are central in astronomy and mechanics. Planetary orbits are conics with the sun at a focus. The same polar equation that classifies conics will become an orbit equation.

The next optional project follows that thread. It asks why an ellipse is the natural curve for a planet, and why equal areas swept out by the radius vector correspond to equal times.

When is a Cartesian standard equation the better language?

Standard equations such as x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2=1 put a center at the origin, while polar form puts a focus at the pole. In your own words, why might you choose one description or the other?

Cartesian form is convenient for axes of symmetry and translations of the center. Polar form is convenient when the important point is a focus, as in an orbit.

before:
Power series

The simplest infinite polynomial is

1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots.

For a fixed value of x, this becomes a numerical series. The same formula can converge for some inputs and diverge for others.

That is the first new question:

\text{For which \(x\)-values does the infinite polynomial make sense?}

A polynomial with infinitely many terms

Start with

1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots.

If x=\frac12, then the series becomes

1+\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\cdots.

This is a geometric series with ratio \frac12, so it converges.

If x=2, then the series becomes

1+2+4+8+\cdots,

which diverges.

If x=1, then the series becomes

1+1+1+1+\cdots,

which diverges.

If x=-1, then the series becomes

1-1+1-1+\cdots,

whose partial sums are

1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ldots.

Those partial sums do not approach one number, so the series diverges.

The same expression

1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots

therefore behaves differently at different x-values. It converges at x=\frac12, but diverges at x=2, x=1, and x=-1.

A finite polynomial does not have this issue. For example,

1+x+x^2+x^3

is defined for every real number x. There are only four terms to add. An infinite polynomial needs a convergence test at each input.

Power series centered at <m>0</m>

A power series centered at 0 is a series of the form

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^n = c_0+c_1x+c_2x^2+c_3x^3+\cdots.

The constants c_0,c_1,c_2,\ldots are called the coefficients of the power series.

The word “power” comes from the powers

1,\ x,\ x^2,\ x^3,\ldots.

For each fixed x, the power series becomes the numerical series

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^n.

It may converge or diverge. The set of all x-values where it converges is called the interval of convergence.

Why does an infinite polynomial need a domain?

A finite polynomial such as 1+x+x^2+x^3 is defined for every real x. The infinite expression 1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots is not. In your own words, why does a power series become a numerical series at each input, and why can the same formula converge at one x and diverge at another?

There is no last term to add. At each fixed x, you must ask whether the partial sums settle. Geometric series already show that the answer depends on the size of x.

Example

Consider

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x^n.

This is the series

1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots.

For a fixed x, it is a geometric series with ratio x. Therefore it converges when

|x|<1,

and diverges when

|x|\ge 1.

So its interval of convergence is

(-1,1).

Later we will use the geometric series to represent a familiar function. For now, the important lesson is simpler: a power series comes with a domain, and that domain must be found.

 Center of a power series

Power series do not have to be centered at 0. They can be centered at any real number a.

For example,

1+(x-3)+(x-3)^2+(x-3)^3+\cdots

is built from powers of x-3. Its center is 3. At x=3, every term after the first is 0, so the series becomes

1+0+0+0+\cdots.

The center is always included in the interval of convergence.

Power series centered at <m>a</m>

A power series centered at a is a series of the form

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n(x-a)^n = c_0+c_1(x-a)+c_2(x-a)^2+\cdots.

The number a is called the center of the power series.

The expression x-a measures the signed distance from x to the center. That is why convergence will be controlled by

|x-a|.

Power series usually converge near their center and fail farther away.

Why does a power series have a center?

A power series centered at a is built from powers of x-a. In your own words, why is the center always a point of convergence, and why is distance from that center the quantity that controls the rest of the story?

At x=a, every term after the constant is zero, so there is nothing infinite left to add. Farther from the center, the powers (x-a)^n grow or shrink according to |x-a|.

Example

Find where the power series

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{x-3}{2}\right)^n

converges.

For a fixed x, this is a geometric series with ratio

r=\frac{x-3}{2}.

It converges when

|r|<1.

Thus

\left|\frac{x-3}{2}\right|<1.

Multiply by 2:

|x-3|<2.

This means

1<x<5.

Now test the endpoints.

At x=1,

\frac{x-3}{2}=-1,

so the series becomes

1-1+1-1+\cdots,

which diverges.

At x=5,

\frac{x-3}{2}=1,

so the series becomes

1+1+1+1+\cdots,

which diverges.

Therefore the interval of convergence is

(1,5).

The interval is centered at 3, with distance 2 to each endpoint.

 Radius and interval of convergence

The examples suggest a pattern. A power series converges in a symmetric region around its center. The endpoints need separate attention.

Radius of convergence

For a power series

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n(x-a)^n,

exactly one of the following happens.

  1. The series converges only at its center x=a. Then the radius of convergence is

    R=0.

  2. The series converges for every real number x. Then the radius of convergence is

    R=\infty.

  3. There is a positive number R such that the series converges absolutely when

    |x-a|<R

    and diverges when

    |x-a|>R.

    The endpoints

    x=a-R \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=a+R

    must be tested separately.

The interval of convergence is the full set of x-values where the series converges. It depends on the radius and on what happens at the endpoints.

Why the convergence set is an interval

Here is the main idea.

Suppose the power series

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n(x-a)^n

converges at some point x_1\neq a. Let

r_1=|x_1-a|.

Then the terms

c_n(x_1-a)^n

approach 0, so their absolute values are bounded. That means there is some number M such that

|c_n(x_1-a)^n|\le M

for all n.

Now choose any x closer to the center than x_1 is:

|x-a|<|x_1-a|.

Set

q=\frac{|x-a|}{|x_1-a|}.

Then

0\le q<1.

For each n,

|c_n(x-a)^n| = |c_n(x_1-a)^n| \left(\frac{|x-a|}{|x_1-a|}\right)^n \le Mq^n.

But

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} Mq^n

is a convergent geometric series. By comparison,

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |c_n(x-a)^n|

converges. So the original power series converges absolutely at every point closer to the center.

This explains the shape: once a power series converges at one point, it converges at all points closer to the center.

The opposite statement follows by the same logic. If the series diverges at some point, it must diverge at every point farther from the center. Otherwise convergence farther out would force convergence closer in.

That is why the convergence set is an interval centered at a, with possible choices about the two endpoints.

 Why is the convergence set always an interval?

A power series converges in an interval of some radius R around its center, with endpoints left to be tested. In your own words, why can the set of convergent inputs not be a scattered collection of points, and what do the three possibilities R=0, R=\infty, and 0<R<\infty mean?

If the series converges at some point, it converges absolutely at every closer point. That forces a solid interval around the center, possibly degenerating to a single point or expanding to the whole line.

infinite radius

Find the radius of convergence of

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n!}.

At x=0, the series equals 1. For x\ne0, use the Ratio Test. Let

a_n=\frac{x^n}{n!}.

Then

\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \left|\frac{x^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\cdot \frac{n!}{x^n}\right| = \frac{|x|}{n+1}.

As n\to\infty,

\frac{|x|}{n+1}\to0

for every fixed real number x. Since the ratio limit is always less than 1, the series converges for every x.

Therefore

R=\infty

and the interval of convergence is

(-\infty,\infty).

This series will become one of the most important series in calculus.

 radius zero

Find the radius of convergence of

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n!x^n.

Again use the Ratio Test. Let

a_n=n!x^n.

Then

\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \left|\frac{(n+1)!x^{n+1}}{n!x^n}\right| = (n+1)|x|.

If x\neq0, then

(n+1)|x|\to\infty.

So the series diverges for every x\neq0. At the center x=0, the series becomes

1+0+0+0+\cdots,

which converges.

Therefore the series converges only at x=0, and

R=0.

Not every power series gives a useful function on an interval. Some collapse to a single point.

 Endpoint testing

The radius tells us what happens inside and outside. It does not tell us what happens at the endpoints.

The reason is simple: the Ratio Test often gives the limiting value 1 at the endpoints, and the Ratio Test is silent when the limit is 1.

Why must endpoints be tested separately?

The radius decides the open interval of guaranteed absolute convergence. The two endpoints are another story. In your own words, why can two series share a radius but have different intervals of convergence, and what extra work do the endpoints require?

At an endpoint the geometric safety margin disappears, and you are back to a numerical series. That series may converge, diverge, or converge only conditionally, independently of the interior.

one endpoint included

Find the interval of convergence of

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n}.

For x\neq0, use the Ratio Test on the absolute values:

\left| \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\cdot\frac{n}{x^n} \right| = |x|\frac{n}{n+1}.

As n\to\infty,

|x|\frac{n}{n+1}\to |x|.

So the series converges absolutely when

|x|<1

and diverges when

|x|>1.

The radius is

R=1.

Now test the endpoints.

At x=1, the series becomes

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1n,

the harmonic series. It diverges.

At x=-1, the series becomes

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n}.

This is an alternating harmonic series. It converges by the Alternating Series Test.

Therefore the interval of convergence is

[-1,1).

One endpoint is included, and the other is not.

 both endpoints included

Find the interval of convergence of

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(x-2)^n}{n^2}.

At x=2, every term is zero and the series converges. For x\ne2, use the Ratio Test on absolute values:

\left| \frac{(x-2)^{n+1}}{(n+1)^2}\cdot \frac{n^2}{(x-2)^n} \right| = |x-2|\frac{n^2}{(n+1)^2}.

As n\to\infty,

|x-2|\frac{n^2}{(n+1)^2}\to |x-2|.

Thus the series converges absolutely when

|x-2|<1,

or

1<x<3.

The radius is 1, centered at 2.

Now test endpoints.

At x=1, the series becomes

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}.

This converges absolutely because

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2}

converges.

At x=3, the series becomes

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2},

which also converges.

Therefore the interval of convergence is

[1,3].

 Endpoint checklist

After finding the radius R, do not stop at

|x-a|<R.

Test

x=a-R \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=a+R

as two ordinary numerical series. Use the tests from Chapter : geometric, p-series, comparison, alternating, ratio, root, or term test.

The next section shows why power series are worth this work. Inside their interval of convergence, they can be handled almost like polynomials.

Therefore the interval of convergence is

(1,5).

The interval is centered at 3, with distance 2 to each endpoint.

 Radius and interval of convergence

The examples suggest a pattern. A power series converges in a symmetric region around its center. The endpoints need separate attention.

Radius of convergence

For a power series

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n(x-a)^n,

exactly one of the following happens.

  1. The series converges only at its center x=a. Then the radius of convergence is

    R=0.

  2. The series converges for every real number x. Then the radius of convergence is

    R=\infty.

  3. There is a positive number R such that the series converges absolutely when

    |x-a|<R

    and diverges when

    |x-a|>R.

    The endpoints

    x=a-R \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=a+R

    must be tested separately.

The interval of convergence is the full set of x-values where the series converges. It depends on the radius and on what happens at the endpoints.

Why the convergence set is an interval

Here is the main idea.

Suppose the power series

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n(x-a)^n

converges at some point x_1\neq a. Let

r_1=|x_1-a|.

Then the terms

c_n(x_1-a)^n

approach 0, so their absolute values are bounded. That means there is some number M such that

|c_n(x_1-a)^n|\le M

for all n.

Now choose any x closer to the center than x_1 is:

|x-a|<|x_1-a|.

Set

q=\frac{|x-a|}{|x_1-a|}.

Then

0\le q<1.

For each n,

|c_n(x-a)^n| = |c_n(x_1-a)^n| \left(\frac{|x-a|}{|x_1-a|}\right)^n \le Mq^n.

But

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} Mq^n

is a convergent geometric series. By comparison,

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |c_n(x-a)^n|

converges. So the original power series converges absolutely at every point closer to the center.

This explains the shape: once a power series converges at one point, it converges at all points closer to the center.

The opposite statement follows by the same logic. If the series diverges at some point, it must diverge at every point farther from the center. Otherwise convergence farther out would force convergence closer in.

That is why the convergence set is an interval centered at a, with possible choices about the two endpoints.

 Why is the convergence set always an interval?

A power series converges in an interval of some radius R around its center, with endpoints left to be tested. In your own words, why can the set of convergent inputs not be a scattered collection of points, and what do the three possibilities R=0, R=\infty, and 0<R<\infty mean?

If the series converges at some point, it converges absolutely at every closer point. That forces a solid interval around the center, possibly degenerating to a single point or expanding to the whole line.

infinite radius

Find the radius of convergence of

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n!}.

At x=0, the series equals 1. For x\ne0, use the Ratio Test. Let

a_n=\frac{x^n}{n!}.

Then

\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \left|\frac{x^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\cdot \frac{n!}{x^n}\right| = \frac{|x|}{n+1}.

As n\to\infty,

\frac{|x|}{n+1}\to0

for every fixed real number x. Since the ratio limit is always less than 1, the series converges for every x.

Therefore

R=\infty

and the interval of convergence is

(-\infty,\infty).

This series will become one of the most important series in calculus.

 radius zero

Find the radius of convergence of

\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n!x^n.

Again use the Ratio Test. Let

a_n=n!x^n.

Then

\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \left|\frac{(n+1)!x^{n+1}}{n!x^n}\right| = (n+1)|x|.

If x\neq0, then

(n+1)|x|\to\infty.

So the series diverges for every x\neq0. At the center x=0, the series becomes

1+0+0+0+\cdots,

which converges.

Therefore the series converges only at x=0, and

R=0.

Not every power series gives a useful function on an interval. Some collapse to a single point.

 Endpoint testing

The radius tells us what happens inside and outside. It does not tell us what happens at the endpoints.

The reason is simple: the Ratio Test often gives the limiting value 1 at the endpoints, and the Ratio Test is silent when the limit is 1.

Why must endpoints be tested separately?

The radius decides the open interval of guaranteed absolute convergence. The two endpoints are another story. In your own words, why can two series share a radius but have different intervals of convergence, and what extra work do the endpoints require?

At an endpoint the geometric safety margin disappears, and you are back to a numerical series. That series may converge, diverge, or converge only conditionally, independently of the interior.

one endpoint included

Find the interval of convergence of

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n}.

For x\neq0, use the Ratio Test on the absolute values:

\left| \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\cdot\frac{n}{x^n} \right| = |x|\frac{n}{n+1}.

As n\to\infty,

|x|\frac{n}{n+1}\to |x|.

So the series converges absolutely when

|x|<1

and diverges when

|x|>1.

The radius is

R=1.

Now test the endpoints.

At x=1, the series becomes

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1n,

the harmonic series. It diverges.

At x=-1, the series becomes

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n}.

This is an alternating harmonic series. It converges by the Alternating Series Test.

Therefore the interval of convergence is

[-1,1).

One endpoint is included, and the other is not.

 both endpoints included

Find the interval of convergence of

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(x-2)^n}{n^2}.

At x=2, every term is zero and the series converges. For x\ne2, use the Ratio Test on absolute values:

\left| \frac{(x-2)^{n+1}}{(n+1)^2}\cdot \frac{n^2}{(x-2)^n} \right| = |x-2|\frac{n^2}{(n+1)^2}.

As n\to\infty,

|x-2|\frac{n^2}{(n+1)^2}\to |x-2|.

Thus the series converges absolutely when

|x-2|<1,

or

1<x<3.

The radius is 1, centered at 2.

Now test endpoints.

At x=1, the series becomes

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}.

This converges absolutely because

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2}

converges.

At x=3, the series becomes

\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2},

which also converges.

Therefore the interval of convergence is

[1,3].

 Endpoint checklist

After finding the radius R, do not stop at

|x-a|<R.

Test

x=a-R \qquad\text{and}\qquad x=a+R

as two ordinary numerical series. Use the tests from Chapter : geometric, p-series, comparison, alternating, ratio, root, or term test.

The next section shows why power series are worth this work. Inside their interval of convergence, they can be handled almost like polynomials.
